COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES

V
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
ABSTRACT
Computational Design approaches enable the systematic creation of designs 
through computing processes and algorithms. These approaches facilitate 
the emergence of systematic design practices and processes, contrasting 
with conventional artefact-based production methods. In this thesis, 
we study the application, feasibility, and effectiveness of computational 
methods in the context of Graphic Design, with a specific focus on layout 
and typography challenges. Our investigation explores the use of compu-
tational techniques for designing responsive designs and automating tasks, 
ranging from routine operations to visual exploration. 
Initially, the main challenges and opportunities for implementing 
computational methods in Graphic Design scenarios were identified, 
and various approaches were developed based on the characteristics of these 
challenges. We conducted experiments to examine how computational 
techniques promote the creation of responsive designs. These experiments 
involved creating reactive and interactive moving posters, developing and 
testing an environmentally responsive generative poster system, and 
developing an interactive installation to create typographic compositions 
based on audience snapshots. In these experiments, context -aware envi-
ronmental data were utilised to define, modify, and adapt visual features 
to different audience behaviours and environmental conditions.
Subsequently, we analysed the potential of computational automation 
approaches in supporting contemporary Graphic Design practices. In this 
sense, we experimented with Evolutionary Computation techniques for gen-
erating posters from user-given content. In this context, we experimented 
with evaluation metrics, strategies, and interactive methods to enable users 
to express their design preferences. Similarly, we introduced a greedy type-
setting approach, which was applied in developing a design tool for the online 
creation of typographic designs and a public art installation. 
Due to their elemental shape and historical significance, our investi-
gation primarily focused on poster designs. Nevertheless, we conducted 
preliminary experiments to evaluate the potential of computational approaches 
in producing other types of designs, including print designs, such as books 
and album covers, and digital designs, such as a website generator and two 
internet artworks.
Results indicate that computational approaches significantly facil-
itate the creation of responsive designs, enhancing audience engagement 
and message communication. Moreover, our research reveals the trans-
formation potential of computational design in improving graphic design 
processes, automating routine tasks, and supporting designers in discovery 
and exploration.

Artificial Intelligence;

COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
RESUMO
As abordagens de Design Computacional possibilitam a criação sistemática 
de artefatos de design por meio de processos computacionais e algoritmos. 
Essas abordagens propiciam a emergência de práticas e processos sis-
temáticos de design, contrastando com as práticas convencionais centradas 
na criação de objetos únicos. Nesta tese, estudamos a aplicação, viabilidade, 
e eficácia do uso de processos computacionais no contexto de Design Gráfico, 
com ênfase especial em tarefas tipográficas e de layout. Deste modo, este 
trabalho abrange a utilização de técnicas computacionais para o desenho 
de artefatos de comunicação responsivos e a automação de tarefas de design, 
abrangendo tarefas de rotina habituais até tarefas de exploração visual.
Identificamos os principais desafios e oportunidades para a utilização 
de métodos computacionais no contexto do Design Gráfico, e são desen-
volvidas diferentes abordagens para responder às características e aos desa-
fios identificados. Numa primeira fase, exploramos de que forma as técnicas 
computacionais promovem a criação de artefatos de design responsivos. 
Este trabalho envolveu a concessão de cartazes animados reativos e inte-
rativos, o desenvolvimento e teste de um sistema de cartazes generativos 
que responde ao ambiente, e a criação de uma abordagem interativa para 
a criação de composições tipográfica baseada em retratos da audiência. 
Nestas experiências, são empregues dados sensíveis ao contexto ambiental 
para definir, modificar e adaptar as características visuais dos artefatos 
a diferentes comportamentos da audiência e condições ambientais.
Numa segunda fase, exploramos o potencial das abordagens com-
putacionais para automatizar e suportar as práticas contemporâneas de 
Design Gráfico. Nesse sentido, desenvolvemos abordagens de Computação 
Evolucionaria para a criação de cartazes em que o conteúdo é fornecido 
pelo utilizador. Neste contexto, desenvolvemos métricas e  estratégias 
de avaliação para cartazes, juntamente com métodos que possibilitam 
aos utilizadores expressarem interativamente as suas preferências visuais. 
De modo semelhante, introduzimos uma abordagem gulosa para a compo-
sição tipográfica, e aplicamo-la no desenvolvimento de uma ferramenta 
online para a criação de composições tipográficas, bem como numa insta-
lação de arte pública.
Devido à simplicidade da sua forma e ao seu significado histórico 
na disciplina, o nosso trabalho concentrou-se principalmente no desenho 
de cartazes. No entanto, desenvolvemos abordagens preliminares para 
avaliar o potencial das técnicas computacionais na produção de outros 
tipos de artefatos de Design Gráfico, incluindo artefatos impressos (como 
livros e capas de discos) e digitais (como um sistema gerativo de websites 
e duas obras de arte para a Internet).
Palavras-Chave
Computação Centrada no Humano;
Criatividade Computacional; 
Design Computacional; 
Design Gráfico; 
Inteligência Artificial.

VIII
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
Os resultados dos processos de avaliação demonstram que as abor-
dagens computacionais facilitam a criação de artefatos responsivos, permi-
tindo aumentar o envolvimento do público com os artefatos e a comunicação 
da mensagem. Além disso, a nossa pesquisa revelou o potencial transformador 
do Design Computacional na melhoria dos processos de Design Gráfico, 
possibilitando a automatização de tarefas de rotina e apoiando os designers 
na descoberta e na exploração visual.

003 PRELUDE  AND  FOUNDA TIONSI
INTRODUCTION
Technological advances profoundly impact various social and eco-
nomic aspects of our societies. Graphic Design (GD), which is the activity 
responsible for organising the way that people visually communicate their 
messages, has undergone an interdependent development along with 
technological improvements (Antonelli, 2008; Cooper, 1989; McLuhan, 1994). 
Throughout time, GD has continuously evolved its practices and media, 
adapting to the ever-changing technological landscape and the zeitgeist  
of different eras. As a result, GD has become one of the most ubiquitous 
activities in contemporary organisations (Bailey, 2008; Frascara, 2022; 
Helfand, 2001; Meggs & Purvis, 2016).
Throughout the history of GD, algorithmic approaches have been 
employed to facilitate creative processes, even before the advent of modern 
computers (Armstrong, 2016; Shim, 2020). Since the creation of Typog-
raphy (c. 1450), the exploration of algorithmic methods to create visual and 
communication designs has been documented (Boden & Edmonds, 2009; 
Galanter, 2016). In fact, traditional typography and letterpress techniques 
inherently follow a systematic and algorithmic approach, as typographers 
select and arrange individual modules to create designs. Since the early 
twentieth century, modular approaches and grids have been ordinarily 
employed to facilitate and restrict the organisation of large amounts 
of information within layouts and simplify the creation of visual variations 
on designs (Armstrong, 2016; Hollis, 2002; Reas et al., 2010).
The initial explorations of computers in the field of GD took place 
during the advent of personal computation. During the early 1960s, Douglas 
Engelbart and Stewart Brand presented a word processing software during 
their influential Mother of All Demos (1968). Several years later, Xerox PARC’s 
researchers developed the first suite of applications and services to support 
office automation, along with the first computer with Graphical User Inter-
face (GUI), the Xerox Alto. This machine introduced the concept of electronic 
typesetting and What You See is What You Get (WYSIWYG) manipulation 
of visuals, allowing users to directly manipulate visuals on the screen and 
then print them (Moggridge, 2006; Sproull, 2018). 
From that time onwards, the history of GD and Typography became 
closely connected with the history of personal computers. As GUI-based 
computers equipped with Desktop Publishing (DTP) software became 
increasingly available in the latter decades of the twentieth century, graphic 
designers became among the first professionals to experience the impact 
of computers on their works (Blauvelt, 2011c). From then on, one person 
operating a computer had control over most typographic and design pro-
cesses. This democratisation of access to GD tools promoted experimen-
tation, leading to a profound modification of the profession, creating new 
media, and promoting the emergence of novel aesthetics (Armstrong, 2009; 
Blauvelt, 2011c; Manovich, 2001; Triggs, 2003). Today, graphic designers are 
1

004PRELUDE  AND  FOUNDA TIONSI
recognised as multidisciplinary professionals whose practice can embrace 
a wide range of visual design activities over several media (Bailey, 2008; 
Helfand, 2001).
Nowadays, most graphic designers primarily use the computer as 
a tool for producing designs using conventional Computer-Aided Design 
(CAD) software. However, in the last decades, a growing number of graphic 
designers are exploring the potential of computation as a meta-tool. They 
employ Computational Design (CD) to generate their own tools, mainly 
through creative coding frameworks, thus embracing and exploring novel 
design practices (Blauvelt, 2011c; Levin  & Brain, 2021; Maeda, 2000).
As a result, these designers are experimenting with novel processes, 
leveraging their computer programming skills to create custom authoring 
tools to execute a specific idea and design task. They explore different 
strategies to generate design using these approaches, creating computa-
tional processes with different levels of autonomy, expertise, and expressive 
power. By embracing these computational tools, designers can explore, 
conceptualise, and experiment with novel design solutions, allowing them 
to discover innovative approaches and new design possibilities. Further -
more, computational processes enable the automation of several routines 
and time-consuming tasks, allowing designers to work more efficiently 
and effectively (Maeda, 2004, 2019; Manovich, 2001). In this way, CD 
methods empower designers to push the boundaries of their creative 
possibilities and explore new aesthetics, allowing them to have more time 
to focus on the creative aspects of their work.
CD, in the context of GD, also introduces a shift in the role of graphic 
designers. Rather than focusing on producing one individual artefact, 
they can craft their own recipes, systems, and methods to create various 
designs in a systematic way. These experiments have already had a signif-
icant impact on both commercial and research practices in GD. They have 
fostered the emergence of designs characterised by collaboration and 
flexibility outcomes (Armstrong & Stojmirovic, 2011; Blauvelt, 2008). 
In contemporary GD, there is an increased focus on creating designs 
that facilitate dialogue and engage with the audience, and CD methods 
have played an instrumental role in the emergence of such designs. As digital 
media and computation become more integrated into our daily lives and 
environments, novel methods of communication in these new scenarios 
are necessary (Laurel, 2009; Manovich, 2020). We observed this in the 
recent emergence of new commercial design trends and specialisations, 
such as dynamic branding and visual identities, cross-media responsive 
and adaptive designs, and the growing popularity of the Information Vis-
ualisation field.
In addition, recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI), particu-
larly in the field of Computational Creativity (CC), have opened new pos-
sibilities for GD. By integrating AI into GD practices, designers have 
the potential to transform the way they conceive, create, and experience 
design (Conrad, 2021; Manovich & Arielli, 2023). This integration pro-
motes the development of more efficient generative design procedures 
and the exploration of techniques that enhance audience engagement 
with the designs.

005 INTRODUCTION1
1
Physical computing refers to the 
use of electronics, sensors, actuators, 
and microcontrollers to sense 
the physical world and control design 
artefacts (Banzi & Shiloh, 2022).
This investigation is motivated by the need to explore how CD 
methods can be more actively applied in the professional context of GD, 
explicitly focusing on typography and layout design challenges. The primary 
objective of this thesis is to investigate the employment of computational 
procedures in various scenarios and tasks within the GD realm, especially 
for the development of typographic and layout designs. Our work placed 
particular emphasis on poster designs. We have chosen posters as the 
primary artefacts for this research due to their historically significant and 
established role in GD. Posters have long been recognised as one of the 
most important artefact for visual communication, holding a special place 
in the creative practice of graphic designers. They serve as the standard 
medium for self -reflective exercises or expressing their thoughts and 
concerns (Blauvelt, 2011b). Also, due to their single-page nature and simple 
information hierarchy, posters allow us to transpose our findings to other 
types of design.
Computational approaches enable the creation of designs that respond 
and adapt to context and audience-aware data, innovatively approaching 
the customisation potential of digital media. Designers using computational 
methods like Computer Vision (CV) and physical computing  1 can use 
gathered dynamic data to create designs that more effectively engage the 
audience (see Part II). 
On the other hand, CD methods can encapsulate and recreate activ-
ities typically performed by graphic designers on their day-to-day. One key 
aspect of this is the use of computational techniques that allow the devel-
opment of methods to automate procedures in GD, including routine and 
time-consuming tasks. Moreover, we identified specific use of computational 
methods, particularly AI-based methods such as Evolutionary Computation 
(EC), which can facilitate visual exploration and discovery in the context 
of the GD, leading to the production of innovative and unexpected visual 
designs (see Part III). Furthermore, recent advancements in Machine Learning 
(ML) and automatic EC approaches offer opportunities for further auto -
mation methods, including their integration into traditional CAD software. 
Therefore, the use of CD processes has the potential to reshape 
and streamline the creation of visual designs. Designers who embrace 
computational methods assume a role more akin to curating the outcomes 
of computational processes rather than solely being the producers them-
selves. In such cases, designers create visuals by crafting and guiding 
the computational processes, leading to a symbiotic relationship between 
designers and computational tools.
Although the primary focus of this work is the study of computational 
methods in the context of poster design, the outcomes of this thesis can 
be extrapolated to other artefact beyond posters. Thus, to demonstrate 
the generalisability of the findings presented in this research, we developed 
a series of experiments conducted to generate other designs, including 
print designs, such as books and music album covers, and digital designs 
and websites (see Part IV). By expanding the scope of the research to 
include other media formats, we demonstrate the versatility and applica-
bility of CD methods and our findings in the generation of layouts in various 
design contexts.

006PRELUDE  AND  FOUNDA TIONSI
With this thesis, we intend to explore and further extend the appli-
cation of CD techniques in the fields of GD, with a particular focus on typo-
graphic and layout problems and tasks. By conducting this investigation, 
we contribute in a multidisciplinary way by exploring the potential of CD 
methods to enhance the efficiency and creativity of designers and show-
casing the possibilities of automation in GD and typographic practices.
1. 1 RESEARCH ST A TEMENT
The research hypothesis is that the use of CD approaches within the context 
of GD and Typography promotes the emergence of innovative communi-
cation methods and design techniques while also streamlining the auto-
mation of design processes. The automation enabled by CD extends from 
specific and routine tasks to those focused on exploration and discovery.
This thesis revolves around developing computational GD and Typog-
raphy experiments while examining the feasibility and effectiveness of the 
employed computational methods. This study is concerned with under -
standing how these computational approaches impact both the design 
process and outcomes. Within the scope of this thesis, we consider that 
computational methods encompass a wide range of code-based approaches, 
varying in terms of autonomy, expertise and expressive power. The explored 
computational approaches range from rule-based procedures to more 
sophisticated techniques, such as EC, CV, and ML. Based on this research 
hypothesis, the following three research questions emerge.
A.   CAN CD SUPPORT THE CREA TION OF DESIGNS  
THA T PROMOTE AUDIENCE ENGAGEMENT AND 
EFFECTIVEL Y COMMUNICA TE THEIR MESSAGES?
We aim to study the potential of computational approaches in fostering 
the crafting of designs that promote innovative communication modes 
with their audience, especially in the current context of the contemporary 
widespread use of digital media. Therefore, we investigate whether com-
putational procedures can be used to create tailored and customised designs 
which aim to enhance audience engagement and effectively communicate 
the design’s message. Due to the reactive nature of digital media, we will 
focus our research on data-driven approaches.
B.    WHA T ARE THE AUTOMA TION POSSIBILITIES  
OF INTEGRA TING CD TECHNIQUES INTO GD PRACTICES, 
PARTICULARL Y IN ADDRESSING TYPOGRAPHY AND 
LAYOUT CHALLENGES?
CD procedures have been successfully explored in GD for automation, 
encompassing support for common routine tasks and facilitating discovery 
and exploratory processes. However, their regular adoption by graphic 
designers in their professional practice remains limited. We aim to explore 

007 INTRODUCTION1
the automation possibilities that integrating computational techniques into 
contemporary GD workflows can offer, with a specific focus on addressing 
typography and layout challenges. This research focuses on understanding 
the challenges and opportunities of using computational approaches 
for automation in the GD context. Additionally, we aim to investigate 
the most suitable and effective approaches within each GD task and assess 
the degree of control graphic designers can exercise over these approaches.
C.   WHA T LIMIT A TIONS EMERGE FROM THE EMPLOYMENT  
OF CD IN GD AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES?
While exploring CD approaches presents multiple opportunities and advan-
tages for graphic designers, its widespread and everyday adoption still 
faces several barriers. These barriers arise from various factors, such as 
the technical expertise of the design professionals, usability limitations, 
and technological constraints. We study and identify the limitations, chal-
lenges and constraints arising from the application of the CD approaches 
under experimentation. Additionally, we examine how these limitations 
may impact the overall effectiveness and feasibility of incorporating com-
putational approaches into GD and typography practices and processes. 
Furthermore, we investigate and propose potential strategies to overcome 
these limitations.
To answer the research questions mentioned above, we intend to pursue 
and attain the following objectives.
1.  Review the background and the state of the art of computational 
visual generation, with a specific focus on typography and layout 
design approaches;
2.  Identify the key challenges associated with the application of CD 
in the field of GD;
3.  Propose and develop practical experiments to further study the  
impact of using computational techniques to create responsive 
digital media artefacts;
4.  Propose and develop practical experiments to investigate the poten-
tial impact of CD techniques in automating GD processes in the 
domain of poster design;
5.  Evaluate the impact and applicability of the developed approaches 
in other typography and layout design contexts beyond poster designs.
The scope of this thesis is related to Human-Centred Computing, particularly 
focusing on the computational creation of visual designs for communication. 
In the domain of GD and Typography, we have identified that computational 
approaches vary in terms of autonomy, expertise and expressive power. Designers 
remain primarily responsible for selecting the most suitable strategy by 
evaluating the advantages and disadvantages of each approach.

008PRELUDE  AND  FOUNDA TIONSI
The analysis of related work has identified two major opportunities 
for CD in the context of this thesis: (i) promoting the emergence of prac-
tices for creating responsive and customised designs; and (ii) supporting 
the automation of specific design tasks, including both routine and visual 
exploration tasks. In this thesis, we conducted experiments considering 
the two presented opportunities, selecting the most appropriate compu-
tational approach based on the needs of the work. We explored approaches 
with lower autonomy to study the potential of responsive practices (see 
Part II). On the other hand, we focus on approaches with higher autonomy 
and expertise concerning design automation tasks (see Part III). 
This work is grounded in addressing practical challenges and prob-
lems faced by graphic designers in their daily practice. Thus, the experi-
ments are developed and evaluated within this context. Although the 
primary exploration artefact of this thesis is the poster, we have also 
conducted experiments to extend the applicability of our findings to other 
typography and layout design domains (see Part IV). 
The experiments that were conducted present an experimental and 
authorial nature. In this sense, in the developed approaches, we are more 
focused on the value of the obtained outcomes than on questions related 
to user experience and interface design.
1.2 CONTRIBUTIONS
This thesis makes contributions to the field of Human-Centred Computing, 
particularly in the application of CD methods to generate GD artefacts. 
It also explores the intersection and application of computing with the 
fields of Arts and Humanities, GD, and publishing, incorporating the 
experimentation of AI techniques in these domains. The main contribu-
tions of this thesis are summarised as follows.
LITERA TURE REVIEW
We conducted a literature review addressing the current background and 
state of the art in topics relevant to this thesis (see Chapter 2). We reviewed 
the use of algorithmic methods to create visual Art and Design, as detailed 
in Section 2.2. Additionally, we analysed the background and related work on 
the computational creation of visual designs in Section 2.3. Lastly, Section 2.4 
classifies the use of CD in the context of Typography and layout, consid-
ering their autonomy, expertise and expressive power. This classification 
not only facilitates the definition of opportunities to work within the 
context of this thesis but also informs the development of subsequent 
approaches. We also analysed related work of specific problems that are 
beyond the main scope of this thesis, including the generation of typo-
graphic portraits (see Section 4.1) and music album cover designs (see 
Appendix E).

009 INTRODUCTION1
RESPONSIVE MOVING POSTER DESIGN APPROACHES
We proposed a set of approaches for developing responsive moving poster 
designs, a type of digital media that resembles traditional poster designs 
while incorporating dynamic visual elements. These approaches enabled 
the development of digital designs that modify themselves based on envi-
ronmental data, promoting new visualisation experiences for their audi -
ence. We experimented with reactive and interactive approaches (see 
Chapter 3 and appendices A and B). In this context, we explore CV, phys-
ical computing, and georeferenced data to modify the features of designs. 
Additionally, we experimented with stochastic methods to introduce 
variation in several designs. The resulting design outputs adapt their style 
and message to respond to different data flows from the audience or envi-
ronment. This contribution led to the following two publications.

Vision Techniques for Moving Poster Design. Ergotrip Design: Journal of

3(2017 – 2018), 120 – 128. https://doi.org/10.34624/etd.v0i3.19011

https://doi.org/10.21606/drs.2022.741
In the context of this contribution, we organised a hands-on workshop to 
study and preliminarily evaluate the potential of using physical computing 
in this context.2 These approaches were the foundations for developing 
the two following contributions.
ENVIRONMENT ALL Y RESPONSIVE POSTER INST ALLA TION
We created a responsive poster design generator and presented it as an 
installation in the Coimbra Historic Centre (CHC) in Portugal for four 
weeks, from March to April 2019. The installation was named  Desenhar 
Cartazes com/para o Caminho. 3 This generative system produces designs 
based on data collected from the surrounding environment of the site 
where it is placed (see Chapter 3 and Appendix C). This system uses geo-
-referenced data from public datasets, and data gathered directly from the 
physical environment nearby, using CV and physical computing. New designs 
are created sequentially based on a template. Nonetheless, random factors 
are used to increase visual variation. Over time, the system evaluates 
the effectiveness of its creations, beginning to replicate outputs (or parts 
of them) that have previously proven successful in similar environmental 
conditions. We placed the installation in four shop windows of various 
traditional businesses located on different streets of CHC, one week per 
shop. The placement of this installation was aligned with the 21st Cultural 
Week of the University of Coimbra (UC) and was partially funded by the 
same institution.4 This contribution resulted in the following publication.

 EVOLUTIONARY APPROACHES FOR 
THE GENERA TION OF POSTER DESIGNS
We iteratively developed three evolutionary approaches for creating poster 
designs based on input text and incorporating interactive definitions of 
visual features by users (see Chapter 6). This evolutionary approach takes 
inspiration from the traditional typography design process conducted in 
nineteenth-century print houses. Their development enables the evolution 
of designs at varying levels of autonomy, expertise, and expressive power,  
allowing users to control the evolutionary process and algorithm evaluation 
interactively by specifying desired visual characteristics for the outputs. 
We developed methods for analysing the initial text inputs, employing 
Natural Language Processing (NLP) using both neural techniques and 
lexicon-based techniques. These methods enable the automation of tasks, 
such as line division and identifying the parts more emotionally related 
to the input content. We conducted experiments to explore automation 
possibilities and assess the performance of these approaches. Additionally, 
several outputs generated using these approaches were publicly displayed 
in some artworks and exhibitions. The development of this approach 
resulted in three publications.

 INVESTIGA TION OF POSTER DESIGN EVALUA TION 
MEASURES AND FITNESS ASSIGNMENT STRA TEGIES
In our evolutionary experiments, we introduced a set of evaluation meas-
ures for assessing poster designs. These measures go beyond aesthetic 
features and consider typography features and the representation of content 
semantics (see Chapter 6). In general, the present measures can cover 
the assessment of features related to the legibility of content, the quality 
of the visual and typographic features of designs, and whether the place-
ment of the typography in the designs conveys the semantic meaning of the 
content. In these experiments, we examined various automated fitness 
assignment strategies that handle measures in objective evaluation func-
tions or as constraints. These experiments included using multi-criteria 
hardwired fitness functions and multi-objective optimisation approaches.
The first experiment (Section 6.1) explored a multi-criteria hardwired 
fitness function strategy that considers legibility and aesthetic measures 
(typography and layout). In the second experiment (see Section 6.2), we 
experimented with three evaluation strategies, including a multi-criteria 
hardwired fitness function, a multi-objective optimisation approach, and 
a hybrid approach that combines features of the other two. These strate-
gies assess the outputs based on ten measures categorised into three 
objectives: legibility; aesthetics ( alignment, regularity, balance, nega-
tive-space fraction, composition security, and font pairing); and the conveyance 
of semantics through design elements (layout, colour, and typeface). In the 
third experiment (see Section 6.3), we proposed a fitness assignment 
strategy that incorporates two legibility constraints (legibility of text 
and grid appropriateness) and the evaluation of aesthetics ( alignment, 
balance, justification, regularity, typeface pairing, and negative space fraction) 
and semantics (layout, typography, and visuals). 

012PRELUDE  AND  FOUNDA TIONSI
We develop methods to enable users to interactively guide the eval-
uation, including defining the measures’ weight in the evaluation and 
defining the fitness assignment strategy. Thus, users can modify the eval-
uation method based on the goals of their own project. This contribution 
resulted in the following two publications.

GREEDY TYPESETTING METHOD
We developed a typesetting method that generates typographic composi-
tions using a greedy approach based on an initial text input (see Chapter 7). 
This method also incorporated a neural NLP approach to analyse the 
emotional tone of the input, which then informs the automatic definition 
of the visual and typographic features of the design. The method iteratively 
arranges the text on posters, continuously adjusting the visual style of the 
selected typeface until the text is entirely readable (see Section 7.1).
We conducted a series of workshops involving Portuguese upper -
-secondary students to collaboratively design and develop an online inter-
face for public use of this tool.9 The main goal of these workshops was to 
make it easier and faster for people to create their own designs and present 
their own thoughts, especially young individuals (see Section 7.2). During 
the workshop, we developed a parametric interface for fine-tuning the 
outputs of the tool, and participants created posters using only the tool 
and also combining it with other techniques. Moreover, we conducted 
evaluation experiments with the system to examine and analyse the per -
formance of this method and how the outputs are perceived by its audience 
(see Section 7.4). The workshops' outcomes, processes, and posters were 
publicly presented at Convento São Francisco (CSF) in Coimbra, Portugal 
(2023). The workshops were a mediation project of CSF in the context of 
the Primaveras Estudantis: da crise de 1962 ao 25 de Abril exhibition.10 Fur-
thermore, the development of this method served as the foundation for the 
development of the public art installation described next.
PUBLIC ART INST ALLA TION  ESSYS* SHARING #UC
We created a media art installation titled ESSYS* Sharing #UC, which 
presents a collection of poster designs representing the content shared 
online on Twitter about the city and the UC, Portugal (see Section  7.3).

013 INTRODUCTION1
In this installation, the audience may see generated poster designs that 
feature tweets related to the university and city of Coimbra. New posters 
are autonomously and dynamically generated based on an ongoing search 
and classification of the emotional charge of tweets about the city. The typog-
raphy and visual features of the posters are defined based on this classifi-
cation, and the posters are composed using the previously presented greedy 
typesetting method. The installation is designed as a hybrid experience, 
accessible both in a physical art gallery and online.11 Alongside the posters, 
users may listen to an ever-changing sonic composition based on the same 
emotional context by the ESSYS system (Seiça et al., 2018). In the physical 
installation, it was also possible to see a live stream of the online installa-
tion running. These installations serve as a mirror, in the physical public 
space, to the online perceptions surrounding a particular place. Further-
more, the audience can contribute to the installation by indirectly influ-
encing the creation of its audiovisuals through their tweets. The ESSYS*: 
Sharing #UC installation was exhibited at the Francisco Tropa’s MUSEU  
art gallery of Círculo de Artes Plásticas de Coimbra (CAPC), Portugal, 
from August 2021 to December 2021.12 A preliminary study for this instal-
lation was presented in the performance sessions of xCoAx 2021 confer -
ence.13 More recently, in May 2022, a version of this installation was featured 
in a session of the commemoration of 250 years of the Faculty of Science 
and Technology of UC (FCTUC). 14 The development of this installation 
resulted in two following publications.

 COMPUT A TIONAL GENERA TION OF BOOKS 
AND ALBUM COVERS
We conducted two experiments to investigate the potential of computational 
approaches in generating print designs other than posters, thereby further 
studying the potential of CD in the identified opportunities over other 
media. We developed generative systems for creating books and album 
cover designs. We created a procedural approach for book generation 
that automates text and image composition based on predefined rules 
derived from specialised literature (see Section 9.1 and Appendix E). This 
approach was implemented within the DTP software Adobe InDesign,  16 
enabling users to have the flexibility to modify and fine-tune the generated 
designs within their natural work environment. Besides automating type-
setting, the system promotes visual and conceptual exploration by allowing

COMPUT A TIONAL CREA TION OF WEB PAGES
We experimented with the computational creation of web designs to study 
the potential and opportunities of CD in digital media. We have developed 
a generative website system and two internet artworks. 17 The generative 
system creates brutalist web pages based on an input token (see Section 
10.1 and Appendix F). This system is primarily designed to promote visual 
and interaction exploration for web page design. Users also can fine-tune 
the outputs through an interface. Furthermore, we developed two internet 
artworks using a template strategies approach to define their visual fea-
tures. The first artwork, Portraits of No One, is an online version of the name-
sake physical installation (see Appendix G), which generates audiovisuals 
by recombining input data from the audience (see Section 10.2). 18 The 
second artwork, titled Sonar, showcases a collection of written testimonies 
from several writers about the Portuguese Carnation Revolution (see 
Section 10.3).19 Users can interactively select a specific location and testi-
monials, presented through a composition combining illustration and typog-
raphy. This contribution resulted in three following publications.

017 INTRODUCTION2
1.3 DOCUMENT OUTLINE
The present thesis is organised into five main parts. In this first part, 
we introduce the motivation, opportunities, goals, and contributions of our 
work. We also establish the foundation and background for our research 
by reviewing the use of CD approaches in the context of GD and Typog-
raphy. In the second part, we provide a comprehensive description of our 
work related to the development of responsive designs. In the third part, 
we present our work focusing on the use of CD approaches to automate 
the generation of poster designs. The fourth part presents our experiments 
that investigate the applicability of the previously discussed approaches 
in domains other than poster design, including both print and digital media. 
The last part synthesises the work carried out in this thesis, offering an 
overall conclusion, answering our research questions, and outlining poten-
tial future work.
Part I contains two chapters, including this chapter. Chapter 2 pro-
vides the background concepts and foundations for developing this work. 
In the first section, we define the core topics to frame the work of this 
thesis. Section 2.2 presents the historical background of employing sys-
tematic and CD approaches in visual art and design. Next, Section 2.3 
offers the background on algorithmic GD and Typography. Following this, 
Section 2.4 proposes a model for classifying the use of CD in the context 
of typographic and layout design and organises related work in this model. 
Finally, Section 2.5 concludes with a summary of the chapter's main points.
Part II investigates the use of CD to create responsive designs and 
studies how these media foster new GD practices and designer -audience 
relationships. Chapter 3 covers three experiments, including reactive and 
interactive moving poster designs as well as an environmentally responsive 
poster generator that creates designs based on environmental data. These 
experiments are presented in greater detail in appendices A, B, and C. 
Chapter 4 describes Photomaton, an installation of a computational system 
that creates designs based on audience data. This chapter describes the 
techniques explored and the evaluation experiments conducted. Chapter 5 
defines our conclusions on responsive design practices based on the 
work developed.
Part III further studies the employment of CD for the automation 
of GD. It is composed of three chapters. Chapter 6 describes our experi-
mentation with an EC for creating poster designs and the development of 
autonomous measures for evaluating poster designs. Chapter 7 describes 
our experiments on greedy typesetting of poster designs and presents the 
corresponding evaluation experiments. Similar to Part II, Chapter 8 pro-
vides an overview of our work and presents the final conclusions.
Part IV concerns the investigation of the applicability of CD to other 
domains than posters. Chapter 9 summarises our experiments on the 
computational generation of other types of print designs, including book 
designs and music album covers. Additional details regarding these exper-
iments are included in appendixes D (books) and E (album covers). Sim-
ilarly, Chapter 10 outlines our experiments on the computational creation 
of digital designs. This includes a brutalist web page generative system, as 

018
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
well as two artworks titled Portraits of No One and Sonar. Appendix F pro-
vides a detailed description of the web page generative system. Appendix 
G discusses our previous work on the physical installation of Portraits of 
No One, while Appendix H presents the earlier research related to the 
selection and search of testimonies for the Sonar artwork. Chapter 11 
concludes with a summary of the conclusions derived from the work pre-
sented in this part.
Lastly, Part V, which comprises Chapter 14, synthesises the work 
conducted in this thesis, providing the overall conclusions, answers to our 
research questions, and indications for future work.
1.4 RESEARCH METHODOLOGY AND DESIGN APPROACH
The work presented in this thesis focuses on the application of CD 
approaches in the context of GD practices. In this sense, we conducted 
experimental and exploratory work that integrates computational features 
into the design process, primarily to address challenges in layout and 
typography.
In this context, we experiment with a practice-based research meth-
odology by using a research-through-design approach (Frayling, 1993; 
Zimmerman et al., 2007). This involves the iterative development of design 
experiments aimed at discovering new knowledge through design processes 
that explore the application of computational methods in different sce-
narios. This research approach enabled the handling of CD approaches 
in the multidisciplinary context of visual and graphic communication.
The work presented in this thesis is set within a specific application 
context, exploring an iterative process that involves making, testing, 
reflecting, and remaking. This approach creates knowledge through the 
creation, deployment, and observation. This way, instead of seeking uni-
versal knowledge and guidelines, we focus on discovering context-dependent 
knowledge tailored to the specific application at hand.
The experiments we conducted are intended for application in real 
contexts and presented through various public formats, such as workshops 
and public installations. These displays are not treated as separate from 
the research; rather, they serve to study both the technical outcomes and 
audience interaction with the designed systems.
Throughout the development of this thesis, the methodology evolved 
in tandem with the experiments. Early exploratory projects helped refine 
both the working directions and the evaluation criteria. Each practical 
investigation served not only as a design experiment but also informed 
subsequent experiments. 

019 PRELUDE  AND  FOUNDA TIONSI
FOUNDA TIONS
This chapter outlines the foundations for the thesis, introducing key con-
cepts and providing historical context on the use of CD approaches in GD 
and Typography. Section 2.1 introduces the core topics that frame this thesis. 
Section 2.2 examines the historical use of systematic and CD approaches 
to generating visuals. Section 2.3 provides a comprehensive overview 
of historical and background knowledge related to Computational GD. 
Section 2.4 reviews the current state-of-the-art research and proposes 
a model for classifying and analysing CD approaches in typographic and 
layout design. Finally, Section 2.5 summarises the key points of the chapter.
2. 1 CORE TOPICS
This section introduces the concepts central to this thesis, including 
Typography and Layout, GD, CD, and CC. 
2. 1. 1 TYPOGRAPHY AND LAYOUT
Typography refers to the art or technique of giving our language a visual 
form by arranging types or glyphs (Bringhurst, 1997; Reinfurt, 2019). There-
fore, Typography is the craft that concerns the arrangement of text and 
other visual elements into a canvas with the intent of conveying a message 
(Lupton, 2014; Spiekermann, 2008; Walker, 2001). This canvas could be 
a page, a computer screen or even a wall in a building. As a craft, Typog-
raphy shares some characteristics and concerns with writing, text editing 
and GD (Bringhurst, 1997). The action of setting typographic composition 
is called typesetting. Until the emergence of electronic typesetting and 
DTP software, typographers were the ones responsible for creating typo-
graphic graphic designs (Spiekermann, 2008). 
The term layout refers to the process (and the result) of arranging 
different elements in a design, such as text, headings, images, and captions  
(Herling, 2008). It involves creating a visual system, often based on a grid, 
to organise the content (Lupton, 2014).
Letterpress, also known as Traditional Typography, is a printing 
method with independent, movable, and reusable pieces (usually produced 
on metal or wood) representing a letter form or symbol using a printing 
press (Meggs & Purvis, 2016). The invention of Typography is credited 
to the German inventor Johannes Gutenberg in the mid -fifteenth century, 
when he printed the first typographical book, a forty-two-line bible pop-
ularly named the Gutenberg Bible. Another similar printing technique, 
Xylography, also employed movable wood pieces to stamp on textiles and 
2

020PRELUDE  AND  FOUNDA TIONSI
paper. This technique probably originated in China before the fourth 
century and was known and widely used in Europe, particularly for pro-
ducing illustrations. Nevertheless, it revealed disappointing results for 
printing textual information, as it was not possible at that time to produce 
woodblock types with satisfactory durability and visual quality, especially 
in small sizes (Meggs & Purvis, 2016).
The invention of Typography triggered one of the most significant 
leaps in human social development (McLuhan, 1962, 1994). Until then, 
book production was a slow and expensive handcraft. From  then on, we 
could use typographic compositions to materialise, document and store 
our knowledge and information (Meggs & Purvis, 2016). As a result, knowl-
edge spreads more rapidly, increasing literacy rates and changing people’s 
habits of perception.
The history of Typography is related to both the history of technology 
and culture. Each social and technical advance reflects itself in typographic 
and layout design (Spiekermann, 2008). In this sense, the classification 
of type designs is based on principles like those employed for the classi-
fication of periods in Art and Architecture, for instance, by Robert Bring-
hurst (1997, pp. 12 – 15) or Ellen Lupton (Clark, 2014, pp. 16 – 17; Lupton, 
2014, p. 42). Thus, Typography developed synchronously with the techno-
logical shifts of the time, referencing and adapting its characteristics to new 
media and social behaviours (Ambrose & Harris, 2006; Cooper, 1989; 
McCoy, 2006). Today, it remains a central aspect of designing visuals, 
including books, videos, and websites.
Over the years, various typographers and graphic designers have 
developed experimental typography practices, offering new ways of seeing 
and reading (Triggs, 2003). These practices explore innovative visual 
languages, embrace technological advances, and use new media to enhance 
the expressiveness of typographic design and challenge audiences (Dair, 
2000; Poynor, 1998).
2. 1.2 GRAPHIC DESIGN
GD describes the process (or the resulting product) of the intentional 
organisation of text and images to communicate a message. This process 
comprises the identification, information, advertising, or decoration of 
a message, and generally, the resulting designs combine these four char -
acteristics (Bailey, 2008; Hollis, 2001). The necessity for efficient commu-
nication is the main reason for the existence of GD; in other words, this 
discipline was born out of the need for someone to have something to com-
municate with someone else (Frascara, 1988). Although this need has 
always existed, GD was only named and recognised as an independent 
discipline in the first half of the twentieth century. It includes various 
communication and advertising activities such as typography, illustration, 
print, and photography (Eskilson, 2007; Harland, 2011).30 Nowadays, GD 
is one of the most ubiquitous disciplines, embracing a wide range of activ-
ities and media, from identity / branding activities to information design 
and advertising. It also comprehends a broad spectrum of working media, 
including the design of print media, e.g. books and posters, location-specific 
design, e.g. signs and signage, and digital media, e.g. websites and digital 
products (Bailey, 2008; Helfand, 2001; Hofmann, 1965; Hollis, 2001). 
30
The term GD was only defined, in 1922, 
by William Addison Dwiggins (1922 / 1999) 
as a blending between common sense 
and artist talent, to provide a more 
professional standing than the, back 
then, common terms of “commercial 
artist” or “graphic artist” (Frascara, 2004; 
Heller, 2006). However, it was only 
popularised after the Second World War, 
when the discipline progressively started 
to acquire some degree of professionalism 
(Bailey, 2008; Byfield, 2008; Meggs 
& Purvis, 2016).

021 FOUNDA TIONS2
The practical and theoretical advances in the discipline led to new 
academic proposals for replacing the term GD with “Communication 
Design” in the early 1970s and later “Visual Communication” in the late 
1980s and early 1990s (Byfield, 2008). These renaming proposals aimed 
to counteract the overstating that the term GD places on the final outcomes 
(i.e. the graphics) and the omission of its primary objective of creating 
effective communications (Frascara, 2004). The term “Communication 
Design” reflected the expanding possibilities of the discipline as well as 
the reflection promoted by the, at the time, popular new media and com-
munication theories such as the one proposed by Marshall McLuhan (1994; 
McLuhan & Fiore, 2008). Later, “Visual Communication” was suggested 
as an alternative term to restrict the scope of the discipline to visual fields 
(Byfield, 2008). According to Jorge Frascara (2004), the term “Visual 
Communication Design” is a more appropriate description of the field 
once it includes the three essential elements of the profession: a method 
(design); an objective (communication); and a medium (vision). Never -
theless, neither term ever came into sufficiently widespread acceptance 
to surpass the usage of GD outside the academy.
GD works cannot be appreciated in social isolation, and they require 
the use of common communication codes and languages to be perceived 
by the audience (Forlizzi & Lebbon, 2002; Frascara, 1988; Harland, 2011). 
Thus, GD artefacts present a zeitgeist nature, and graphic designers’ prac-
tice demands cultural and social awareness and constant research about 
the domain where the design is being developed and presented (Ambrose 
& Harris, 2006; Shaughnessy, 2010). Furthermore, GD changes in synchrony 
with the state-of-the-art technological innovation of the times, and it is one 
of the first disciplines to be impacted by digital technologies and media 
(Blauvelt, 2011c; Cooper, 1989; Helfand, 2001).
Evaluating the quality and performance of designs is a challenging 
task impacted by several factors. According to Jorge Frascara (1988, 2022), 
the quality and performance of every GD artefact should be measured 
by its communication value and the consequent changes, knowledge, 
behaviours, or feelings it produces in the audience. Thus, their overall 
quality should not be determined only based on their aesthetic and tech-
nical features. Similarly, Adrian Shaughnessy (2010) states that the eval-
uation of a GD artefact is subjective, and designers not should only evaluate 
the final outcomes based on the communicative, technical, and aesthetic 
features but also on professional aspects of work, such as whether the 
work was profitable or if the client is satisfied with the outcome. The eval-
uation of a GD artefact is, then, a contextual and subjective task that con-
cerns the impact of this artefact on people and the environment. 
In this way, graphic designers are primarily responsible for evaluating 
their design processes and editing (or curating) the results, taking into 
account the design's features and its context of communication and vis-
ualisation (Frascara, 1988; Shaughnessy, 2010). During the design process, 
designers decide whether their designs are fully aligned with the require-
ments of the briefing and the expectations of the client while communi-
cating with the audience. Nevertheless, the outcomes of these processes 

022PRELUDE  AND  FOUNDA TIONSI
may fail, and several designers are also exploring the inclusion of research, 
audience-centred processes, and interdisciplinary methodologies to find 
appropriate ways to reach the audience (Forlizzi & Lebbon, 2002).
Design is a discipline that bridges engineering and the arts, incor -
porating both artistic elements and scientific thinking (Cross,  2006; 
Harland, 2011). However, unlike other creative fields, such as Architecture 
or Literature, GD has developed with comparatively less theoretical and 
critical discourse (Bailey, 2008; Harland, 2015). Currently, there are various 
interpretations and adaptations of GD Research, with some designers also 
developing independent and commercial work that integrates research 
and experimental features (Bailey, 2008). Christopher Frayling (1993) 
indicated three types of design research: research into/about, for, and through 
design (Bailey, 2008; Shaughnessy, 2010). Research into/about design is the 
conventional concept of research concerning the research about design 
according to the perspectives of history, sociology, cultural studies, phi-
losophy, or technology. Research for design is a preparatory research 
approach that supports the process of design that creates design outcomes, 
such as market and consumer research. Finally, research through design 
is an approach that explores the development of new knowledge through 
design practice and the employment of their methods and practices. 
Thus, the resulting design processes present an open and interactive nature 
which is modified and considers the characteristics of the design scenario.
In this thesis, we explore a research through design approach, focused 
on the development and documentation of innovative CD processes in 
the context of GD and typography and the study of their outcomes and 
potentially transformative nature. We consider that designs' overall quality 
and performance depend on their communicational value. In the context 
of this thesis, we use the term GD to describe the discipline and the pro-
cesses responsible for the creation of visual communication designs, with 
the same significance as the terms “Communication Design,” “Visual 
Communication Design,” and “Visual Design.”
2. 1.3 COMPUT A TIONAL DESIGN
CD focuses on the creation of designs or design tools through systematic 
and algorithmic processes that involve computing, including features such 
as randomisation or data-drivability (Levin & Brain, 2021; Lorusso, 2021; 
Maeda, 2019; Shim, 2016, 2020; R. Yu et al., 2021). It contrasts with tradi-
tional artefact-based design methods, offering a dynamic and iterative 
approach (Groß et al., 2018; McCormack et al., 2004; Reas et al., 2010). CD 
has been explored across various creative domains, including the process 
of creating architecture, furniture, visuals, or even text.
In creative domains, software tools are used either for production 
— where software is used to produce visuals — or for conception — where 
software is used to create new visuals (Reas et al., 2010). CD primarily 
involves the conception (J. M. Cunha, 2022; Worrall, 2020). CD Practi-
tioners often develop custom software to create new tools, systems, and 

023 FOUNDA TIONS2
methods for design, primarily using creative coding frameworks (Armstrong, 
2016; Maeda, 2004). 31 CD methods have facilitated the development of 
design processes where computation serves as a tool to create other tools, 
enabling a complete exploration of digital media (Blauvelt, 2011c; Kusters 
& King, 2001). We do not consider direct manipulation of visuals through 
conventional CAD software (e.g. DTP or graphic editors) as part of the 
realm of CD. As David Worrall (2020) and João M. Cunha (2022) state, 
the term “computerised design” is used to describe these standard tools. 
Therefore, computational designers are not constrained by the possibilities 
offered by conventional computerised design software. Nevertheless, some 
computerised design software allows for experimentation with computa-
tional methods and approaches by customising existing operations through 
scripting.
We observed an increase in the use of computational methods in the 
context of creative domains, including those related to visual generation. 
In recent decades, there has been a noticeable increase in the number 
of creative coding frameworks, as well as the publication of several works 
on this subject, such as Form + Code in Design, Art, and Architecture (Reas 
et al., 2010), Generative Design (Bohnacker et al., 2012; Groß et al., 2018), 
Data-driven Graphic Design (Richardson, 2016), or Code as Creative Medium 
(Levin & Brain, 2021).
The use of CD approaches in GD practice has raised several consid-
erations about the future direction of the profession. Kostas Terzidis (2009) 
and Andrew Blauvelt (2011c) consider that code literacy will promote 
a new generation of designers who use computer programming as a tool 
to create another tool, i.e. meta-designers. Thus, there is currently advocacy 
for the mandatory inclusion of CD techniques in GD programmes (Amiri, 
2011; Hansen, 2019; Levin & Brain, 2021).
In the context of the generation of creative artefacts, two main 
perspectives on the representation of creative concepts exist: (i) descrip-
tive; and (ii) procedural (Xiao et al., 2020). As the name indicates, a descrip-
tive representation describes the artefact in some way the artefact, whether 
low or high level, complete or partial. On the other hand, a procedural 
representation is related to an algorithm that, once executed, produces 
the artefact being represented. Like descriptive representations, the pro-
cedural representation can also be low or high-level, complete, or partial. 
Xiao et al. (2020) further describe each representation type.
Over time, several terms and designations are used in tandem, and 
more or less interchangeably, to characterise different computational 
approaches to produce designs, with Algorithmic Design and Generative 
Design (GenD) being popular denominations (Agkathidis, 2015; J. M. Cunha, 
2022). These terms are sometimes used ambiguously and inconsistently 
to express the same approach (I. Caetano et al., 2020; R. Yu et al., 2021). 
Algorithmic Design refers to design processes that involve algorithms 
(R. Yu et al., 2021). On the other hand, GenD concerns design practices 
where algorithmic approaches are employed to  create new designs sys-
tematically (Agkathidis, 2015; I. Caetano et al., 2020; de Bleser, 2016; Galanter, 
2008a). Algorithmic and generative approaches do not require the use of 
computers (Carvalhais, 2016; Galanter, 2016). Examples of Algorithmic 
31
Creative coding involves using computer 
programming to develop experimental 
and creative projects, often with 
expressive and aesthetic  purposes. 
(Greenberg, 2007; Mitchell & Bown, 2013; 
Rodenbroöker, 2022).

024PRELUDE  AND  FOUNDA TIONSI
Design and GenD systems may include natural language instructions, 
biological or chemical processes, computer programs, machines, self-or -
ganising materials, mathematical operations, and other procedural inven-
tions (McCormack et al., 2004; Singh & Gu, 2012). 
GenD is a popular approach and term in the fields of art and design. 
It refers to the process of creating and developing methods that generate 
multiple design variations rather than producing a single unique design 
(Reas et al., 2010). These systems are often endowed with some autonomy, 
using, for instance, random or semi-random features (Boden & Edmonds, 
2009; McCormack et al., 2004; Pearson, 2011; R. Yu et al., 2021). The role 
of generative designers involves both creating and curating. Generative 
processes are employed to create designs for multiple media and disciplines, 
allowing the generation of animations, imagery, forms, audio, and typog-
raphy (Galanter, 2016; McCormack et al., 2004). In Visual Design and Art, 
GenD is closely related to Generative Art. Indeed, the term generative has 
become synonymous with computational for many people.
We may categorise computational GenD procedures and systems 
into five main non-exclusive categories: (i) grammar-based techniques, 
which involve the specification of rules and their recursive application 
to generate designs, e.g. L-Systems (Lindenmayer, 1968) and Shape Gram-
mars (Knight, 1998; Stiny & Gips, 1972); (ii) evolutionary techniques, which 
create designs through the simulation of the process of natural selection 
and reproduction, see e.g. Colin G. Johnson and Juan J. Romero (2002) 
or Matthew Lewis (2008); (iii) self-organising emergent techniques, which 
allow the emergence of a design out of self-organised components, e.g. 
Swarm Intelligence (Jacob & Gerald, 2008) and Cellular Automata (Adamatzky 
& Martínez, 2016); (iv) parametric techniques, which involve the associ-
ation of a relationship between a set of parameters and the features of 
the outputs (I. Caetano et al., 2020; Oxman, 2017; Reas et al., 2010; Wood-
bury, 2010; R. Yu et al., 2021); and (iv) generative deep learning techniques, 
which generate designs by mimicking patterns in data, see e.g. David Foster 
(2019) or Giorgio Franceschelli and Mirco Musolesi (2021).
In the context of this thesis, we present and document the devel-
opment of a set of generative CD approaches for creating GD and typo-
graphic artefacts. We use “Algorithmic Design” to describe systematic 
approaches that generate designs algorithmically, including those that do 
not rely exclusively on computational techniques.
2. 1.4 COMPUT A TIONAL CREA TIVITY
CC, also known as Artificial Creativity, is an AI field focused on studying 
how creativity can be artificially modelled in computational systems. It also 
explores the potential of these systems to function as autonomous creators 
and co-creators (Colton & Wiggins, 2019; Veale et al., 2019; Wiggins, 2006). 
Research in CC is motivated by diverse viewpoints, understandings, and 
goals that could be arranged in a spectrum between engineering-mathe-
matical and cognitive-social oriented approaches (Guckelsberger, 2020; 
Pérez y Pérez, 2018). CC systems are developed to address various creative 
problems, such as image generation, musical composition, poetry, games, 
or storytelling (Loughran & O’Neill, 2017).

025 FOUNDA TIONS2
CC systems are designed to support, analyse, or create processes 
that generate novel (original and new) and valuable (useful and appropriate) 
outcomes through computational methods with creative intent (Boden, 
2004; Colton & Wiggins, 2019; Jordanous, 2012; Ritchie, 2007; Machado 
et al., 2007; Ventura, 2016; Wiggins, 2006). However, there are varying 
opinions on how to define creativity within a CC system. 
Margaret A. Boden (2004) considers novelty, value and surprise 
as the fundamental characteristics of the products of creative processes, 
assuming that the same processes can be evaluated according to two per-
spectives: (i) psychological creativity perspective, or P-Creativity, in which 
people come up with something innovative according to their point of view; 
and (ii) historical creativity perspective, or H-Creativity, in which the 
products are something that has never been created before by anyone, in 
other words, it is considered novel in a historical way. Moreover, Margaret 
A. Boden also proposed a framework to study creativity in AI and identified 
three primary forms of creative processes: (i) combinational creativity, 
based on the combinations of existing ideas or concepts; (ii) exploratory 
creativity, based on the exploration of structural conceptual spaces; and 
(iii) transformational creativity, based on the transformation of a given 
dimension of the conceptual space. 
On the other hand, Geraint A. Wiggins and Simon Colton (Colton 
& Wiggins, 2019; Wiggins, 2006) consider that CC systems are those that 
perform tasks and exhibit behaviours that unbiased observers would con-
sider to be creative whenever conducted by people. This characterisation 
of CC allows for the definition and assessment of creativity without the 
need to define it, albeit it makes the assessment of CC systems dependent 
on the observer (Jordanous, 2012). Similarly, Dan Ventura (2016) proposes 
to assess the behaviour of a CC system based on the presence, or lack of, 
of three characteristics: (i) novelty, i.e. the quality of the system’s outcomes 
of being novel; (ii) value, i.e. the usefulness of the outcome products; and 
(iii) intentionality, i.e. the system’s capability of having a goal or an intent.
CC systems can be divided into four primary categories (Machado 
et al., 2007; J. M. Cunha, 2022; Karimi et al., 2018; Shneiderman, 2007): 
(i) computer-aided creativity (or creativity supporting tools), which support 
user creativity; (ii) co-creative systems, which produce creative artefacts 
through collaboration between humans and computational agents; (iii)  
creative task analysis software, which analyses creative tasks; and (iv)  
autonomous creative systems (or artificial artists), which generate creative 
artefacts from ideation to creation autonomously.
The evaluation of creativity in CC approaches is a challenging task 
mostly because there are still open questions about how to define what 
creativity is, even in people, and creativity cannot be measured directly 
and quantitatively. Thus, CC systems cannot be evaluated as conventional 
software (Ritchie, 2007). Consequently, Anna Jordanous (2012) proposed 
a Standardised Procedure for Evaluating Creative Systems (SPECS), a meth-
odology to understand and evaluate the creativity of CC systems. SPECS 
requires that CC researchers and developers first adopt and clarify the defi-
nition of creativity and the standards the system should satisfy before 
evaluating their system’s creativity and outcomes.

026PRELUDE  AND  FOUNDA TIONSI
In the context of computational GD, CC approaches and systems 
have been employed in multiple related tasks, from the generation of basic 
communication shapes (e.g. type designs and symbols) or visual assets 
(e.g. vector and raster graphics) to the composition of print and digital 
finished artefacts (e.g. books and web pages). 
In this thesis, we explore the computational co-creation of GD and 
typographic artefacts both autonomously and collaboratively. We adopted 
a methodology to evaluate the developed experiments, initially defining 
the characteristics of the outputs that must be satisfied and studying the 
potential impact of their support on designers' creativity.
The next subsections will compressively present the current state 
of the art in the field. This way, CC approaches reveal a high potential 
to increase the productivity of graphic designers and may give rise to new 
design practices (Lopes, Parente, et al., 2020). They also enable the auto-
mation of certain design tasks and stimulate the exploration of new con-
ceptual and visual possibilities. 
2.2 ALGORITHMIC VISUAL ART AND DESIGN
The exploration and use of algorithmic approaches in creative domains can 
be traced back many centuries, predating the invention of computers (Boden 
& Edmonds, 2009; Carvalhais, 2016; Galanter, 2016). These approaches 
explore systematic processes, such as randomisation or combinational 
methods, to produce or assist in the creation of creative artefacts.
The earliest applications of combinational methods are related to the 
creation of visual patterns (Galanter, 2016; Hargittai & Hargittai, 1994; 
Levin & Brain, 2021). Geometric, mathematics, and iterative methods 
are explored in creating patterns for various forms and shapes, including 
mosaics, textiles, jewellery, calligraphy, furniture, and architecture. Exam-
ples of decorative and expressive pattern-making techniques date from 
ancient times to the present. Systematic production of patterns is observ-
able in centuries-old patterns such as Scottish tartans or Islamic decora-
tive tiles, as well as in the engravings of Albrecht Dürer, the Victorian 
wallpapers of William Morris, or the textiles of Charles and Ray Eames 
(Galanter, 2008b; Reas et al., 2010). For instance, Islamic decorative tiles 
and designs (see Figure 2.1) were characterised by being created through 
highly ordered geometric systems, whereas the placement of individual 
elements in the compositions was not decided by the craftsmen or the archi-
tect but was rather dictated by manually executed compositional rules 
and symmetry-based algorithms (Galanter, 2016). 
Combinatorial thinking systems were already employed in ancient 
times. In East Asia, in the fourth century BCE, the use of I Ching, the Book 
of Changes, an oracular system based on chance combinations of 64 sets 
of six-line hexagrams, was already documented.

027 FOUNDA TIONS2
At about the same time, the ancient Greek philosopher and polymath 
Aristotle made use of combinatorial thinking in his work Politics. In a text 
denominated On the Part of Animals (350 BCE / 1912, bk. 4, sec. 1290), Aris-
totle discusses the methods for designing a city and presents a combinatory 
method for the generation of potential animals and cities. This method 
involved identifying the essential parts of each animal or city, listing the 
alternatives for each essential part and recombining the alternatives in a 
valid manner (W. J. Mitchell, 1977; W. J. Mitchell & Chin, 2009).
Before the twentieth century, algorithmic methods were used spo-
radically to design creative artefacts, particularly in musical compositions 
and architecture.
Several musical composers explored algorithmic methods in their 
creative processes over the centuries. Around 1020, in the Middle Ages, 
Guido d’Arezzo developed a method to compose melodies to accompany 
a text based on a scheme that assigns a pitch to each vowel (Kirchmeyer, 
1968; Roads, 1996). Evidence of similar algorithmic processes is also found 
in the other music of composers such as Johann Sebastian Bach, Franz 
Schubert, and Béla Bartók (Edwards, 2011). In the seventeenth century, 
Marin Mersenne, in his work Harmonie Universelle (1636), 32 argued that 
music is only algebra translated into sound (Zielinski, 2008). This idea has 
also been explored by Athanasius Kircher, one of his contemporaries, in 
their theoretical works,  e.g. Musurgia Universalis  (1650) 33 or Phonurgia 
Nova (1673),34 as well as in his combinatorial boxes Cassetta Matematica  
and Arca Musarithmica the mid-seventeenth (Carvalhais, 2016).
In eighteenth-century Western Europe, some games explored the 
introduction of a certain amount of randomness in the composition of 
musical and performance processes, often through throws of dice. The most 
well-known is the Musikalisches Würfelspiel, 35 used by several musicians 
such as Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, which allowed to assemble 176 snippets 
of prepared music in a sequential score based on the throw of the dice 
(Boden & Edmonds, 2009; Cope, 2017; Edwards, 2011; Galanter, 2016; 
Pearson, 2011). Other examples include Der allzeit fertige Polonaisen und 
Menuettcomponist of Johann Philipp Kirnberger (1757)36 or Gioco Filarmonico 
(1790) attributed to Joseph Haydn.37
In the nineteenth century, we find more examples of combinatorial 
systems to aid music composition, such as the Kaleidacousticon or the 
Quadrille Melodist (Carvalhais, 2016).
Architecture has always been fertile ground for the exploration 
of algorithmic methods. In the fifteenth century, Leonardo da Vinci explored 
combinatorial methods in the design of central-plan churches (Frankl, 
1968; W. J. Mitchell, 1977). He began using a basic spatial form (square, 
octagon, dodecagon, or circle) and, next, he systematically added circular, 
semi-circular, or octagonal spaces to the design, according to certain 
geometric rules. This process permitted the creation of conceivable designs 
for a central-plan church without requiring much creative effort. In the six-
teenth century, the architect Andrea Palladio presented in his treatise

028PRELUDE  AND  FOUNDA TIONSI
I Quattro Libri dell’Architettura (1570)38 where he presented and analysed 
a set of grammatical rules for creating architectural designs (W. J. Mitchell & 
Chin, 2009; Stiny & Mitchell, 1978). In the 1820s, the architect Jean-Nicolas-
-Louis Durand proposed complementary generative approaches in his work 
Partie Graphique des Cours d’ Architecture 39 to the creation of neoclassical 
architecture from the combination of different building elements (Hanna 
& Barber, 2001).
Algorithmic techniques are also explored in the context of other 
creative fields. Some artists explore these kinds of processes to help in 
specific tasks. For instance, in the sixteenth century, while creating paint-
ings, Pieter Bruegel the Elder determined the colour distribution in these 
paintings by chance through a roll of dice (Berge, 1986). Moreover, Albrecht 
Dürer described in some of his theoretical works, such as the Underweysung 
der Messung, mit dem Zirckel und Richtscheyt, in Linien, Ebenen unnd gantzen 
corporen (1525), 40 systematic approaches for the creation of geometric 
patterns. Furthermore, combinatorial methods were also explored for the 
creation of artefacts. An example of the combinatorial creation of visuals 
is the popular nineteenth-century myriorama 41 card games (see Figure 2.2, 
Wilden, 1987). In the context of text generation, the poet and language 
researcher Georg Philipp Harsdörffer proposed a word creation machine, 
the Fünffacher Denckring der Teutschen Sprache (1636). 42 This machine 
enables the generation of all existing potential words in the German lan-
guage by the combination of morphemes (Cramer, 2005).
In the early twentieth century, Marcel Duchamp created several 
artworks based on the exploration of motion, environmental light, and 
mechanical aesthetics. Examples include the series of paintings Nude 
Descending a Staircase (1911–1918), the artwork The Bride Stripped Bare by 
Her Bachelors (1915–1923), and the rotoreliefs machines (see Figure 2.3) 
featured in his Anemic Cinema film from 1926 (Popper, 1993). He also 
developed one of the earliest examples of an algorithmic system for image 
generation, the 3 Standard Stoppages, created between 1913 and 1914. This 
system consists of a set of wooden slats to be used as “units of measure.” 
The slats were created based on the drop of one-metre thread onto a canvas 
strip, and then wood slats were cut to preserve the random curves the 
threads assumed upon landing (Reas et al., 2010).
In 1920, Tristan Tzara published the Dada Manifesto on Feeble Love 
and Bitter Love (1987), which presented a set of introductions to create 
a Dada poem (Cramer, 2002). In 1922, the architect Louis Henry Sullivan 
published A System of Architectural Ornament, which describes a series 
of processes and methods to systematically create ornaments that repro-
duce organic shapes created based on geometrical constructs (Phillips, 
2008). In 1926, Le Corbusier wrote Les Cinq Points d’une Architecture Nou-
velle (1931),43 describing five architectural principles that characterise his 
technique. The five principles are (i) pilotis, i.e. replacing the ground floor 
supporting walls with concrete columns, (ii) the free designing of the ground 
plan, (iii) the free design of the façade, (iv) long horizontal windows, and 
(v) roof gardens. Le Corbusier’s five points of architecture can be consid-
ered an example of an algorithmic system since it not only describes an
