of a building (Beilharz, 2004). The Villa Savoye is a classic example of the 
incorporation of these five principles. 
During the first decades of the twentieth century, László Moholy-Nagy 
produced artistic work, arguing that the static principles of classical art 
should be replaced by the dynamic principles of universal life (Moholy-Nagy 
& Kemeny, 1985). His Light Prop for an Electric Stage (see Figure 2.4), also 
named Light-Space Modulator, presented in 1930, clearly reflects these 
reactive and dynamic principles. This object creates lighting effects through 
its mechanical rotation and the reflectivity of light on space in its aluminium 
surfaces (Moholy-Nagy, 1930; Reas, 2001). Similarly, Alexander Calder 
and their mobiles explored the relationships between environmental 
factors such as the air (Popper, 1993; Reas et al., 2010). 

030PRELUDE  AND  FOUNDA TIONSI
In 1947, the American magazine Popular Science Monthly published 
the article Even Necktie Designers Can Use Electrons, where it was suggested 
that oscilloscope visuals could be a useful resource for designers to get 
ideas and inspiration for textile patterns (Githens, 1947). At around the 
same time, Ben F. Laposky (1953, 1969) and Herbert W. Franke (1985) used 
oscilloscopes and long-exposure photography to create abstract images 
(see Figure 2.5). Other visual artists and photographers explored similar 
uses of long-exposure photography to capture light motion, e.g. Man Ray, 
Pablo Picasso, or Gjon Mili (Keimig, 2016; Levin & Brain, 2021).
In 1948, Norbert Wiener (1961) introduced cybernetics as the study 
of how human beings, animals, and machines control themselves and com-
municate to promote a novel way of thinking about systems that can reach 
goals by adjusting themselves under environmental feedback. Joseph 
C. R. Licklider (1960) further expanded Norbert Weiner’s ideas, expressing 
that computers and humans can develop symbiotic cooperative relation -
ships to cooperate in decision-making and control complex situations. 
Relatedly, Douglas C. Engelbart (1963) stated that computers and AI should 
collaborate and support human intelligence rather than attempt to repli-
cate (or replace) human cognitive functions. Also, in the 1960s, Marshal 
McLuhan (1962) predicted that electronic media were progressively creating 
an increasingly interconnected “global village”. Some years later (McLuhan, 
1994; McLuhan & Fiore, 2008a), he also stated that future technological 
advances will develop new communication environments and media, pro-
moting new human perceptions of the world. Around the same time, 
Theodor H. Nelson (1965) defined hypertext and hypermedia as part of 
a space of writing and reading where texts, images, and sounds could be 
electronically interconnected and linked. Thus, readers / writers can choose 
their own path through the information in this space.
In parallel, advancements and studies in visual generation were 
observed. Bell Laboratories researcher Kenneth C. Knowlton developed 
BELFIX (1964), a computer technique to produce animated movies. In 
1967, Wally Feurzeig and Seymour Papert introduced a programming lan-
guage created to introduce programming to young children named LOGO 
(Papert, 1980). It enables the production of line graphics, commonly known 
as turtle graphics, by drawing the path of a small triangular robot named 
turtle around a screen. Aristid Lindenmayer introduced Lindenmayer Systems, 
or L-Systems (1968), formal grammatical structures that model plant life 
states and growth. Over time, L-Systems has been applied to generative art 
and design to create abstract patterns as well as two-dimensional and 
three-dimensional rendering of artificial plant-like structures in stills and 
animations, e.g. Przemyslaw Prusinkiewicz and James Hanan (1989). 
In the 1960s, several technological advances also concerned the inter-
action between computers and people. Ivan Sutherland (1965) presented 
the SketchPad, an interactive approach in which computer users can directly 
manipulate visuals on a screen without having to write code-based rep-
resentation, using a light pen, and see the results visuals in real-time 
(see Figure 2.6). In the same year, the United States Defense Department’s 
Advanced Research Projects Agency (ARPA) began discussing the devel-
opment of ARPANET, the early version of the Internet (Roberts, 1986).

031 FOUNDA TIONS2
Soon after that, in 1968, Douglas Engelbart, assisted by Stewart Brand, con-
ducted the presentation of the so-called Mother of All Demos (see Figure 2.7). 
Here, he presented the oN-Line System (NLS), computer hardware and 
software that include early versions of fundamental computing elements 
like windows, hypertext, the mouse, and word processing (Engelbart & 
English, 1968).
Along with these technological advances, in 1968, Steward Brand 
began publishing the Whole Earth Catalog (WEC). This publication was 
the consequence of enthusiasm about computation and counter-culture 
movements (see Figure 2.8). Under the subtitle “Access to tools”, the WEC 
presented a compendium of tools, i.e. ideas, practices, or low-cost tech-
nologies, which aimed to promote the process of people finding their 
own inspiration and conducting their own education (Blauvelt, 2011c; 
Brand, 1968). The catalogue presented an always work-in-progress and col-
laborative nature, functioning as (Brand, 1968, p. 2) “an evaluation and 
access device” and being continually revised according to readers’ sugges-
tions. WEC anticipated personal computing and the Internet, promoting 
a broader cultural and critical attitude towards computers (Armstrong, 2016; 
Blauvelt, 2011).
At that time, these advances and works started to spread the idea 
that a new information technology era was close, and the computer would 
significantly impact that (Kapoor, 1972; Shanken, 2002). However, access 
to computers was still restricted to a few academic and corporate institu-
tions. The widespread use of computers by individuals continued to present 
significant challenges. Computer programmers needed to create programs 
for mainframe computers using punched cards or tape, and the visual 
output devices were very few, restricted to the screens and some plotters 
(Armstrong, 2016; Franke, 1972).
Many artists associated with several popular 1960s and 1970s artistic 
movements (such as Concrete Art, Serial Art, Op Art, and Conceptual Art) 
began exploring algorithmic processes as a source of inspiration for their 
artistic production. They incorporated techniques such as input processing, 
variation, and randomisation into their work (Armstrong, 2016; Galanter, 
2016; Reas et al., 2010). The work of Sol LeWitt is a notable example of this 
approach. In his texts Paragraphs on Conceptual Art (1999a) and Sentences 
on Conceptual Art (1999b), first published in the 1960s, LeWitt stated that 
in Conceptual Art, the  idea is the  key part of a conceptual artwork. This 
indicates that conceptual artworks should be created from a set of instruc-
tions and/or rules, with all decisions planned in advance. Thus, the execu-
tion of the artwork is a perfunctory affair. Several of LeWitt's works are 
examples of this algorithmic production method (Marzona & Grosenick,

032PRELUDE  AND  FOUNDA TIONSI
2005). For instance, in the Wall Drawing series (see Figure 2.9), LeWitt 
defined a set of instructions for designing a wall drawing. Subsequently, 
drawings were created by draftsmen who interpreted the instructions during 
the drawing process (LeWitt, 2016; Reas, 2004). In other works, such as 
Serial Project, I (ABCD) (1966) or Incomplete Open Cubes (1974), LeWitt 
explored combinatorial and interpretative approaches (Marzona, 2004).
The use of similar approaches by other artists at that time was also 
observable. As early as the 1950s, Victor Vasarely developed an approach 
to creating preliminary scale drawings, or so-called Programmations, in 
which he used a modular colour system. Also, Andy Warhol’s studio, infor-
mally named Factory, was known for Warhol instructing his assistants to 
create different variations of his silkscreen prints (Watson, 2003). In the 
1960s, Warhol's works were often based on patterns created by repeating 
a basic tile system (Marzona & Grosenick, 2005). The artists Donald Judd 
and Bridget Riley explored similar repetition and loop processes in their 
work (Marzona, 2004; Reas et al., 2010). Hans Haacke explored and exploited 
the biological and social systems in artworks such as Condensation Cube  
(1965), Ice Stick (1966) and MOMA-Poll (1970) (Alberro, 2016; Shanken, 
2002). Other artists also documented artistic processes based on rules 
and instructions, including Allan Kaprow, Bruce Nauman, Carl Andre, 
Ellsworth Kelly, Josef Alberts, Joseph Kosuth, Les Levine, Mel Bochner, or 
On Kawara (Boden & Edmonds, 2009; Galanter, 2016; Shanken, 2002). 
Several early computer artists who had access to computers devel-
oped custom computer programs and methods to create drawings. Many 
of these artists used computational approaches to create geometric draw-
ings, employing probability theories and pseudo-random number gener -
ators to introduce elements of disorder into their compositions (Nake, 
1968; Noll, 1967; Mohr, 1971; Nees, 1968). Examples can be seen in artworks 
by computer artists such as Frieder Nake, A. Michael Noll, Manfred Mohr, 
and Georg Nees (see Figure 2.11). On the other hand, several artists used 
random number generators to determine the features of the elements in 
their compositions, e.g. Charles A. Csuri in his artworks Feeding Time (1966) 
and Random War (1967, see Figure 2.12).
Other computer artists experimented with digitalisation methods, 
scanning an input image, converting it to greyscale, recreating the same 
image using symbols that depict the different shades of grey of the input 
image, and finally drawing the resulting composition with a plotter. Exam-
ples include the Mona by the Numbers (see Figure 2.10) of H. Philip Peterson 
(1965), created using only pairs of decimal digits (Levin & Brain, 2021; 
Mezei, 1967), or the series Studies in Perception (1968) created using the 
BELFIX method by Kenneth C. Knowlton and Leon D. Harmon. Back then, 
it was also popular to experiment with algorithmic approaches to reproduce 
images using typewriters (Poynor, 2014; Tullett, 2014). With the democ-
ratisation of personal computers, these approaches were extended to digital 
media, giving rise to artistic movements such as Radio Teletype Art or 
ASCII Art (Stark, 2001). Bob Neill’s Book of Typewriter Art (1982) is a clear 
example of this since it was sold with a program for Commodore PET 
that produced a printout of a portrait of Prince Charles of the UK.

033 FOUNDA TIONS2
The creation of modular composition, especially composed of elemen-
tary shapes, was also explored by early computer artists (see Figure 2.13). 
Manuel Barbadillo developed an alphabet of modules to create images over a 
grid (Hertlein, 1876; Barbadillo, 1976). Edward Zajec created images from a 
set of combination rules and varying probabilities of occurrence (Zajec, 1976). 
Similarly, Paul Brown used a computational system to generate modular tiles 
from a set of simple rules (Brown, 2014).
Several artists created work through transformation methods such 
as geometric translations or morphing between distinct drawings (see 
Figure 2.14). Charles A. Csuri also created artworks by applying geometric 
transformation methods to distort input drawings (Glowski, 2006). Leslie 
Mezei produced drawings employing similar approaches (Mezei, 1967, 1976). 
Vera Molnár generated drawings by modifying line drawings using random 
translations (Molnár, 1976). Similarly, the Japanese Computer Technique 
Group researchers from the IBM Scientific Data Centre of Tokyo explored 
diffusion, deformation, and metamorphosis methods to produce drawings 
(Dietrich, 1985; Reichardt, 1968a).
Many artists also explored the advances in computers to generate 
animations. Between 1965 and 1984, Stan VanDeBeek and Lillian F. Schwartz 
created computer-generated sequences for abstract films using the BELFIX 
computer technique (Kane, 2015; Reas et al., 2010). In 1966, John Whitney 
created the computer-generated film Permutations (see Figure 2.15) using 
GRAF, a Fortran programming library developed by Jack Citron in IBM 
(Citron & Whitney, 1968; Dietrich, 1985; Whitney, 1968). Soon thereafter, 
in the late 1970s and early 1980s, Larry Cuba created experimental anima-
tions based on mathematical operations, e.g. translation, rotations and reflec-
tions (Harris et al., 2019).
In the late 1960s, Roman Verostko began to develop a drawing soft-
ware named Hodos, which he used over the following years to create pen-
plotted paintings made of various scribers, such as brushes, pens, or pencils. 
Kerry A. Morgan and Melanie Pankau (2019) present a compressive over-
view of his work. In his later text, Epigenetic Pairing: Software as Genotype 
(1990), he establishes an analogy between the biological process of epi -
genesis and his artistic practice. He stated that the code is equivalent 
to an artistic concept, or the DNA, of an artwork; in other words, it suggests 
that the physical materialisation of a code-based artwork is epigenetic 
since it creates a phenotype (e.g. a painter or a drawing) from a genotype 
(i.e. code).
In 1973, Harold Cohen introduced the first version of AARON (H. Cohen, 
1973, 1995), one of the earliest creative AI systems designed to generate 
drawings using a rule-based approach (Dietrich, 1985; Galanter, 2016; Reas et al., 
2010). Through the years, Cohen continually added features and expanded

AARON's capabilities, from a system that produces simple black-and-white 
outline shapes to creating scenes of people dancing surrounded by colourful 
vegetation (H. Cohen, 1979, 1988).
Algorithmic approaches were also explored in literature and music 
during the advent of computation. In the 1960s, François Le Lionnais and 
Raymond Queneau founded the Ouvroir de Littérature Potentielle (Oulipo), 
a collective focused on examining and exploring mathematics procedures 
and combinatory structures in the context of literature (Berge, 1986). Also, 
William Burroughs explored cut-up techniques of writing, which involved 
randomisation (Reas et al., 2010). On the other hand, musical composers 
such as John Cage, Karlheinz Stockhausen, La Monte Young, Cornelius 
Cardew and Brian Eno worked with stochastic and rule-based procedures 
in the creation of musical scores and compositions (Edwards, 2011). Some 
composers such as Iannis Xenakis, Lejaren Hiller and Leonard Isaacson 
developed computational methods to generate generative music, such as 
the musical piece Illiac Suite for String Quartet (1957) of Hiller and Isaacson 
or the Stochastic Music program (1962) of Xenakis (Boden & Edmonds, 2009; 
Edwards, 2011).

035 FOUNDA TIONS2
Influenced by the creative experimentation with algorithmic methods, 
in 1962, Bruno Munari and Giorgio Soavi introduced the concept of Pro -
grammed Art when they organised the exhibition Arte Programmata. Arte 
cinetica. Opera moltiplicate. Opera aperta ,44 firstly in the Olivetti Gallery, 
in Milan, Italy, and, later, in Germany and the United States (Caplan, 2022; 
Munari, 2016). In this exhibition, they presented a set of programmed 
works that, in opposition to “traditional art”, allowed the viewer to observe 
the artwork in continuous variation. Similary, Jack Burnham, in Beyond 
Modern Sculpture work (1968), examines how contemporary science and 
technology (or technics) can tranform artistic sculpture practices. He argues 
that technological and scientific advancements have potentially to funda-
mentally reshaped both the intentions and forms of sculpture, moving 
from traditional object-making to system-oriented practices.
Throughout that period, several other events and exhibitions have 
also been concerned with this relationship between Art and Information 
Technologies, both from a theoretical and practical point of view. Examples 
include the individual Georg Nees exhibition Computergraphik (1965) in 
Erlangen, Germany; the 9 Evenings event (1966) in New York, USA; the 
Cybernetic Serendipity  exhibition (1968b), held at the Institute of Contem -
porary Arts in London, UK; The Machine: As Seen at the End of the Mechanical 
Age exhibition (1968), in Museum of Modern Art in New York (MoMA), New 
York, USA; the Software exhibition (1970), held at the Jewish Museum of 
New York, USA; or Information exhibition (1970), in MoMA, USA.
In the later quarter of the twentieth century, new computational 
techniques and models were introduced, encouraging the exploration of new 
methods for generating visuals. As early as the 1970s, Benoit B. Mandelbrot 
(1983) introduced fractal geometries exhibiting self  -similarity across all 
scales. These kinds of shapes were later applied to create computationally 
abstract patterns and generate natural objects and landforms, such as clouds 
or mountains. Stephen Wolfram (1983) introduced Cellular Automata (CA), 
a computational decentralised model that defines the behaviour of a grid 
of cells based on a set of simple rules. Each cell in the grid could be either 
white or black, with its state changing over time according to the rules. CA 
systems have proved to have the ability to emulate many properties of living 
systems and are often employed in creative domains. John Conway’s Game of 
Life (Gardner, 1970) is one of the most notable examples. Andrew Adamatzky 
and Genaro J. Martínez (2016) present a compressive collection of examples 
of using CA to generate visuals.
Ken Perlin (1985) presented an algorithm to produce naturalist 
sequences of random numbers that later was named Perlin Noise. This algo-
rithm was explored in computer graphics to generate organic-seeming 
textures, visual effects and motion, e.g. John C. Hart (2001) or Holger Lip-
pmann (2012). Craig Reynolds (1987) presented a set of algorithmic models 
and strategies for steering the behaviour of animated characters. These 
strategies allow the coordination of the animation of the artificial agents as 
being part of swarms, flocks, herds, shoals, and schools. The most popular 
model presented was the Boids model for flocking / swarming behaviour. In 
this model, each agent movement is defined by three rules: (i) separation, 
i.e. steer to avoid crowding local flockmates; (ii) alignment, i.e. steer towards

036PRELUDE  AND  FOUNDA TIONSI
Figure 2.18. Galápagos installation 
at ICC, Tokyo, Japan. Karl Sims. 1997.  
© Karl Sims.
the average heading of local flockmates; and (iii) cohesion,  i.e. steer to move 
towards the average position of local flockmates. Several authors explored 
these models to generate images and videos. Gary Greenfield and Penousal 
Machado (2014) and Mahsoo Salimi (2021) present a good overview of the 
use of these strategies in creative domains. 
EC has been explored in the development of various creative appli-
cations. In the realm of visual generation, EC works are frequently referred 
to as Evolutionary Art. The first employment of EC to generate visuals 
was presented by Richard Dawkins in the book The Blind Watchmaker (2006), 
first published in 1986. In this book, he proposed a method for the evolu-
tion of tree-like artificial creatures named biomorphs (see Figure 2.16).  
Dawkins also provided a computer program alongside the book, allowing 
users to interactively evolve creatures by selecting their favourites—the 
ones that would survive and reproduce in the next generation. Later, in 
an appendix published in a later version of the same book (1991), Dawkins 
explored the same method to evolve shapes that resemble letterforms. 
Soon, in the 1990s, William Latham, in collaboration with Stephen Todd, 
developed computer programs which allow the interactive creation of 
nature-inspired forms (Paul, 2015; Todd & Latham, 1992). 
They explored these forms in multiple media, from pictures (Latham 
& Todd, 1989) to videos and animations (Todd et al., 1991) or virtual reality 
environments (Latham et al., 2021). These programs were developed based 
on an experimental rule-based drawing system, Form Synth (see Figure 2.17), 
explored by Latham earlier (Latham, 1989). 
Karl Sims explored methods to simulate the evolution of images/  
organisms around the same time in his two installations: Genetic Images  
(1993) and Galápagos (1997). In both installations, Sims allowed the viewers 
to influence the evolution of the organisms by interactively evaluating the 
presented organisms. Moreover, in Galápagos (see Figure 2.18), Sims also 
explored the evolution of animations and the locomotion of virtual crea-
tures by combining evolutionary approaches with neural networks.
In the following years, EC was employed to generate several visuals. 
Examples include abstract vector images, e.g. Steven Bergen and Brian J. 
Ross (2012), or Eelco den Heijer (2013); figurative illustrations, e.g. Kenichi 
Nishio et al. (1997) or Jon McCormack (2019); or even animations, e.g.  
Sims (1994), Jeffrey J. Ventrella (1994), Tatsuo Unemi (2000, 2003), or 
David A. Hart (2007). Moreover, EC techniques were also employed in the 
creation of interactive experiences and installations, e.g. A-Volve by Christa 
Sommerer and Laurent Mignonneau (1997) or Eden by Jon McCormack 
(2001, see Figure 2.19). Matthew Lewis (2008) and Tiago Martins (2021, 
sec. 3.2) offer comprehensive overviews of the field.
In the 1990s and 2000s, computer programming became increasingly 
accessible to the general public. During this time, several creative coding 
frameworks and tools were developed, promoting software literacy among 
artists and designers and fostering more regular creative experimentation 
with computers and code.
The necessity of general software literacy was first claimed by Theodor 
H. Nelson in the twofold book Computer Lib / Dream Machines (1974), in which 
he stated that (Nelson, 1974, p. 303) “everybody should understand com-
puters.” In this book, Nelson focused on literacy issues in the Computer 
Lib section and covered the potential of the computer as a medium

037 FOUNDA TIONS2
in the Dream Machines section. He argued that due to society's immersion 
in media, it was imperative that people be able to control this environment 
to make the best use of it. He argues that if more people knew about com-
puters, they would be more capable of imagining new ways of communi-
cating, looking to shape what would have, instead of being focused on the 
technicalities of placing the parts together (Reas & Fry, 2014).
In 1999, Maeda published the book Design by Numbers (DbN), where 
he argues that computer programming is the most natural tool of expres-
sion in computational media. He stated that designers and artists need 
to enhance computer programming to explore and exploit the full poten-
tial of computational media (Maeda, 2001). In addition, he also presented in 
the DbN programming language and Integrated Development Environment 
(IDE) designed to create a friendly framework to introduce the basic ideas 
of computing programming to creative practitioners (see Figure 2.20). 
Thus, users were able to create programs using a limited set of commands 
and functions and simultaneously run the same programs in a screen grid 
of one hundred by one hundred pixels. Although DbNitself is no longer in 
use, the project had a huge influence on the subsequent development of 
creative code tools, particularly the Processing project initiated in 2007 by 
Ben Fry and Casey Reas, two of Maeda’s students (Greenberg, 2007; Reas 
& Fry, 2014). 45 
Like DbN, Processing is developed to facilitate creative practitioners 
in creating code-generated visuals, e.g. two-dimensional forms, motion 
graphics, or interactive experiences. Processing implements and extends 
the Java language through simplified syntax and methods to make it easy 
to access visuals and interactive methods (Reas & Fry, 2014). Over the years, 
the Processing community has grown, and it is now the most responsible 
for the importance of the CD practice. Currently, it is the mainstream pro-
totyping tool for code-based generation of designs and artworks (Pearson, 
2011; Richardson, 2016). Although the first version was based on Java 
language, several additional projects were spun off from Processing, most 
notably Arduino 46 and p5.js.47
Visual programming approaches  48 were also explored for creative 
experimentation, especially in audio synthesis. In the 1980s, Miller Puck-
ette began to work on a visual programming interface to create interactive 
computer music scores at Institut de Recherche et Coordination Acous-
tique / Musique, Paris, France (Puckette, 1988). In the 1990s, an extended 
version of this software, developed by David Zicarelli, was released com-
mercially, such as Max / MSP  by Opcode System.49 Since 1999, it has been 
published and supported by Cycling ‘74. In 2004, Cycling’74 released its 
own set of video extensions, Jitter, including real-time video, OpenGL 
graphics and matrix processing capabilities. Puckette also presented the 
visual programming language Pure Data (1997) for creating interactive 
computer music and multimedia works.50
In the following years, a collective of creative code practices, com-
posed of joreg, Max Wolf, Sebastian Gregor, and Sebastian Oschatz, pre-
sented VVVV, a node-based visual programming language focused on the 
generation of real-time audiovisuals manipulated by physical interfaces 
(Brüll et al., 2006).51 Similarly, NodeBox is a computer application designed 
to create two-dimensional visuals in an easy-to-use manner for creative

038PRELUDE  AND  FOUNDA TIONSI
practitioners.52 It was first released in 2002 as a text-based approach, being 
developed at the Experimental Media Research Group of the Sint Lucas 
School of Arts, Antwerp, Belgium, by Frederik De Bleser and Tom De 
Smedt, under the research coordination of Lucas Nijs (de Bleser, 2016; 
de Smedt et al., 2011). Several versions of NodeBox have been launched, 
including three main versions, a web-based version (NodeBox Live), and 
one OpenGL  -optimised version. The initial and OpenGL versions were 
developed as cross-platform libraries for graphics programming in Python. 
Later versions were created as visual programming tools to address the 
language syntax challenges some creative practitioners face.
Beyond Processing and the first version of NodeBox, other text-based 
tools were also developed. In 2002, Just van Rossum from LettError studio 
developed DrawBot, a programming environment and framework for gen-
erating two-dimensional visuals on Python programming.53 In 2005, Chris 
Coyne, John Horigan and Mark Lentczner launched the Context Free  soft-
ware to create images from a set of written instructions in Context Free 
Design Grammar, an extension of context-free grammars to model two-di-
mensional structures from a set of simple primitives, e.g. squares and 
circles (Coyne, 2004).54 In the same year, Dave Griddths began developing 
Fluxus, a live coding environment for three-dimensional graphics, music 
and games written in one LISP dialect called Racket (Blackwell et al., 2013, 
sec. 6.3).55 In 2005, Zachary Lieberman, Theo Watson and Arturo Castro 
developed the toolkit OpenFrameworks 56 for producing high-performance 
visuals that blend multiple media elements, e.g. visuals, sound, and videos, 
etc., either with audience interaction or not (Perevalov, 2013).
Nowadays, conventional creative production software also allows 
the insertion of code-based functions and scripting to manipulate or create 
visuals. Adobe Creative Suite software allows users to define expressions, 
automation commands, or even scripting in their working environment 
in an easy-to-learn structure that supports the use of JavaScript language 
(Adobe Systems, 2016; McWilliams, 2003).57 The three-dimensional Houdini 
animation application developed by Side Effects Software is well-known 
for its node-based procedural approach, which includes operators for mod-
elling, particle simulation, animation and audio, compositing, dynamic 
simulations, shading and rendering (Side Effects Software, 2022).58 Rhino3D 
computer graphic application presents a node-based visual programming 
language, named Grasshopper 3D, that enables users to generate new geom-
etry or mutate existing ones (Bachman, 2017).59
The emergence of creative coding tools and frameworks facilitated 
the use of code and computers in creative and artistic fields in the late 
twentieth and early twenty-first centuries.
Many authors have continued experimenting with computer pro-
gramming to procedurally generate images in recent years. Ed Burton 
(1995) presented ROSE (Representation of Spatial Experience), a system to 
create two-dimensional representations inspired by the typical children's 
drawings from a general form and structure of three-dimensional objects. 
Mathew Lewis (1998) made a digital print with a computerised drawing 
machine replicating hand-drawn sketches. Julius von Bismarck and Ben-
jamin Maus (2009) presented a drawing machine, Perpetual Storytelling 
Apparatus, which created never- -ending illustration stories using “patent

Dörfelt (2012) designed a group of computer-generated faces that appear 
to be hand-drawn. More recently, David Ha et al. (2017) trained a neural 
network model, the Sketch-RNN, to be drawn based on the millions of 
doodles collected from the Quick, Draw! game (Jongejan et al., 2017). Also, 
they launched a web application (Ha et al., 2017) that allows users to start 
a sketch and model complete it.
On the other hand, other authors used computational methods 
to create different types of images and graphics with different purposes 
and styles. John F. Simon Jr. developed Every Icon (1997), an autonomous 
artwork that generates signs through the combination of black and white 
squares in a grid-constrained canvas (see Figure 2.22). From 1998 to 2002, 
Vasa Velizar Mihich created various abstract and colourful images based 
on rules (Mihich, 2007). In the early 2000s, Jared Tarbell created images 
exploring emergent behaviours (Tarbell, 2012). 60 Around the same time, 
Marius Watz employed algorithmic processes to create images character-
ised by well-defined geometrical forms and vivid colours (Richardson, 
2016; Watz, 2014). ART+COM studio (2004) developed the Dual Gardens 
installation, which presents a digital garden where plants and flowers grow 
based on a computational approach. 
Leonardo Solaas developed the Dreamlines system (2005), which 
generates images based on a web search for a given user input. From 2004 
to 2014, Casey Reas developed the Process series (2010), where a formal 
written description of a process is translated into computer instructions 
to generate images. Along with Reas, artists like Joshua Davis (2023) and 
Zachary Lieberman (2023) explored data-driven and generative methods 
to create various image collections. 
Advances in creative computing have also led to the development 
of reactive and interactive artefacts, showcasing a range of artistic, visual, 
and performative qualities. In the 1990s, the artist Scott Snibbe explored 
the interactive creation of images in works such as Motion Phone (1995), 
Bubble Harp (1997), and Haptic Sculpting (1998). Dag Svanæs began to 
develop a series of an experiment concerning the fundamental properties 
of interaction (Svanæs, 1997). In this testing interaction, Painting with 
Interactive Pixels,  he designed a simple tool that allows users to assign 
behaviours to pixels and interact with the resulting display. The art col-
lective calc and Johannes Gees developed the collaborative art project

individual parts. John H. Holland 
(1998) presents a good overview 
of these kinds of behaviours.

040PRELUDE  AND  FOUNDA TIONSI
Communimage (1999), where thousands of people participated in the 
creation of a digital mosaic made up of GIF images. The Tmema collective 
(composed of Golan Levin and Zachary Lieberman) created the interactive 
installation Reface [Portrait Sequencer] (2007), which allowed the audience’s 
faces to be captured and mashed up with other faces to create new ones.  
Takashi Kawashima and Aaron Koblin created the crowdsourcing digital 
artwork Ten Thousand Cents (2008) by requesting Amazon's Mechanical 
Turk workers to collectively paint a US $100-dollar bill. Telcosystems 
presented a live audiovisual performance named Mortals Electric (2008), 
featuring visuals generated parametrically by the user as well as by envi-
ronmental data. Similarly, Ryoji Ikeda produced audio-visual installations 
and performances based on the visual translation of audio in multiple 
visual styles, e.g. Test Pattern series (2008) or Superposition (2012). Jono 
Brandel and the electronic duo Lullatone (Shawn James Seymour and 
Yoshimi Tomida) launched Patatap (2014), a web application that enables 
users to create audio-visual performance based on predefined sounds and 
animated imagery using a computer keyboard. More recently, the chore-
ographer Bill T. Jones and Google Creative Lab produced a series of inter-
action studies named Body, Movement, Language (2019), in which participants 
use their bodies to place their own spoken words in the space around them.
This literature review demonstrates that algorithmic practices have 
been employed in art and design throughout history, even before the advent 
of modern personal computation. We observed that from the early days 
of computation, various computational techniques have been explored in 
artistic contexts, including those related to visual generation. Additionally, 
this historical perspective illustrates and documents that algorithms and 
computational methods effectively support artistic practices over the 
centuries.
2.3 ALGORITHMIC GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY
Systematic approaches have played a key role in the history of GD and 
Typography, assisting in assembling layout elements and integrating var -
iations within the same designs (Armstrong, 2016; Shim, 2020). These 
approaches are characterised by modular, grid-based, rule-based, or par -
ametric features.
Early examples include, for instance, the modular Gothic Alphabet (2011) 
designed by Albrecht Dürer through the repetitive combination of a square 
module, or the method Schriftsystem (1878), created by Friedrich Soennecken, 
to design glyphs modularly using metal elements (Levin & Brain, 2021). However, 
at the beginning of the twentieth century, the use of these approaches became 
widely documented. Modernist and avant-garde artists, including construc-
tivists, de Stijl members, futurists, and suprematists, started designing com-
munication artefacts such as posters, books, and typefaces. They explored 
new visual vocabularies and techniques, drawing inspiration from the aesthetics 
and processes of machinery (Armstrong, 2016; Meggs & Purvis, 2016). These 
visual vocabularies and techniques resulted in communication artefacts fea-
Figure 2.22. Every Icon. John F. Simon Jr. 
1996. © John F. Simon Jr.

041 FOUNDA TIONS2
turing sans-serif typefaces, modular grid systems, and asymmetric layouts 
(see Figure 2.23). For instance, Philip B. Meggs and Alston W. Purvis (2016, 
Chapters 13–15) and Richard Hollis (2001, Chapter 2) present a comprehensive 
overview of these transformations.
The search for an ideal, clear objective communication, divested 
of subjectivity and ambiguity, became the predominant lecture model 
for the Bauhaus school, founded in Weimar in 1919, being disseminated 
by its teachers such as Johannes Itten, Josef Albers, Herbert Bayer,61 Lazlo 
Moholy-Nagy,62 Paul Klee and Wassily Kandinsky, György Kepes, among 
others (Meggs & Purvis, 2016). These artists and designers advocated the 
organisation of information into modular and mathematically constructed 
grids to promote legible, objective, functional and harmonious typographic 
compositions as well as to create visual variations (see Figure 2.24). Ellen 
Lupton and J. Abbott Miller (2019) present a broad discussion about the 
impact of Bauhaus research in the development of this objective vocabu-
lary. Subsequently, the New Typography Movement (1928 / 1998) by Jan Tsch-
ichold opened these ideas to the GD industry in a clear and accessible 
manner (see Figure 2.25).
After World War II, some graphic designers sought systematic 
approaches to manage the vast amount of information being generated in 
mid-twentieth-century society (Armstrong, 2009; Bailey, 2008; Meggs & 
Purvis, 2016). These designers defined an innovative visual style, exploring 
a new way of organising information into graphic icons, diagrams, table 
systems, and grids. This led to the development of novel and effective 
methods of communication with the audience, giving rise to a design style 
known as the International Typographic Style  or Swiss style. Among the 
designers associated with it, we found names such as Armin Hofmann, 
Emil Ruder, Josef Müller-Brockmann, Karl Gerstner, Ladislav Sutnar, Max 
Bill, Rodolph de Harak, and later Otl Aicher, Massimo Vignelli and Wim 
Crouwel. Grids and design style systems allowed these designers to create 
new layouts using algorithmic thinking by selecting and variating the visual 
features of layout elements based on a limited number of parameters, such 
as size, weight, and proximity (Armstrong, 2016). Thus, these grid-based 
approaches enable the accommodation of a wide variety of data and, 
simultaneously, that each design is distinct while speeding up the design 
process and creating artefacts that relate to other communication materials 
(Reas et al., 2010).
The Unigrid system was developed in 1977 by the Park Service Divi-
sion of Publication, led by Vincent Gleason and Massimo Vignelli (2012), 
for the visual unification of the United States National Park Service. This 
system is a notable example of applying the principles mentioned earlier

042PRELUDE  AND  FOUNDA TIONSI
to layout design, enabling the design of a brochure to suit the needs of 
each park while also maintaining organisational identity (Reas et al., 2010). 
This way, each designer can make their own decisions about the brochure's 
layout, adapting it to different functions and proportions. This allows them 
to maintain their individual visual style while working within a larger visual 
system. Other well-known examples include, for instance, the Boîte la 
Musique (1959, see Figure 2.26), the pioneering flexible visual identity of 
Karl Gerstner, the Olt Aicher visual identities and materials for Lufthansa 
(1962, in collaboration with Tomás Gonda, Fritz Querengässer, Hans 
Roericht) and 1972 Summer Olympic Games in Munich (see Figure 2.27), 
Germany or the McGraw-Hill Publishers paperback cover designs, during 
the 1950s and 1960s, by Rodolph de Harak.
Ladislav Sutnar was one of the first designers to prophesy that tech-
nological advances would change the way we relate and communicate. In 
the text Visual Design in Action (2016), he claimed that new technologies 
impact GD, and he states that the same advances will influence GD's 
consumption and production processes. In 1963, Karl Gerstner published 
the book Designing Programmes (2019), presenting his method and approach 
to design — the “programmes” — and unveiling how these systems can 
generate a broad range of design solutions. The presented approach reduces 
the creative process to the acts of selection and permutation of attributes; 
therefore, he defines the design process as “pick out determining elements 
and combine them” (Gerstner, 2019, p. 9). In this sense, he mapped the 
design process as a search for an organised inventory of possibilities (Hollis, 
2002). His processes are exhaustively analysed and further translated into 
a logical language that the computer can understand in his later book 
Compendium for Literates (1974). Similarly, other of Gerstner’s contempo-
rary graphic designers revealed similar design approaches. In 1965, Max 
Bill (2016) stated that his artworks and designs grew from structured, or 
rule-based, methodology. In 1967, Emil Ruder (see Figure 2.28), in his book

Typographie (2009), presented how a highly constrained set of elements 
can be combined to create a wide range of compositions, exemplifying this 
idea by combining one line and dot into 36 distinct compositions. In his 
book Graphic Design Manual (1965), Armin Hofmann presents a set of rule-
based exercises that he did with his students. At that time, systematic and 
rule-based GD approaches were also explored in 1973 by Donis A. Dondis 
(1979) and, in 1979, by Wucius Wong (1991). In his later text, the Swiss style 
designer Josef Müller-Brockmann stated that work with a grid system is an 
expression of “clearly intelligible, objective, functional, and aesthetic quality 
of mathematical thinking” and promotes a rational creative and technical 
production of visuals (Müller -Brockmann, 1981, p. 10, see Figure 2.29). 
At about the same time, several artists experimented with algorithmic 
approaches for generating design visuals. In the 1930s, it was developed 
sets of modular graphic elements to construct custom lettering and illus-
trations through arranged and rearranged geometrical forms in many ways 
(Biľak, 2020). Patrona Grotesk, published by Czechoslovakian Slévarna 
Písem in 1931, and Fregio Mecano published by Italian Nebiolo Foundry 
in 1934, are two well-known examples. Likewise, in the 1940s, Joan Trochut 
developed SuperTipo Veloz, a collection of type modules published by José 
Iranzo foundry. Recently, in 2004, this system was digitalised by Alex 
Trochut and Andreu Balius (Arroyo & Balius, 2022). In 1960, Bruno Munari 
made a game called ABC con Fantasia 63 for the Italian Danese design company 
when he designed 26 linear and circular elements that can be combined 
to write any letter of the alphabet or create other imaginative shapes (Levin

044PRELUDE  AND  FOUNDA TIONSI
& Brain, 2021). Some years later, Bruno Munari (1966) presented a method 
to design posters “without end,” i.e. posters that are not designed as single 
entries, presenting no edges, that can be placed and connected side by 
side to form a poster of any size. Around the same time, Sol LeWitt pre-
sented The Plan for a Conceptual Art Book (1971), when he compiled a set 
of formal instructions to create an exhibition catalogue bearing how to 
draw lines and typography (Cramer, 2002). 
In the 1970s, Win Crouwel convinced that current typefaces were not 
appropriate for machine displaying, designed the experimental typeface 
The New Alphabet (1970), optimised for visualisation in CRT screens (see 
Figure 2.30). In this typeface, the letters were aligned both horizontally 
and vertically within a grid and composed with only horizontal, vertical, 
and diagonal strokes. This way, Crouwel sought a type of design for the 
new computer age, which, according to him, is not based on written or 
drawn examples of the past (Hollis, 2001). 
The first approaches to automating and computerising typesetting 
were noticeable in the 1960s and 1970s. In 1963, the company Rocappi 
presented a workflow based on a computer-generated tape that made 
it possible to typeset text with little (or even without) human intervention 
(Seybold, 2018). Some years after, in 1973, researchers at the Xerox Palo 
Alto Research Center (PARC) built Xerox Alto (see Figure 2.31), the first 
computer designed to support a Graphical User Interface (GUI) based 
on a desktop metaphor and a suite of applications and services to support 
office automation. Besides the computer, the Alto workstation also included 
a black-and-white display about the size of a sheet of paper, a keyboard, 
a keyset, a mouse, and a network connection via Ethernet (Sproull, 2018). 
Alto introduced the idea of electronic typesetting, enabling users to manip-
ulate the elements on the screen and print them next. The publishing tools 
developed in PARC were a set of standalone applications, each designed 
to prepare a different document content.64 In text typesetting, Alto intro-
duced two multi-font text document editors, Bravo (command-based) and 
Gypsy (GUI-based), and the Interpress page description language (Sproull, 
2018). Alto is also made available with SuperPaint, an eight-bit pixel painting 
system (Shoup, 2001). These innovations support Alto with WYSIWYG 
tools, enabling users to observe on the screen the characters and layouts 
that will also be printed in the final document, establishing the foundation 
for the general availability of DTP applications. Then, innovations of Xerox 
PARC were made available commercially with the release, in 1981, of the 
Xerox 8010 Star workstation (Moggridge, 2006; Sproull, 2018).
In 1984, the PostScript programming language created by John Warnock 
and Charles Geschke was launched by Adobe Systems (Adobe Systems, 1990; 
Warnock, 2018). This language enabled the description and rendering of 
computer graphics, allowing the designer to define the appearance of every 
point on a page to within a thousandth of a millimetre. The new language 
quickly became the standard for describing designs, replacing phototype-
setting processes and enabling the development of early digital printing 
tools. The invention of the PostScript language allowed the development 
of several DTP software applications. Also, in 1984, Paul Brainerd created

045 FOUNDA TIONS2
Aldus and began to develop DTP software. In the same year, Apple released 
the Apple Macintosh — the first successful mass-market desktop personal 
computer with a graphical interface. Soon after that, in 1985, Apple intro-
duced the Apple LaserWriter printer, while Aldus made PageMaker available 
to Macintosh. PageMaker enabled users to create, stylise, and combine 
typographic and imagery elements in documents and print the created 
documents (Meggs & Purvis, 2016). The introduction of Macintosh and 
PageMaker allowed DTP to be made feasible and economically practical. 
From then on, one person operating a computer could control most of the 
typography and layout production processes (Bailey, 2008; Meggs & Purvis, 
2016). This turned GD into an  interdisciplinary field, profoundly modi -
fying its professional nature and democratising its production methods 
(Blauvelt, 2011c; Cooper, 1989; Triggs, 2003). Nevertheless, the initial 
adoption of these digital technologies was very limited (Byfield, 2008).
In the 1980s, the first experiments were developed to enrich people’s 
visualisation and interaction with documents. Apple developed HyperTalk, 
a programming language for the Apple HyperCard application, an early 
hypermedia system which allowed people to create hypertextual relations 
between regions of the same document (Moggridge, 2006; Reas et al., 2010). 
Around the same time, Steven Feiner, Sandor Nagy, and Andries van Dam 
presented the Electronic Document System (EDS) Navigation System (1982), 
an experimental system for designing, developing, and presenting com-
puter-based documents. It enabled people to visualise documents composed 
of pages that include pictures and actions. The system consisted of sepa-
rate programs for laying out and drawing pictures, graphically specifying 
the contents of pages, chapters, and their interconnections, and displaying 
the document for user interaction.
In the later 1980s, many designers started to embrace computerised 
and DTP tools to explore primitive digital media in order to create inno-
vative visual languages and forms. These designers explored the traditional 
design and typesetting rules, creating and incorporating Postmodern and 
Poststructuralist concepts such as Open Works or Multiple Meanings (Bailey, 
2008; Guffey, 2015; Heller, 2004; Lupton & Miller, 1996; Poynor, 2003). 65 
The democratisation of these DTP tools and the emergence of this post -
modern design practice allowed experimental typography and type design 
practices that blended craftsmanship, historical revivalisms, and techno-
logical aesthetics, which were progressively incorporated as part of the 
design processes (Triggs, 2003).

In the 1970s, theorists such as 
Umberto Eco (2006), Roland Barthes 
(2006), and Michel Foucault (1979) 
explored the idea that texts can be 
interpreted in multiple ways. They 
argued that meaning is not fixed but 
open to various interpretations. In the 
following decades, graphic designers 
adopted this concept, creating works 
that encouraged audiences to decode 
and interpret them in different ways,

These characteristics were observable in the works of Postmodern 
(also named New Wave) graphic designers such as April Greiman (see Figure 
2.35), Barbara Kuhr, Dan Friedman (see Figure 2.32), David Carson, Edward 
Fella, Fred Woodward, Gail Anderson, Jeffery Keedy, John Plunkett, Jon 
Wozencroft, Katherine McCoy (see Figure 2.33), Katie Salen, Paula Scher, P. 
Scott Makela, Rudy VanderLans, Wolfgang Weingart (see Figure 2.34), Zuzana 
Licko, or the studio 8vo (Mark Holt and Hamish Muir, Michael Burke, and 
Simon Johnston). These designers established what Frances Butler (1995) 
denominated as “new demotic typography,” a design practice that presents 
a poststructuralist critical approach to design characterised by visual com-
plexity, layering and experimentation, in which the printer pages are so fully 
packed that many of its layers become invisible. Publications such as Emigre 
(1984 – 2005) by Rudy VanderLans and Zuzana Licko, Octavo (1986 – 1992) 
edited by 8vo, or Fuse (1991 – 2012) edited by Jon Wozencroft and Neville 
Brody, became playgrounds for exploration, discussion, and dissemination 
of experimental type design and typography, being a showcase of the capa-
bilities of digital technologies in the context of typography, to the magazine 
editorial design and the selection of feature works (Heller, 2004; Triggs, 2003). 
Postmodern designers also explored and exploited the thereupon 
technological advances to create experimental new kinds of designs defined 
by the technological experimentation and the crossover between distinct, 
or even opposite, styles (Blokland & Rossum, 2016; Lupton & Miller, 1996; 
Triggs, 2003). Examples include Template Gothic (1990) by Barry Deck, 
Dead History (1990) by P. Scott Makela, Oakland (1985) and Narly (1993) 
by Zuzana Licko, FF Reactor (1993) by Tobias Frere-Jones, or Exocet (1991) 
or Manson (1992) by Jonathan Barnbrook.

During the 1990s, the development of the World Wide Web (WWW)
allowed the Internet to move from academic settings into homes every-
where. The Internet presented a window of opportunity to GD professionals, 
allowing for new ways of communicating and disseminating information 
and creating and designing websites.  Meanwhile, no-code and alternative 
Web Design and development tools, such as Macromedia Flash and Director, 
emerged and gave the opportunity to develop experimental and distinctive 
websites, building the foundations for an intense period of visual explo-
ration on the web (Reas et al., 2010; Vinh, 2011). Flash and Director had 
their own built-in programming languages, ActionScript and Lingo, respec-
tively. These languages permitted code-based access to a wide range 
of interactive features, from the state of a simple button rollover to fully 
dynamic animation generated entirely by code, leading to a high impact 
on the development of the WWW in the early 1990s (Richardson, 2016). 
Although during the early time of the web, the designs denoted significant 
constraints, e.g. limited computer screen sizes or the required use of web-
safe fonts, several designers such as April Greiman, Clement Mok, Jessica 
Helfand, or Paola Antonelli (see Figure 2.36) notably worked with these 
limitations (Meggs & Purvis, 2016). 
At the turn of the millennium, GD had already adopted the computer 
as its primary tool and the Internet as its main distribution media, enabling 
creative practitioners to experiment with new ways of thinking, making, 
collaborating, and distributing their designs. Nowadays, contemporary 
Typography and GD are no longer restricted to physical surfaces and com-
puterised tools and are embracing a multitude of strategies ranging 
from architectural to digital media and virtual spaces.
The widespread access to computers and the Internet has trans-
formed work processes and tools across nearly all disciplines, including 
GD. Consistently with other periods in the past, GD evolved in synchrony 
with the technological advances of each era, becoming one of the first 
disciplines significantly impacted by the rise of computers (Blauvelt, 2011c; 
Cooper, 1989).
Since the latter years of the twentieth century, many designers began 
to explore computers as more than just editing suites, looking to computers 
as media in their own right. These designers explored computer program-
ming to overcome the limitations of mainstream computerised tools 

048PRELUDE  AND  FOUNDA TIONSI
(Maeda, 2004; Reas et al., 2010; Richardson, 2016). This exploration led to 
the emergence of computational GD practices. Designers began using 
computation to automate certain tasks and explore new conceptual and 
visual possibilities, resulting in novel types of designs. Moreover, the emer-
gence of these computational approaches comes with a paradigm shift in 
the role of the designer, who begins to create processes that enable the cre-
ation of designs instead of designing the final solution (Bohnacker et al.,  
2012). In other words, the design concept is translated into a computer 
program that systematically crafts multiple design possibilities from the 
original concept.
Early research in the computational GD field was focused on text 
formatting and typesetting. In the 1980s, Donald E. Knuth and Michael F. 
Plass (1981; Plass, 1981) developed an algorithm to break pages, avoiding 
widows and orphans. They also employed the developed approach to 
typeset a two-column dictionary. Soon after that, Knuth introduced the 
parametric typeface design language Metafont (1982) and the TeX typeset-
ting system (1991), allowing everyone to produce a book using a structural 
markup language and a set of commands. Arno J. H. Peels et al. (1985) 
presented COBATEF, a context-based text format system which enables 
automatic text-element recognition and establishes the foundations for 
a fully automatic presentation based on predefined layouts. Jock D. Mack-
inlay (1986) developed a framework for automated graphic presentation 
named APT that automatically designs two-dimensional presentations of 
information. Steven Feiner (1988)  addressed the problem of creating the 
automated layout of graphical displays by developing the GRIDS system, 
which creates layouts based on a set of encoded rules, including the grid, 
legibility and the element structure displayed. Richard Furuta et al. (1982) 
presented a comprehensive overview of the early digital typesetting systems 
as well as the issues and challenges of the field at that time.
In 1978, Muriel Cooper and Ron MacNeil created the Information 
Landscape project and founded the Visual Language Workshop (VLW) at 
the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), USA, to encourage 
graphic design students to seek novel forms, methods, and techniques for 
graphical communication (Conrad, 2021; Reas et al., 2010). Through the 
VLW, Cooper and her students explored the possibilities created by the 
emerging electronic media to pioneer new forms (Cooper, 1989; Meggs & 
Purvis, 2016, see Figures 2.37 to 2.40). Later, in 1985, VLW became a part 
of the MIT Media Laboratory. In the subsequent decades, the VLW team 
explored multiple designs for electronic media through the employment 
of tailor-made software tools, either with research or professional proposals. 
In 1986, VLW began working together with IBM to explore ideas that 
supplement the mechanical process of graphic design (Musgrave & Cooper, 
1996). In this collaboration, multiple cover designs were created for the 
journals Perspectives in Computing and IBM Systems as well as several cor -
porate technical publications of IBM, e.g. IBM Journal of Research and Devel-
opment. Other works developed in VLW include the dynamic multi-layer 
compositions created by Muriel Cooper and Suguru Ishizaki in 1988 through 
variation of text and image characteristics such as size, placement, colour

and opacity (Cooper, 1989, see Figure 2.40); the interactive three -dimensional 
Typographic Space created by David Small, Ishizaki Suguru, and Muriel 
Cooper (1994), the experimental interactive three-dimensional information 
space, Financial Viewpoints, developed by Lisa Strausfeld (1995); or the 
navigable Virtual Shakespeare environment created by David Small (1999).
Since the 1990s, John Maeda has been exploring code as an expres-
sive medium for crafting several visual artefacts, such as drawing machines, 
posters, books, and new media installations. His work laid the foundation 
for creative coding and introduced a new way of looking at and thinking 
about code in visual design. Between 1994 and 1999, Maeda also created a 
series of book-inspired applications, Reactive Books (Maeda, 2005).66 These 
books present a collection of visuals that interactively are controlled by 
user inputs, introducing the concept of reactive graphics (see Figure 2.41) 
(Maeda, 2000, 2004). Each book explores a single type of input source to 
generate the visuals: microphone, mouse, time, keyboard, and video. The

first book, named Reactive Square (1994), presents ten squares that respond 
to audio from a microphone. The second book was Flying Letters (1995), 
where the mouse position was used as a way of playing with digital-type 
forms. The third book presents 12 playful clocks, called 12 o’clocks (1996), 
that display the time in a specific digital format. The fourth and last pub-
lished book, Tap, Type, Write (1998.) displays compositions of letters 
moving and rearranging themselves in various patterns, allowing users to 
interact with them using the keyboard. The last book was supposed to be 
named Mirror Mirror and use video input as the primary interaction input; 
however, it was not published since the publisher, Digitalogue, closed its 
doors in 2000. In 1996, Maeda also designed a series of ten posters for the 
Japanese type foundry Morisawa by varying and repeating the visual attrib-
utes of the Morisawa logo using the Adobe PostScript language (Maeda 2000, 
see Figure 2.42).
LettError design studio, founded by Just van Rossum and Erik Blokland, 
also began to employ random processes and parametric design methods 
to design several typographies and type design scenarios. In 1989, they 
released the typeface Beowolf (originally called Random Font), the first 
typeface with random programmed behaviour, which takes a unique shape 
every time it is printed (Barrett et al. , 2000; Blokland & Rossum, 2016). 
Consequently, each point of the glyphs moves randomly when printed 
using the PostScript language (see Figure 2.43). As a result, when printed, 
the glyphs always take an uncertain and distinct shape on the page. Fur -
thermore, LettError explored the use of computational design scripts and 
tools to automate several tasks and generate visual identities and typo-
graphic artefacts, such as books, calendars, type specimens, stamps, and 
even their portfolio (Blokland & Rossum, 2016; Middendorp, 2018).
In the 1990s and 2000s, multiple artists and designers developed 
work concerning the generation of web-based compositions exploring the 
novel aesthetics and interactive possibilities of the primitive web. 
Between 1996 and 2011, Born Magazine (Kean et al., 1996) published 
innovative explorations of typographic composition in digital media, uti-
lising moving and interactive features to create new ways of experiencing 
and reading text. In the 1990s, Mark Napier created a series of Internet 
artworks that concerned the generation of layouts. Shredder (1998) decon-
structs the elements of a collection of preselected websites, e.g. text, images 
and source code, and generates new abstract layouts (see Figure 2.44). 
Similarly, Riot (1999) combines the elements of the last three visited web-
sites. The art collective JODI (Joan Heemskerk and Dirk Paesmans) created 
web designs exploring and exploiting the compositions possibilities of the 
early web, e.g. wwwwwwwww.jodi.org (1995), asdfg.jodi.org (1998), or SOD 
(1999). Janet Cohen et al. developed the Unreliable Archivist (1998), a website 
that allows users to adjust the visual features of the online gallery äda’web 
through a parametric interface with four slides: language; images; style; 
and layout. Cornelia Sollfrank and Panos Galanis created the Net.Art gen-
erator (2003), which generates web pages from a combination of images 
gathered from many online sources based on user text input.

051 FOUNDA TIONS2
Others created custom drawing tools with interactive behaviours 
distinct from mainstream computerised tools. Tomoko Takahashi devel-
oped Word Perhect (1999), a word processor with a hand-drawn interface 
that generates rude and handwritten text designs. In the same year, Ben 
Fry developed FugPaint (1999), a painting program that replies directly 
to the user’s drawing commands. Comparably, Adrian Ward developed 
Auto-Illustrator (2001), a graphics editor and design application that com-
prises a set of uncontrollable drawing functions and, therefore, allows for 
the introduction of randomness in the drawing process. Golan Levin 
developed Yellowtail (2000), an interactive application for the gestural 
creation of real-time abstract animations. John F. Simon Jr. presented 
Mobility Agents (2005), a drawing software that extends user-drawn lines 
by adding new lines connected to the originals. More recently, Zachary 
Lieberman created Ink Space (2015), a drawing software that uses an accel-
erometer to move user drawings in three-dimensional space.
Since the turn of the millennium, several creative coding frameworks 
have been made available, encouraging graphic designers to begin devel-
oping their own programs and work directly with software, e.g. Processing, 
NodeBox or OpenFrameworks (Armstrong, 2016; Blauvelt, 2011c; Bohnacker 
et al., 2012; Richardson, 2016). These frameworks present different purposes, 
letting users code either graphically or textually (see Section 2.2). Moreover, 
most of these tools and frameworks are released under an open-source 
licence and are supported by strong user communities. The Magic Book  
(2020) framework is a clear example of this. This project was created 
to facilitate the design, production, and self-publishing of books in various 
formats by a group of researchers, faculty, and students of the Interactive 
Telecommunications Program (ITP) at the New York University TISCH. 
Several computerised GD software programs also allow the users to include 
code-based expressions and scripting. Accordingly, several libraries and 
frameworks were developed to facilitate code operations inside these 
scripting environments. For instance, the Scriptographer (Lehni, Puckey, et al., 
2001; Womack, 2011; Womack & Lehni, 2006) was created to facilitate 
writing scripts for Adobe Illustrator (see Figure 2.45). In a similar way, the 
Basil.js library (T. Davis et al., 2013; Zeller et al., 2014) also provides friendly 
and accessible tools for scripting and automation in Adobe InDesign (see 
Figure 2.46).67
These digital experiments and technological advances have impacted 
GD processes, leading to the development of an experimental GD practice 
characterised by collaborative and flexible outcomes (Armstrong & Sto-
jmirovic, 2011; Blauvelt, 2011c; McCormack et al., 2004; Shaughnessy, 2013).

052PRELUDE  AND  FOUNDA TIONSI
Today, graphic designers focus on creating designs that actively engage 
and interact with their audience. In other words, they aim to produce work 
that fosters a dialogue with viewers. CD tools are the driving force behind 
the emergence of these kinds of artefacts. While most explorations are 
digital, some examples also exist in physical media, as seen in the work of 
graphic designers like Daniel Eatock,68 Luna Maurer (see Figure 2.47),69 or 
Marco Neves (2016).
While there are no certainties about the future of design practices, 
recent digital media and CD tools are promoting a profound change in the 
discipline (Blauvelt, 2011c; Shim, 2020). Graphic designers' successful 
adaptation to these new scenarios will likely play a crucial role in deter -
mining their future professional success (Shaughnessy, 2012).
In this sense, many authors have presented theories and insights 
regarding the potential directions of future GD-related practices and 
processes. Lev Manovich (2001) considered computers to be universal 
mass communication tools. Nevertheless, he emphasises that new media 
is not a simple digitalisation of old media; instead, it must share five main 
key principles: numerical representations, modularity, automation, vari-
ability, and transcoding. Brenda Laurel (2006, 2009) stated that computer 
technologies, especially ubiquitous computing, have the potential to create 
novel narrative experiences, envisioning the advent of a new design par -
adigm named Design Animism. 
Andrew Blauvelt (2008) introduced the concept of Relational Design 
as a new practice that explores GD’s performative dimensions and facili-
tates users’ social interactions in an era. The Relational Design practice is 
characterised by the inclusion of performative, pragmatic, programmatic, 
process-oriented, open-ended processes, and participatory elements. 
Although this practice is connected to digital media, it is not only limited 
to it. Later, Blauvelt (2011c) argues that designers must learn how to use 
computers as meta-tools to create their own tools. Adrian Shaughnessy 
(2012) reinforces the idea of shifting in the GD practice, considering that 
we are entering into a Post-Graphic Design Age, where design skills will serve 
as a “passport” to achieve various other goals. Alessandro Ludovico (2012) 
argues that new digital media and technologies promote a post-digital 
print practice, defined by the expansion of print and the hybridisation of 
editorial designs. David Reinfurt (2019) proposed a design curriculum that 
treats GD as a liberal art that informs the dissemination of information 
and knowledge across other disciplines. This curriculum is centred around 
three fundamental subjects: typography, gestalt principles, and interface 
design. On the other hand, Demian Conrad (2021) believes that the crea-
tion of graphic variation using computer programming is one of the main 
purposes of GD in the post-digital age.
Hugh Dubberly (2008) believes that the increase in computer pro-
cessing power is enabling us to move from a “mechanical-object ethos” to 
an “organic-systems ethos.” This way, designers will move from the role 
of an expert to a collaborator in the future complex systems. Similarly, 
Paola Antonelli (2008) suggests that we are moving toward an organic, 
system-based approach to design. She believes that biomimicry and nano-
technology will significantly impact future design practices. From her 
perspective, the future of design involves creating artefacts that reflect 
these advancements.

053 FOUNDA TIONS2
Luna Maurer, Edo Paulus, Jonathan Puckey, and Roel Wouters pub-
lished the Conditional Design manifesto (2008), presenting an approach to 
design that emphasises the process and utilises logic to manage external 
inputs. Inspired by complex structures and emergent behaviours, this 
design collective experimented with creating visuals based on self-imposed 
conditions and rules (Paulus et al., 2013). This way, the presented approach 
allows the emergence of generative designs from shared processes of 
chance, time, and instruction. Other designers have explored similar 
approaches, employing conditional and collaborative methods to create 
visuals based on rules-based systems and various inputs. We highlight 
works such as the Utilitarian Poster series (1998, 2010, 2013, see Figure 
2.48) or Pens  Paper image series (2014) by Daniel Eatock or the socially 
constructed Incidental flyer (2009) by BERG studio.
Helen Armstrong and Zvezdana Stojmirovic (2011) adapt Participa-
tory Design to the GD context, allowing designers to address audience 
requirements by creating scalable, adaptable, and unfinished projects. They 
considered that participatory projects should be based on these four fea-
tures: (i) community, i.e. designs should establish platforms for social 
interaction; (ii) modularity, i.e. designs must be thought in a modular way; 
(iii)  flexibility, i.e.  designs must easily adapt to unexpected conditions; 
and (iv) technology, i.e. designs should be developed taking into consid-
eration algorithmic processes, enabling the recombination and extension. 
More recently, Kate Compton (Compton & Mateas, 2015; Compton, 
2019) and Elena Petrovskaya et al. (2020) proposed a collaborative type of 
creativity supporting system, the Casual Creators. This type of system 
enables the integration of generative approaches into creative processes, 
democratising access to creativity tools in an engaging, autotelic, and 
enjoyable manner.
In recent decades, Conceptual  70 and Critical Design  71 experiments 
have emerged and gained popularity among designers. These approaches 
concern the development of speculative, fictional, and imaginary design 
experimentations to examine the consequences, implications, and possi-
bilities of future relationships between science, technology, and humans. 
These approaches incorporate several design practices such as Design Fiction 
(Bleecker, 2009; Sterling, 2009), Speculative Design (Dunne & Raby, 2013), 
Critical Making (Ratto, 2011), or Experimental Futures (Candy & Kornet, 2019; 
Luria & Candy, 2022). Instead of focusing on commercial goals, these 
approaches aim to develop design proposals that address and explore 
critical issues likely to arise in the future.
Currently, digital media and computers are becoming increasingly 
ubiquitous and seamlessly integrated into our everyday environment  
(Laurel, 2009; Manovich, 2020). Today, we find ourselves surrounded by 
displays, ranging from the screens of our mobile phones to large public 
billboards, and we are gradually extending screen-based behaviours into 
the physical world. Consequently, computational processes have signifi-
cantly influenced professional GD, often supporting the creation of visuals 
for digital media, including imagery, animations, and typography. As a 
result, CD approaches are now being explored across various domains 
related to GD. In the scope of this thesis, we identify three main domains: 
branding; symbol design; and layout design.

054PRELUDE  AND  FOUNDA TIONSI
Since the turn of the millennium, the use of CD approaches in 
branding has become increasingly prominent. These methods are employed 
to handle, react to, and respond to various types of data inputs and cir -
cumstances. These approaches allow designs to satisfy the complexity of 
present-day institutions (Armstrong & Stojmirovic, 2011; Blauvelt, 2011a; 
Richardson, 2016). While experiments with dynamic branding were iden-
tified in the twentieth century (e.g. the Alfred A. Knopf publishing house or 
the Boîte a Musique visual systems), it was not until the 2000s that the 
design of dynamic visual identities became commonplace. The earliest 
uses of computational approaches in this domain also occurred during 
this epoch, such as the data-driven logomark for the Rhizome blog (2001) 
or the Golan Levin experiments with interactive logographs (Levin, 2001). 
Ulrike Felsing (2010), Irene van Nes (2013), and Tiago Martins et al. (2021) 
present good overviews of the domain of dynamic visual identities.
Recently, graphic designers have been experimenting with CD 
methods to introduce flexibility and variations on their visual identities’ 
designs. Several designers explored data-driven approaches to create 
reactive branding that adapts to different contexts, like visual identities 
such as Casa da Música (Sagmeister & Walsh, 2001), Poetry on Road litera-
ture festival (B. Müller et al., 2002, see Figure 2.50), the Decode exhibition 
(Schmidt, 2009), the Norwegian Nordkyn peninsula (Neue, 2010), or the 
Design and Multimedia programmes of UC (S. M. Rebelo, Martins, et al., 
2019). Also, there were explored generative approaches to create visual 
variation on visual identities. Examples include the Walter Expanded visual 
identity programme (Felsing, 2010, pp. 166 – 173, see Figure 2.49), the evolving 
logo (Schmitz, 2006), the Monadnocz logomark (Catalogtree & Issler, 2007), 
as well as Ollo (Bibliothèque, 2011) and Llun Negra  72 (Rodenbröker & 
TwoPoints.Net, 2022) visual identities. More recently, logotype generators 
have been developed, experimenting with both evolutionary and ML. 
Evolutionary approaches include the works of Junji Saikawa and Takehisa 
Onisawa (2014), Sérgio M. Rebelo et al. (2018), as well as the MarkMaker 
system (Gambell & Hooikaas, 2015). Examples of neural generators are 
Looka Logo Maker (2016), Logopony (2016), My Brand New Logo (Monokai, 
2018), and Brandmark (2022).
Using computational methods in symbol design encompasses cre-
ating functional (glyph) and pictorial (pictograms and ideograms) designs. 
There are various experiments that involve the modification of pre -designed 
symbols, such as the evolving font deformations experiment (Lewis & But-
terfield, 2000), Galagagos (A. Chen & Woo, 2012), PALETTE (Yoshida et al., 
2010), TypeAdviser (J. Cunha et al., 2016), and Ådea (Lopes, Correia, et al., 
2020b, 2020a) generative systems. The recombination of parts from pre-
designed diverse symbols to create new ones is observable in works like 
Slitscan (J. Keller, 2006), FontMixer (Oppenhäuser, 2008), and genoTyp  
(Schmitz, 2004) letter shapes generators, as well as the ICONATE gener -
ator (Zhao et al., 2020) and the conceptual emoji creator Emojinating  
(J. M. Cunha et al., 2019, 2020, see Figure 2.51). 
Approaches for creating visual variations of glyphs are observable 
in the works of Peter Cho (1999), Andreas Lund (2000), Tatsuo Unemi 
and Megumi Soda (2003), Yeohyun Ahn (Ahn & Jin, 2016; T. Lee & Ahn, 
2020, see Figure 2.52), Jéssica Parente et al. (2018, 2020, see Figure 2.53). 
These types of CD approaches are also employed in the works Here to There

055 FOUNDA TIONS2
(I/O, 2007), mis.shap.en.ness (Ali, 2010b), and Growing Data (onformative, 
2011), as well as in the creation of the Gothic Lab typeface (Murit & Pro-
duction Type, 2016). Similarly, evolutionary approaches were employed 
to generate a variety of symbols, including calligraphic glyphs (Levin et al., 
2001), Japanese fonts (Wada & Hagiwara, 2003), modular type designs 
(Kuzma et al., 2009; T. Martins et al., 2015, 2016), stencils templates 
(T. Martins, Correia, et al., 2018, see Figure 2.54), anthropomorphic symbols 
(Dorris et al., 2004), emoticons (Dozier et al., 2005), or warning symbols 
(Piper, 2010). Recently, neural models have also begun to be explored for 
creating symbols. Examples include the AIfont typeface (Process Studio, 
2019a), the AImoji emoji set (Process Studio, 2019b), and the Hongyi Yang 
et al. generative icon systems (2021). 
Other generative approaches explore parametric techniques to 
introduce the visual variation of outputs. Examples include the three-di-
mensional shape generator SuperShape (Ali, 2010a), the type design 
approaches Letter Spirit (McGraw Jr, 1995), and Lego Font Creator (Lehni, 
Lehni, et al., 2001), N O R M A L S T Y P E (N O R M A L S, 2012), Phase 
(Hanzer & Zia, 2018), GrammarType (T. Martins, Rebelo, et al., 2018), and 
LetterSpecies (Pereira et al., 2019, 2020) systems. Data-driven approaches 
handling visual variation of symbols based on data include Laika (Fluckiger 
& Kunz, 2009), TYPEFACE (Huang, 2010), typeEm (Maçãs et al., 2019), 
FaceType (Maher et al., 2022), and SpeechTyper (Parente et al., 2022).
CD approaches are also explored for supporting layouts and typo-
graphic design. The following section offers a comprehensive overview of 
CD practices in this domain.
We also observed computational explorations in other domains 
related to GD that are beyond the scope of this thesis. For example, CD 
techniques show significant potential for Data and Information Visualis -
ation. Some notable examples include Arc Diagrams (Wattenberg, 2002), 
Understanding Shakespeare (Thiel, 2010), Visualizing Empires Declines (P. Cruz 
& Machado, 2011), Feltron Annual Reports (Felton, 2014), the hexagonal 
gridded maps of Evgheni Polisciuc et al. (2016), Planck (Matsuda, 2017), 
All Roads to Rome (Reimann et al., 2017), or Field of Leaves (Silva et al., 2022). 
Comparably, CD approaches have been successfully employed in the gen-

056PRELUDE  AND  FOUNDA TIONSI
eration of abstract images, as seen in projects such as Daily Sketches (Lieb-
erman, 2016), Prima Materia (Vallejo, 2018), or Shared Visual Abstractions 
(T. White, 2019). Similarly, they have been explored in the creation of visual 
patterns, evident in works like PSC31 (Wilson, 2003), the evolutionary tile 
system of Carl Anderson et al. (2008), or Abstract_ (Karmann et al., 2015), 
or even video and animation, as demonstrated in the works of Marc Downie 
(2002), Jonathan J. Harris (2007), Chris Milk (2012), Doyeon Kim et al.  
(2020), and Peggy Chi et al. (2020).
This section provides essential background for the experiments 
presented in later chapters of this thesis by examining how designers 
have historically used algorithms and systematic approaches to structure 
visual communication and graphic design. It also reveals that systematic 
and algorithmic approaches have been key strategies in this discipline 
throughout its evolution. Examples of these approaches include modularity, 
rule-based designs, and, more recently, procedural generation. Additionally, 
this research contextualises the potential of using computational approaches 
in GD scenarios, both in terms of specific design tasks and examining their 
broader implications for GD practice.
