057 FOUNDA TIONS2
2.4  COMPUT A TIONAL DESIGN APPROACHES 
IN TYPOGRAPHY AND LA YOUT
The democratisation of computer access allowed designers, artists, and 
researchers to explore CD methods for creating grids, layouts, and typog-
raphy, encouraging new design practices and media. These approaches are 
developed using custom software or scripting methods in computerised 
Desktop Publishing (DTP) tools.
Several works have contributed to the automation of layout gener-
ation without directly producing designs. Instead, they focus on the rep-
resentation and facilitation of the layout generation process. Greg J. Badros 
et al. (2001) developed Cassowary , an incremental linear arithmetic con-
straint-solving toolkit for adjusting element size in a layout. Angelo Di Iorio 
et al. (2008) proposed the XML-based template language Topological 
Abstract Layout Language, allowing users to describe layouts based on high-
-level topological properties (e.g. similarity, proximity, importance, grouping) 
instead of geometric features. They also developed an engine for handling 
this representation. Ludwig Zeller et al. (2013; 2014) created the typesetting 
scripting library Basil.js, which facilitates the scripting and automation 
in Adobe InDesign. Similarly, the Magic Book (2020) framework simplifies 
books' design, production, and self-publishing in multiple formats. This 
framework employs the markup language AsciiDoc  to represent and visually 
format content, guiding the generation of documents in various formats.73
Other works focused on developing metrics, heuristics, and measures 
for typography and layout designs. Steven J. Harrington et al. (2004) pro-
posed a non-linear heuristic measure for evaluating document design 
quality comprising nine measures: alignment, regularity, separation, balance, 
white-space fraction, white-space free flow, proportion, uniformity, and page 
security. Simon Lok et al. (2004) introduced a technique for computing 
visual balance using lightness weight maps from images. Helen Y. Balinsky 
et al. (2009) introduced two measures for calculating the alignment and reg-
ularity of a page based on the extraction and counting of the “alignment 
lines” (i.e. illusory contour elements of the layout structure). Zoya Bylin-
skii et al. (2017) present a ML model that estimates the relative importance 
of different visual elements in GD layouts and data visualisations. This 
model is trained using a crowdsourced collection of annotations from 
hundreds of designers, who provided data through human clicks and 
importance annotations. More recently, Yuxi Xie et al. presented CanvasEmb 
(2021), a large-scale pretrained model for visual layout representation that 
unveiled some potential in layout auto-completion and retrieval.
Regarding the use of CD for directly impacting the creation of designs, 
we observed that works can be either research-oriented or application -
-oriented. Research-oriented works concern comprehensive studies of com-
putational techniques to automate design tasks and processes. In contrast, 
application-oriented works are developed to address a specific design 
project. Despite this distinction, both types of work can be classified based 
on autonomy, expertise, and expressivity power. 
73
AsciiDoc is a plain text markup 
language used to represent and 
visually format text. It offers a range 
of functions to represent various 
types of textual elements. For more 
information, visit https://asciidoc.org 
(visited: 7 July 2025).

058PRELUDE  AND  FOUNDA TIONSI
Autonomy refers to how a computational procedure can operate 
independently without requiring human intervention (Russell & Norvig, 
2016). A fully autonomous procedure produces outcomes without any 
human input, whereas a system with low autonomy frequently requires 
human intervention.
Expertise (or expert performance) refers to the depth and breadth 
of domain-specific knowledge that enables a computational procedure 
to make informed decisions within a specific domain (Ericsson et al., 2018; 
Russell & Norvig, 2016). A procedure with high expertise relies on sourced 
specialised knowledge, while a procedure with low expertise cannot make 
informed judgments.
Expressive power refers to the range of outcomes a computational 
procedure can represent and produce (Russell & Norvig, 2016). A procedure 
with high expressive power produces outcomes that can be significantly 
diverse in characteristics and diversity, while a procedure with low expres-
sive power produces constrained and similar outcomes.
Considering these concepts, we analysed computational design 
approaches for producing layouts and typography across various media. 
With the understanding that related work in the field might overlap across 
different domains, we have grouped the work into four main strategies: 
(i) template, (ii) stochastic, (iii) expert , and (iv) cooperative.
template strategies involve creating designs based on predetermined 
visual and typographic features. These production processes typically have 
low autonomy and expertise, requiring designers to define and describe 
visual features and their variations, with results heavily dependent on user 
input. Also, they exhibit low expressive power, as the outcomes present 
limited visual variation.
stochastic strategies involve producing designs through stochastic 
methods, typically incorporating randomness with minimal constraints 
and restrictions. These processes can exhibit high autonomy, operating 
independently without user interaction, and have been explored with 
varied levels of expressive power. However, they often present low expertise, 
relying on randomness.
expert strategies allow for the autonomous creation of designs with 
minimal human input that rely on domain-specific expertise instead. These 
procedures typically exhibit high autonomy and expertise, using specialised 
knowledge from rule-based systems, ML models, predictive methods, and 
automated evolution. They have been explored with varying levels of 
expressive power, ranging from highly controlled outcomes to more flexible 
and diverse ones.
cooperative strategies involve low autonomy since they require 
human participation or guidance during the design process. Including 
co-creative design processes, these strategies can vary in expertise, incor -
porating domain-specific knowledge to make human collaboration more 
efficient and less time-consuming. While template strategies focus on 
modifying base artefacts based on inputs, these strategies concentrate 
on generating new artefacts. As a result, they offer a wider variety of outputs 
and exhibit greater expressive power.
The following subsections comprehensively describe each strategy 
supported by related work.

059 FOUNDA TIONS2
2.4. 1 TEMPLA TE STRA TEGIES
template strategies involve creating designs based on specific inputs and 
a predefined set of visual and typographic features determined by the 
designer. This approach allows designers to control the visual aspects 
of the outcomes tightly, with any variations being predefined and minimal. 
The computational procedure automatically processes the inputs and 
adjusts the design accordingly. Inputs can range from simple interactive 
elements to the complete content that needs to be displayed. The gener -
ative processes of these strategies exhibit low expertise, relying on simple 
rules or direct mappings between inputs and visual features. Designs 
created using these strategies have low autonomy, as they depend heavily on 
human inputs for generation or modification. Also, they exhibit low expres-
sive power, producing similar outcomes and featuring limited visual variety.
These strategies are used to automate design creation for different 
purposes and in distinct media. Liqun Chen et al. (2002) developed a 
document representation structure, the Document Representation for Scal-
able Structure (DRESS),  which enables the creation of documents that 
adapt themselves to various display sizes. They tested the proposed rep-
resentation by applying this structure to content from existing web pages. 
Mira Dontcheva et al. (2007) developed a system for creating card-like 
banners with content obtained from multiple websites based on users’ 
preferences. LUST developed PolyArc (2011b), an interactive installation 
for the 22 nd International Poster and Graphic Design Festival of Chaumont, 
in 2011 (see Figure 2.56). This installation enables visitors to make their 
own poster based on a template and add it to an archive by sending a text 
message or posting a tweet (M. Webster, 2013). Jonas Pelzer developed 
Temper (2018), a template-based website generator that enables users 
to dynamically insert content and define website styles based on a prede-
fined set of options. In the same year, Sara Orsi presented the Whole Web 
Catalog (2018), a web system that populates a template web page with 
information related to an input term and retrieved from several databases 
to this term, gathered using multiple popular web APIs (e.g. New York 
Times, Wikipedia, and Youtube). Thomas Winters and Kory W. Mathewson 
proposed TEDRIC (2019), a system to create slide presentations using 
template layouts defined based on a set of topic suggestions and the typical 
flux of TED presentations.74
template strategies produce outcomes with limited visual variation. 
To overcome this limitation, many approaches combine templates with 
stochastic methods and rules, such as minimal constraint processing 
and probabilistic methods, to introduce controlled variation in the features 
of the outputs. Winfried H. Graf developed LayLab (1995), a constraint-based 
framework to support the creation of dynamic multimedia layouts based 
on a predefined layout template. Alan Borning et al. (2000) proposed a web 
design generator based on page layout templates and constraints previously 
defined by users (see Figure 2.57). Charles Jacobs et al. (2004) developed 
a page layout system that composes text and imagery elements, adapting 
them to different grids based on constraints related to the types of elements 
and viewing conditions (see Figure 2.58). Evan Schrier et al. (2008) pro-

060PRELUDE  AND  FOUNDA TIONSI
posed a system that generates adaptive layouts based on constraints and 
grid templates. These layouts allow the elements to be adapted to different 
viewing conditions and types of content. Niranjan Damera -Venkata et al. 
(2011) presented a template-based probabilistic framework for generating 
document layouts that adapt to variable content. Mikko Kuhna et al. (2012) 
proposed a semi-automated system for creating digital magazine layouts 
using a user-selected template and data from image feature extraction. 
Niraj Ramesh Dayama et al. (2020) combined layout optimisation with 
templates to create grid layouts using integer programming. This approach 
ensures that the outputs comply with a set of restrictions and conventions. 
They also developed GRID, a wireframing tool that suggests alternative 
layout designs.
Other works have utilised aesthetic criteria to guide content place -
ment within templates. Helen Y. Balinsky, Jonathan R. Howes, et al. (2009) 
presented the Aesthetically-Driven Layout (ADL) engine, which automat-
ically generates documents containing text and images. This system 
uses a template with static objects and predefined areas, dynamically 
filling these spaces with content while adhering to the aesthetic prin -
ciples proposed by Helen Y. Balinsky, Anthony J. Wiley, et al. (2009). Xuyong 
Yang et al. (2016) created a system to generate magazine covers from a set 
of images and textual descriptions based on predefined layout templates 
and design principles.
Many approaches allow users to modify template features directly 
through an interface. While these methods enable some adjustments, they 
remain limited. Users can make specific visual tweaks but cannot alter 
fundamental aspects of the design. Between 2008 and 2010, Benjamin 
Stephan and Christoph Haag developed several posters optimised for 
cost-effective reproduction using parametric modelling and bash scripts  
(Stephan & Haag, 2011). The Poster Machine installation (2013), designed 
by Luiz Ludwig, allowed users to modify a template poster design by manip-
ulating a series of physical knobs and switches (see Figure 2.59). Florian 
Schulz proposed a tool that interpolates website components based on 
predefined parameters (Schulz, 2016). Vânia Oliveira et al. developed Var-
ianType (2020; 2019), a tool to create moving posters based on a template 
design in which these features are modelled by parameters. Similarly, the 
Artic paper company, Patrik Hübner, and the design agency JUNO created 
Munken Creator (2022), an online tool to create moving posters by modifi-
cation of parameters to promote Artics’ Munken paper gamma and the 
typeface Munken Sans. 
Several works have explored data-driven approaches to define or 
influence the features of a template. For example, the Annual Report for 
Mondriaan Foundation (2009), designed by Studio Mind Design, used 
content analysis to modify and style a graph-based visualisation throughout 
the pages of the report. This visualisation highlights key topics and provides 
a non-chronological reading experience. LUST developed a set of Adobe 
InDesign scripts to automatise the design of the book I Read Where I Am  
(2011a). These scripts are used to perform simple tasks informed by the 
book's content, such as colourising words based on their frequency in the

text and generating the table of contents and glossaries. (Maffei, 2019, see 
Figure 2.60). Vladimir V. Kuchinov presented the Generative Gatsby book 
(2013) in which the content of F. Scott Fitzgerald’s novel, The Great Gatsby 
(1925), is typeset according to the musical scores of nine “big band” jazz 
from the 1920s. 
These data-driven approaches are often used to create series and 
collections of designs based on the same template, such as book covers. 
For instance, the design studio Carvalho Bernau used a data-driven method 
to design the covers of the main paperback collection of Octavo Publicaties 
(2008), basing their designs on the book contents. Pedro Cruz et al. (2010) 
developed a tool for generating visuals that reflect the occurrence of spe-
cific words in the text. This tool includes several visualisation models and 
is used by the FBA. design studio to create book covers (see Figure 2.61). 
Similarly, Lígia Duro et al. (2012) and Variable Studio (Ignac & Kuchinov, 
2017) developed systems to generate book covers based on book textual 
content and structure. In addition to book covers, similar approaches are 
also employed in other domains, such as the generation of data-driven 
illustrative designs, e.g. Generative World Cup project (2022), wallpapers, 
e.g. Spamghetto (2010), or even banknotes, e.g. Block Bills designs (2017).
template strategies can also be combined with live data streams 
to create designs responsive to environmental context, especially data 
from the audience captured using CV and sensors. Stefan Sagmeister 
and Ralph Ammer (2006) designed a reactive projection composed of 
a virtual spider web with the sentence Being not truthful works against me 
woven into it. The web remained sticky except in the shadow of passers-by. 
LUST developed the Camera Postura (2014) installation for the Netherlands 
Film Festival. This installation created posters that matched users' gestures 
with scenes where similar gestures were performed in popular movies 
from the festival (see Figure 2.62). The resulting posters are created based 
on several templates. The matching scenes were then used as backgrounds 
for the poster, with added information about the chosen movie, such as 
title, credits, nominations, and awards (RNDR, 2018). Åkestam Holst 
agency developed two reactive billboards for the Swedish pharmacy chain 
Apotek, using data from the surrounding environment to animate the 
behaviour of a central character. The Blowing in the Wind billboard campaign 
(2014) uses data recorded by ultrasonic sensors to make the hair of a woman 
model be tousled by the "wind" of the passing trains. Similarly, the Coughing 
Billboard (2016) employed a smoke detection sensor, causing the person 
depicted in the poster to start coughing whenever someone smoked nearby. 
The interactive collective YesYesNo created the interactive urban installa-
tion Más Que la Cara (2017) in Houston, USA. This installation used face-
tracking technologies to react to the facial expressions of passers-by, 
creating customised facial masks in response. Daniel Givens presented 
the gallery Computerized Forms (2017), showcasing digital poster designs 
whose elements react to audio inputs. Daniel Lopes et al. developed a 
reactive poster for the music festival Olhos Music Fest (2018), where the 
viewers’ eyes are placed on the poster and move in sync with the sound. 
João Couceiro e Castro et al. developed Máquina de Ouver (2019), a system

062PRELUDE  AND  FOUNDA TIONSI
that turns speech recordings into typographic compositions. The visual 
features are based on a predefined typographic mapping (see Figure 2.63). 
More recently, Beatriz Dias (2021) designed digital posters that react to an 
audio input. 
In addition, other template-based works have used interactive 
animation to introduce content variation and visual flexibility in designs. 
Ariel Malka created various forms of interactive typography, allowing users 
to read while interacting with the content. Two of her popular artworks 
include Javascriptorium (2006) and He Liked Thick Word Soup (2014). Studio 
Feixen created a reactive digital poster design for Oto Nové Swiss, a con-
temporary music and sound festival (Pfäffli et al., 2017). Users can interact 
with the poster on a specific web page using their mouse, with each mouse 
movement producing a sound, enabling users to create their own music 
by interacting with the poster. Furthermore, Serafim Mendes developed 
the Post-Print project (2020), a collection of 15 posters that allows the 
audience to interact and engage with them through an augmented reality 
bespoke application.
In conclusion, template strategies enable the creation of designs 
based on inputs while allowing designers to control the visual features 
tightly. Designers must predefine the expected outputs' visual features 
and the range of possible variations. Inputs can vary from simple interac-
tions to complete content that needs to be displayed. Consequently, designs 
produced with these strategies often exhibit low autonomy, expertise, and 
expressive power.
These strategies are effective for generating designs across various 
purposes, styles, media, and viewing conditions, although they offer limited 
variation. However, some template approaches incorporate minimal sto-
chastic and knowledge-based methods to introduce visual variation within 
the constraints of the template. Similarly, interface manipulation and 
data-driven methods are commonly used to modify template features, 
whether for creating new designs or adjusting pre-existing ones. Thus, 
template strategies are appropriate for cases where controlled outputs 
and input-driven approaches are necessary.
2.4.2 STOCHASTIC STRA TEGIES
stochastic strategies involve producing outcomes where features are 
defined by stochastic methods, often incorporating low expertise and some 
randomness. In contrast to template strategies, stochastic strategies 
generate designs without a predefined base. These strategies offer high 
autonomy, as the computational process operates independently without 
human intervention. They can also exhibit varied expressive power, be used 
for different tasks, and produce designs with a range of diversity.
Due to the nature of the typographic and layout design, fully random 
procedures have almost no practical applications. However, incorporating 
stochastic strategies with minimal constraints and rules can be useful 
for promoting diversity and generating visual assets for designs. For example, 
Karsten Schmidt developed a generative system (2008) to create distinct 
book covers for Faber and Faber’s print-on-demand collection, Faber Finds.

Each book cover featured a decorative frame created by randomly com-
bining a set set of modular abstract elements designed by Marian Bantjes. 
The generated frame was then integrated into a template layout using the 
b-hmmd typeface designed by Michael C. Place (Armstrong & Stojmirovic, 
2011; Bohnacker et al., 2012). FIELD studio created 10000 Digital Paintings 
(2011), a series of abstract illustrations to use on the promotional materials 
of paper manufacturer G.F. Smith (see Figure 2.64). Each illustration 
represents a random close-up view of a virtual sculpture created through 
a generative process (Walters et al., 2011). From 2001 to 2014, Andreas Gysin 
and Sid Vanetti developed a series of generative promotional posters and 
flyers for The Puddle (2014), an electronic music festival held in Zürich, 
Switzerland (see Figure 2.65). The visual designs were generated using 
a software program (the page build) that allowed the creation of visual 
patterns from random numeric sequences. Alexander Moskovkikh (2017) 
created an experimental website featuring random generative suprema-
tism-like illustrations. Additionally, the design studio MuirMcNeil gener-
ated 8,000 distinct covers for issue number 94 of Eye using HP Mosaic  
software, which enables the printing of variable data from a single seed 
vector file (Walters et al., 2017).
Similarly, several works use stochastic strategies to create random 
variations of previously created designs. Denis Klein developed Crossing, 
Mixing, Mutating (2012), a tool for generating variations of a layout design 
inspired by genetic operators. He later, with Bastian Werth and Lisa Reimann 
(as LESS Studio), updated this tool and released it as a plug-in for Adobe 
InDesign, named Evolving Layout (2016). Jon Gold (2016) introduced a declar-
ative and permutational design approach, the René, that creates multiple 
combinations of web components randomly permuting a set of user-defined 
visual features. Based on René, Simon Takman and Carl Albertsson launched 
BillUI (2019), a Sketch application plug-in for generating design variations. 
Also, Janne Aukia introduced Uibot (2019), a web application that randomly 
varies the styles of a dashboard.
Many works have explored stochastic strategies with limited exper-
tise to support design discovery and exploration tasks. They ensure that, 
although the outcomes are generated using stochastic methods, they 
maintain minimal viability and structure. Stephen M. Hart and Liu Yi-Hsin 
(1995) approached layout generation as a rectangular packing problem for 
integer linear programming, creating layouts that fit as many objects as 
possible on a canvas without overlap. C. Brian Atkins (2004) proposed a 
method for designing a photo collection page layout based on randomly 
seeded hierarchical page partitions, aiming to maximise the canvas coverage 
without photo overlap; however, this work did not address text placement. 
Benedikt Groß and Julia Laub created a series of generative poster designs 
(2007) using Adobe InDesign scripting, experimenting with random-based 
design techniques (see Figure 2.66). The design studio LUST developed 
the installation Poster Wall for the 21st Century (2008) for the Graphic Design 
Museum in Breda, Netherlands (see Figure 2.68). This installation was 
a physical and online display, generating 600 posters daily using ran-
dom-based methods and content from various internet sources (Armstrong 
& Stojmirovic, 2011). João Batista S. de Oliveira (2008) proposed two 
recursive division methods for placing elements on both single and multi-

-column grid layouts. One method involves randomly placing previously 
defined rectangular items on a page, such as in a sales brochure, while the 
other method randomly arranges varied items on pages divided into columns, 
as seen in newspapers. 
Recently, several designers have been hosting workshops to promote 
the use of stochastic  strategies for incorporating variations in designs. 
Tim Rodenbröker (2018) led the Programming Posters workshop, where 
participants created a set of animated and interactive posters. Furthermore, 
Edwin Jakobs and the RNDR studio conducted a workshop (2019) in Politec-
nico di Milano, Italy, focused on designing posters using stocasthic -based 
visuals and data scraped from various online sources (see Figure 2.67). The 
results are eight sets of 20 posters depicting diverse topics, such as “Airplane 
Spotting,” “Perceptions of God,” or “Space Oddities” (Benedetti, 2020).
In summary, stochastic strategies produce outcomes where features 
are defined autonomously by processes involving little or no expertise, often 
relying on randomness. These strategies can show varied expressive power, 
allowing for the creation of a wide range of designs with diverse charac-
teristics. However, because typographic and layout design require func-
tionality, entirely random procedures are not practical in this context and 
do not create complete designs. Their uncontrollable nature means they 
only produce suitable results by chance.
Nevertheless, these strategies can be valuable for generating visual 
assets and introducing variation within a design or its specific parts. They are 
most effective when combined with minimal expertise. In such cases, 
this approach can support the discovery and exploration stages of GD 
processes. Several graphic designers have recently explored these features 
in workshops, recognising their potential.

2.4.3 EXPERT STRA TEGIES
expert strategies enable the design of outcomes with minimal human 
input (high autonomy), relying on domain-specific expertise. This expertise 
can be incorporated into the system with varying levels of adaptability 
and complexity, including rule-based systems, probabilistic generative 
approaches, or automated evolution. The purpose of these systems can 
vary, from managing specific design tasks (like image placement or colour 
palette selection) to more comprehensive tasks (like generating an entire 
book or website). These strategies have been explored with different levels 
of expressive power and expert performance, ranging from highly controlled 
to more flexible and diverse outcomes.
Automatic evolution employs the use of EC to autonomously evolve 
a set of candidate solutions to a problem. This process includes the auto-
matic evaluation, ranking, and selection of individuals based on automated 
fitness assignment schemes. A key challenge in using these approaches is 
developing suitable fitness assignment strategies (Machado et al., 2008).
Automatic evolution approaches are used to create designs across 
different media using various evaluation strategies. Matthias Fuchs (2000) 
introduced an evolutionary approach for optimising picture placement 
on a web page, aiming to enhance the aesthetic appeal of the composition 
by reducing blank space. Similarly, Eldan Goldenberg (2002) employed 
an evolutionary algorithm to automatically generate page layouts with the 
goal of minimising space wastage. Lisa Purvis et al. (2003) developed 
a multi-objective optimisation approach to generate document layouts 
that satisfy certain content and layout constraints, as well as certain desired 
design properties proposed by Steven J. Harrington et al. (2004). Susanne  
Boll (2007) and Philipp Sandhaus et al. (2010, 2011) used evolutionary 
algorithms to optimise photo layouts based on design rules, including a 
method for transforming a blog into a photo book by incorporating genetic 
algorithms and various aesthetic criteria. Lukas Günthermann and John 
Kingston (2018) developed an evolutionary approach for creating websites 
that adhere to classical web design principles and aesthetics, with the 
colour scheme automatically defined based on an input logo. More recently, 
Daniel Lopes et al. (2022) introduced the evoDesigner system, which auto-
matically evolves designs within the Adobe InDesign environment, focusing 
on their novelty and visual appeal (see Figure 2.69).
Probabilistic methods are employed by various expert  strategies 
to create new designs for various purposes and media. Many of these 
strategies focus on designing wireframes, especially for digital media, rather 
than producing finished designs. Jerry Talton et al. (2012) proposed a 
method that uses Bayesian grammar induction to learn design patterns 
from a dataset of web pages, enabling the generation of new designs. Ying 
Cao (2012) introduced a generative probabilistic framework for arranging 
input artwork into a page in a manga layout style. Ildus Ahmadullin and 
Niranjan Damera-Venkata (2013) developed a Bayesian probabilistic model 
for newspaper typesetting, which divides available layout space into regions 
and optimises content placement within these regions based on given 
content. Yunke Zhang et al. (2017) created a system that automatically

the evoDesigner system. Daniel Lopes, 
João Correia and Penousal Machado.

066PRELUDE  AND  FOUNDA TIONSI
generates digital banner designs using a style parameter learned from 
training examples. Alibaba Group introduced the Luban system (2018; Liu 
et al., 2019), which uses deep learning and reinforcement learning 75 tech-
niques to generate advertising posters. Xinru Zheng et al. (2019) proposed 
a content-aware Generative Adverbial Network (GAN) for creating mag-
azine layout proposals, including the typesetting of text and images. Jianan 
Li et al. (2019, 2021) developed LayoutGan, a GAN model designed to 
generate wireframe layouts of relational graphic elements. Akshay Gadi 
Patil et al. (2020) presented Recursive Autoencoders for Document Layout 
Generation (READ). This ML-based method uses heuristics to learn hier-
archies and distributions of elements in layouts and automatically generate 
document layouts. Guolong Wang et al. (2020) proposed the Deep Element 
Selection Network (DESN) method, which employs a reinforcement 
learning framework for selecting the appropriate elements for a given 
poster design. Mengxi Guo et al. (2021) proposed LayoutT - CVAE, an end-
to-end wireframe GD layout generation model that integrates a transformer 
model with a conditional variational autoencoder to handle layout gener-
ation tasks. Kotaro Kikuchi et al. (2021) focused on optimising layout 
generation by exploring the latent space of a pretrained GAN model. Samuel 
von Tucher developed PosterGAN   (2021), a poster generator that uses a 
GAN network trained on 12,000 designs to create new posters (see Figure 
2.70). Chenhui Li et al. (2022) employed a deep generative approach to 
create banner layouts that combine images with simple text. This approach 
uses a semantic visual saliency detection network to propose text regions 
and a discriminative deep aesthetics scoring model to evaluate the aesthetic 
quality of the generated designs.
In addition, several works focus on the autonomous generation of 
designs using specialised domain-specific expertise, such as rules and heu-
ristics. Many of these efforts are centred on creating web pages and user 
interfaces. Alexander Kröner developed DesignComposer (1999), an auto-
mated web page layout generator that uses a combination of constraints, 
rules, and pattern techniques to create layouts. Krzysztof Gajos and Daniel 
S. Weld introduced the SUPPLE (2004), a method that automatically 
adapts user interfaces to both device specifications and user characteris-
tics. This method employs an optimisation algorithm that uses constraints 
and heuristics to adjust layout and element sizes. Ranjitha Kumar et al. 
(2011) developed the Bricolage algorithm, which generates new designs by 
transferring the stylistic features of one web page onto the content of 
another. Wenyuan Yin et al. (2013) introduced an automatic social media 
snippets generative system that extracts and analyses the information 
from online articles and generates text-overlaid images. Flipboard news 
aggregator developed Duplo (Ying, 2014) layout engine, which creates news 
magazines tailored to their content using heuristics such as the volume 
and flow of text and the presence and placement of images. Similarly, the 
VOX news website used the SB Nation system (Young, 2014), also known 
as the River. This system dynamically generates new layouts based on 
a responsive grid and a set of rules and heuristics to utilise all available 
space efficiently.

067 FOUNDA TIONS2
Similarly, other forms of domain-specific expertise have been explored 
in creating print designs, such as magazine covers, newspapers, and image 
banners. Jesús Gonzalvez et al. (2002) applied a greedy simulated annealing 
algorithm to generate multi-column newspaper layouts. Thomas Strecker 
and Leonhard Hennig (2009) proposed a grid-oriented placement method 
for creating newspaper layouts, which minimises wasted space while con-
sidering newspaper design aesthetic measures. Paul Cleveland (2010) 
proposed a method for generating style-based design layouts based on the 
spatial interrelationships between text and graphics and also proposed a 
system to implement these principles. Ali Jahanian et al. (2012) defined a 
framework for magazine cover design known as the Automatic Design of 
Magazine Covers (ADoMC). This framework determines the visual saliency 
of an input image and uses this information to design the covers automat-
ically. They later adapted this framework to create the R-ADoMC system 
(2013), which recommends improvements on magazine cover designs 
based on visual attributes such as colour and balance; however, this rec-
ommendation system does not consider the employed typeface. NETFLIX 
(2016) introduced an approach for designing movie cover art that identi-
fies and extracts the most “interesting” parts of an image (e.g. a character's 
face or the sharpest region) to define image cropping and text placement. 
Yu-Ting Qiang et al. (2019) developed a method to automatically create 
scientific poster designs by extracting contents from research papers. Sou 
Tabata et al. (2019) proposed an automatic method for generating magazine 
layout proposals from input texts and images. These proposals are created 
randomly according to a set of minimum conditions and are evaluated 
using a magazine dataset.
 expert strategies enable the autonomous and effortless creation 
of designs with minimal human intervention for various purposes and 
media. The performance of these strategies depends on the quality of their 
domain-specific expertise, and the outcomes reveal varying levels of expres-
sive power. They use various computational approaches, including automatic 
evolution, probabilistic generative methods, and other specialised tech-
niques such as rules or heuristics. However, the generative procedures can 
be computationally heavy and difficult to control. Also, many approaches 
focus not on creating finished designs but on establishing hierarchies 
or developing grids and wireframes.
The quality of outcomes often relies on pre-existing annotated 
knowledge, data, or base knowledge defined by experts. This can be chal-
lenging to model in GD and Typography due to their subjective and soci-
ocultural aspects. Despite these challenges, these methods are valuable 
for facilitating the design process and completing specific tasks. Methods 
like automatic evolution and GANs offer significant potential for discov-
ering visual variations and novel ideas in an informed way.
2.4.4 COOPERA TIVE STRA TEGIES
cooperative strategies involve human participation or guidance during 
the generation process, leading to varying levels of autonomy. These strat-
egies can include both collaborative and co-creative design processes 
between computational systems and humans. They may vary in expertise, 

068PRELUDE  AND  FOUNDA TIONSI
with some incorporating domain-specific knowledge to make collaboration 
more efficient and less time-consuming, such as filtering out invalid out -
comes. Like expert strategies, cooperative strategies have been explored 
for various purposes, including specific and general design tasks, and offer 
different degrees of expressive power.
A traditional example of a collaborative strategy is Interactive Evo-
lutionary Computation (IEC), which relies on human evaluation to guide 
the evolutionary process. Hideyuki Takagi (2001) provides a comprehen-
sive overview of this approach. IEC has been successfully applied to col-
laboratively generate designs across various media and for diverse purposes. 
Richard Gatarski (1998, 2002) developed an IEC system that automatically 
evolves digital banners using user click-through rates as the fitness metric. 
Nicolas Monmarché et al. (1999) created Imagine, a system that iteratively 
evolves CSS stylesheets for websites. This work was later extended by 
Antoine Oliver et al. (2002) to evolve the positioning of elements on web 
pages. Sunyoung Park (2007) created an evolutionary web page generator, 
the Evo-Web, that employs an IEC approach to evolve CSS stylesheets. 
Deniz Cem Önduygu developed the Gráphagos system (2010), which evolves 
several types of document layouts (see Figure 2.71). The system starts with 
randomly generated designs composed of different visual elements (such 
as text, shapes, and images) and interactively evolves the position, scale, 
and rotation of these elements. Sonomi Kitamura and Hitoshi Kanoh (2011) 
used an interactive approach to evolve the visual characteristics of poster 
designs. Ken Ishibashi and Kazunori Miyata (2013) interactively evolve 
grid layouts. Davy Sorn and Sunisa Rimcharoen (2013) employed an IEC 
approach to create web page templates, evolving both HTML pages and 
CSS stylesheets. Unlike other methods, users do not evaluate the entire 
design but rate each section individually.
IEC approaches have demonstrated their capability to evolve a wide 
variety of designs while incorporating the subjectivity of human evaluation. 
However, they often lead to user fatigue, resulting in a loss of interest and 
inconsistent evaluations (Lewis, 2008; Machado et al., 2008; Takagi, 2001). 
Several works combined human evaluation with domain-specific expertise 
to address this issue, primarily using evaluation measures. For instance, 
Joe Geigel and Alexander C. P. Loui (2000) created an evolutionary system 
that automatically designs page layouts for photo albums, using automatic 
evaluation based on user-defined measures such as page balance, spacing, 
and emphasis. Juan C. Quiroz et al. (2007) developed a system to evolve 
user interface designs. The system outputs were evaluated using a weighted 
combination of IEC with measures based on user interface design guide-
lines. In this system, users only need to select the best and worst candidate 
solutions from a subset every few generations rather than every generation. 
Later, Juan C. Quiroz et al. (2009) created a brochure evolution method 
where the user guides the evolution by assessing only a small subset of the 
individuals. Alongside these user-based subjective heuristics, the individ-
uals are also evaluated using a set of objective heuristics for document 
design. Cosimo Birtolo et al. (2009) interactively evolved colour palettes 
to apply in user interface panels. Their approach combined both comput-
able measures and user feedback to guide the choice of colours. Following

069 FOUNDA TIONS2
this, Luigi Troiano and Cosimo Birtolo (2014) explored a similar approach 
to generate hierarchical menu layouts, considering accessibility, user pref-
erences, and a set of standard guidelines. Carlos Glez-Morcillo et al.(2010) 
developed an evolutionary system for creating single-page designs called 
GAUDII (see Figure 2.72). This system directly queries users about their 
preferences at the beginning of layout generation. It then evolves designs 
using an interactive method, only requesting users to choose the most 
interesting designs. Andreas Dyroy Jansson and Bernt Arild Bremdal (2018) 
presented a system that interactively creates web designs, employing 
a dynamic fitness function that changes over time based on user feedback 
and a neural model.
Similarly, other IEC systems have explored methods to filter out 
unsuitable candidate solutions from the evaluation process automatically. 
Fei Yu et al. (2014) developed an approach that designs book covers using 
IEC and a clustering method to reduce user fatigue. Zahra Sheikhi Darani 
and Marjan Kaedi (2017) proposed a method to decrease user fatigue in 
the IEC of visual designs by employing a candidate elimination algorithm 
to predict and remove inappropriate genotypes. They evaluated this method 
in a book cover design scenario. Alfredo Milani and Silvia Suriani also 
proposed an indirect human evaluation method in their online evolutionary 
system AdaN (2004), which generates layouts for digital newspapers. This 
system indirectly evaluates designs based on user behaviour metrics such 
as the number of news clicks, total time spent on the website, and time 
spent reading each article.
Similar collaborative approaches are also used with methods other 
than evolutionary computation. Frederik De Bleser (2016) developed Logic 
Layout, an interactive design tool that uses ranges and constraints to create 
generative poster designs without programming (see Figure 2.74). Nolwenn 
Maudet et al. (2017) researched how practising graphic designers structured 
layouts for both digital and print media, leading to the introduction of two 
collaborative tools that explore these strategies: Contextify, which creates 
a layout based on reading conditions and Linkify, which creates layouts 
through the inter-relationship between properties of the layout’s elements. 
Hsin-Ying Lee et al. proposed the Neural Design Network (2020) layout 
generator tool to handle the creation of layout wireframes from given 
user-specified constraints. Sanket Biswas  et al.  (2021) introduced the 
DocSynth model, a GAN-based approach for generating layouts guided by 
a reference layout image given by the user. Shunan Guo et al. presented 
Vinci (2021), a system that automatically generates posters using a deep 
learning-based technique based on user preferences and allows subsequent 
editing of the results. In contrast, Harrison S. Gerard created a series of 
graphic designs named Fallen Objects (2020) based on generative text 
descriptions provided via a text prompt in the GPT-2.
Other works employ computational approaches to generate designs 
based on previously prototypal designs. Anabela Caetano et al. (2002) 
created JavaSketchIT, a tool that produces user interfaces in Java GUI from 
hand-drawn sketches provided by users. Tony Beltramelli presented Pix-
2Code (2018), a deep neural approach that generates functional interfaces

070PRELUDE  AND  FOUNDA TIONSI
by extracting features from interface sketches. Several follow-up projects 
have explored similar approaches, including Sketch2code (Robinson, 2019), 
Ink to Code (Microsoft Garage et al., 2018), and Uizard (2019).
Recommendation and suggestion systems are among the most 
popular layout collaborative-based applications. Xiaofan Lin developed 
Active Layout Engine (ALE, 2006) to adjust existing designs for changed 
content within a specific formal template, a process that he called Vari-
able Data Printing. ALE can also generate new layouts using methods for 
text fitting in arbitrary geometrical regions or image crop and placement. 
The ALE specify the constraints the final document should satisfy. Brian 
Lee et al. developed the browser extension Adaptive Ideas (2010), which 
allows for automatic searching in a web page database using a subset 
selection algorithm based on simple attributes such as background colour, 
primary font, and grid layout. Similarly, Luis A. Leiva (2012) introduced 
the Adaptive CSS Engine (ACE) method to incrementally adapt a web page 
based on user interactions. More recently, deep generative approaches 
have been explored in these contexts. Peter O’Donovan et al. (2014) pre-
sented an energy-based approach for designing single-page layouts based 
on design principles, including predicting perceived visual importance, 
alignment detection, and hierarchical segmentation. They later extended 
this tool into DesignScape (2015), an interactive suggestion tool for design. 
Yang Li et al. (2020) developed a transformer-based system to auto-com-
plete partial layout designs of mobile applications. Amanda Swearngin et 
al. (2020) presented Scout, a layout exploration tool for creating alternatives 
supported in high-level constraints such as alternative design elements, 
grouping, and placement preferences. Kamal Gupta et al. (2021) used a 
transformer model to complete a layout based on an input sequence. Lukas 
Bruckner et al. (2022) proposed two neural approaches (a Graph Neural 
Network and a transformer model) to create recommendations for user 
interface elements based on given element constraints.
Design tools and no-code services have recently employed compu-
tational strategies with some expertise to support and recommend variations 
to users during their design process. Ucoz Media launched uKit AI (2015), 
an online service that uses neural approaches to analyse an existing website 
and proposes refinements to the layout (see Figure 2.73). Similarly, the 
WIX company developed its Advanced Design Intelligence system (Weiner, 
2016) to create websites based on user preferences and data gathered 
online. Comparable online services, such as BookMark (2019) or HU2La 
(2019), have since been released. Kashyap Todi et al. (2016) developed the 
SketchPlore tool, a real-time layout optimiser that can deduce the designers’ 
subsequent actions for enhancing usability and aesthetic appeal. 
In conclusion, cooperative strategies use computational processes 
with low autonomy, requiring human participation or guidance to generate 
new outcomes. Different levels of domain expertise can be used in these 
strategies to facilitate user interaction. These strategies can produce a 
wide range of designs through various methods, including IEC, constraint 
processing, and deep generative techniques. They are applicable to both 
specific and general tasks and vary in expressive power.
Figure 2.74. Logic Layout interface. 
Frederik De Bleser. 2016. © enigmeta.

071 FOUNDA TIONS2
These strategies can involve human designers in the computational 
process. Determining the exact impact of human involvement is challenging. 
Lower autonomy can lead to user fatigue, while higher autonomy and exper-
tise can make the systems more difficult to control and guide. Despite 
these challenges, cooperative strategies offer valuable support, primarily 
through recommendation systems and engines, which related work shows 
can improve the efficiency of design production.
2.5 SUMMARY
In this chapter, we established the theoretical and conceptual foundations 
for the research presented in this thesis. We began by defining key concepts 
to contextualise our investigation, including Typography and Layout, GD, 
CD, and CC. In this section, we also highlighted the research through 
the design nature of this investigation.
We then provided a brief overview of the background knowledge 
relevant to this research. We began by examining algorithmic methods 
in Art and Design, focusing on visual generation. Next, we studied the 
historical use of algorithms in GD and Typography. Finally, we reviewed 
related work on using CD for Typography and layout, encompassing 
research and application-oriented works. 
Our review of related work revealed that CD approaches for gener-
ating typography and layout vary in autonomy , expertise , and expressive 
power. These differences allowed us to categorise them into four main 
strategies: template, stochastic, expert , and cooperative. We have 
comprehensively described each strategy and provided examples.
template strategies involve generating designs from predefined 
inputs and set visual features, resulting in low autonomy, expertise, and expres-
sive power. While offering limited variation, they are effective across various 
purposes and media. They can also incorporate minimal stochastic methods 
and specialised expertise to introduce some variation into the designs.
stochastic strategies, characterised by high autonomy and low 
expertise, are useful for generating visual assets and introducing variation 
into existing designs. Despite their uncontrollable nature and challenges 
in producing valid designs, these methods are valuable for discovery tasks. 
They can present varied expressive power.
expert strategies enable the autonomous creation of designs based 
on domain-specific expertise, offering varying levels of expressive power. 
The quality of the results depends on the depth of the provided expertise 
and can address diverse tasks with multiple purposes.
cooperative strategies involve low autonomy , requiring human 
intervention or guidance to generate outcomes. They can incorporate 
different levels of domain expertise and expressive power, handling both 
specific and general design tasks. Although they can lead to user fatigue 
or control challenges, these strategies are valuable for improving design 
efficiency, primarily through tools like recommendation engines.

The second part of this thesis presents our investigation of Computational 
Design (CD) responsive approaches in Graphic Design (GD), specifically 
focusing on Poster Design and examining their impact on developing new 
communication approaches for engaging the audience. In Chapter 3, we 
present our preliminary study on developing responsive techniques for 
moving poster designs. This includes creating reactive and interactive 
moving posters as well as an environmentally responsive poster generator 
demonstrated in an urban installation. Chapter 4 presents Photomaton as 
an interactive installation for autonomously creating typographic compo-
sitions combining user portraits with texts. Finally, in Chapter 5, we define 
responsive design practices based on insights and conclusions drawn from 
these development experiments. 

075 II DESIGNING  RESPONSIVEL Y
PRELIMINARY EXPLORA TION 
OF RESPONSIVE POSTERS
3
This chapter presents our preliminary research on the impact of CD in 
creating responsive designs. These designs adapt their visual features and 
elements dynamically, responding to environmental data in real-time. 
In this sense, we developed three experiments that explore computational 
approaches to create responsive moving posters. The primary intent of these 
experiments was to determine whether adding responsiveness to designs 
has the potential to enhance the engaging and communicative qualities 
of GD artefacts. Also, we were motivated to examine the challenges of using 
CD in this context.
Poster design is among the most well-established, enduring, and 
resilient design practices, having played a key role in visual communication 
throughout history (Blauvelt, 2011b; Sontag, 1999). Even in ancient times, 
primitive types of posters were already observable, and over the centuries, 
they adapted, changing their characteristics and production methods as 
technology advanced (Blauvelt, 2011b; Guffey, 2015). This way, they have 
adapted to novel social and technological contexts while maintaining 
their fundamental purposes of conveying messages (Hollis, 2001; Meggs 
& Purvis, 2016).
Over time, CD and Computational Creativity (CC) methods have 
been used in GD. Chapter 2 provides an overview of how computational 
techniques are explored in the context of GD and Typography. We observed 
that these computational methods have led to the emergence of responsive 
designs, where visual features and elements dynamically adapt to data 
during visualisation and production. For example, responsive designs might 
change based on real-time data feeds or environmental factors such as 
location or time. We found that responsiveness has the potential to create 
designs that encourage audience engagement, indicating they can effectively 
communicate their messages. 
Moving poster designs are a recent type of design that, although 
resembling traditional posters, incorporate animation and video to enhance 
the message delivery, aiming to engage their audience better. These posters 
serve various purposes, including advertising, entertainment, and educa-
tion. Although they deviate from traditional posters in their use of motion 
and digital elements, moving posters are designed to adhere to the con -
ventions, standards, and formats of classic print poster designs (Benyon, 
2016; Schaub, 2022). The rise of these approaches is amplified by the 
increased proliferation of digital media in physical spaces and the wide -
spread use of mobile computing in contemporary times (Conrad, 2021). 
Unlike their traditional print counterparts, moving posters are typically 
crafted for mass digital display rather than for mass print production.

076
II DESIGNING  RESPONSIVEL Y
There is no typical way of animating a moving poster, ranging from 
simple animations to more complex filmic posters, often employing 
loop-based animations and video. The Moving Poster Archive (Schaub, 2022) 
offers a wide collection of examples. Moreover, we have recently noticed 
an increase in discussions about moving posters at various GD events and 
conferences, including the Le Signe Design Biennale (Chaumont, France),76 
the Golden Bee Graphic Design Biennale (Moscow, Russia),77 the DEMO Fes-
tival (Amsterdam, Netherlands),78 or the Weltformat Poster Festival (Lucerne, 
Switzerland).79
As moving posters gained popularity, several designers started incor-
porating reactive and interactive behaviours, experimenting with compu-
tational technologies like physical computing, Computer Vision (CV), or 
Augmented Reality. 
Within this context, we identified template strategies as the most 
effective approaches for creating responsive designs (see Section 2.4). 
These strategies enable designers to predefine action and adaptable visual 
elements, linking them to data so that animations and visuals adjust auto-
matically in response to data. By using this type of strategy, designers can 
maintain control over the features of the outcomes, ensuring consistency 
in the message while adding dynamism and potentially creating a tai-
lored visualisation experience for the audience. Also, stochastic and 
expert-based methods can be integrated into these templates to introduce 
controlled visual variation in the design or generate assets for the visuals.
We conducted three experiments using various computational 
methods to develop responsive moving poster designs that dynamically 
adjust their visual features based on environmental data. In these exper -
iments, we explored methods that included techniques that directly collect 
data from the environment, such as CV and physical computing, as well 
as accessing online georeferenced data.
The first experiment focuses on creating reactive moving poster 
designs. These reactive designs are context-aware artefacts in which fea-
tures and elements respond to data primarily related to the location where 
the poster is displayed. These data add dynamism to the design without 
altering its core information and content. We developed two reactive 
designs, each exploring different data acquisition techniques. In the first, 
we experimented with CV and georeferenced data. On the other hand, in 
the second, we explore the use of physical computing. The development 
of this last design included the creation of a template and the testing and 
evaluation of these templates in a hands-on workshop. In this workshop, 
participants modify and experiment with the resulting moving posters 
that react to sensor data, allowing us to preliminary study the customisa-
tion and engagement possibilities of these types of data and media.
The second experiment involved creating a series of seven interac-
tive moving posters. These posters are designed to inform viewers about 
the causes and effects of current environmental issues and climate change. 
In these posters, we explored an interactive approach where visual responses 
to real-time environmental data by adapting the posters’ content, poten-
tially introducing new meaning to the viewers. We used CV, physical

computing, and georeferenced data to read environmental data. To pre-
liminary assess the posters’ effectiveness and engagement, we conducted 
testing sessions with people and compared these interactive versions to 
both static print and simple animated posters.
The third experiment introduced an environmentally responsive 
poster generator, which creates designs based on data and detected envi-
ronmental patterns. This poster adjusts itself by adding or removing 
variable elements, with some features defined by data collected through 
CV and physical computing. This poster is composed of variable visuals 
whose characteristics and lifespan are influenced by environmental data. 
Also, the system learns over time, replicating successful designs or elements 
that previously captured people’s attention under similar conditions. We 
assessed this approach by placing it in an urban environment. Moreover, 
we evaluated the visualisation capability, as well as the quality of the visuals 
and animations, through evaluation sessions with people. 
Although these experiments present a preliminary nature, they 
indicate methods that can enhance message transmission and provide 
more engaging visual experiences for the audience. The following sections 
describe the experiments and summarise the conclusions obtained.
3. 1 REACTIVE MOVING POSTERS
We began by exploring the impact of creating reactive moving posters. 
Reactive moving posters are artefacts where elements and features can 
respond to environmental data. These data introduce dynamism to the 
design without altering its core information and content. These initial 
experiments primarily intended to investigate various data -gathering 
techniques to understand their potential application in this context. We 
experimented with real-time environmental data collected through CV, 
sensors, and georeferenced data. In this context, we aimed to avoid random 
methods, which might create autonomous moving posters but would not 
establish environmental responsiveness. Both experiments are developed 
using Processing. 
In the first experiment, we created a moving poster with elements 
that reacted to CV and online georeferenced data. CV data enabled real-
time interaction between the audience and the poster, while georeferenced 
data, which changes more gradually, allowed the poster to respond only 
to the environmental features of the site where it is displayed, independent 
of the audience. We chose these types of data for their ease of access 
through existing frameworks, as well as the widespread availability of 
cameras and internet access on contemporary devices.
This poster contains reactive elements that can sequentially change 
their visual appearance. It features three types of elements: boxes, spheres, 
and letterforms. Each element has a different animation to the audience’s 
motion, precisely the position of the viewer’s face. Initially, these elements 
are two-dimensional shapes, which reveal a three-dimensional aspect only 

078II DESIGNING  RESPONSIVEL Y
in response to the data (see Figure 3.1). On the other hand, the colours of 
the elements are determined by the air temperature at the location where 
the poster is displayed, using georeferenced weather data (see Figure 3.2). 
Appendix A (sec. A.1) provides further details on the development of this 
poster and the visual translation of audience and georeferenced weather 
data into modifications on the poster.
In the second approach, we created moving posters whose elements 
respond to sensor data collected through physical computing. While this 
approach allows us to capture non-visual data from the environment, 
it requires the development of a custom interface for both poster display 
and data acquisition. To achieve this, we developed a template poster and 
a code framework to simplify the rendering of reactive elements, the mapping 
of sensor data to visuals, and managing the communication between 
the Arduino microcontroller (which captures the sensor data) and the 
poster via serial communication.
These posters consist of typography and geometric elements (see 
Figure 3.3). This approach presents a slightly greater expressive power, ena-
bling the dynamic creation of visual geometric shapes in multiple locations. 
We tested this approach in a hands-on workshop, where non-specialist 
participants modified these posters and assigned responses to different 
physical sensors, creating print and moving posters. 80 Figures 3.4 to 3.6 
document the workshop and the results. Appendix A (sec. A.2) provides 
further details on the development of the poster, the framework, and 
the workshop.

Our observation reveals that both approaches successfully created 
reactive moving posters. The widespread availability of capture cameras 
in devices and the straightforward application of contemporary CV frame-
works simplify the development of reactive posters, making this technique 
accessible and practical for various applications. Although using sensor 
data requires more setup, custom physical interfaces can provide the same, 
or even more, tailored audience experiences.
In both approaches, we focused on methods that enable poster 
elements to respond quickly to feedback from viewers. However, in the 
first experiment, we used georeferenced weather data, which changes 
gradually and has limited or no direct impact on the audience. This weather 
information was used to adjust less noticeable design elements. This 
approach seems to enhance the poster’s dynamism, especially when viewed 
sporadically over time, thereby mitigating the repetitive nature of the 
designs. However, further testing is needed to understand how different 
data types, which are not directly retrieved from the surroundings, impact 
our design decisions.
We observed that only a few inputs are needed to introduce reactivity 
into a poster. CV and sensor data are particularly effective techniques 
for creating reactive elements, enabling real-time interaction and instant 
responses to audience movement. These methods hold significant promise 
for delivering more engaging and customised visual experiences compared 
to traditional print or moving posters.

Despite using template strategies, the variations in the output 
designs of both approaches highlight the potential for controlled visual 
changes. The reactivity introduces variations in designs without funda-
mentally modifying the poster’s message. Therefore, we do not consider 
that it significantly affects how people perceive the poster’s message. 
Nevertheless, this study is preliminary, and further testing and 
development are required to fully understand the potential of these methods, 
as well as the impact of reactive posters on the comprehension of the 
message by the audience.
3.2 INTERACTIVE MOVING POSTERS
Interactive moving posters are responsive digital designs where features 
and elements respond to data, modifying the core content or adding sup-
plementary information. These data are mainly gathered from the envi-
ronment, primarily related to the audience and the location where the 
poster is displayed. In contrast to reactive moving posters, where data 
does not alter the core content, interactive moving posters use animation 
techniques to dynamically change the core content and introduce new 
information based on data values. These posters can feature visuals that 
respond both reactively and interactively.
We developed a collection of seven interactive moving posters called 
Metamorphosis, which address current environmental issues on Earth. These 
posters aim to inform viewers about the causes and consequences of ongoing 
environmental problems, with a particular focus on human impact. The 
animations were designed to introduce new communication significance 
in the posters’ message, with different animation stages reflecting the 
possible data variations. The subjects covered include air pollution, bio-
diversity loss, deforestation, global warming, noise pollution, rubbish 
production, and water pollution. Each poster is a self-contained commu-
nication artefact reflecting a different subject. However, all share common 
visual features to ensure visual cohesion and are, therefore, recognised as 
a collection. Our main goal is to conduct a preliminary study to see if the 
introduction of interactive dynamism in visuals enhances the communica-
tive value of the posters. Appendix B includes detailed information on the 
development of these posters as well as the preliminary evaluation exper-
iments conducted.
This experiment employs data acquisition methods similar to those 
used in previous experiments. In some posters, we used stochastic  
strategies to introduce visual variation, such as simulations and generative 
methods. These posters can be displayed physically (see Figure 3.7) or online 
(see Figure 3.8), requiring only a video camera and microphone.
Briefly, this collection of posters is designed to reflect the selected 
environmental issues, using audience interaction and environmental data 
to illustrate their consequences. The air pollution poster displays the real-
time air quality and pollutant levels for the location where the poster is 
Figure 3.7. Prototype of the physical 
installation setup, displaying the Rubbish 
Production poster in motion.

082II DESIGNING  RESPONSIVEL Y
visualised. The biodiversity loss poster simulates species extinction, where 
human presence accelerates extinction. The deforestation poster highlights 
the impact of human activity on forests. The global warming poster simu-
lates glacier melting based on the local temperature at the viewing location. 
Similarly, the noise pollution poster becomes increasingly distorted as 
environmental noise rises. The rubbish production poster simulates the 
accumulation and decomposition of rubbish, warning about human impact 
on litter production. Finally, the water pollution poster visualises litter in 
the ocean, adding new items when a viewer is detected. Figure 3.9 presents 
the designed posters.
We preliminary assessed the poster designs with users. The primary 
aim of this evaluation session was to determine how effectively these 
posters conveyed their intended message as well as the impact of the 
interactive features on it. We conducted 11 evaluations with participants 
aged 22 to 30 who viewed and interacted with the posters online through 
an online user survey. In these sessions, the posters were evaluated indi-
vidually, focusing on visual quality and how the interactive features impacted 
message comprehension compared to print and animated versions. Also, in 
the end, we conducted a preliminary evaluation of the overall effectiveness 
of using animation and interactivity in moving poster designs. Appendix B 
provides further details about each poster, the approach used, and the 
preliminary evaluation conducted.
The participants found the posters attention-grabbing and consid-
ered their subjects easy to understand. In the context of these posters, 
most participants considered that animation and interactivity helped to 
transmit messages effectively. Nevertheless, we recognise that further 
testing is needed to understand better how animation and interactivity 
help and improve message comprehension, particularly for more complex 
messages. Also, some participants noted that the interactive versions could 
sometimes be unnecessary or difficult to understand. 
Our results also indicate that designers should be careful about 
adding animation and interactivity when designing this type of poster. 
Our experimentation reveals that designers should include such features 
only when expected to enhance the poster’s communication value. More-
over, when such features are added, designers must ensure that interactions 
are simple, provide clear feedback, and are accessible for the audience 
to understand.

3.3  ENVIRONMENT ALL Y RESPONSIVE

We developed an environmentally responsive moving poster that adjusts 
its design based on environmental data from the surroundings where it is 
being visualised. Like previous experiments, this context-aware system 
uses CV, physical computing, and online georeferenced data to gather 
environmental information. Our primary goal is to create a design that 
integrates with and responds to the dynamics of the physical surroundings. 
Moreover, this poster system can adapt its generation processes based on 
received environmental feedback. Appendix C includes detailed informa-
tion on the development of the system, the installation process, and the 
preliminary evaluation experiments conducted.

In conclusion, our findings indicate that interactive moving posters 
can be effective in conveying messages. Our experimentation also suggests 
that the added interactivity must be straightforward enough for the audi-
ence to understand. Otherwise, it may have the opposite effect.

084II DESIGNING  RESPONSIVEL Y
The proposed poster generator creates designs using environmental 
data from its surroundings. It combines template-based and stochastic 
methods using static and variable visual elements (see Figure 3.10). Static 
visuals include fixed information, such as technical details or location, 
which remain unchanged by environmental factors. In contrast, the system 
dynamically places variable visuals, and environmental data and feedback 
influence their characteristics (such as position, style, and colour). Initially, 
the poster displays only static parts and, over time, modifies its design by 
adding and removing variable visuals. These visuals are placed on the 
poster with a defined lifespan that decreases as they remain visible. Visuals 
stay visible on the poster until their lifespan expires.
Variable visuals are rewarded by extending their lifespan based 
on audience behaviour in the environment surrounding the installation. 
The system scans the environment and assigns rewards based on three 
main questions: (i) “How many people are near the installation?;” (ii) “How 
close the people are to the installation?;” and (iii) “How many people are 
attentive to the installation?.” For each person detected in the system’s 
video feed, it calculates the distance between the camera and the person 
and checks whether the same person is looking directly at the installation. 
We use a body detection method to recognise people on the captured video 
and a face detector to check if we can assign a face to the detected bodies. 
If a face is detected, the system further checks for the presence of eyes to 
confirm attention. The higher the arithmetic mean of the lifespan of var-
iable visuals, the more the system considers the design successful. 
New variable visuals are placed on the poster using two methods: 
random generation, where a new shape’s attributes are influenced by random 
and environmental data and generation based on experience, where a previ-
ously successful shape is reused. When adding a new variable visual to the 
poster, the system considers previous designs that successfully captured 
viewers’ attention under similar conditions. If previous designs successfully 
gained audience feedback, the system is more likely to replicate them 
or elements of them. Otherwise, it is more likely to generate a new variable 
visual randomly. Figure 3.11 displays several posters created with this system.
We experimented by deploying our system as a physical installation 
called “Desenhar Cartazes com / para o Caminho” in the Coimbra Historic 
Centre (CHC) between March and April 2019.81 The installation was placed 
in four shop windows within the neighbourhood, spending one week at 
each location, with system data reset between sites to ensure site-specific 
outputs (see Figure 3.12). This neighbourhood allowed us to test the system
