II DESIGNING  RESPONSIVEL Y
in environments with varying conditions and people fluxes. The chosen 
shops represented different types of businesses. Figure 3.13 provides 
an overview of the installation locations. In each location, passers-by were 
made aware of the system’s presence in the shop window. The system did 
not record or store any personal data or images; only the presence of people 
was detected. Across these four weeks, the system identified 12,722 pas-
sers-by (an average of 490 per day and 3,430.5 per week). 
We observed that local environmental conditions, such as temper -
ature, luminosity, and passer-by patterns, influenced the generated designs, 
indicating that the system can create posters that adapt to surrounding 
environmental data, reflecting various conditions in urban space. These 
adaptations included changes in the visual properties of the posters, such 
as colour saturation, the number of dynamic elements in the composition, 
and the lifespan of these elements. 
We conducted evaluation sessions with participants to preliminary 
assess the system’s ability to communicate environmental features and 
whether its adaptive capabilities were visible in the output designs. These 
sessions involved 35 participants, aged between 20 and 34, from diverse 
professional backgrounds. These sessions showed that most participants 
recognised the environmental conditions reflected in the outputs. However, 
the system’s adaptive capabilities were only slightly noticeable over time, 
mainly when the similarity value was higher. Also, participants found the 
generated outputs visually appealing. 
Furthermore, our observations during the installation revealed that 
the generated designs are more noticeable in urban spaces due to their 
reactive nature than traditional print designs. This allows us to draw 
a preliminary conclusion that the system’s capability to adapt designs 
in real-time to the current environmental context enhances visibility 
and engagement. Nevertheless, some testing participants suggested that 
incorporating more environmental data and reactive elements could give 
the poster’s audience a more distinctive visual experience.
3.4 FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS
This chapter presented a preliminary study investigating the effects 
of responsiveness and computational approaches in creating responsive 
moving posters. Our primary intent was to determine whether adding 
responsiveness to visual design has the potential to enhance the engaging 
and communicative qualities of GD artefacts. In this context, we were also 
motivated to examine the challenges of using CD. To explore this, we 
developed several preliminary experiments in the creation of responsive 
moving posters. 
Moving posters are a recently popular motion design artefact that 
translates the features of traditional poster design into a digital context 
while maintaining the format and visual characteristics of traditional print 
posters. This artefact reflects the ability of GD, over time, to evolve along-

087
 PRELIMINARY  E XPLORA TION  OF R ESPONSIVE  P OSTERS3
side technological advancements. This study also provides insights and 
approaches exemplifying the future relevance and potential of computa-
tional technologies impacting GD artefacts, particularly in moving posters. 
These approaches have the potential to modify, expand, and distribute 
visual designs, especially as computational and digital media become more 
prevalent in our daily lives (Benyon, 2016; Blauvelt, 2011; Manovich & 
Arielli, 2023). 
This chapter presents three preliminary experiments focused on 
developing computational moving posters that dynamically respond to 
environmental data. We used template strategies in these experiments, 
which we identified as the most effective approach for creating responsive 
designs. This method allows designers to set actions for visual elements 
and link them to data, allowing control over design features while adding 
dynamism. Also, we included stochastic methods to add visual variation 
to the designs.
The first experiment explored designing reactive moving posters, 
where their visual elements respond directly to environmental data and 
audience behaviour without fundamentally changing their core content. 
We explored two approaches and various methods of gathering data from 
the environment, assessing their potential use in this context. In the 
first approach, we designed posters that responded to computer vision 
and georeferenced online data, while in the second, we developed posters 
that reacted to sensor data. To support this second approach, we developed 
a framework to connect physical sensors to the poster and tested its use 
in a hands-on workshop, where participants adapted a template moving 
poster to create their own versions that reacted to real-world sensor data.
Both approaches effectively demonstrated the potential for intro-
ducing reactivity into moving posters. Although our study presents a pre-
liminary nature, we found that CV and sensor data are highly effective for 
creating reactive elements, allowing for real-time interaction. This indicates 
that these methods could provide a more engaging and customised poster 
visualisation experience than traditional print or static moving posters.
In the second experiment, we created seven interactive moving 
posters focused on climate change, aiming to inform viewers about envi-
ronmental issues and human impact. These interactive approaches use 
environmental data to adapt both the message and content of the resulting 
posters interactively. These data were also collected through CV, physical 
computing, and access to geolocalised data.
We evaluated these posters with people to assess how well they 
conveyed their intended messages and preliminary to determine the impact 
of the interactive features. Participants found the poster subject easy 
to recognise, considering that the interactive version was more effective 
in conveying their messages than traditional print or only moving posters. 
However, some participants found that interactivity could make the message 
more challenging to understand under certain contexts. Therefore, the 
findings indicate that interactivity and animation can improve the com-
municative impact of moving posters; nevertheless, when designing such 
posters, designers must ensure that interactions enhance the message and 

088
II DESIGNING  RESPONSIVEL Y
that they are simple, provide clear feedback, and are easy for the audience 
to understand. Although interactive moving posters show promise for cre-
ating more customised and dynamic poster visualisation experiences, 
further testing is needed to understand how interactivity impacts message 
comprehension across diverse audiences.
In the third experiment, we explored a template strategy providing 
greater autonomy and expertise  in data use. This approach was designed 
to modify the poster’s visual features and create, place, and select visuals 
based on the gathered data. This way, we developed an environmentally 
responsive moving poster that adapts its design based on real-time envi-
ronmental data gathered from its surroundings. This poster consists 
of static and variable visuals, with CV, physical computing, and georefer -
enced data used to adjust its visual elements dynamically. While static 
visuals remain unchanged, variable visuals are influenced by environmental 
data and audience interaction, with their lifespan extended based on factors 
such as the number of people nearby, their proximity to the installation, 
and their attention to the poster. Moreover, the system gains expertise 
over time, replicating successful designs or parts of them that previously 
captured people’s attention in similar conditions.
We tested the system by installing it in four store windows in urban 
space over four weeks. This installation demonstrated its ability to create 
a variety of designs from scratch, indicating that it can effectively reflect 
varying environmental conditions in its designs. We also observed that 
the generated designs stood out in the surrounding environment, providing 
more noticeable visual experiences. 
Preliminary evaluation sessions with people showed that most par-
ticipants could recognise most of the environmental conditions reflected 
in the outputs and found them visually appealing. However, the system’s 
adaptive expertise was only slightly noticeable to participants. Overall, the 
findings suggest that this system uses a more autonomous and expert 
template strategy, which has proven capable of producing visually appealing 
results that reflect the nearby environmental conditions. Nevertheless, 
the method for introducing expertise into the system could be improved 
by incorporating design knowledge that goes beyond just considering the 
audience’s attention.
The developed experiments demonstrate the feasibility of using 
template strategies to create dynamic and responsive artefacts, where 
the designers define and control the possible visual variations in advance. 
Our findings show that both reactive and interactive approaches can help 
improve the communication value of posters compared to traditional print 
and classic moving posters. This indicates that these methods have the 
potential to create more memorable posters tailored to time, audience, 
and location. However, we consider that the visualisation experience of 
both types of posters differs. Reactive designs modify only the posters’ visual 
features without changing their core message. In contrast, interactive 
posters allow for gradual communication of the message through interac-
tion, which suggests that this approach makes the experience more personal.

089
 PRELIMINARY  E XPLORA TION  OF R ESPONSIVE  P OSTERS3
While both experiments (reactive and interactive) focused on methods 
that respond quickly to viewer feedback, the first approach used slowly 
changing georeferenced online data (weather information) to adjust the 
colour of design elements. We indicate that this method can help to mit -
igate the repetitive nature of these designs, especially when viewed spo-
radically over time. However, further testing is needed to understand how 
these types of environmental data and the designer’s decisions affect the 
perception of reactive posters over time.
On the other hand, we consider that a method similar to the one 
explored in the last experiment is more suitable for public spaces with 
many visual stimuli. The poster continuously adjusts while maintaining 
a uniform base, which we consider helps keep the audience attentive to 
design changes over time without becoming tiresome. This experiment 
demonstrates a reactive approach focused on location rather than the 
audience. The findings indicate that creating reactive designs based on 
location may be more effective for maintaining appeal over time with 
regular audiences. However, if the goal is to create personalised artefacts, 
we consider an approach focused on audience movement (as seen in the 
first two experiments) more suitable.
Overall, the findings indicate that these methods could enhance 
message transmission and provide more engaging visual experiences for 
the audience. template strategies demonstrated flexibility by allowing 
designers to define data-driven actions, such as animations or procedures, 
to modify and create new designs. Also, stochastic and expert-based 
methods were effective in introducing visual variation within templates 
or generating assets for the visuals.

090
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES

091
 II DESIGNING  RESPONSIVEL Y
PHOTOMA TON
In this chapter, we present and document the development of Photomaton, 
an interactive installation that automatically generates artworks consisting 
of typographic illustrations of users’ faces and text. This installation works 
like a traditional photo booth but uses only black typographic elements 
to render the user’s facial image. It employs a CD approach to create por-
traits made exclusively of letter shapes. Moreover, we used a template  
strategy to combine the generated image with a text chosen by the user. 
The chosen text is automatically typeset using an autonomous generative 
approach. Our primary motivation for this work was to study whether 
designers can use a generative and responsive approach to create traditional 
print artefacts. In this context, we further explored using CV techniques 
to inform the generation of GD artefacts. 
This work was part of a commercial project commissioned by Fundação 
Cupertino de Miranda, Portugal. The installation is part of the permanent 
exhibition Torre Literaria: A Simplificação e o Louvor da Literatura Portuguesa, 
dedicated to Lusophone literature, which officially opened in October 
2020. It is housed in a continuous helical tower spanning four floors, sit -
uated in one of the main squares of Vila Nova de Famalicão, Portugal. 82 
The installation is designed for a custom space, insulated from the main 
exhibition by a curtain, in a room thematically related to the subject of 
self-portrait in literature. 
The installation consists of a wall-mounted box with a touchscreen, 
a camera (on top), and two light boxes surrounding it (see Figure 4.1). It 
is connected to a hidden computer. The client and the exhibition architect 
defined the space and the installation’s main hardware. The primary objec-
tive of the installation is to allow visitors to create custom typographic 
compositions, fostering a closer connection between the exhibition’s 
artefacts and its audience. This way, the installation aims to encourage 
deeper reflection on self-portraits in literature while also providing a more 
interactive and engaging museum experience.83 We have collaborated with 
the museum team since the beginning of the exhibition design process, 
actively participating in the various stages of the project. Figures 4.2 and 4.3 
provide visual documentation of the evolution of the installation space 
across different construction phases.
Photomaton requires users to create, view, and modify the generated 
typography compositions in real time. Therefore, an automatic approach 
was required to typeset these compositions. We designed a computational 
method to automatically typeset compositions that include (i) a typographic 
composition depicting the user’s facial image and (ii) a text the user 
selects. The letter compositions are generated through a design approach 
that assembles letterforms to create typographic portraits, reflecting 
the users’ facial images. We also developed a generative approach to typeset 
text compositions.

II DESIGNING  RESPONSIVEL Y
For this installation, we developed three distinct techniques for 
creating typographic portraits, each exploring a different typesetting 
mechanism based on a different unit of written language. Specifically, 
we created methods to generate portraits using (i)  text, (ii)  words, and 
(iii) glyphs. Each method creates typographic portraits with different 
balances between the readability of the imagery and the textual content. 
Given the installation’s requirements, we preferred the method that pro-
duces more recognisable outcomes, specifically the one that uses glyphs.
We developed an approach to typeset the text within a given space 
using a predefined font. Additionally, we conceived a template-based approach 
to integrate the typographic portrait with the text. We evaluated the gener-
ated outputs with people to study (i) the legibility of the typographic portraits 
and (ii) user satisfaction with the system and its outputs. The following 
sections present related work on typographic portraits and comprehensively 
describe the process behind the production of the installation.
4. 1 BACKGROUND ON TYPOGRAPHIC PORTRAITS
Since prehistoric times, petroglyphs, signs, and simple figures have been 
combined with paintings in caves in various locations worldwide, comple-
menting the spoken language (Meggs & Purvis, 2016). The invention of 
the movable type allowed for the mass production of printed materials, 
dramatically reducing the time and cost of producing written communi-
cation (Bringhurst, 1997; Eskilson, 2007; Meggs & Purvis, 2016). Printing and 
typesetting technologies thus became the primary technologies for storing 
knowledge and transforming human perception habits (Lupton, 2014; 
Spiekermann, 2008). As people became familiar with typography, visual 
artists, writers, and designers began to explore typographic shapes beyond 
their phonetic function. They experimented with typesetting text and 
words to create images, adding new meaning and expressiveness into text 
or replicating images.
Initial experiments date back centuries, with some of the earliest 
examples found in ancient Greece. Examples include the pattern poetry  
of Simmias of Rhodes (c. 300 BCE) or the work of Theocritus (c. 250 BCE). 
Until modern times, similar approaches have been occasionally explored 
in various alphabets and languages, e.g. the pictorial writing of Arabic 
calligraphy, especially exploring zoomorphic compositions (Blair, 2006; 
Teparić, 2013), the Hebrew micrography (Avrin, 1984), the seventeenth-
-century poems The Altar (1899, p. 25) and  Easter Wings (1899, pp. 48 – 49) 
in the book The Temple of George Herbert, the poem Un Coup de Dés Jamais 
N’Abolira le Hasard (1914)  84 from Stéphane Mallarmé or the book Cal-
ligrammes: Poèmes de La Paix et de La Guerre (1925) 85 from Guillaume Apol-
linaire (see Figure 4.4).
Nevertheless, during the Modern art movements, which emerged 
in the first half of the twentieth century, the visual shapes of the letters 
were definitively explored as visual shapes of their own, separated from 
their phonetic function. Cubist artists such as Pablo Picasso, George Braque, 
Figure 4.1. Illustration of user 
interaction with Photomaton. Illustration 
by Tiago Martins.

093
 PHOTOMATON6
and Fernand Léger used typographic elements and words as pictorial and 
decorative elements in their artworks (Marcus, 1972). Similarly, futurist 
artists rejected “harmonious design” and proposed a novel typographical 
layout, coined Parole in Libertá,86 creating dynamic and non-linear compo-
sitions characterised by expressive word use (Meggs & Purvis, 2016). 
The Concrete Poetry movement explored non-standard layouts to 
embed textual meaning within compositions, using various glyphs, lan -
guages, alphabets, and typesets (Polkinhorn, 1993). Concrete poets often 
also explored the subject of self-portrait both in its conceptual form, 
e.g. Fernando Aguiar’s Auto-Retrato em Forma de Soneto (1993, p. 458, 
see Figure 4.5),87 or in its visual shape, e.g. Duarte’s Sin Título (Gutierrez, 
1993, p. 418). 88 These artistic experiments influenced later movements, 
with letterforms continuing to be used as pictorial elements by artists such 
as Kurt Schwitters, John Heartfield, Geroge Grosz, Iliá Jdaniévitch, and 
El Lissítzky.
Although occupying a lower status than other design artistic practices, 
Typewriter Art was popular among hobbyists, artists, and poets (Carlsson 
& Miller, 2012; Poynor, 2014). Alan Riddell (1975) and Barrie Tullett (2014b) 
provide comprehensive overviews of examples. The portrait was one widely 
explored subject, e.g. the typed portrait of Queen Elizabeth and Duke of 
Edinburgh by Dennis W. A Collins (Riddell, 1975, pp. 70 – 71), the Portrait 
of Franklin D. Roosevelt by Roger van Braekel (Tullett, 2014, p. 31), or the 
Self-portrait of Eduardo Kac (Tullett, 2014, p. 222).
With the advent of personal computing, many individuals began 
exploring similar approaches to generate artworks in both physical and 
digital media, leading to the emergence of movements such as Radio Tel-
etype Art and ASCII Art. Early examples include Mona by the Numbers  
by H. Philip Peterson (1965), created using a mechanical plotter, and the 
image series Studies in Perception (1968), created using the BELFIX system 
by Kenneth C. Knowlton and Leon D. Harmon (Levin & Brain, 2021; Mezei, 
1967). Section 2.2 provides a comprehensive overview of early typography-
-based computational art.
Recently, CD methods have been employed to generate typographic 
portraits autonomously. Yoshi Sodeoka (2004) created ASCII BUSH , 
a video artwork when two American presidential speeches, from George 
W. Bush (on 12 January 2003) and George H. W. Bush (on 6 March 1991),

II DESIGNING  RESPONSIVEL Y
were digitally rendered using only characters. Gui Borchert (2007) pro-
duced a series of typographic portraits created by an automated algorithm 
based on character mapping. Jeff Clark (2008) adapted a word-filling 
algorithm to automatically fill shapes with words, creating works like the 
Obama Word Portrait with repetitions of texts such as ‘HOPE’, ‘CHANGE’, 
and ‘YES WE CAN’ (see Figure 4.6). Jonathan Feinberg (2010) used a ran-
domised greedy algorithm to depict images with words, placing words of 
different sizes over darker parts of the image to minimise gaps. Sergio 
Albiac (2016) used code to generate typographic portraits from collages 
of typographic textures based on user input. More recently, Yeohyun Ahn 
created the Typographic Selfie + Code (2020a, 2020b) collection, which 
consists of typographic “selfies” created from user-submitted pictures and 
descriptions, transcribed into text and combined with literary and philo-
sophical passages to form typographic textures. Moreover, interactive 
artworks that respond to video streams of environmental captures often 
manipulate typography and other visual elements, e.g.  Text Rain (1999) 
developed by Camille Utterback and Romy Achituv, For All Seasons (2005) 
by Andreas Müller, You Fade to Light (2009) by Random International, 0,16 
(2013) by Aram Bartholl and Portrait on the Fly (2015) by Laurent Mignon-
neau and Christa Sommerer. 
The use of the CD approaches for generating typographic portraits 
focuses on creating imagery that does not involve users’ participation 
in the creation process. In other words, these works did not require a live 
creation of the portraits, nor were the users involved in creating the por-
traits. The exception is Sergio Albiac’s experiment, where portraits are 
created based on the procedural placement of previously generated typo-
graphic compositions as textures within an image. With this in mind, our 
work develops an approach that involves the autonomous and direct 
placement of typographic forms.
4.2 APPROACH 
We developed an interactive installation that allows the visitors of the exhi-
bition Torre Literária to create compositions combining their own portraits 
made of letters and text from their favourite authors featured in the exhi-
bition. This section presents our approach to developing the installation 
software and hardware components.
The installation’s main hardware components include a computer, 
a USB camera module, and a touchscreen, with the camera placed on top 
of the screen. We also designed the side lamps to evenly illuminate the instal-
lation’s space and the camera support (see Figures 4.7 and 4.8).
As mentioned, user interaction with the installation occurs in a ded-
icated space resembling a traditional photo booth kiosk. Users begin 
by approaching the installation space and closing a curtain. The interaction 
starts with selecting the interaction language, either English or Portuguese 
(see Figure 4.11a). Before starting to interact, users are required to agree 
with the privacy policy employed in the installation. The first screen dis-

 PHOTOMATON6
plays an overview of the privacy policy in a pop-up window above a blurred 
video capture (see Figure 4.11c). Users can confirm their agreement or read 
more about the policy (see Figure 4.11d). If they choose to read more, 
they can review the entire policy page by page before deciding whether 
to continue interacting.
After agreeing to the privacy policy, users see a video capture with 
the region of interest for the generation of portrait highlighted on the screen 
in a mirror-like style. This region includes the area of the face plus a preset 
margin around it (see Figure 4.10). The highlighted region will be rendered 
in the typographic portrait, while the rest of the image will be ignored. 
This feature handles the recognition of multiple faces (group portraits) by 
adjusting the region to enclose all detected faces. A bounding rectangle 
indicates when a face is detected and shows the area to be rendered in the 
portrait. This way, users know when a face is being detected or not. If no face 
is detected, the region of interest is centred in the middle of the capture.
When the image framing pleases them, users press the button to take 
a picture. Following, a countdown of three seconds to the image capturing 
begins, and a snapshot is taken at the end (see Figure 4.11f). When the pho-
tograph is taken, a camera shutter sound effect is played, and the lamps 
brighten briefly before and after the capture. The system then generates 
and presents the portrait to the user. If users are pleased with the portrait, 
they select the option to continue (see Figure 4.11g); otherwise, they can 
retake the picture.
After confirming their portrait, users must select a text from a list pre-
sented, each identified by a bottom with the author’s name (see Figure 4.11h). 
The selected text is typeset along with the portrait (see Figure 4.11i). Users 
can select another text whenever they want, and the portrait is updated.
When users are satisfied with the composition, the system saves 
the image to a database and requests the users to provide their email 
to send the digital version of the composition (see Figure 4.11j). Finally, 
a four-digit code is provided for downloading the portrait from the muse-
um’s website (see Figure 4.11k). Furthermore, the digital version of the por-

trait is sent to the user’s email. Users can save the code and request a print 
version of the portrait in various formats and sizes on the exhibition desk. 
When the interaction finishes, the system presents a message reminding 
users not to leave the curtain open (see Figure 4.11l). Figure 4.9 presents 
the workflow for user interaction with the system.
When there is no active interaction, the system enters screensaver 
mode, automatically creating typographic portraits based on photographs 
of the writers in the exhibition (see Figures 4.11b and 4.12). After a certain 
period of inactivity, the system resets the current composition and re-en-
ters screensaver mode.
We used the off-the-shelf OpenCV  89 face detector, the LBP cascade 
classifier, to automatically detect faces in the captured video and calculate 
the region of interest accordingly. The final version of the system was 
created as an executable application that runs on any computer with 
Microsoft Windows and a webcam. This interaction workflow was designed 
and fine-tuned based on the requirements of the team of Fundação Cuper-
tino Miranda and the exhibition’s curators. Earlier versions included QR 
codes for users to access their portraits and the option to automatically 
turn off the use of the region of interest detection. However, the museum 
team decided to remove these features from the final implementation. 
The following subsections comprehensively present the process and methods 
behind generating portraits and outputs.
4.2. 1 PORTRAITS’ GENERA TION 
We explored various visual approaches for creating portrait illustrations, 
each focusing on a different core element of the written language. The first 
experiment revolved around the text, the second concerned word type-
setting, and the third used the smallest typography element, the glyph. 
These explorations allowed us to achieve results with varying levels of 
granularity, precision, recognisability of the input image, and readability 
of the textual content used to render the image. Our primary focus was 
creating compositions resembling images by arranging typographic forms 
without incorporating other visual variables such as colours or contours.

posed methods.

These approaches share an initial preprocessing step for the image. 
Firstly, the captured image is converted to greyscale. Then, the brightness 
value of each pixel is calculated and normalised within a minimum and 
maximum threshold. All the parameters mentioned in these approaches 
are configurable, providing flexibility to adjust and calibrate the outputs 
based on the conditions in the installation space. Also, the approaches 
allow the export of portraits as raster and vector files. This feature allows 
museum visitors and staff to reproduce the generated outputs in the format 
and media they want.

II DESIGNING  RESPONSIVEL Y
We conducted preliminary experimental testing for all three pro-
posed approaches to generate various types of images. In each experiment, 
we tested different configurations to evaluate the extent to which the input 
image remains recognisable as a typographic portrait and to analyse how 
each parameter affects the visual properties of the portrait. For our input 
image, we used the same photograph (see Figure 4.14). As input text in the 
two first experiments, we used the poem Eu Nunca Guardei Rebanhos , 
written by Alberto Caeiro.90
Together with the museum, we analysed the advantages and draw-
backs of each approach. Each proposed approach enables the design of 
portraits with different commitments regarding the readability of the text 
and the imagery. The outputs of the first experiment (based on the text) 
are closer to a text than an image, i.e. the portraits are more to be read 
than seen. Alternatively, the portraits generated using the second and third 
experiments are closer to an image. Also, the smaller the typographic 
elements used by the system, the more detailed the outcomes are, as the 
textual content’s readability is not the portrait’s primary focus. We selected 
the approach based on glyphs as it offered the highest level of recognisa-
bility for the input image. Below, we provide a comprehensive description 
of each approach.

EXPERIMENT BASED ON TEXT
We began by exploring an approach based on text. Therefore, we developed 
a system that composes an input text using glyphs that dynamically change 
their weight to depict an input image. Each letter is positioned within 
a rectangle proportional to the size of the image. The weight of each glyph 
adjusts dynamically based on the average brightness of the corresponding 
area in the input image. Glyphs positioned over darker areas of the image 
have a higher weight than those over lighter areas.
To implement this approach, we started by converting the image 
to greyscale and calculating the brightness values. The system then type-
sets the input text from left to right and top to bottom within a rectangular 
area proportional to the input image. For each glyph, the system computes 
the mean brightness of the pixels within its occupied area. This brightness 
average determines the weight of the glyph. Glyphs positioned over darker 
areas will appear bolder than those over lighter areas. The text is aligned 
to the left, and word hyphenation is not applied. If a word exceeds the right 
boundary of the text area, it is moved to the following line. This generative 
process is outlined in Algorithm 4.1.
Algorithm 4.1. Generation of typographic portraits based on text.
1: Read inputImage and inputText from the file.
2: Convert inputImage to greyscale.
3: Get imageSize (width and height).
4: Calculate the brightness for each pixel in the greyscale image.
5: Set textArea (width [w] and height [h]) proportional to imageSize.
6: startingPosition (x, y) = (0, 0).
7: currentPosition = startingPosition.
8: FOR each word IN inputText DO
9:  FOR each glyph IN word DO
10:   Calculate occupiedArea of the glyph.
11:   Calculate the meanBrightness of pixels under the occupiedArea.
12:    Set glyphWeight based on meanBrightness (Bold in dark areas, light in 
bright areas)
13:   Place the glyph at currentPosition with glyphWeight.
14:    IF currentPosition.x + occupiedArea.w > textArea.w THEN
15:    currentPosition.x = 0
16:    currentPosition.y += occupiedArea.height
17:   ELSE
18:    currentPosition (x,y) += occupiedArea (width, height).
We conducted tests with various configurations to explore the range 
of visuals generated by this approach. This experiment requires using type-
faces that offer a wide range of weights to represent different shades of 
grey. We employed a stencil-type family created by the Evotype  system

featuring our colleague João M. Cunha.

(T. Martins, Correia, et al., 2018) for this purpose. These typefaces enable 
the creation of typographic portraits with varying shades of  grey by pro-
viding a continuous range of font weights. Figures 4.15 and 4.16 present 
typical portraits generated using this approach.
The portraits created with this approach effectively depict the input 
images while maintaining the readability of the text. We observed that 
increasing the number of text lines adds more detail to the portrait (see 
Figure 4.15). Additionally, increasing the difference between the minimum 
and maximum thickness of the glyphs enhances the contrast in the portrait. 
We also experimented with using a monospaced typeface for creating 
portraits. However, we found that the resulting portraits lost readability 
due to the emergence of white rivers within the typeset text, necessitating 
an increase in the text leading (see Figure 4.16).
EXPERIMENT BASED ON WORDS
In the second experiment, we explored the creation of typographic portraits 
through word arrangement. In this approach, the size, weight, and hori-
zontal motion of the typeset words are determined based on the brightness 
of the input image. 
Figure 4.15. Two typographic portraits 
created using text of different sizes: one 
with 40 text lines (left) and one with 100 
text lines (right).
Figure 4.16. Two typographic portraits 
created using text and different typefaces: 
a monospace typeface (left) and 
a regular-width font (right).

101
 PHOTOMATON6
To implement this experiment, we started by converting the image 
to greyscale and calculating its brightness. We then apply a brightness 
quantisation filter to the image and subdivide it using the quadtree algo -
rithm (Samet, 1984). The quadtree is created from the brightness uniformity 
within each image region, and it is simplified by removing uniform white 
areas and merging adjacent regions with similar sizes and brightness values 
(see Figure 4.17).
Next, the typesetting of words is carried out. We provided the system 
with a collection of typefaces, each with details about its horizontal motion 
and weight. The system determines the average brightness for each quad 
in the quadtree and selects a suitable typeface accordingly. Lighter and more 
extended fonts are chosen for lighter quads, while heaviest and more 
condensed typefaces are used for darker quads. A word from the text is 
then selected and oriented based on the longer side of the quad. The system 
calculates the appropriate size for the occupy word, ensuring it fills the entire 
text box width. If the word does not entirely fill the quad width, additional 
words are added recursively until the space is filled. Figures 4.18 and 4.19 
display some outputs of this approach. Algorithm 4.2 provides an overview 
of this generative process.
Preliminary testing results of this approach revealed its capability 
to generate typographic portraits while preserving the main characteristics 
and readability of the original image. Although the entire text may not be 
readable, small text fragments (words) are legible. Also, the readability 
and size of the words are constrained by the size of the resulting quads. 
Figure 4.18 displays two typographic portraits with different levels 
of colour aggregation between the quads during the simplification process 
of the quadtree.
The visual quality of the generated results heavily relies on the choice 
of typefaces. Type families with a wide range of horizontal motion and 
weights are needed to create visually contrasting outputs. This way, exten-
sive type families such as Titling Gothic FB 91 or Interstate 92 produce higher-
-contrast outputs. The use of less extensive type families leads to outputs 
with reduced contrast (see Figure 4.19).

Algorithm 4.2. Generation of typographic portraits based on words.
1: Read inputImage, inputText, and typefaces from the file.
2: Convert inputImage to greyscale.
3: Calculate the brightness for each pixel in the greyscale inputImage.
4: Apply brightness quantisation filter to the inputImage.
5: Subdivide the inputImage using the quadtree algorithm.
6: Remove uniform white areas from the quadtree.
7: Merge adjacent quadtree regions with similar size and brightness.
8: FOR each quad IN quadtree DO
9:  Select a typeface by mapping the quad brightness to font stretch.
10:  Set orientation to the longer side of the quad (vertical or horizontal).
11:  currentPosition (x, y) = quad (x, y).

EXPERIMENT BASED ON GLYPHS
In the last experiment, we explored a more pictorial approach than the 
previous ones. This method focuses on placing glyphs over the darker 
regions of the input image to create a typographic image that resembles it. 
By varying the size and density of the glyphs, we can achieve different 
shades of grey.
Like the second experiment, the generation process starts with 
calculating the quadtree of the input image based on brightness (see Figure 
4.20). This quadtree information is then used to determine the glyph 
placement that forms the portraits. Each quad of the quadtree is filled with 
glyphs of varying sizes and quantities based on their brightness level. 
Lighter quads are filled with smaller glyphs, while darker quads are filled 
with more glyphs of a broader range of sizes.
The method for placing glyphs in each quad can be described as 
follows: if the brightness of a quad is below a predefined threshold, we ini-
tialise the glyph placement in that quad. Otherwise, the quad is ignored, 
and no glyphs are placed within it. Based on the average brightness of the 
quad being filled, four aspects are determined: (i) the number of font sizes 
that can be used; (ii) the minimum area a glyph must cover with non-white 
pixels (larger for lighter quads); (iii) the maximum number of consecutive 
failed attempts to place glyphs (higher for darker quads); and (iv) the 
space around the glyph (more so for lighter quads). Once these aspects 
are defined, glyph placement begins. For each selected font size, starting 
from the largest, the system randomly places glyphs of random characters 
from a given text at random positions and angles within the quad until 
the maximum number of consecutive failed attempts is reached. A place-
ment is successful if the glyph covers the minimum or a greater area of 
non-white pixels. When a glyph is placed, it is drawn on the input image 
in white with a white outline, with the outline thickness equal to the pre-
defined space around the glyph.
This generative process can be configured to attain different results. 
For instance, different levels of detail can be achieved by changing the range 
of font sizes that can be used (more extensive ranges of font sizes tend to 
create more detail) or by adjusting thresholds of the quadtree decompo-
sition (more quadtree rectangles tend to create more detail). Adjusting 
these parameters also influences the ability of the system to create smooth 
gradients. The contrast of the portraits can be adjusted by setting the 
amount of overlap between the letters (more overlays create darker regions) 
and the space around them (more space creates lighter  regions). This 
process is outlined in Algorithm 4.3.
Figure 4.20. Results of the quadtree 
simplification process. The image 
at the left presents the quadtree 
of the input image. On the right,

104II DESIGNING  RESPONSIVEL Y
Algorithm 4.3. Generation of typographic portraits using glyphs.
1: Read inputImage, inputText, fontSizes from the file.
2: Convert inputImage to greyscale.
3: Calculate brightness for each pixel in the greyscale inputImage.
4: Subdivide the inputImage using the quadtree algorithm.
5: Set brightness threshold.
6: FOR each quad IN quadtree DO
7:  IF quad brightness < threshold THEN
8:   Set minimum nonWhitePixelArea for glyph (larger for lighter quads).
9:   Set failed glyph maxAttempts placement (higher for darker quads).
10:   Set spaceAround each glyph (more for lighter quads).
11:  FOR each fontSize IN fontSizes, starting from the largest DO
12:   failedAttempts = 0.
13:    WHILE glyphPlacement = false   
OR failedAttempts < maxAttempts DO
14:    Select a random character from inputText.
15:    Choose a random position and angle.
16:     IF the glyph covers at least the nonWhitePixelArea THEN
17:     Place the glyph at the selected position and angle.
18:     failedAttempts = 0.
19:    ELSE
20:     failedAttempts +=1
The preliminary testing results demonstrate that the approach can 
create typographic portraits that capture the main features of the input 
image. Figures 4.21 and 4.22 present some of the obtained outputs with 
different levels of detail and contrast. Also, this method has proven capable 
of running in real-time using video capture.93
Although this approach compromises text readability, it successfully 
captures the key visual features observed in the portraits created in the 
previous experiments. These features include the smooth transitions from 
darker to lighter areas observed in the first experiment and the high con-
trast observed in the second experiment. After analysing the experimental 
results of all experiments and considering the advantages and disadvantages, 
this approach was selected to continue the development of the installation 
in collaboration with the museum team.
4.2.2 OUTPUT COMPOSITION
The installation’s final outputs include a typographic portrait of the user 
and a text they select. The outputs must also include technical information 
about the museum and the installation. This information includes the log-
otype of Fundação Cupertino de Miranda, details about the selected text 
(title, author, and publication year), and the date the portrait is generated.

(visited: 7 July 2025).

105 PHOTOMATON6
We used a template strategy to facilitate the creation of the outputs. 
Each output is divided into three sections. The typographic portrait occu-
pies the top portion and takes up most of the available space. The portrait 
is always created in a square ratio. The text is positioned in the middle 
part of the composition, below the portrait, and occupies the same height, 
regardless of the text length. Finally, the technical information is placed 
at the bottom. Figure 4.23 schematics the template used. The outputs are 
designed in the ISO 216 A series paper format, which follows a 1:√2 ratio. 
The outputs are exported as vector files, allowing them to be printed at 
any size. Figure 4.24 displays some typical outputs.
The exhibition’s staff selects the texts available in the installation, 
which may change over time. Texts are dynamically incorporated into 
the installation by placing text files, formatted in a specific way, into a des-
ignated folder. The first line of the text file should include details such 
as the button label, authors’ names, publication year, and title, separated 
by a special character that we define as the dollar sign ($). Subsequent

lines contain the actual text, with pilcrows (¶) indicating line breaks 
and silcrows (§) indicating section breaks. By default, the system interprets 
changes in text lines as line divisions. The text dividers, both at the section 
and line levels, can be adjusted parametrically and modified when needed.
Users can select the text from a specific interface screen (see Figure 
4.11h). We have developed an automatic typesetting method to compose 
the chosen text in the output. This method calculates the font size for 
a rectangular area of different dimensions. Since most texts are too long 
to fit entirely in the output, our typesetting method considers cutting 
marks provided with the text. The method operates as follows. Firstly, 
it subdivides the text into sections based on the provided section marks, 
then composes the text line by line using a default text size and leading. 
If a section does not fit within the available space, the method progressively 
reduces the font size (and text leading) until it fits.

This process is repeated for each section until the text is typeset 
at the smallest possible font size or until it is no longer possible to fit 
the next section. We empirically define the minimum font size as eight 
points. If the next section cannot be placed, the system retains the best 
setup achieved up to that point. Special characters replace line and para-
graph breaks to standardise the text. By default, the system uses a slash (/) 
for line breaks and a double slash (//) for paragraph breaks. Lines are treated 
as sections if the text does not have identified sections. The typesetting 
method can be configured to attain different results, including selecting 
a random starting point in the text. Algorithm 4.4 summarises this type-
setting procedure.
Algorithm 4.4. Text Typesetting and output composition.
1: Initialise template with three sections: portrait, text, and info.
2: Load selected text and logo from the file.
3: Extract the title, author and year from the text file’s first line, split by $.
4: Split the remaining text into sections (§) and lines (¶).
5: Replace section markers (§) with “//” and line breaks (¶) with “/”.
6: Set default fontSize and leading.
7: stopped = false.
8: FOR each section IN sections DO
9:  FOR each line IN lines DO
10:   Calculate line length.
11:    WHILE line does not fit in availableSpace  
OR fontSize >= minimum DO
12:    fontSize =- 1.
13:   IF the line cannot fit THEN
14:    Retain the best fit for the current section.
15:    stopped = true.
16:    BREAK
17:  IF stopped == true THEN
18:   BREAK
19: Place the generated typographic portrait.
20: Typeset the text.
21: Place technical info (logo, title, author, year, and date).
4.3 EV ALUA TION
In collaboration with the museum staff, we identified key installation 
design and development goals. First, the installation must generate por -
traits using only letterforms that clearly depict the users’ facial features, 
ensuring they can easily recognise themselves in the generated portraits. 

108
II DESIGNING  RESPONSIVEL Y
Second, users should also be able to select a text to accompany their por-
trait. Third, the final composition must be aesthetically pleasing and 
satisfying to the user. Finally, the interaction and portrait generation 
process should take about one minute, excluding the time required to enter 
the email address and accept the privacy policy.
We tested a prototype version to assess whether the proposed instal-
lation meets these goals. Thus, we set up a functional prototype of the instal-
lation and invited individuals passing through to use it (see Figure 4.25). 
46 users participated in these evaluation sessions, primarily students 
and faculty from the design and multimedia programmes at UC, Portugal. 
These evaluation sessions specifically focused on the installation’s ability 
to produce recognisable portraits and satisfactory results in alignment 
with the museum’s goals. However, this evaluation also included assessing 
the system’s core capability: its ability to generate recognisable portraits 
and deliver satisfactory user results.
Each test session began with a brief introduction to the installation’s 
purpose and context. Next, we invited users to experiment with the instal-
lation and create their own typographic portrait. We also let users know 
they could make multiple portraits until they were satisfied and recognised 
themselves. During the testing sessions, users accessed the portraits 
by scanning a QR code and were not required to enter their email or accept 
the privacy policy. Figure 4.26 presents the different stages of interaction 
with the prototype used in the evaluation sessions.
During testing, we recorded two measures: (s1.1) the number of 
portraits generated and (s1.2) the time taken to achieve a satisfactory 
result. At the end of their physical interaction, we asked users three ques-
tions verbally: (s2.1) “To what extent do you recognise yourself in the 
portrait?”; (s2.2) “How much do you appreciate the final composition?”; 
and (s2.3) “Would you like to provide any comments on the installation 
or the generated output?”. For the first two questions of the second stage 
(s2.1 and s2.2), users were requested to rate their responses on a scale 
ranging from 1 to 5. A score of 1 indicated that users did not recognise 
themselves (s2.1) or did not visually appreciate the portrait (s2.2), while 
a score of 5 indicated full recognition or a high level of appreciation. The 
quantitative results of the testing sessions are presented in Tables 4.1 and 
4.2. All collected data in these evaluation sessions are available at https://
pf.dei.uc.pt/4/eval-results.xlsx (visited: 7 July 2025).

The testing results reveal that, on average, users generate approxi-
mately one portrait per interaction, which takes about one minute (s1.1). 
Furthermore, most users recognise themselves in the generated portraits 
(mean [x̅ ]: 4.44; median [x̃]: 4.00) and express high levels of satisfaction 
with the results (x̅ : 4.60; x ̃: 5.00). These findings demonstrate that the 
installation successfully fulfils the museum’s goals. Analysing the visual 
results generated in these sessions, we observed that the output portraits 
successfully captured distinct facial expressions and rendered high-contrast 
features with smooth transitions from darker to lighter areas, capturing 
the continuous colour transitions present in the input images.

II DESIGNING  RESPONSIVEL Y
The comments provided by users in response to question s2.3 were 
highly valuable in identifying areas for improvement in the installation. 
Many comments focused on the step where the user combines the text 
with the portrait. For instance, participants suggested that (i) the selected 
text should somehow influence the generated portrait, (ii) the variety 
of texts available is limited, and users recommended expanding the selec-
tion by including more writers or randomly selecting a portion of a text 
from the chosen writer, and (iii) the default writer should be randomised 
rather than always being the first one listed. These suggestions were included 
in the development of the final version of the installation. However, we could 
not control the number of texts available, as the museum staff selects them 
dynamically. Also, allowing the selected text to alter the portrait was con-
sidered inefficient, as the portrait is generated before the text is chosen.
Based on the interactions observed during the tests, we concluded 
that all users were able to use the installation without encountering sig-
nificant issues. We also observed that the installation’s interface effectively 
guided users through the steps to generate the desired output, and many 
users enjoyed creating and viewing the experience.
These tests also enabled us to evaluate the technical aspects of 
the installation, particularly the performance of the face detection and 
cropping mechanism. The system performed well despite the diverse range 
of faces tested. Also, as mentioned earlier, the installation’s outputs are 
exported as vector graphics, enabling their use in various media and sizes. 
To validate this capability, we designed several visual applications where 
the output, either fully or partially, serves as the primary visual element. 
Figures 4.27 and 4.28 present some examples of the visual applications we 
have designed.
4.4 FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS
We introduced Photomaton, an interactive installation to integrate a per -
manent exhibition dedicated to Lusophone literature. It allows users 
to create designs by combining typographic portraits with text from the 
exhibition. This project was part of a commercial design challenge issued 
by Fundação Cupertino de Miranda, Portugal. The development of this 
installation included both the software and specific hardware components, 
such as the side lamps in the installation space and the camera support.
We used a computational approach to automate the creation of these 
portraits. This approach involved developing a generative process that 
creates portraits by placing glyphs on a canvas based on user snapshots. 
We also implemented a template strategy to combine the portraits and text, 
along with an automatic typesetting method to compose the text.
For this installation, we developed three distinct methods to create 
typographic portraits, each exploring a different unit of written language: 
text, words, and glyphs. Each method produces portraits with different 
visual styles, balancing the text’s readability with the image’s recognisability. 
Portraits based on text had more readable content, while those created 
with words and glyphs more closely resembled the input images. Thus,

the use of smaller typographic elements produced more detailed outputs. 
Together with the museum team, we chose the glyph-based approach for its 
superior recognisability of the input image.
We evaluated the installation to determine how well it met the 
museum’s requirements. We tested a prototype of the installation with 
46 participants, assessing user interaction, portrait recognition, and people 
satisfaction with the results. Most users recognised themselves in the por-
traits and were pleased with the outputs. The average interaction time was 
about one minute, aligning with the museum’s requirements. This evalu-
ation also allowed us to test technical aspects of the installation, such 
as the face detection and cropping mechanism. The system performed 
well across the diverse range of faces tested. We also designed several 
applications for the outputs in various media, formats, and sizes, demon-
strating their visual versatility due to their vector graphic format.
Photomaton was publicly presented during the inauguration of the 
Torre Literária exhibition in October 2020 (see Figures 4.29 and 4.30). Since 
the installation outputs can be reproduced in various sizes, the museum 
staff decided to offer a print-on-demand service. This service lets people 
purchase the generated outputs in three sizes: postcard (A6), A4, and A3 
(see Figure 4.31). At its opening, the exhibition and installation received 
extensive media coverage, including features in national newspapers such 
as Observador,94 and Público 95 and on the Portuguese television channel RTP. 96
In summary, this project demonstrates the application of CD methods, 
particularly template and stochastic strategies, in a commercial design 
context. It highlights their potential for customising visual designs based 
on individual input.

COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES

115
 II DESIGNING  RESPONSIVEL Y
RESPONSIVE  
DESIGN PRACTICES
5
Part II of this thesis explores the development of responsive designs. These 
designs adapt their visual features and elements dynamically adjust in 
response to real-time data. In this sense, responsive posters use context -
-aware and data-driven computational techniques to adjust their features 
based on audience behaviour or environmental conditions where they are 
being displayed. The primary goal of this research was to explore the 
potential of responsive CD approaches to enhance audience engagement 
and create more effective communicative design artefacts.
After reviewing related work on layout and typographic design, we 
focused on template strategies, which were identified as the most effec-
tive for creating responsive designs (see Section 2.4). This approach allows 
designers to set up actions for visuals and link them to data, making the 
animations adjust automatically. This way, designers can control the fea-
tures of the outcomes while adding dynamism to them.
We conducted experiments using various computational methods 
to adjust visuals based on environmental data. These methods included 
techniques that directly collect data from the environment, such as CV 
and physical computing, as well as accessing online georeferenced data. 
We explored both the development of reactive and interactive approaches. 
In reactive approaches, the visuals respond directly to environmental 
changes and audience behaviour without fundamentally changing their 
core message. In contrast, interactive approaches use collected data to adapt 
both the message and content of the outcome. We also occasionally incor-
porated stochastic methods to introduce visual variation to the designs.
These experiments include three preliminary studies (Chapter 3) 
and an interactive installation called Photomaton (Chapter 4).
In the first preliminary experiment, we developed reactive moving 
posters that adjusted their visuals based on current environmental con-
ditions (see Chapter 3, sec. 3.1). We explored two approaches and various 
methods of gathering data from the environment, assessing their potential 
use in this context. The first involved creating posters whose visuals reacted 
to CV and georeferenced online data, while the second focused on posters 
that reacted to sensor data. To support this last approach, we created 
a template poster with a framework for connecting physical sensors and col-
lecting data through them. This approach was further tested in a hands-on 
workshop, where young participants without design experience adapted 
this template to create moving posters that reacted to physical-world data. 
In the second preliminary experiment, we designed seven interac-
tive moving posters that address current climate changes (see Chapter 3, 
sec. 3.2). These posters aimed to raise awareness about environmental 

116
II DESIGNING  RESPONSIVEL Y
issues and human impact. We used a template strategy with responsive 
visuals, where animations react interactively to data inputs, particularly 
audience-related data. These data were also collected through CV, physical 
computing, and access to geolocalised data. We preliminary evaluated 
the posters with people to assess how well they conveyed their intended 
messages and to determine the impact of the interactive features. Evalu-
ation results show that, despite the interactivity, the message was easily 
recognisable on all posters. Participants considered interactive posters 
to be more effective in conveying their messages than traditional print 
or only moving posters. However, some participants noted that in certain 
contexts, the interactive elements could make the message more challenging 
to understand.
Our experiments successfully demonstrated the potential of reactive 
and interactive moving posters. Despite their preliminary nature, the 
results indicate that CV and sensor data are effective methods for creating 
reactive and interactive elements, enabling real-time interaction and 
immediate response to audience movement. This suggests that these 
methods could provide a more engaging and customised poster visualis-
ation experience compared to traditional print or moving posters. 
Both experiments focused on quick responses to audience feedback. 
Nevertheless, in the first experiment, we explored slowly changing geo-
referenced data (weather information) to adjust the colour of design 
elements. We suggest that this method can help to mitigate the repetitive 
nature of these designs, especially when viewed sporadically over time. 
However, further testing is needed to understand how these types of envi-
ronmental data and the designer’s decisions affect the perception of reac-
tive posters over time.
Our findings show that both reactive and interactive approaches 
can help improve the communication value of posters compared to tradi-
tional print and classic moving posters. This indicates that these methods 
can create more memorable posters tailored to time, audience, and location. 
However, we consider that the visualisation experience of both types of 
posters differs. Reactive designs modify only the posters’ visual features 
without changing their core message. In contrast, interactive posters allow 
for gradual communication of the message through interaction, which 
suggests that this approach makes the experience more personal.
Both experiments demonstrate the feasibility of using template  
strategies to create dynamic and responsive artefacts, where the designers 
define and control the possible visual variations in advance. However, 
our findings also indicate that when designing such posters, designers 
must ensure that interactions enhance the message and that they are 
simple, provide clear feedback, and are easy for the audience to understand.
In the third preliminary experiment, we introduced an environmen-
tally responsive poster generator that creates designs based on data and 
detects environmental patterns (see Chapter 3, sec. 3.3). This system also 
uses a template strategy with greater autonomy and design expertise, auto-
matically creating, positioning, and selecting visuals instead of merely 
modifying existing features. The poster adjusts itself by adding or removing 
variable elements, with some features defined by data collected through 

117
 RESPONSIVE  DESIGN  P RACTICES7
CV and physical computing. The system also uses stochastic methods 
to increase visual diversity. Environmental data affects the duration these 
visuals remain displayed, depending on the attention of nearby people. 
Moreover, the system gains expertise over time, replicating successful 
designs or parts of them that previously captured people’s attention 
in similar conditions.
We tested the system by installing it in four shop windows in urban 
space over four weeks. This installation demonstrated its ability to create 
a variety of designs from scratch, indicating that it can effectively reflect 
varying environmental conditions in its designs. We also observed that the 
generated designs stood out in the surrounding environment, providing 
more noticeable visual experiences. Afterwards, we conducted a set of 
preliminary evaluation sessions to assess how well the system communi-
cated environmental features and whether its adaptive capabilities were 
evident in the designs. The results showed that most participants could 
recognise most of the environmental conditions reflected in the outputs 
and found them visually appealing. However, the system’s adaptive expertise 
was only slightly noticeable to participants. Overall, the findings indicate 
that this system uses a more autonomous and expert template strategy, 
which has proven capable of producing visually appealing results that reflect 
the nearby environmental conditions. Nevertheless, the method for intro-
ducing expertise into the system could be improved by incorporating design 
knowledge that goes beyond just considering the audience’s attention.
We consider that this strategy is more suitable for public spaces 
with many visual stimuli. The poster continuously adjusts while maintaining 
a uniform base, which we suggest helps keep the audience attentive to design 
changes over time without becoming tiresome. This work demonstrates 
a reactive approach focused on location rather than the audience. Our 
findings indicate that creating reactive designs based on location may be 
more effective for maintaining appeal over time with regular audiences. 
However, if the goal is to create personalised artefacts, we consider an 
approach focused on audience movement (as seen in the first two exper -
iments) more suitable. Nevertheless, further testing and evaluation are 
necessary to understand how these design choices and environmental data 
impact the effectiveness and user experience of the system over time.
In Chapter 4, we presented an interactive installation called Pho-
tomaton for a permanent exhibition on Lusophone literature. This instal-
lation, created as part of a commercial design commission by Fundação 
Cupertino de Miranda in Portugal, uses a template strategy to generate 
compositions that combine typographic portraits with user-chosen text. 
Its development process included both software and custom hardware 
components. We explored three methods for generating typographic por-
traits using different written units (text, words, and glyphs), and the results 
varied in how recognisable the image was and how legible the text appeared. 
For the final implementation, we selected the method that produced the 
most detailed and recognisable images, which utilised glyphs. Furthermore, 
we developed an automatic method that optimises text typesetting to fit 
the available space on the template.

118
II DESIGNING  RESPONSIVEL Y
We conducted evaluation sessions with people who were considering 
the museum’s requirements for the installation. The findings revealed that 
participants recognised themselves in the portraits and expressed high 
satisfaction with the outputs. The sessions demonstrated that the system 
performed well with various faces, and the outputs proved versatile enough 
to be applied across different media, formats, and sizes.
While the outputs followed a fixed template, they incorporated 
visuals that responded to user data obtained through CV (a snapshot of 
the user) and the user’s direct selection of text. This experiment demon-
strates how template strategies can be used to create new designs rather 
than just customising existing ones. It also indicated how responsive visuals 
can be integrated into traditional static designs, enabling user participation 
and customisation. This approach remains a template rather than a 
cooperative strategy, with human input limited to providing data for 
generating parts of the design rather than altering the design features 
themselves. In other words, user data are used to adjust specific elements 
of the layout without changing the overall design features. Nonetheless, 
the approach includes some level of expertise, particularly for executing 
specific tasks such as creating typographic portraits or text typesetting.
The approaches presented in this part of the thesis had low expres-
sive power, resulting in outputs with limited visual variation. The findings 
show that these low expressive power approaches have the potential to 
create responsive designs with data-driven modifications while the designer 
retains control over the main features. The findings also indicate that a few 
variations in features are sufficient to add dynamism to designs.
Two of these works were based on proposals commissioned by two 
Portuguese cultural entities: UC (the installation “Desenhar Cartazes com /
para o Caminho”) and the Fundação Cupertino de Miranda (the installation 
Photomaton). We consider these experiments successful examples of how 
CD techniques can be effectively integrated into contemporary GD prac-
tices. Both projects received coverage in regional and national Portuguese 
newspapers and news agencies. They also highlight the potential for CD 
to lead to new design services and outcomes. For instance, the development 
of the Photomaton project unexpectedly resulted in the creation of a print-on-
-demand service for selling compositions. As digital media and environ-
mental data-reading techniques, such as CV, continue to advance, we 
consider that GD processes and practices will increasingly rely on com-
putational strategies, resulting in more responsive outcomes.
The works presented in this part of the thesis illustrate how respon-
sive and data-driven approaches might produce tailored and customised 
designs. The findings indicate that these methods might be useful for 
improving message transmission and potentially offering more engaging 
visual experiences for the audience. template strategies demonstrated 
flexibility in modifying and creating designs by allowing designers to pre-
define data-driven actions, such as animations or procedures. Also, sto -
chastic and expertise-based methods have proven useful for introducing 
further visual variation into templates or generating assets for these visuals.

119
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
Part III
DESIGNING 
AUTOMA TICALL Y

120
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
The third part of this thesis presents our investigation into using Compu-
tational Design (CD) approaches to automate Graphic Design (GD) prac-
tices. We consider that this automation supports routine tasks and 
facilitates the discovery and exploration processes. This research comprises 
two main experiments. In the first set of experiments, detailed in Chapter 6, 
we employed Evolutionary Computation (EC) to generate poster designs 
based on user inputs. We describe three iterative approaches for evolving 
various visual features, exploring different evaluation methods, and devel-
oping interactive methods for users to express their preferences. Then, in 
Chapter 7, we introduced a greedy typesetting method applied to designing 
posters. The development of this method includes co-design workshop 
sessions and the creation of the media art installation ESSYS* Sharing 
#UC. Finally, in Chapter 8, we present conclusions on automating poster 
design practices based on the insights gained from these works.

121
 III DESIGNING  AUTOMA TICALL Y
EVOLUTIONARY  
POSTER COMPOSER
6
This chapter presents our research on using EC to generate posters auton-
omously. EC offers significant potential for automating tasks in GD by 
replicating essential actions that graphic designers perform during their 
daily work, including the simultaneous exploration of different visual 
perspectives. However, effectively translating people’s desires and prefer-
ences into EC approaches remains challenging. cooperative evolutionary 
approaches, such as Interactive Evolutionary Computation (IEC), have 
proven capable of evolving a wide variety of designs while incorporating 
human evaluation subjectivity in the evolutionary processes. Nevertheless, 
these strategies may lead to user fatigue, loss of interest, and inconsistent 
evaluations (Lewis, 2008; Takagi, 2001). On the other hand, automatic 
evolutionary approaches can achieve results with minimal user effort, 
but communicating user preferences in these cases can be challenging 
(Lewis, 2008; Machado et al., 2008). Chapter 2 presents an overview of the 
use of CD in Typography and GD, including evolutionary approaches.
The primary goal of the work presented in this chapter is to explore 
how automatic approaches can support design tasks and be integrated into 
contemporary GD practices. We focus on developing generative systems 
that exhibit enhanced domain expertise and greater autonomy while enabling 
users to share their preferences and guide the system’s output generation.
This study involves three iterative experiments using a Genetic 
Algorithm (GA) to generate typographic poster designs from user-provided 
inputs. The proposed approaches are inspired by letterpress design pro-
cesses from nineteenth -century print houses characterised by their highly 
algorithmic nature. Back then, typographers created posters, often in 
consultation with clients, by selecting and arranging typography, ornaments, 
and wood-engraved illustrations to fill a matrix (Meggs &  Purvis, 2016). 
The design choices were very pragmatic: lengthy sentences were composed 
in condensed typefaces, while shorter ones were composed in extended 
typefaces. Also, the most important parts of the content were highlighted 
using bigger and bolder typefaces. This study draws parallels between the 
interaction dynamics of typographers and clients back then and the current 
relationship between computational systems and users. Figure 6.1 presents 
examples of posters representative of this historical period.
The three experiments follow a similar workflow. In each, users start 
the generation by inputting the contents. The system then generates a random 
population of candidate solutions (or poster designs) and evolves these 
designs based on the users’ desired features. We have developed methods 
that let users express their intentions and preferences to evaluate the evolved 
individuals. Moreover, we ensured these systems could evolve designs auto-
matically using predefined default values without user interaction.

122
III DESIGNING  AUTOMA TICALL Y
In each experiment, we explored different evolution and evaluation 
approaches, using various measures and rules to assess the generated 
designs’ legibility , semantics, and aesthetic qualities.
The first experiment uses a GA to autonomously evolve the type-
setting of posters only composed of black-and-white typography. These 
designs are created based on user-provided text and designed using the same 
type family. The fitness of each candidate solution is computed through 
a multi-criteria hardwired fitness assignment strategy. This strategy con-
siders three criteria: (i) layout, which assesses the effective use of canvas 
space; (ii) legibility (or text coverage), which checks if the text on the poster 
is legible; and (iii) typography, which measures how closely the typeface 
matches a predefined desired typeface. Users can influence the evolutionary 
process by influencing the fitness assignment’s typography criterion by 
interactively adjusting the desired features for the typeface (horizontal 
motion and weight). We experimented with this approach to evolve posters 
for various contents, applying different user preferences.
The second experiment also uses a GA to generate typographic 
poster designs from a text input. However, in that case, the candidate 
solutions are assessed based on three criteria: (i) legibility , (ii) aes-
thetics, and (iii) semantics. Each criterion is computed by considering 
a set of design measures and rules. We developed three distinct automatic 
evaluation strategies: a multi-criteria hardwired fitness function, a multi-
-objective optimisation approach, and a hybrid strategy combining elements 
from both. Users can also select the expected visual preferences of the 
outputs, the preferred fitness assignment strategy, and the evolutionary 
and evaluation preferences. We use a Natural Language Processing (NLP) 
lexicon-based method to automatically extract information from the text, 
such as colours, emotions, and sentiments, and divide it into lines. These 
data are used to adjust the input text, fitness assignment scheme, and 
system parameters, including identifying the parts of the text with strong 
Figure 6.1. Two typical English 
letterpress posters from the nineteenth 
century. © Rafael Dietzsch and Michael 
Twynam’s collection.

123
 EVOLUTIONARY  P OSTER  C OMPOSER6
emotional impact that we determined should be highlighted in the layout. 
Using different evaluation strategies, we experimented with this approach 
to understand its behaviour and effectiveness in evolving posters for 
various contents.
The third experiment uses a GA to autonomously evolve posters 
that include both text and imagery provided by users. Building on the second 
experiment, it incorporates improvements based on previous results and 
feedback. We explored the designs’ constrained evolution, experimenting 
with stochastic ranking selection and static penalty methods. The fitness 
assignment uses a hardwired scheme that considers a combination of 
aesthetic and semantic criteria, along with legibility constraints. 
Users can restrict the GA’s search space through a dedicated inter-
face by specifying the desired range of visual variation in the outputs. They 
can also customise the evolutionary and evaluation parameters in the same 
interface. We integrated an emotion recognition NLP method that com-
bines lexicon-based and Machine Learning (ML) techniques to identify 
emotionally significant parts of the text and divide it into sentences. Fur-
thermore, this system allows users to characterise each emotion and incor-
porate this information on evolution.
The following subsections provide detailed descriptions of each 
experiment, with the final subsection presenting the main findings and 
conclusions from our investigation.
6 .1 GENERA TING JUSTIFIED TYPOGRAPHIC POSTERS
The first experiment uses a simple GA to automatically arrange a set of 
text boxes into a fully justified typographic poster. The posters feature 
black typography from the same type family on a white background. The 
system starts by initialising and evolving a population of posters based 
on a provided text. Subsequently, text boxes’ position, size, and visual 
features have evolved. The posters were created in portrait orientation, 
following the ISO 216 A series paper format (with a 1:√2 ratio). We limited 
the search space by constraining the placement of text boxes to a 16 × 24 
modular grid. Figure 6.2 displays a screenshot of the system’s interface.
A poster’s genotype is a sequence of arrays that define the width, 
height, and font of each text box in the poster (see Figure 6.3). The phe-
notype of the poster is a visual representation, where the text is displayed 
in text boxes encoded in the genotype arranged in a specific grid and size. 
As shown in Figure 6.4, these phenotypes are generated by drawing each 
text box and positioning the text content at the centre of each box. This 
experiment was implemented using Processing in Python mode.
