The posters’ content is uploaded as a text file, with a specific char -
acter separating the lines. By default, the pilcrow (¶) symbol is used. After 
processing the text, the system generates a random population of posters 
and then evaluates the resulting individuals  based on a multi-criteria 
hardwired fitness assignment strategy. 
The fitness of each individual is calculated as the weighted sum of 
three criteria: (i) layout, i.e. how effectively the space on the poster is used; 
(ii) legibility (or text coverage), i.e. how legible the poster content is; and 
(iii) typography, i.e. how closely the poster typefaces matches the desired 
target typeface. Based on empirical analysis, we allocated 30% of the total 
evaluation to the layout measure, 50% to the legibility measure, and 20% 
to the typography measure. It ensures that the system focuses on creating 
legible and fully justified posters while optimising outputs according to 
user preferences once valid designs are achieved. The following equation 
summarises this fitness calculation:
)6.1  (  
where f(p) represents the overall fitness score of an individual poster p, and 
ly, lg, and tp denote the layout, legibility, and typography scores, respectively.
Ranking selection is applied as a selection strategy.97 The individuals 
are selected for breeding using a Stochastic Universal Sampling (SUS) 
method.98 New generations are created using variation operators, particu-
larly crossover and mutation with a set probability. This process continues 
until an individual with maximum fitness is found, the set number of 
generations is reached, or the user stops the evolution.
We implemented an elitist approach to address this, passing on the 
best individuals from generation to generation. Figure 6.5 and Algorithm 
6.1 outline the GA’s behaviour in this experiment. Users can influence the 
evolution by expressing their typographic preferences for vertical motion 
and weight, using the arrow keys to define a target typeface (see Figures 
6.2 and 6.4). Adjustments can be made before or during evolution. Type-
faces must be preloaded into the experiment with metadata described in 
a CSV file, including horizontal motion ratio and weight.
6 .1 .1 INITIALISA TION
The initial population is seeded with randomly generated genotypes, each 
created based on the provided text file. A text box is created for each line 
in the text file. The width is determined based on the text character length, 
with the value set randomly between 25% of the length and four times the 
character count. The height, representing the leading between lines, is

III DESIGNING  AUTOMA TICALL Y
6. 1.2 VARIA TION OPERA TORS
New candidate solutions are generated by applying variation operators. 
Below are the genetic operators used in this experiment to manipulate the 
proposed representation: mutation and crossover.
CROSSOVER
The crossover operator recombines features from two selected parents. 
We employed a uniform crossover method, where each gene in the descend-
ant’s genotype is randomly selected from one of the parents.99 The process 
begins by selecting two parents using a SUS method. Then, for each gene, 
the corresponding gene in the offspring is randomly chosen from one of 
the parents based on a predefined crossover probability.
MUTATION
The mutation operator introduces random changes to the genotype and is 
applied with a certain probability to the resulting offspring. We designed 
this mutation operator to ensure that any possible solution can be achieved 
through employing it, i.e. the search space is fully connected with mutation. 
To achieve this, we developed seven types of mutation operators, 
each with an equal chance of being applied to an individual. When mutated, 
an option is selected from the available choices for each gene type (width, 
height, and font).
The seven developed operators are as follows. The independent muta-
tion operator randomly flips all genes in the genotype with a low probability, 
typically set at 2%, and changes their values to a random one. Gene muta-
tion randomly selects a text box on the genotype and replaces all its genes 
with new randomly generated ones. Gene value mutation randomly selects 
a value within a gene and replaces it with a new random value. As the name 
suggests, gene swap mutation randomly selects two text box genes and 
swaps their positions (width and height). Similarly, the value swap mutation 
selects and swaps two values from two randomly chosen text box genes. 
The change text box width mutation runs on all the text box width values 
in the genotype and randomly decides whether to maintain or modify the 
width with a low probability, typically set at 2%. When a modification 
occurs, the width can either increase or decrease, with both modifications 
having an equal probability. Finally, the change font mutation randomly 
decides whether to change each text box’s font value, replacing it with a 
new random one with a low probability, typically set at 2%.
6. 1.3 EVALUA TION CRITERIA
Each candidate solution is evaluated based on three criteria: (i) layout, 
(ii) legibility, and ( iii) typography. The layout measures how effectively 
space is utilised, legibility (or text coverage) evaluates how clear and easy 
to read the text on the poster is, and typography considers how closely the 
poster’s typefaces align with the user’s preferences. This evaluation scheme 
allows users to express their typographic preferences, which are incorpo-
rated into the typography measure.
99
Uniform crossover is a genetic

The poster layout is assessed by comparing the placement of text boxes in

used, the text boxes are evenly spaced by height, and each text box fills 
the width. This similarity is calculated by measuring the differences in size

posters. The results are normalised between 0 and 1, where 1 represents 
the maximum possible difference. The final layout score (ly) is the inverse

LEGIBILITY
The legibility, or text coverage,  measure assesses whether the text within 
each text box fits its allocated space without overflowing, ensuring the 
content does not exceed the text box’s width.
Legibility is measured by computing the variation between the poster 
and text box widths when the text content is rendered. We implemented 
three different modes to calculate this measure: (i) linear, which measures 
the absolute difference, whether the text is longer or shorter than the 
text box; (ii) non-linear, which is similar to the linear mode but doubles 
the difference if the text is longer than the poster width; and (iii) truncate, 
which calculates the distance only if the text width exceeds the poster 
width, and if it does not, the difference is zero. The variation (V ) of text 
box i for each mode is calculated as follows:

TYPOGRAPHY
The typography measure assesses how well the fonts used in the posters 
align with user preferences. Users specify a preferred typeface for the poster, 
and this measure evaluates how closely the design matches the specified 
weight and horizontal motion features. Designs that closely match these 
preferences receive higher scores.
This measure is computed by comparing the typefaces in each text 
box with the user-specified typeface by measuring the distances in weight 
and horizontal motion. Typefaces are preloaded with sequential informa-
tion about their weight and horizontal motion information, allowing for 
distance computation between them. Users can choose their preferred 
weight and horizontal motion via a dedicated interface in the system.
Similar to other measures, these distances are normalised between 
0 and 1, where 1 represents the maximum distance, and 0 indicates no 
distance. The final typography score (tp) is the inverse of the arithmetic 
mean of these normalised values across all text boxes, as described below:

6. 1.4 EXPERIMENT AL EVALUA TION
We conducted an experimental evaluation to study and analyse the effec-
tiveness of the developed approach’s effectiveness in generating typographic 
poster designs and assessing the creative value of its outputs. This way, 
we experimented with this system to study its behaviour, aiming to answer 
two main questions: (i) “Can the system create fully legible posters?” and 
(ii) “How do users’ preferences influence the evolution of poster designs?”. 
This way, we assess the outputs of the evolutionary approach com-
pared to those generated based on a simple random search algorithm using 
the same typeface and content.100 The objective of this evaluation was to 
verify whether the evolutionary approach produces legible posters and to 
assess the quality of the generated designs compared to those produced 
by random generation. To do that, we implemented a random search  
algorithm to generate a random population from one generation to another 
and only keep the best individual for the next generation. The experimental 
parameters are defined empirically and summarised in Table 6.1.
The top chart in Figure 6.7 presents the fitness progression of the 
best individual for each generation, comparing the random  search and 
evolutionary approaches. The evolutionary approach exhibits a consistent 
incremental improvement in fitness for the best individuals. In contrast, 
the random search may occasionally produce high-fitness outputs. However, 
the fitness progression is inconsistent, relying more on the system’s capa-

Although the typography measure makes up only 20% of the fitness 
function, we observed that the system frequently selects fonts that closely 
match the user-defined target font (see Figure 6.10). The typography measure 
is not fundamental for creating legible compositions but plays a significant 
role in optimising the output designs, mainly when legible posters have 
already been achieved. Its lower weight in the fitness function allows the 
system to favour other fonts if the target typeface makes typesetting dif -
ficult, e.g. if the target typeface is too wide for the available space.
Additionally, we used this approach to create designs for two design 
installations. The first features a series of posters inspired by the student 
protests of May 1968 in France and 1969 in Portugal, both of which com-
memorated their 50th anniversaries at that time (see Figures 6.11 and 6.12). 
The second consists of posters generated using this evolutionary approach, 
then deformed using a simple pixel deformation algorithm that shifts pixels 
to neighbouring locations, with colourisation applied afterwards (see

We found that the approach effectively produces legible designs 
while incorporating user preferences into the evolutionary process, espe-
cially when these preferences still allow for creating legible posters. Fur -

creation of typographic posters and headlines. However, we also noted

commercial contexts, either for generating final outputs or in combination

6.2  EXPLORING MUL TIPLE FITNESS 
ASSIGNMENT STRA TEGIES
The second experiment focuses on using a GA to evolve typographic posters 
from user-provided text and exploring different fitness strategies for auto-
matically evaluating these designs. The primary goal of this system is 
to create designs that optimise the use of space on the poster, reflecting the 
design philosophy and aesthetics of nineteenth-century designs. It involves 
maximising the use of different typographic resources while ensuring that 
the most emotionally significant parts of the contents are visually empha-
sised. Also, this system aims to assist designers during the discovery stages 
of their processes by allowing users to adjust and  fine-tune visual and 
evolutionary parameters throughout the evolution process.
Each poster is represented by a set of features and text boxes, each 
with its own set of attributes. The genotype of each poster is structured 
as a sequence of sets. Subsequent sets represent text box attributes, 
including typeface, font weight, height, and font size (as a percentage of 
height). As the poster content can vary, the number of text boxes and, 
consequently, the size of the genotype may also vary. Figure 6.15 shows an 
example genotype. 
The place and dimensions of text boxes are constrained according to a 
one-column grid with multiple rows, and the text is centrally aligned. 
Perceptive poster designs (phenotypes) are generated by rendering the 
text boxes according to the information encoded in the genotype, using 
HTML Canvas and web technologies, parti cularly the JavaScript library 
P5.js, to handle the visual creation.
We developed an NLP lexicon-based approach to automatically 
estimate the input text’s most sentimentally and emotionally significant 
part. This method also establishes a connection between the text content 
and certain colours. This analysis helps to identify key content that is more 
semantically significant and should be emphasised visually. Moreover, 
the system also automatically divides the text into lines.
Posters are evaluated based on three categories of measures: (i)  
legibility , which evaluates whether the content is fully legible on the 
poster; (ii) aesthetics, which evaluates if the poster is visually appealing; 
and (iii) semantics, which evaluates whether the design features conveys 
the emotional meaning of its content. We implemented three strategies 
to assign fitness to individuals: a multi-criteria hardwired fitness function 
strategy, a multi- objective optimisation strategy, and a hybrid strategy 
combining a hardwired fitness function with one multi-objective optimi-
sation part.
The system operates as follows: the generative process begins by 
processing and analysing the input text to identify associated emotions, 
sentiments, and colours using the developed lexicon-based approach. The 
evolutionary process begins by creating a random population of poster

III DESIGNING  AUTOMA TICALL Y
designs. These designs are then evaluated according to the user-selected 
fitness assignment strategy. Next, the system evolves a population of 
designs. Tournament selection is used to choose individuals for the next 
generation. Variation operators, such as crossover and mutation, are applied 
to create new offspring. Elitism is employed to combine these new indi-
viduals with the best individuals from the current generation. This evolu-
tionary process continues until a stopping criterion is met, either a set 
number of generations or user interruption. Figure 6.16 and Algorithm 6.2 
outline the system workflow.
Algorithm 6.2. Pseudocode for the evolutionary approach used in the 
second experiment.
1: Analyse the input text to extract emotions, sentiments, and colours.
2: Initialise the population of individuals' genotypes.
3: termination = false.
4: WHILE termination != true DO
5:  Map individuals into phenotypes. 
6:  Evaluate individuals based on specified criteria.
7:  Calculate the fitness of individuals.
8:  offspring = [].
9:  FOR n from 0 TO eliteSize-1 DO
10:   ADD population[n] to offspring.
11:  FOR i from eliteSize TO populationSize/2 DO
12:   Select two parents from population using tournament.
13:   ADD parents TO offspring.
14:   IF random(0,1) <= crossoverProbability THEN
15:    Apply uniform crossover on the parents.
16:   For  each individual IN parents
17:    IF random(0,1) <= mutationProbability THEN
18:     Apply mutation on the individual. 
19:  population = offspring.
20:   IF generationNumber > maximumGenerations  
OR user stopped evolution THEN
21:   termination = true.
22:  generationNumber++.
This system allows users to interactively define evolutionary features 
and parameters, select the fitness assignment strategy, and express their 
visual preferences for the outputs through an interface. Regarding the 
fitness assignment strategy, users can choose their preferred approach 
and, depending on the strategy, define the weights for each criterion or 
specify what objective should be optimised. In evolutionary settings, users 
can adjust parameters such as population size, number of generations,

137
 EVOLUTIONARY  P OSTER  C OMPOSER6
variation operator probabilities, and elite size. Users can control the visual 
features of the outputs, including the poster size, letter case, available 
typography colours, background colour, and the range of typefaces and 
font weights. Users can also adjust these preferences throughout the gen-
erations, directly influencing an ongoing evolutionary process. Figure 6.17 
displays a screenshot of the system interface.
Users can export outputs at any stage of the evolutionary process. 
When exporting, four files are downloaded: vector (SVG file) and raster 
(PNG file) versions of the phenotype, the genotype (JSON file), and the 
output content (text file). Figure 6.18 displays typical outputs generated 
by this system.
Users can integrate new typographic and colour options into the 
system by updating specific configuration files. The typography configu-
ration file stores details about the line division of text and the available 
typefaces (including available weights, pairing scores with other typefaces 
and paths to typefaces files). Similarly, the colour configuration files contain 
information about the colours and tones available.
We conducted two evaluation experiments to analyse the system’s 
performance, its possible commercial uses, and the visual features of the 
outputs. The first experiment assessed the system’s exploratory potential 
and the effectiveness of the three proposed fitness strategies by evolving 
posters with various text lengths and purposes. The second experiment 
involved creating an online tool integrated with the Twitter API to generate 
poster designs for content retrieved automatically. In this evaluation 
experiment, we also explored evolving background colours instead of 
typography colours. The following subsection comprehensively describes 
the system and the evaluation experiments conducted.
6.2. 1 INPUT PROCESSING METHOD
We have developed a lexicon-based method for analysing the semantics 
and structure of input text. This analysis detects sentiments, emotions, 
and colours related to the content. These data are then used to inform 
the visual features of the outputs.

Input processing starts with segmenting the text into lines using 
a sentence boundary detection algorithm (Reynar & Ratnaparkhi, 1997). 
The resulting longer sentences are then further subdivided based on a 
random factor within an optimal threshold and predefined line length 
range. As the character length of a sentence approaches this optimal threshold, 
the probability of dividing the sentence increases. This threshold is set 
randomly within a predefined range for each subdivision, resulting in more 
organic and irregular text breaks. The maximum threshold and range are 
specified in the typography guidelines sheet.
The analysing process works at the word level. Once the text is 
segmented, it undergoes preprocessing for lexicon analysis by (i) expanding 
contracted word forms, (ii) replacing abbreviations and slang expressions 
with their formal equivalents, (iii) converting words to their base forms 
(lemmas), (iv) replacing negations with antonyms, (v) removing stop 
words, and (vi) performing text tokenisation. The preprocessed tokens 
are then analysed by searching them in a word-emotion association lexicon 
developed by Saif Mohammad and Peter Turney (2010) and a word-colour 
association lexicon created by Saif Mohammad (2012a, 2012b). 
These lexicons were created through manual annotation and cover 
the most commonly used terms in the English language. The emotion and 
sentiment lexicon connects around 15,000 words to positive and negative 
sentiments and the eight basic and prototypical emotions delineated 
by Robert Plutchik (1980): anger, anticipation, disgust, fear, joy, sadness, 
surprise, and trust. The word-colour lexicon, on the other hand, measures 
the strength of associations between 14,000 words and 11 distinct colours: 
black, blue, brown, green, grey, orange, purple, pink, red, white, and yellow.
The results of the emotion and sentiment analysis are grouped by 
text line, enabling the system to identify the most emotionally and senti-
mentally charged sections. Based on this information, the system calculates 
an optimal semantic layout, giving more prominence to lines with higher 
emotional intensity.
On the other hand, the results of the word-colour analysis are aggre-
gated globally by colour intensity and stored in a list sorted by inten-
sity. The intensity value represents the cumulative score of occurrences 
in the text by each colour. 
This method enables users to customise the results generated by 
the input processing module. They can modify the lexicon used for analysis 
and also configure how visual and typographic features, as well as colours, 
relate to the content by updating specific configuration files. We developed 
this method using the NLP libraries finNLP  102 and Natural 103 libraries, as 
well as the Merriam- Webster Dictionary API.104

6.2.2 INITIALISA TION
The initialisation operator creates a random initial population of posters. 
Each individual is randomly assigned the colour configuration and text 
box genes. The colour configuration genes are determined by randomly 
selecting a base colour and its tint percentage from the available options 
defined by users.
Tint percentages are chosen randomly in increments of 20%, ranging 
from 20% to 100%. Black and white are the only colours that do not support 
tints. Default base colours are specified in a dedicated configuration colour 
file. By default, ten base colours are defined: black (#000000); red (#CC1948); 
yellow (#EED524); blue (#0468BF); brown (#A63F03); green (#29A683); 
grey (#35536B); orange (#F28705); purple (#800080); and pink (#F44ABF).
The number of text boxes is defined by the number of lines resulting 
from the content-splitting process. For each line, a text box is created with 
proprieties defined at random. The typeface and its weight are randomly 
chosen from the available options. The height of the text boxes is also 
selected randomly but adjusted to ensure that all the text boxes occupy 
all the available space on the posters’ canvas. The operator ensures this 
by generating a random sequence of numbers equal in length to the number 
of text boxes, with the sum of the sequence matching the number of rows 
in the grid. Next, the sequence is shuffled, and each value is assigned 
to a text box. Finally, the font size is set to 100% of the text box height. 
Default typefaces and their properties are specified in the typography 
configuration file.
6.2.3 VARIA TION OPERA TORS
The population evolves using variation operators. This section describes 
the genetic operators (crossover and mutation) used to manipulate the 
population while preserving the validity of the generated individuals.
CROSSOVER
The crossover operator exchanges genes between two parents’ posters 
to create new offspring. We use a uniform crossover method, where genes 
are randomly selected from either parent using a roulette wheel selection 
process. For each gene position, it randomly determines which parent will 
contribute the gene based on a specified crossover probability. This oper-
ator does not crossover genes related to height, ensuring that all offspring 
remain valid with text boxes that fully occupy the height of the posters.
MUTATION
The mutation operator makes random changes in the individual genotype 
based on a certain probability. The operator randomly decides whether 
the individual will be mutated for each candidate solution. If selected, one 
of three specific mutation methods will be chosen to apply. We have designed 
these three mutation methods to ensure this operator covers all the search 
space. Each operator has an equal chance of being chosen.

140
III DESIGNING  AUTOMA TICALL Y
The independent mutation method randomly selects a gene and a 
parameter within that gene to mutate. If a colour configuration gene (colour 
and tint) or the font weight parameter is chosen, it randomly assigns a new 
value from the available options. If the height parameter of a text box is 
selected, it randomly picks two genes, making sure at least one has a height 
greater than one, and then decides which gene will increase or decrease 
in height. This selection is made randomly unless one of the selected genes 
has a value of 1. In that case, the gene with the lower value will increase 
its height, while the other will decrease. When the font size parameter is 
selected, it changes by 1%, with the change direction being random unless 
the value is at its minimum or maximum.
The specialised mutation method is a customised version of the inde-
pendent mutation method that only mutates the highest text box on the 
individual and the font size parameter. We introduced this method because 
we noticed that evolution often slowed down and settled on designs with 
one large text box. Even with the most condensed typeface, the content 
could not be fully displayed in these cases. We developed this method 
to target the parameters causing these issues. It is an optional method and 
can be activated or deactivated as needed. 
When used, this method randomly chooses to mutate the height 
genes or the font size of the highest text box. If the height is selected, it 
decreases the height of the highest text box and increases the height of 
another randomly chosen text box. If the font size is chosen, it adjusts the 
font size by 1%, with the direction of the adjustment being random, unless 
the size is at the maximum (100%) or minimum (30%). The minimum font 
size of 30% was set based on the observation of the smallest viable font size 
that does not compromise the legibility of the design.
As the name indicates, swap mutation randomly selects two text 
boxes and swaps their gene values.
6.2.4 EVALUA TION CRITERIA
In this experiment, the posters were evaluated based on three main eval-
uation criteria: (i) legibility, (ii) aesthetics, and (iii) semantics. These 
categories were defined to evaluate both the effectiveness of the message’s 
communication, legibility , and the quality of its visual language, aes-
thetics and semantics (Frascara, 1988). legibility examines whether 
the content on the poster is readable while optimising the use of white 
space. aesthetics assesses the visual appeal of the poster design, evalu-
ating it according to specific aesthetic principles for typographic posters, 
which include (i) alignment, (ii) regularity, (iii) balance, (iv) negative space 
fraction, (v) compositional security, and (vi) typography pairing. semantics 
assesses how effectively the visual characteristics of the posters convey 
the meaning of their content, emphasising the parts with greater emo-
tional intensity.
Determining the overall quality of a poster is a subjective and con-
text-dependent task influenced by various subjective human factors. Graphic 
designers are primarily responsible for iteratively evaluating and editing 
their outcomes based on the design briefing, the design tradition, and 
the clients’ expectations (Frascara, 1988; Shaughnessy, 2010).

141
 EVOLUTIONARY  P OSTER  C OMPOSER6
To align with this subjective evaluation nature of the GD processes, 
we implemented three automatic strategies for assigning fitness to the 
designs generated by the system: a multi-criteria hardwired fitness assign-
ment approach; a multi-objective optimisation approach; and a hybrid 
approach which combines features of the two other approaches. This 
strategy provides different ways to influence the system’s creative process 
and various methods of combining the three evaluation criteria. Users can 
switch between these fitness assignment strategies during the evolutionary 
process, allowing them to choose the most appropriate approach at each 
moment based on their observations of evolution. Next, we detail each 
criterion.
LEGIBILITY
The legibility criteria evaluate how legible the content on the poster is 
while also aiming to minimise negative space on posters (the area on 
posters coloured with background colour). 
The legibility score (LG) of each text box (t) is calculated by taking 
the absolute difference between the width of the poster and the rendered 
text box width. This difference is then normalised to a score between 0 and 
1. A score of 0 is assigned when the text width is at least double the poster 
width, indicating poor legibility. Conversely, a score of 1 is assigned when 
the text width fits within a specific range close to the poster width, typically 
set at one-third of the poster length, indicating good legibility . This is 
represented by the following equation:
)6.6  (
 
where Wp is the width of the poster p and w(i) is the width of the content 
of the text box i when rendered.
The overall legibility score is the weighted arithmetic mean of the 
scores for all text boxes. The weight of each text box in this mean is auto-
matically calculated based on its height. This calculation is expressed as 
follows:
)6.7  (
 
where lg is the overall legibility score of a poster p, LG(p, i) is the legi-
bility score for each text box i in poster p (see Equation 6.6), h(i) is the 
height of each text box i, and H  is the height of poster p.
AESTHETICS
The aesthetics criterion evaluates how well a poster design meets a set 
of six aesthetic measures specifically for typographic posters. These meas-
ures are based on work by Steven J. Harrington et al. (2004) but have been 
adapted to suit the context of typographic poster designs. We excluded 
white-space free-flow, proportion, and uniform separation measures from 
the initial proposed set of measures as they are unrelated to our one-column 

142
III DESIGNING  AUTOMA TICALL Y
grid layouts. This way, we included a font pairing measure based on the 
principles outlined by Ellen Lupton (2014) and Robert Bringhrust (1997) 
since proper typeface pairing is crucial for a harmonious layout.
The six aesthetic measures for evaluating a poster are (i) alignment, 
(ii)  regularity, (iii)  balance, (iv)  negative-space fraction, (v)  composition 
security, and (vi) font pairing. Each measure is scored on a scale from

The alignment measure assesses the horizontal uniformity of the text 
by measuring the distance between the horizontal position of the left edges 
in neighbouring text boxes. The closer the distance between text boxes, 
the higher the alignment score. The alignment score is determined by 
creating a histogram of the left edge positions of text boxes and comparing 
the distance between the adjacent positions. This distance value is then 
normalised according to the width of the poster. The  overall alignment  
score (align) is the arithmetic mean of all distances, expressed as follows:
)6.9  (

and Wp is the width of the poster p.
The regularity measure (reg) checks how uniformly the text boxes 
are spaced vertically on the poster by looking at the distances between the 
top edges of adjacent boxes. The process is similar to the alignment but 
uses a histogram of the top edges rather than the left edges. Also, the value 
is normalised based on an optimal height, where all text boxes occupy the 
same height on the poster. We can represent it as:

The balance measure indicates how visually balanced the poster is. 
In this experiment, we only measured the central balance, as the content 
is centre-aligned, and the poster must be horizontally justified. We deter-

The negative space fraction ( neg) measures the balance of negative 
space (background-coloured areas) on the poster. It calculates the absolute 
difference between the current percentage of background colour and a set 
optimal threshold, typically 50%. A score of 1 is given if this percentage 
matches the threshold. As the percentage deviates from the threshold, the 
score decreases, reaching 0 when the background colour coverage falls 
outside the threshold range. This can be represented as:
)6.15  (

The composition security measure (comp) checks whether text boxes 
near the poster’s edges appear secure rather than “falling off” the edges. 
It is determined by the minimum distance between the top and bottom 
edges of all text boxes in the composition, normalised on a scale from 0 
(indicating that the text box is on the edge) to 1 (indicating that at least 
the text box is placed at 10% of the poster’s height). This measure is

SEMANTICS
The semantics criterion evaluates how effectively the posters’ visual 
characteristics convey the emotional meaning of their content. We defined 
the parts with more significant emotional and sentimental impact as 
those that must be highlighted in the layout compared to less emotionally 
charged ones. Furthermore, the typography colour should align with the 
content, as colours matching the message can enhance communication 
(Mohammad, 2012a). 

145

The semantics value of a poster is the weighted sum of three meas-
ures used to evaluate the appropriateness of (i) layout (seLy), (ii) colours 
(seCol), and (iii) typefaces (seTyp). The overall semantics score (se) ranges 
from 0 (poor semantics) to 1 (perfect semantics), as illustrated in:
)6.18  (
 
where w1, w2, and w 3 are the weights assigned to the layout, colour, and 
typeface measures, respectively. Users can deactivate any of these measures 
and adjust their weights in the interface, customising the evaluation process 
based on their preferences.
The appropriateness of the layout is determined by calculating the 
distance between each text box’s height and its optimal semantic height 
(op), which is computed in advance based on an optimal semantic layout. 
The overall layout appropriateness  value (seLy) is the arithmetic mean of 
all distances, normalised on a scale from 0 (where the sum of distances 
exceeds the poster height) to 1 (indicating no distance), as shown below:
)6.19  (
 
where Np is the number of text boxes i in the poster p, h(i) and op(i) is the 
height and optimal semantic height of textbox i, and Hp is the poster height, 
representing the maximum possible deviation.
The appropriateness of colour is calculated based on the results of 
word-colour analysis performed beforehand. The typography’s colour 
conveys the semantic meaning when it corresponds to the colour most 
associated with the text. The colours are ranked by their intensity score 
with the content. The colour appropriateness value is the normalised 
distance (dc), on a scale from 0 to 1, in the number of positions on the list 
between the used and the optimal colour (the top of the list). We also 
developed a method to evaluate how well colour tints align with the content, 
which the system can optionally use. Essentially, if a colour is strongly 
related to the content, its tint percentage should be higher, and vice versa. 
The optimal tint value is determined by dividing the number of available 
tint percentages by the colour’s relationship intensity with the content 
(its position on the list). The tint appropriateness value is the normalised 
distance (dt) calculated, similar to the colour appropriateness. The overall 
colour appropriateness score (seCol) is the weighted arithmetic mean of 
the two scores (colour and tint) for all text boxes in the poster p, as stated in:
)6.20  (
 
where Np  is the number of text boxes in poster p , dc(i)  is the distance 
between the colour of text box i and the optimal colour, MCp is the maximum 
possible distance for colour, dt(i) is the distance between the tint of text 
box i and the optimal tint, and MTp is the maximum possible distance for 
tint. wcol and wtint are the weights assigned to the colour and tint appro-
priateness scores, respectively.

The appropriateness of a typeface is evaluated by determining whether

The typeface’s global appropriateness (tpGlobal) is related to whether 
the typeface shape conveys the overall sentiments and emotions found in 
the poster content, according to the mapping between visual features and 
emotions defined by users. It is calculated as the arithmetic mean of the 
distances between the features of the typefaces used on the poster and 
the expected features for the most recognised emotion or sentiment,

6.2.5 FITNESS ASSIGNMENT 
We implemented three automatic strategies to evaluate the fitness of indi-
viduals: (i) a hardwired fitness  function approach; (ii ) a multi -objective 
optimisation approach; and (iii) a hybrid approach.
The hardwired fitness assignment strategy is based on the premise 
that high-quality posters must fully satisfy all criteria, each weighted dif -
ferently in the fitness function. This way, the quality of the poster is com-
puted as the weighted sum mean of the three criteria, as summarised in:
)6.26  ( 
where f(p) represents the overall fitness score of an individual poster p , 
and ly, ae, and se represent the legibility , aesthetics, and semantics  
scores, respectively. Also, w1, w2, and w3 are the weights assigned to each 
criterion in the evaluation schema. The default weight distribution for 
each criterion is 90% for legibility, 5% for aesthetics, and 5% for seman-
tics. We defined this default weight scheme to ensure that the system 
primarily focuses on optimising legibility , prioritising the creation of 
a readable poster regardless of the text length or emotional and sentimental 
context before addressing other criteria. However, users can adjust and 
fine-tune the weight of each criterion over generations through the inter-
face based on their observations and preferences.
The multi-objective optimisation approach uses an Elitist Non-
-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm (NGGA-II, Deb et al., 2002) to 
assign fitness to the generated posters. This approach values posters that 
create innovative and distinctive relationships between the three criteria 
(in that case, considered objectives), whether through optimisation, min-
imisation, or balance. The fitness is determined by the rank of the front 
where the individual is placed in the non-domination sort of the population. 
The population is organised into fronts, and the crowding distance is used 
to select individuals during the tournament.105 Since this strategy can be 
destructive to the population, we have implemented a custom elite mech-
anism that retains all individuals on the non-dominated front in the elite 
pool, ensuring that at least 50% of the population comes from the new 
offspring. Users can also specify which objective they want to optimise. In 
such scenarios, it only stores on elite individuals meeting these preferences.
The hybrid approach combines a hardwired fitness function with 
a multi-objective optimisation strategy. This strategy considers that 
high-quality posters are both legible and exhibit distinctive relationships 
between the semantics and aesthetics objectives, whether through 
balance or optimisation / minimisation. The fitness of each poster is based 
on the weighted sum of the legibility measure (the fixed part) and the 
relationship between the semantics and aesthetics objectives (the 
multi-objective part). The relationship between aesthetics and semantics 
is computed using NGGA-II, similar to the multi -objective optimisation 
strategy, but focusing on these two objectives. The following equation 
summarises this calculation:
)6.27  (

The w1 and w2 represent the weights assigned to each part of the evaluation

We also introduced an elite mechanism for this hybrid strategy, 
where the elite poll may vary if the top-ranked individuals share the same 
legibility score and are placed in the non-dominated front regarding the 
multi-objective evaluation of aesthetics and semantics. As in the multi-
-criteria hardwired strategy, users may define and refine the weights of each 
part in the mean.
6.2.6 EXPERIMENT AL EVALUA TION
We tested the current system to explore and analyse how the three different 
fitness assignment strategies influence the evolution of posters. The testing 
experiments involved evolving posters with contents of varied lengths 
and purposes. This way, we evolved poster designs using the three proposed 
fitness assignment strategies with the same text content and settings. 
We used only one type family for easier comparison and did not assess the 
appropriateness of a typeface for the semantics criteria.
The experimental parameters and fitness function weights were 
determined empirically and are summarised in Table 6.3. Table 6.4 lists 
the text content used. We did not change any preferences during the evo-
lution, and all available colours were used. Posters were generated using 
the Bureau Grot type family.106
In the experiment using the hardwired fitness function, we used 
the default set of weights, using a high legibility weight over the other 
criteria (see Table 6.5). Figure 6.19 presents several examples generated 
with this strategy.

The results reveal that this strategy allows the creation of legible 
and finished posters from scratch. However, we observed that posters with 
the same content show reduced visual diversity in colour and layout. We 
also found that the  visual diversity in results is related to the emotional 
and sentimental analysis of the content: texts with weak or evenly distrib-
uted emotional charges tend to produce more varied poster designs. In 
contrast, texts with strong emotional charges result in less diversity. Similar 
patterns are observed with typography colour. Also, we noted that the 
system generates outputs faster with longer texts due to fewer layout 
options. For the same reason, extended text content creates more similar 
poster populations.
Posters with high fitness values were achieved within a few gener -
ations, with faster evolution in the early stages compared to the later stages. 
Figure 6.20 presents the progression of fitness and criteria scores in the pop-
ulation. Although the fitness did not reach the maximum theoretical value, 
the top individuals in the population achieved high fitness values and 
evaluation scores in both legibility and semantics, exceeding 0.9 out of 1. 
On the other hand, we observed that high aesthetics evaluations are less 
common. Our analysis reveals that the evaluation of these criteria is more 
constrained by content features. Also, we noted that these criteria are 
often constrained by legibility since the readable layouts may not align 
with all aesthetic measures. Never theless, aesthetics criteria scores 
did increase over the generations.

The multi-objective optimisation strategy assigns fitness to posters 
based on their non-domination ranking within the population. We consider 
that this approach promotes novelty by encouraging and favouring the 
evolution of designs that exhibit distinct relationships among the three 
evaluation criteria, which serve as evaluation objectives. Figure 6.21 pre -
sents examples of typical posters generated using this strategy.
The experimental results reveal that this fitness assignment strategy 
cannot guarantee the generation of fully readable posters (see bottom row 
of Figure 6.21). Our analysis indicates that it sometimes prioritises opti-
mising aesthetics or semantics over legibility . For the same reason, 
legible posters are also discarded from the population in favour of unread-
able ones. We found that the probability of generating legible posters

The experimental results demonstrate that this hybrid strategy also 
enables the creation of legible and finished poster designs. We noted that 
the visual diversity of posters is slightly greater compared to the multi-
-criteria hardwired fitness strategy. We also observed that these posters 
also closely resemble letterpress aesthetics. This increase in visual diver -
sity seems to be due to the multi-objective part, as best-ranked posters do 
not need to fully satisfy aesthetics and semantics but instead need to 
present a non-dominant relationship between them. Also, this strategy 
produces well-evaluated poster designs more quickly when the content is 
longer. However, as the text length increases, the visual diversity of the 
generated outputs decreases.
Figure 6.25 illustrates the progression of fitness within the popula-
tion and the scores for the corresponding criteria. To fully understand the 
fitness progression with this strategy, both charts must be viewed together, 
as the relationship between aesthetics and semantics objectives is 
represented by the rank of the front to which the individual belongs rather 
than by a quantitative value. While fitness values do not reach the theo-
retical maximum, high values can be achieved within a few generations. 
This strategy achieves similar or higher fitness and legibility evaluations 
than the multi-criteria hardwired strategy. However, the evolution is slower. 
On average, the aesthetics have lower evaluation values due to their 
specific dependencies. In contrast, semantics evaluation is lower and 
more variable than other strategies. 
We also noted that this strategy is less destructive than the multi-
-objective optimisation approach. In the earlier stages of evolution, the 
evaluations of aesthetics and semantics criteria are similar to or even 
higher than those in later stages. In some early stages, the average evalu-
ation for these criteria in the population can exceed the evaluations of the 
best -ranked individuals. Our analysis reveals that this occurs because

legibility acts as a constraint, disregarding designs that prioritise aes-
thetics or semantics instead of legibility. Nevertheless, the evaluation 
scores for aesthetics and semantics are highly influenced by the con-
tent’s characteristics.
Although poster evolution can be influenced by various factors, 
including context, textual content, and user-related aspects, the experimental 
results revealed that both the multi-criteria hardwired and hybrid strategies 
effectively enable the autonomous generation of finished posters. Overall, 
these strategies performed similarly. The hybrid strategy achieved slightly 
better results in terms of visual diversity and legibility evaluation. 
On the other hand, the multi-criteria hardwired strategy performed slightly 
better in terms of semantics evaluation and evolutionary convergence speed. 
The multi-objective optimisation strategy, however, produced unstable 
populations and did not consistently generate readable and finished posters, 
mainly when the content was neither too long nor too short. Nevertheless, 
this strategy created individuals with superior aesthetic evaluations 
and encouraged the development of more visually diverse populations.
6.2.7 POSTER GENERA TOR TOOL
To evaluate the practical effectiveness of this evolutionary approach, we 
developed a tool that uses the proposed system to automatically generate 
poster designs from input strings retrieved from Twitter, exploring the 
potential system’s automation capabilities.
This tool features an interface that allows users to search the Twitter 
API by tweet text, username, or hashtag. Users can also specify whether 
the tweet selection should be based on popularity, newness, or a combi-
nation of both. When a search is performed based on a standard Twitter  
API search, the tool retrieves the tweet that best matches the input term. 
The input processing module then analyses the tweet’s text and starts 
the automatic generation of poster designs. The interface is documented 
in Figures 6.26 and 6.27. 
We used the hybrid fitness assignment strategy for this tool because 
our previous evaluations reveal that it produces more visually diverse 
designs by exploring various relationships between semantics and aes-
thetics while still ensuring legibility. Since this tool focuses on automatic

We observed that the system, in a single poster, often favours type-
faces from the same type family, such as  Bureau Grot or Titling Gothic FB. 
We infer that this is due to these families offering a wide selection of font 
styles, ensuring that at least one typeface fits different text box sizes and 
features while maintaining good visual pairing because of their shared 
design traits.
Regarding background colours, the system often selects the same 
colour set across different evolution runs for specific content. As expected, 
it converges to well-evaluated outputs more quickly when the content 
is longer because there are fewer possible solutions and the search space 
is more constrained. However, we noted that longer text content tends to 
produce more similar outputs and populations across different runs.
We also observed that posters with high legibility scores have been 
generated within a few generations. The legibility criterion, due to its 
high weight in the fitness assignment scheme, as expected, acts as a restric-
tion. Consequently, we observed that the evolution process is faster in the 
early stages, focusing primarily on achieving a legible layout. In the later 
stages, the system focuses on making minor adjustments to the aesthetics 
and semantics features of the posters.

6.3 EVOL VING WITH DESIGN CONSTRAINTS
In the third evolutionary experiment, we employed a constrained evolu-
tionary approach to generate poster designs from input texts and imagery. 
Similar to the other experiments in this chapter, the primary goal of the 
generated posters is to display their content fully. However, we experi-
mented with constraint-handling techniques by using a GA to evolve a 
population of posters and treating legibility measures as constraints the 
outputs must satisfy while evaluating designs based on other measures.
We further expanded the set of heuristic measures for evaluating 
poster designs. The proposed 11 measures are also organised into three 
criteria, encompassing the evaluation of designs in terms of their legibility, 
aesthetic features, and coverage of content semantics. The legibility  
criterion assesses whether all text content is adequately displayed and 
readable within the design, including the evaluation of text legibility and 
grid appropriateness. The aesthetics criterion determines the visual quality 
of the designs, examining aspects like alignment, balance, justification, reg-
ularity, typeface pairing, and negative space fraction. The semantics crite-
rion focuses on assessing how the composed text effectively conveys the 
semantic meaning of the content in terms of layout, typography, and visuals. 
We used a stochastic ranking strategy (Runarsson & Yao, 2000) to evaluate 
outputs, where the legibility criterion is considered a constraint and the 
fitness of each design is determined using the weighted arithmetic mean 
of the semantics and aesthetics criteria. We also explored a penalty 
function strategy to manage elitism and improve the visualisation of the 
outputs in the interface.
As with other evolutionary experiments, this experiment still drew 
inspiration from traditional letterpress typesetting. As a result, this evo-
lutionary system values outputs with diverse typography and visual styles 
and where the layout highlights the most emotionally significant parts 
of the content. However, users have the flexibility to parametrise the system 
to modify the measures and the expected features of outputs.
In this experiment, we used OpenType variable fonts (OTVF) files, 
which enable direct modification of the variation axes of the typeface rather 
than altering the font file. By default, the variation operators act in the weight 
and font-stretch axes. 107 The resulting outputs can feature different text 
alignments (left, centre, or right) and vertical alignments (top, middle, 
and bottom). New typefaces and typographic options can be added to the 
system by updating the system configuration files.
The system also colours the background of the outputs according 
to different styles. By default, three background styles are available: (i) solid 
background, where the background is filled with a solid single colour; 
(ii) gradient background, where the background is created as a linear gra-
dient between two colours; and (iii)  halved triangle background , where 
the background is divided into two triangles with different colours. Users 
can also add new background styles by describing them and including 
the rendering function in a specific file.
107
The font-stretch axis, also known 
as the width axis, is used in OTVF. 
It adjusts the horizontal width 
of a typeface, making it appear more 
condensed or expanded.

160
III DESIGNING  AUTOMA TICALL Y
Each poster comprises a group of visuals, including text boxes (each 
representing a text line) and raster images. We adopted a Domain-Driven 
Design (2015) approach to define the representation of posters, structuring 
the genotype in JSON format. This way, each representational attribute 
is identified by a term commonly used in the GD domain. 
The genotype is organised into two distinct parts. The first part 
focuses on the content and its features. The first component of the geno-
type is an array of objects, with each element on the array describing a text 
box. The number of text boxes does not vary over the evolution, and it is 
defined based on the number of text lines of content. For each text box, 
it stores its content and characteristics, namely the typeface name, font 
weight, vertical motion (or stretch), size, alignment, colour, and case. 
The second component is an array of objects that stores the images. Like 
the text boxes, the number of images on the poster remains constant during 
evolution. For each image, it stores the coordinates (x, y) of their position 
as a percentage-relative value of their size, width, and height, respectively, 
along with the image itself in a Binary Large Object (BLOb) format.
The second part of the genotype focuses on the general features of 
the poster design. The third component of the genotype stores information 
related to the dimensions of the posters, including the size (height and width, 
in pixels) and the margins, represented as percentage-relative values 
and ordered as left, top, right, and button. The fourth component is related 
to the poster background. It includes an integer variable that defines 
the background style of the poster and a two-position array that defines the 
colours used in these background styles in hexadecimal format. The fifth 
component of the genotype is an integer that defines the vertical text 
alignment on the poster. The grid of the poster is inferred based on the 
poster’s characteristics. Figure 6.30 presents an example of a genotype. 
We employ a NLP approach that combines lexicon-based methods 
with ML for emotion recognition in the input text content. The lexicon-
-based approach conducts a local analysis of the text (word level) to iden-
tify the parts of the text with a higher emotional significance, visually 
emphasising them on the layout. Additionally, our method utilises an 
ML-based emotion recognition technique to discern the overall emotional 
tone of the text, identifying the emotions that are related to the text as a 
whole. This method also handles the division of the text into lines. The 
data from this analysis are used to evaluate the layout and visual features 
of the outputs. Moreover, users have the flexibility to map the recognised 
emotions to visual preferences and specific features, allowing for a more 
customised approach to defining the design’s visual elements.
The generative process starts with randomly initialising a population 
of posters. A text box is defined for each line of text, and its characteristics 
and the general poster features are randomly determined from the available 
choices. Tournament selection is used to choose individuals for breeding 
based on their fitness, and variation operators (mutation and crossover) 
are applied to the selected individuals, with a certain probability, to gen-
erate new offspring.

approach and the system workflow.
Users may export one or multiple outputs at any point during the evo-
lutionary process. When a user chooses to export an output, three files 
are downloaded: the vector and raster versions of the phenotype, in SVG 
and PNG format, respectively, and the genotype of the output in JSON 
file. Figure 6.33 displays some outputs generated by the proposed approach.

Algorithm 6.3. Pseudocode of the approach used in this third evolutionary experiment.
1: Import default settings and typefaces from the file.
2:  Analyse the input text to extract emotions (globally and locally) and perform text 
line breaking.
3: DISPLAY analysisResults TO user.
4: WAIT UNTIL user CONFIRMS or MODIFIES analysisResults.
5: DISPLAY system parameters TO the user.
6: Initialise the population of individuals’ genotypes.
7: WHILE user HAS NOT CONFIRMED parameters DO
8:  IF user MODIFIES any parameters THEN
9:   Initialise a new population of individuals' genotypes.
10: termination = false.
11: generationNumber = 0;
12: WHILE termination != true DO
13:  Map individuals into phenotypes.
14:  Evaluate the individuals.
15:   Calculate the objectiveValue of individuals (aesthetic 
and semantic criteria).
16:  Calculate the penaltyValue of individuals.
17:  Compute the staticPenalty of individuals.
18:  Rank population by staticPenalty.
19:  offspring = [].
20:  FOR n from 0 TO eliteSize-1 DO
21:   ADD population[n] TO offspring.
22:  Rank the individuals using Stochastic Ranking.
23:  FOR i from eliteSize TO populationSize DO    
24:   IF random(0, 1) <= crossoverProbability THEN
25:    Select two parents using tournament selection.
26:    Generate a child using uniform crossover.
27:    ADD child TO offspring.
28:   ELSE
29:    Select one individual using tournament selection.
30:    ADD individual TO offspring.
31:   IF random(0, 1) <= mutationProbability THEN
32:    Apply mutation to the individual/child.
33:  population = offspring.
34:   IF generationNumber > maximumGenerations OR user stopped evolution 
THEN
35:    termination = true.
36:   generationNumber++

III DESIGNING  AUTOMA TICALL Y
We conducted experiments to examine the influence of the proposed 
evaluation measures on the evolutionary generation of typographic poster 
designs. These experiments involved the evolution of typographic posters 
using input texts of varying lengths and emotional content. The experiments 
consisted of three stages, each focusing on the evolution of posters based 
on either semantics criterion, aesthetics criterion, or a combination of both. 
This system was developed using web technologies and divided into three 
modules, with input processing and evaluation methods independent of the 
primary approach. We also developed unit and end -to-end testing modules 
for each system part. Phenotypes are rendered according to the information 
encoded in the genotype, using HTML Canvas, particularly exploring the 
JavaScript library P5.js to handle the visual creation.
6.3. 1 INPUT PROCESSING METHOD
The input processing method analyses the user-given text to identify 
its emotional significance. This way, it detects the overall emotional tone 
of the entire text (global analysis) while also identifying the emotions 
associated with specific words within the text (local analysis). As in the 
second experiment, this method is also responsible for automatically 
dividing the provided text into lines. Initially, it divides the text using 
a sentence boundary detection algorithm (Reynar & Ratnaparkhi, 1997). 
After, the resulting longer sentences are further divided based on a random 
factor in a predefined line size range. This process includes implementing 
mechanisms to prevent the occurrence of typographic widows and orphans, 
as well as placing short words at the end of lines, avoiding text division when 
the following lines consist only of small words.
To perform the global analysis, we employed a neural NLP approach 
trained to determine the emotional intensity of a text. This training was 
based on a corpus created from the emotion-intensity annotated multi-label 
text dataset provided by Saif M. Mohammad et al. (2018). The corpus consists 
of a set of human-annotated texts to infer the writer’s emotional state. It 
primarily focuses on short text that is mainly posted on Twitter. The texts 
in the corpus are categorised to determine whether they convey neutrality 
or exhibit one or more of the 11 emotions. These emotions include anger, 
anticipation, disgust, fear, joy, love, optimism, pessimism, sadness, surprise, 
and trust.
Figure 6.32. Workflow of this experiment. 

165 EVOLUTIONARY  P OSTER  C OMPOSER6
The global analysis begins with the processing of the input text for clas-
sification. The classification model is designed to work with text in English. 
This analysis starts by translating the text to English using the IBM Watson 
Language Translator V3 web cloud API. Currently, the method supports text 
translation into forty-eight languages, including Arabic, French, Japanese, 
Portuguese, and Spanish.108 Following translation, the system identifies and 
removes parts of the text that are unnecessary for the emotional classifica-
tion, including removing URLs, hashtags, mentions and emojis. Emojis are 
substituted with their corresponding meanings. The resulting text is then 
classified by the neural network, which identifies the relevant emotions and 
assigns their intensity scores. Finally, the predominant emotions are deter-
mined based on a predetermined threshold score. By default, this threshold 
is set at 0.5.
On the other hand, the local analysis is conducted using a lexicon -based 
approach like the one presented in the second experiment, operating at the 
word levels. This analysis is iteratively applied to each of the resulting text 
lines. The text is first processed for lexicon analysis by (i) handling contrac-
tions, (ii) replacing abbreviations and slang with formal equivalents, (iii)  
substituting emojis with their meanings, (iv) converting negations to anto-
nyms, (v) removing stop words and URLs, and (vi) tokenising the text. Next, 
it performs a lexicon-based analysis of the text by searching the resulting 
tokens in the Saif Mohammad and Peter Turney (2010) word-emotion asso-
ciation lexicon. The emotional score of each line is calculated by summing 
the emotional scores recognised by the words on it.
We used the information from the local analysis to define the poster’s 
optical semantic layout, considering that lines with higher emotional signif-
icance must be typeset with more emphasis than the others. On the other 
hand, the information from the global analysis is used to determine the 
expected visual features of the outputs.
This method was developed as a standalone Node.js JavaScript module, 
including methods to access it via a REST API and input the text via a user 
interface. We also developed the necessary unit tests for the module. 
Throughout the development process, we used natural language processing 
libraries like finNLP  and NLP.js,109, as well as the Express.js framework  110 
and the Merriam-Webster Dictionary API.

6.3.2 INITIALISA TION
The initialisation method generates a new random population of poster 
designs, considering the range of possible features defined by users. A text 
box is created for each line of text, and the typeface, weight, stretch, and 
alignment are selected randomly. However, the weight and stretch are 
chosen within the allowed range for each typeface and as defined by the user. 
The font size is randomly determined within a specified range, and the 
letter case is defined according to user preferences, with the default being 
the mixed case. Typefaces are included in the system through a configu-
ration file that defines the available axis values and the text leading.
The background style and the vertical alignment of the text are also 
selected randomly from the available options unless users have specified 
a particular choice. The background options available are specified in 
a separate configuration file. 
Concerning the colour scheme of posters, if the user does not pre-
define the text and background colour, they are determined based on 
a three  colour scheme generated based on a random seed. The scheme 
is created from a random colour, which is applied to the typography on the 
poster. Based on this colour, it generates the remaining two background 
colours. The main background colour is the complementary colour of the 
random text colour, even if the background styles only use a single colour.111 
The secondary background colour is one of the analogue colours of the 
main background colour.112 To define this colour, a three-colour analogous 
colour scheme is generated based on the main background colour, and one 
of the two analogous colours is selected randomly.
We implemented a contrast checker to ensure the generated colour 
schemes meet a minimum contrast value. When a scheme is generated, 
the system calculates the minimum contrast ratio between all possible 
pairs between the three colours. The contrast ratio is determined by dividing 
the colour pair’s maximum and minimum luminance values. If a scheme 
is created without the proper contrast, a new scheme is generated until 
the criteria are met. Users set the minimum contrast value in the system 
configuration file, with the default value set as 2.5. This contrast checking 
only applies to random colour schemes and is not used for user-defined 
colours. The poster sizes are defined as specified by the users and do 
not change over the evolution. The margins of posters are automatically 
determined based on the minimum predefined values, typography sizes, 
and vertical alignment. Figure 6.34 displays a population of random indi-
viduals created by this system.
6.3.3 VARIA TION OPERA TORS
The poster generation starts with randomly creating a population of posters, 
taking into account user restrictions. Then, we evolve the designs using 
variation operators like crossover and mutation. Next, we describe each 
operator in detail.
111
The complementary colour is the one 
that is located on the opposite side 
of the colour wheel. When two 
complementary colours are used 
together, they create a high 
colour contrast. 
112
An analogous colour is part 
of a group of colours that are located 
next to each other on the colour wheel. 
Analogous colours share a similar 
undertone or hue. 

167
 EVOLUTIONARY  P OSTER  C OMPOSER6
CROSSOVER
The crossover operator creates a new generation by exchanging genetic 
material between two parent individuals. The parents are randomly selected 
using a tournament method with a certain crossover probability. Both 
parents are chosen from the same tournament through a rank-based SUS 
procedure, reducing the chance of selecting the same individuals.
As in two other evolutionary experiments, we employ a uniform 
crossover (Syswerda, 1989), randomly deciding which parent will pass 
down genetic material to the descendant. This way, the background style 
and vertical alignment genes, all text boxes, and images on the new indi -
vidual are flipped to determine which parent will pass down its character-
istics to the offspring. The text boxes and images are transferred to the 
offspring with all their characteristics intact.
We introduced a method to ensure that crossover maintains the con-
trast of the colour palette. Thus, it randomly selects which parent must 
provide the colour scheme globally to the descendant poster, regardless 
of which parent gives the gene.
After the crossover, the margins of new individuals are calculated 
based on the size of the text boxes, vertical alignment, and the predefined 
minimum margin size. This operator does not crossover static values 
on the genotype, such as the content of each text box, the image source, 
and the poster size.
MUTATION
The mutation operator is designed to introduce random variations into 
the genotype. For each individual in the new offspring, it decides if an 
attribute will be changed based on a certain probability. As a result, the 
same individual can have different parts of its genotype mutated, including 
within the same text box. The mutation operation varies depending on 
the attribute being changed. The operators are designed to cover the entire 
search space and only affect attributes the users did not predefine. 
When the background style or vertical alignment is selected for 
mutation, the operator randomly chooses another option between the 
available ones. The process for colour mutation is global. If a colour (either 
for typography or the background) is chosen for mutation, a new colour 
scheme is generated and applied to all colours not predefined by the user.

III DESIGNING  AUTOMA TICALL Y
The mutation can change all text box and image attributes except 
text content or source. When the alignment or the typeface attributes are 
selected, the current value is replaced with one from the available options. 
When selected, the weight and vertical motion of the typeface are defined 
based on the range of available options for the selected typeface. In the case 
of the font size of the text box, it adjusts the size based on random values 
within a specific range, typically between -5 and 5. This range can be con-
figured in the system configuration file. Image features (position and scale) 
also can be mutated. In these cases, a new random value within the avail-
able range is assigned to the selected feature for mutation.
6.3.4 EVALUA TION CRITERIA 
The generated outputs are evaluated based on their ability to effectively 
display the contents and their overall quality in terms of visual language. 
In this experiment, we refine the three evaluation criteria that were pre-
viously proposed: legibility , aesthetics, and semantics. The overall 
value of each criterion is calculated based on a weighted arithmetic mean 
of a set of measures, which are evaluated on a scale ranging from 0 (poor 
score) to 1 (perfect score). The default weight value for each criterion has 
been established through empirical observations. However, users can adjust 
these weights within the interface to align with their preferences.
LEGIBILITY
The legibility criterion assesses whether the text is fully legible in the 
design. In this experiment, the legibility value of each poster is deter-
mined using two measures: (i) text legibility and (ii) grid appropriateness. 
The overall legibility criterion score (lg) is calculated as the weighted 
arithmetic mean of the two values, formulated as:

The text legibility (lgText) measure evaluates whether all text content 
is entirely placed within the text boxes that compose the poster. It is cal-

The text legibility score of each text box is the difference between the text

AESTHETICS
The aesthetics criterion evaluates the visual and typographic features 
of a design. It is then based on six measures: (i)  alignment,  (ii) balance, 
(iii) justification, (iv) regularity, (v) typeface pairing, and (vi) negative space 
fraction. These measures are an advanced version of our previous work 
from the second experiment, influenced by Steven J. Harrington et al. 
(2004) and the traditional typographic principles outlined by Ellen Lupton 
(2014) and Robert Bringhurst (1997). These measures are assessed on a 
scale from 0 (poor score) to 1 (perfect score). The overall aesthetic score 
(ae) is calculated as a weighted average of all measures, similar to the 
approach used in the second experiment (see Equation 6.8). This is defined

The alignment measure evaluates the consistency of horizontal text 
alignment in two main steps. First, it computes the variance in text width 
between neighbouring text boxes. Then, it calculates the arithmetic mean 
of these variances, using the non-linear constant A that controls how fast 
values fall away from 1 as the distance between entries increases. Second, 
it checks the uniformity of line alignment by dividing 1 (the ideal number 
of line alignments) by the number of different line alignments identified 
on the posters. The overall alignment score is a weighted average, with 
width variance contributing 80% and text alignment contributing 20%. 
This score is subsequently normalised within a range from 0 (high width 
variance and different line alignments) to 1 (low width variance and con-
sistent use of a single line alignment). The formula below summarises this 
calculation:

where Np  represents the number of text boxes in poster p, A is a constant 
that controls how quickly values decrease as the distance between entries 
increases, x(i) is the horizontal position of the text box i, and txtAlign(p) 
is a function that calculates the number of unique text alignments in the 
poster p.
We have further developed the balance measure to assess visual 
balance across different text alignments, rather than just central balance, 
as in the second experiment (see subsection 6.2.4). This estimation involves 
calculating each text box’s visual centres and visual weights. However, the 
visual balance centre of a text box i (vc(i)x and vc(i)y) is determined based 
on its line alignment. For instance, if the text box is left-aligned and ver -
tically aligned to the top, its balance centre is the upper-left corner. When 
the vertical alignment is set to centre, the vertical balance centre position 
is visually adjusted, moving one-twelfth towards the top. The visual weight 
(VW) of a text box is calculated by multiplying its area by its optical density, 
as defined in Equation 6.11 earlier. The centre of the visual weight for the 
entire poster (w(p) x and w(p)y), is then computed, considering all text 
boxes, as described in Equation 6.13.
Subsequently, it estimates the expected balance centre of the design 
(bo(p)x and bo(p) y) employing the same method as used for text boxes, 
considering the alignment of the first text box and the same global vertical 
alignment, albeit taking into consideration the full poster size. The overall 
balance score (bal) is determined by comparing the current and expected 
balance centres and poster sizes, as described following:

The justification measure evaluates whether the text fully occupies 
the available space. It is inspired by the traditional aesthetics of nineteenth-
-century letterpress posters, where text was justified using all available 
space. The calculation of this measure is like the text legibility. The overall 
justification score is determined as the arithmetic mean of the justification 
scores of all text boxes. The justification score of a text box is calculated 
by considering the variance between the text width of each text box and 
the available space. The variance value is  normalised, penalising both 
designs with text overflowing and excessive white space. The penalty is 
lower when text fully fits within the poster, being divided by a factor. A lower 
variance results in a higher justification score. A justification score (just) 
of 1 indicates zero width variance, while if the variance doubles the design 
width, the justification is set to 0, as explained below:

The regularity measures how regular the text boxes’ heights are. 
It measures the distances between the vertical positions of the top edges in

constant A to determine the rate at which values decrease as the distance

typefaces used on the poster, considering their categories on typographic 
classification, e.g. serif, mono-space, sans-serif, etc. A design with a high 
typeface pairing score should use typefaces that belong to the same type

tional parts of the content in layout, typography, and visuals. In this sense,

The semantic significance of the layout measure evaluates whether text 
lines that contain more emotional charge are appropriately highlighted 
in the layout. The greater the emotional charge on a line, the higher the line 
of text should be on the design. This calculation is done at the line (or text 
box) level. So, for each text box, it calculates the distance between its height 
and the height in the optimal layout, represented as a percentage of the 
poster’s total height. This measure can operate in two modes: Fixed and 
Relative. In the Fixed mode, it considers that content must fulfil the total 
poster available height. In Relative mode, it only considers the current 
height of the composition, ignoring the empty space. By default, it operates 
in Fixed mode. The overall score for the semantic significance of the layout

It calculates variations in weight, stretch, and type design across fonts

The score for the variable typographic features (weight and stretch)

and expected values. These distances are normalised between 0 (maximum

the recognised emotional levels in the content. The text box with the

no distance. Finally, for each text box, the distance between the current
