6.3.5 FITNESS ASSIGNMENT
We have implemented a multi-criteria evaluation strategy and constraint-
-handling techniques to evaluate the outputs. These techniques ensure that 
the system generates valid posters with legible content. However, a good 
poster must fully satisfy the aesthetics and semantics criteria, with each 
of these criterion carrying a different weight in the evaluation, as summa-
rised below:
)6.49  ( 
where ae(p) and se(p) represent the aesthetic and semantic score for 
the poster p , and w1  and w2 are the weights assigned to ae(p) and se(p), 
respectively. We have set the default evaluation weight to distribute equally 
across two criteria. Nevertheless, users have the flexibility to adjust the 
weight of each criterion in the interface.
In this experiment, we implemented a rank-based selection method. 
This process involves ranking individuals according to both constraint values 
(legibility) and an objective fitness function (aesthetics and semantics). 

176
III DESIGNING  AUTOMA TICALL Y
We used a stochastic ranking approach (Runarsson & Yao, 2000) that 
combines a constraints penalty function and rank-based selection. This 
method arranges the population by comparing adjacent individuals based 
on their evaluation objective functions while considering constraint vio-
lations. Additionally, it introduces a stochastic element to the ranking 
process, allowing some solutions to receive a favourable rank even if they do 
not fully meet the constraints (see Algorithm 6.4). The selection of indi -
viduals is then based on this resulting ranking, following the method 
proposed by James E. Baker (1985).
We employ an elitist process, where the best individuals from the 
current generation are combined with the new offspring. This way, we also 
employ a static penalty function to allow alternative fitness assessments 
of individuals. This function subtracts the constraint value from the objec-
tive evaluation value. Beyond supporting elitism, this alternative fitness 
approach is also used to sort individuals in the interface.
Algorithm 6.4. Pseudocode for the stochastic ranking approach used 
in these experiments.
1: objectiveFProbability = 0.45
2: FOR i IN population DO
3:  FOR j IN population-1 DO
4:   individual1 = population[j]
5:   individual2 = population[j+1]
6:   IF random(0,1) <= objectiveFProbability THEN
7:     IF individual1.objectiveValue > individual2.objectiveValue THEN
8:     SWAP  population[ j] WITH population[ j + 1]
9:    ELSE IF individual1.constraints > individual2.constraints THEN
10:     SWAP  population[ j] WITH population[ j+1]
11:  IF no swap was done in this iteration THEN
12:   BREAK
6.3.6 EXPERIMENT AL EVALUA TION
We conducted evolutionary experiments using the proposed system to 
automatically evolve typographic posters using different texts. These 
experiments were divided into three different stages: (s1) evolving only 
considering semantic criterion; (s2) evolving only considering aesthetic 
criterion; and (s3) evolving considering both criteria, with equal weight 
on each criterion evaluation.
The default weights of each criterion in the objective function are set 
based on empirical observations, aiming to create poster designs inspired by 
the aesthetics of nineteenth-century letterpress posters. Table 6.10 displays 
the weight assigned to each measure in both the semantic and aesthetic 
groups. Due to its subjective nature, in these evaluation experiments, we do 
not consider the evaluation of the semantic significance of the visuals measure. 

177 EVOLUTIONARY  P OSTER  C OMPOSER6
This way, colours and background styles are not considered in the evalu -
ation, and we evolve posters mostly in black and white using a solid back-
ground style. Nevertheless, we also evolved some colourised posters to 
assess the contrast of the colours applied in the outputs.
We conducted the experiments on the client side of a Chromium web 
browser. We loaded eight OTVFs, all of which have weight and stretch 
axes available. The experimental parameters for these experiments were 
empirically defined and are summarised in Table 6.11. In the three evalu -
ation stages, we generated typographic posters for 20 different texts in three 
languages (English, Portuguese, and French). These texts expressed various 
purposes, emotional contexts, and lengths. On average, each input text con-
tained 39.55 characters, divided into 7.15 words, with a maximum of 83 char-
acters and a minimum of 17. The average text line length was 4.15 lines. 
The selected texts, apart from being neutral, were classified by representing 
emotions such as anticipation, disgust, joy, sadness, surprise, and trust. 
Tables 6.12 and 6.13 describe the characteristics of the input text and the type-
faces used in these evaluation experiments.

6.35), we observed that the proposed approach leads to a faster reduction 
in the number of individuals that do not comply with the legibility con-
straints, either in the best individuals or the population average. Individ-
uals evaluated with maximum fitness are present in the population but 
are not legible. A detailed analysis of the grid appropriateness measure 
reveals that the proposed approach can consistently generate and maintain 
individuals who use valid grids. On the other hand, the evolution of text 
legibility is inversely proportional to the constraint penalty value. The 
results also reveal that the fittest individuals at the end of evolution are 
always individuals with all text legible.
The evolution based on the semantic criteria (s1) reveals that 
the evaluated measures (significance of layout and typography) can guide 
the evolution of posters towards designs where the more emotional parts 
of the content are highlighted. The experimental results (see Figure 6.36) 
unveil that the best individual in the population achieves high fitness values 
and scores in both measures. However, the values of the measures stabilise 
after a dozen generations, primarily due to the legibility constraints. 
These constraints restrict the semantic evolution of certain individuals, 

180
III DESIGNING  AUTOMA TICALL Y
as they compromise legibility. In this context, some individuals with high 
semantic scores are not fully legible designs. We also noted that the evolu-
tion of the semantic significance of layout is slightly faster than typography.
The evaluation results reveal that the generated outputs exhibit 
certain parts of the content that are emphasised in terms of layout, typog-
raphy, or both (see Figure 6.37a). This emphasis is primarily directed 
toward the more emotional sections of the content. However, we noted 
that when the emphasis affects both typography and layout, it can sometimes 
become excessive, leading to a visually heavy impact, particularly in designs 
with fewer emotional variations. Additionally, specific design issues were 
observed in the outputs, including non -uniform alignment, unbalanced 
layout, or excessive use of different typefaces.
The outcomes of the aesthetics criteria evolution (s2) indicate that 
it is possible to evolve designs complying with the proposed aesthetic  
measures. Nonetheless, these results also reveal the challenge of evolving 
designs that fulfil all the measures simultaneously. The findings demonstrate 
that the performance of measures depends on the text content, and the 
necessity for legibility limits the range of aesthetic design possibilities.
Results reveal that global fitness increases faster in the initial gener-
ations but slows down as the constraint penalty decreases (see Figure 6.38).

We noted that several individuals in the population achieve higher aesthetic 
evaluation than the best individuals in the population, but they are not legible 
posters. When examining the score of each measure individually, regularity, 
alignment, and typographic pairing progressively increase over the generation, 
both in the fittest individuals and population average. These findings suggest 
that enhancing these measures does not compromise the legibility of the 
posters. On the other hand, balance, justification, and negative space fraction 
maintain relatively stable scores over the generations, with slight decreases 
in scores on the best individuals, while legibility and other aesthetic  
measures increase. The justification score of the best individual was, on 
average, below the population average. Further experimentation is necessary 
to understand how other measures and experimental parameters impact 
their evaluation. However, high scores on these measures result in the cre-

subsequently removed from the population. Due to this, legibility meas-

The visual analysis of the outputs (see Figure 6.37b) reveals that, even 
though they are created with the same input texts, the generated posters 
are more balanced and regular in typographical terms compared with s1  
outputs. Nonetheless, we noticed that in some outputs, less meaningful 
parts of the content are typographically highlighted (e.g. conjunctions), 
making the content more difficult to read.
The results of the evolution combining both aesthetic and semantic 
criteria (s3) indicate that optimising all measures simultaneously is chal-
lenging, as design possibilities are influenced by the text content and its 
emotional impact. The experimental results exhibit an evolutionary pattern 
akin to the two other experiments: faster evolution in early generations 
followed by gradual stabilisation as the constraint penalty values decrease 
(see Figure 6.39). However, we noted that there are individuals with higher 
fitness values in the population, yet they are not legible.
The analysis of the evolution of semantic measures separately 
reveals that their combined evaluation with aesthetic measures presents 
challenges to evolving semantic measures, being constrained by the other 
aesthetic measures. Regarding the significance of layout, this experiment 
indicates that it is restricted by aesthetic measures, showing a relatively 
flat trajectory, with the fittest individuals and the population average 
achieving similar values. The evolution of the significance of typography,  
although exhibiting some improvement in the early generations, stabilises 
faster and remains below the scores achieved in the s1  experiment. The 
results of aesthetic measures resemble the results of s2. Alignment, reg-
ularity, and typographic pairing progressively increase over the generations,

6.4  FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS
We presented our research involving the sequential development of three 
experiments that used a GA to generate poster designs. These designs are 
primarily composed of typography based on user-provided content. The 
proposed approaches are inspired by the traditional design processes 
of nineteenth -century print houses. During that era, typographers often 
worked closely with clients, selecting and typesetting designs with the goal 
of visually emphasising the most important parts of the content while 
attempting to fill all the available space.
while balance, justification, and negative space fraction maintain relatively 
stable scores, seemingly constrained in their progress by legibility criteria. 
We observed a slight evolution of justification scores, which appear to be 
related to the inclusion of semantic measures and the exploration of 
layouts that are not highly valued by other aesthetic measures but, from 
a semantic perspective, are considered superior and enable improved 
content justification.
The visual analysis of the outputs (see Figure 6.37c) reveals an 
increase in the value of aesthetic features compared to s1. Simultaneously, 
it is possible to observe the emphasis on parts with more emotional weight, 
whether through layout or typeface selection, compared to s2. However, 
this emphasis in certain designs should be more pronounced in  some 
posters than others.
Visually observing the results, when their colour scheme and back-
ground style are defined at random (see Figure 6.40), we observed that 
the developed contrast checker enables the colourisation of designs, 
ensuring that the colours pair well with each other and ensuring that poster 
content is legible regardless the background style or colour.

184
III DESIGNING  AUTOMA TICALL Y
Recognising the limitations of existing work in IEC and the automatic 
evolution of designs, we proposed methods that enable users to interac-
tively guide the evolution by expressing their preferences. This approach 
allows users to influence the evolution as it unfolds automatically, which 
we consider results in a more time-efficient and user-friendly process.
The three presented experiments follow a similar workflow in which 
users input content. Subsequently, the system generates a random popula-
tion of poster designs and then evolves these designs, taking into account 
the users’ preferences. We define a set of initial preferences for each exper-
iment based on our empirical observation of the results. Users can further 
customise these preferences using configuration files or an interface.
The first experiment uses a GA to evolve black -and-white typographic 
designs from a user-given text string. In this experiment, users can guide 
the evolutionary process by interactively expressing their typographic 
preferences, specifically regarding horizontal motion and weight. To fitness 
assign the population, we employ a hardwired fitness assignment strategy 
that considers three criteria: (i) layout, which evaluates the effective use 
of space on the canvas; (ii) legibility, which assesses the legibility of text 
on the poster; and (iii) typography, which measures if the chosen typefaces 
align with the user’s typographic preferences.
We conducted an experimental evaluation with this approach to 
determine if it can create fully legible posters and whether user preferences 
influence the evolution of poster designs. The testing results unveil that 
the system can generate legible designs from scratch and that user -expressed 
preferences are noticeable in the results, particularly when these prefer -
ences do not compromise the creation of legible designs.
The second experiment also utilises a GA to generate typographic 
posters from user-provided textual content. However, this experiment 
encompasses a broader expressive power, evaluation methods, and content 
analysis strategies. In this experiment, users can express their desired 
visual preferences and define the range of possible visual variations in the 
outputs through a specific interface and a set of configuration files. 
We have developed a method to automate the selection of the most 
emotional parts of the content, which we decided must be highlighted 
in the design. Also, it allows for a prior definition of the range of visual 
features of the outputs. This method uses a lexicon-based method to rec-
ognise colours, emotions, and sentiments in the input text content. Based 
on the emotional and sentiment analysis, we predict which parts of the text 
are the most important. It also automates the division of the text into lines. 
The designs are evaluated based on three criteria:  (i) legibility , 
which assesses the text’s legibility on the poster; (ii) aesthetics, which 
assesses the aesthetic features of the poster; and (iii) semantics, which 
evaluates if the poster visuals align with the input analysis. Each criterion 
considers a set of distinctive design measures. We have also developed 
three separate automatic strategies for evaluating outputs. These strategies 
include a multi-criteria hardwired fitness function, a multi-objective opti-
misation approach, and a hybrid strategy that incorporates elements from 
both strategies. The system allows the mixed use of these evaluation 
strategies in the same evolutionary run.

185
 EVOLUTIONARY  P OSTER  C OMPOSER6
We experiment with this system to study its behaviour and ability 
to evolve posters for different text contents, with different lengths and pur-
poses, using the different evaluation strategies developed. The results 
showed that the multi-criteria hardwired and hybrid strategies effectively 
generated finished posters, producing similar outputs. The hybrid strategy 
demonstrated slightly better visual diversity and legibility evaluation 
results. Conversely, the multi-criteria hardwired strategy performs better 
in semantic evaluation and convergence speed. In contrast, the multi-
-objective optimisation strategy generates unstable populations and does 
not ensure the creation of legible posters. 
Furthermore, we adapted this system to create an autonomous poster 
generator tool that works with content retrieved online from Twitter, using 
the hybrid evaluation strategy. The results demonstrate that our proposed 
approach can autonomously generate visually diverse and legible posters.
In the third experiment, we further iterate the second experiment 
by presenting a GA for generating poster designs. We also refine evaluation 
criteria, input analysis methods, and the evolutionary process. Thus, in this 
experiment, we evolve poster designs that can be both composed of text 
and imagery provided by the user. The generated outputs are evaluated 
according to the same three criteria but include new evaluation measures. 
The fitness of the candidate poster solutions is assigned utilising a sto-
chastic ranking method which handles constrained evolution by combining 
a hardwired fitness assignment strategy ( aesthetics  and semantics  
criteria) with a penalty function strategy (legibility criterion). In this 
system, users can also restrict the search space of GA by defining the 
variables for a visual generation and adapting the parameters of the evo-
lutionary process.
We experiment with this system to study the system behaviour 
and features of the resulting designs and the different impacts of aesthetics 
and semantics in the objective evaluation function. Despite their prelim-
inary nature, these experiments demonstrate our proposed evolutionary 
approach’s effectiveness in generating legible poster designs and evaluation 
measures to guide the evolution of poster designs for diverse text contents. 
However, evolving multiple measures simultaneously in this constrained 
setting can limit some measures’ progression. This way, further exploration 
is needed to understand individual measures’ progression and their inter-
play with legibility constraints.
The findings of the three experiments reveal the potential of EC in 
supporting GD tasks. The results demonstrated that GAs are capable of 
generating fully finished designs from scratch. Due to its stochastic opti-
misation nature, the results also indicate its capability to assist with both 
automation and discovery tasks. We consider that these evolutionary 
approaches encourage serendipity in visual exploration processes, enabling 
designers to explore numerous design variations and visual contexts 
simultaneously. Also, the experiments reveal that complementary methods 
can be used to automate various design tasks and routines, such as line 
division or colour generation.

186
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
The findings further suggest that the mechanisms for users to express 
their preferences and guide the evolution enable them to overcome some 
limitations of fully automatic evolution while avoiding the potential fatigue 
associated with traditional manual and interactive design techniques. 
Our experiments suggest that evolutionary approaches hold promise 
for commercial applications, both for generating final outputs and inte-
grating with other systems and techniques. Nevertheless, we observed that 
defining the search space and establishing appropriate evaluation criteria 
can be a complex and challenging task impacting the results’ visual quality. 
However, further testing is needed to draw definitive conclusions, especially 
with users.
Although these experiments present promising results for design 
generation, we highlight the need for future research to evaluate measures 
separately, including subjective and personal assessments. We also consider 
it important to experiment with larger populations and varied experimental 
settings, as well as to conduct evaluations involving participants and ad 
hoc testing with design experts. Additionally, phenological testing is needed 
to understand the impact of fitness assignments on the designs.
In summary, the experiment unveils the potential of EC to ease and 
speed up the creative processes in the GD field by offering daily support 
and automation for the tasks of graphic designers, including the ones 
related to visual discovery and production.

187
 III DESIGNING  AUTOMA TICALL Y
This chapter presents our work on developing a greedy computational 
approach to typesetting. Our main goal is to create an automatic method 
to rapidly typeset text based on predefined features. 
The proposed method is based on a local search approach. It starts 
by generating an initial solution, where text boxes are placed with random 
sizes and features. The method then iteratively adjusts these features. 
If the new design is an improvement, it replaces the previous one. This 
process continues until the entire text is fully legible, at which point it stops. 
Although we primarily used this method for generating posters, it can also 
be used to typeset designs of various sizes and formats. Figure 7.1 displays 
several poster designs created using this method.
We developed an automatic generative method for posters to support 
experimentation with this approach. The method uses a neural NLP tech-
nique to detect the emotional tone of the text content. This emotional 
data, combined with information from configuration files, defines the 
visual features of the posters, such as background style and typeface.

The text is automatically divided into lines, and the greedy approach is

this method is focused on emotion recognition, it can be adapted for other 
purposes by employing different classification models and updating the 
corresponding configuration files.
Beyond automatically generating posters, we explored this approach 
by developing an online design tool for creating posters and producing 
the public art installation ESSYS* Sharing #UC.
The tool allows users to interactively create posters with short text 
messages through a user interface. The user interface is designed in col-
laboration with a group of Portuguese upper-secondary students, around 
15 years old, from Escola Secundária José Falcão (ESJF) in Coimbra, Por-
tugal. This collaborative design process took place over seven workshop 
sessions titled Pedir a Palavra. 114 The primary motivation behind this 
collaboration was to create and evaluate a tool that helps people, especially 
young individuals, share their messages and thoughts. 
During the workshop sessions, participants used the interface to 
generate posters or create base designs, which were later combined with 
other techniques to produce the final posters. Figure 7.2 presents some of 
the posters created during these workshops.

On the other hand, the public media art installation ESSYS* Sharing 
#UC is designed to reflect on a city’s online identity through content shared 
about it. In the installation space, visitors can view a collection of posters 
automatically generated by the proposed greedy approach, featuring mes-
sages posted on Twitter about Coimbra. The visual features of these designs 
are determined based on the emotional context recognised in the messages.
The installation has a hybrid nature, being accessible in both online 
and physical forms. In the physical space, visitors can see a selection of 
posters alongside an ever-changing sonic composition created by the ESSYS 
system (Seiça et al., 2018) based on the same emotional context. On the 
other hand, the online version displays posters generated in real time. The 
online installation is also presented on a television screen within the phys-
ical installation. Visitors can indirectly interact with the installation through 
their tweets. ESSYS* Sharing #UC  was developed for the Francisco Tropa 
MUSEU gallery at the Círculo de Artes Plásticas de Coimbra (CAPC), Por-
tugal, and was exhibited from August 2021 to December 2021. Figure 7.3 
shows the installation space.

189
 GREEDY  T YPESETTING  A PPROACH7
We also conducted a study to evaluate the outputs generated by the 
proposed approach, focusing on their communication value, how they are 
perceived, and their potential use in other commercial contexts. The eval-
uation was divided into two parts. First, we experimented with this method, 
generating outputs for different text types and evaluating its performance 
and ability to automatically create posters for various text content. Second, 
we conducted interview-based evaluation sessions with 12 individuals to 
understand their perceptions of the designs regarding expressiveness and 
creativity. During these sessions, we also discussed possible future appli-
cations of the method in different commercial scenarios.
The following sections provide a detailed description of the approach, 
along with the experiments and evaluation sessions conducted.
7.1 APPROACH
The proposed approach uses a greedy method to generate typographic 
designs. It involves two main steps: defining the posters’ visual features; 
and typesetting the content. 
Figure 7.3. Photography of physical 
installation of ESSYS* Sharing #UC  at 
CAPC. 2021. © CAPC. Photography by 
Jorge das Neves.

190
III DESIGNING  AUTOMA TICALL Y
The visual features are automatically defined using mappings stored 
in configuration files. We developed a method that analyses input content 
with a neural NLP emotion recognition technique and assigns visual fea-
tures based on these results. Users can modify this method to accommo-
date different classification results by employing other recognition techniques 
and updating the configuration files accordingly. This approach is developed 
using web technologies.
The generation process consists of three sequential methods. First, 
the input processing method analyses the text content to detect its emo-
tional tone. Next, the styling method determines the visual characteristics 
of the designs based on the data from the input processing method. Finally, 
the typesetting method uses the greedy approach to position the text on 
the poster. The following subsections describe each method.
7.1 .1 INPUT PROCESSING METHOD
The input processing method analyses a given text input to identify its 
emotional tone, similar to the input processing global analysis used in 
evolutionary experiments (see Chapter 6). The recognised emotional tone 
is then used to determine the visual features of the design. This method 
also divides the text into lines.
We trained a neural NLP model to identify the emotional intensity 
of text using a corpus based on the emotion-intensity annotated multi-label 
text dataset by Saif M. Mohammad et al. (2018). This dataset categorises 
texts as either neutral or indicative of one or more of 11 distinct emotions: 
anger, anticipation, disgust, fear, joy, love, optimism, pessimism, sadness, 
surprise, and trust, effectively capturing the author’s psychological state. 
The dataset is primarily designed to analyse tweets.
The analysis begins with text preprocessing for classification. If the 
text is not in English, it is translated using the IBM Watson Language 
Translator V3 API. The system then identifies data related to the text, such 
as URLs and emojis (along with their meanings). Considering the utilisa-
tion of this method with tweets in ESSYS* Sharing #UC, it also recognises 
social media features, including user information, retweet data, hashtags, 
and user mentions. The neural network classifies the text, identifies rele-
vant emotions, and assigns intensity scores. Predominant emotions are 
then determined based on a predetermined threshold score. This method 
also subdivides the text into lines using a sentence boundary detection 
algorithm (Reynar & Ratnaparkhi, 1997) and randomly divides lengthy 
sentences according to a predefined optimal word range.
7. 1.2 STYLING METHOD
The styling method defines the visual characteristics of generated posters, 
considering the emotional data from the input processing method and a 
predefined visual mapping stored in configuration files. These files specify 
the range of possible values to features and the mapping between the 
classification outcomes and visual attributes, including colours (specified 
in the colour configuration file) and typefaces (outlined in the typeface 
configuration file).115

191
 GREEDY  T YPESETTING  A PPROACH7
The method begins by selecting the background style for the posters 
using a Roulette Wheel Selection (RWS) method.116 This selection is guided 
by available options, their corresponding probabilities, and the results 
from the input processing method. There are four background styles: 
(i) solid; (ii) diagonally halved; (iii) solid divided; and (iv) gradient. The solid 
divided  style is used only when two or more emotions are recognised. 
The other styles can be selected for any classification result. If no emotion 
is recognised ( i.e. the content is neutral), the text is displayed in black on 
a white background. These background styles are specified in a namespace 
(or package), allowing for the development of new styles in the future. 
Figure 7.4 provides an overview of these background styles. 
For the colour schemes in these background styles, colours are 
selected using an RWS method that considers a predefined range of colours 
and their associated probabilities for each classification result. Black and 
white are used as neutral colours. Also, a legibility checker ensures that 
the selected colours (both for typography and background) meet specific 
criteria and do not compromise the poster’s legibility.
The solid style involves colourising the background with a single 
solid colour. Initially, the background colour is selected from a set of 
colours associated with the predominant classification result, plus white. 
The selection probability of white colour was empirically defined at 10%. 
The typography colour is then determined. If white is selected for the 
background, the typography colour is chosen from the set of colours asso-
ciated with classification results, similar to the background colour selection 
process. Otherwise, if the background is not white, the typography colour 
is selected from either a neutral colour or a colour related to the second 
most predominant classification result if such a result exists. The proba-
bility of choosing a non-neutral typography colour increases when the 
intensity scores of the two classification results are similar. The closer the 
classification results are, the higher the chance of using a colour related 
to the second most recognised emotion for the typography. If there is no 
secondary classification result, a neutral colour is chosen for the typography.

method that selects options based 
on predefined probabilities, in this case,

It is commonly used in evolutionary 
approaches for selecting individuals 
for breeding, taking into consideration 
their fitness scores. Briefly, it treats 
each individual as a slide of a roulette 
wheel, where the size of each slice 
is proportional to the individual’s 
fitness. John Holland (1992) provides 
a comprehensive overview of this method.

III DESIGNING  AUTOMA TICALL Y
The diagonally halved style involves creating a background compo-
sition with two diagonal triangles. The process starts by randomly selecting 
one of the triangles and colourising it with a colour corresponding to the 
primary classification result from the input processing. Next, the other 
triangle is colourised either with white or a colour related to the second 
most predominant classification result if such a result exists.Typography 
colour is defined as white or black, according to the saturation of the 
selected background colours.
As with other styles, the probability of choosing a non-white colour 
increases when the scores of the two results are closer. If only one classi-
fication result is recognised, the second triangle is coloured white.
The solid divided style creates a composition of rectangles that visually 
represent the classification results of the input text. The height of each 
rectangle corresponds to the classification scores, which are translated 
into percentages of the poster’s height. The filling colour of each rectangle 
is determined using the same mapping method as in other styles. Typog-
raphy colour is limited to black or white to ensure the poster’s legibility. 
The gradient style is analogous to the solid divided style; however, 
instead of colourising rectangles with solid colour, it employs a linear 
colour gradient. Also, it creates a full-height rectangle coloured with a 
gradient of the selected colour to white whenever only one classification 
result is obtained. The position of the gradient endpoint (the white one) 
is placed in the last vertical quarter of the poster, mapped according to 
the classification score, i.e. the higher score near the bottom edge is the 
end of the gradient.
The selection of the poster’s typeface is also based on the classifi-
cation results, according to a predefined set of typefaces defined in the 
typeface configuration file. This file specifies the distribution percentages 
for each typeface according to the classification result. An RWS method 
is employed to choose a typeface, relying on the classification results 
and the selection probabilities outlined beforehand. Additionally, text 
alignment (e.g. right, centre, or left) and text box alignment (e.g. top, middle, 
or bottom) are determined randomly. Figure 7.5 illustrates the correlation 
between typical emotional data and generated posters’ background, colour 
and typographic styles.
7. 1.3 TYPESETTING METHOD
The typesetting method composes the posters using an iterative greedy 
approach to modify the visual features of an OTVF with multiple axes. 
The typesetting procedure begins by creating a grid with the same size as 
the poster with one column and the same number of rows as the computed 
line division. The text lines are positioned into text boxes according to 
the grid’s rows. Consequently, the text leading is defined as the height 
of the rows. The text size is computed based on the leading, looking at a pre-
defined relationship between the text leading and the size for the selected 
typeface. This relationship is outlined in the typeface configuration file. 
By adhering to this procedure, the method ensures the incorporation 

193
 GREEDY  T YPESETTING  A PPROACH7
of traditional leading adjustments based on size, as documented in foun-
dational typography literature, exemplified by works like Robert Bringhurst 
(1997). Subsequently, it verifies whether all the text lines are rendered 
inside of the poster; if so, the generation is finished. Otherwise, if any lines 
extend beyond the poster’s boundaries, it randomly selects an operator to 
change the visual features of the employed typeface. To do that, we devel-
oped two operators: (i) size modifier; and (ii) axis modifier. Both operators 
change the visual features of all text lines. When the selected typeface 
has no variation axes, it only employs the size modifier. This last step is 
repeated until all text lines are rendered within the poster or a high number 
of attempts is achieved.117
The size modifier operator decreases the typeface size in a certain 
increment value. This value is determined based on a predefined range 
for each typeface, which increases along with the number of attempts; in 
other words, as the number of attempts to compose the poster increases, 
the size decreases. When this operator is employed, the grid’s row heights 
are adjusted according to the new text size, and the grid margins increase 
based on the present text box alignment. This operator can be applied 
until a minimum row height is achieved.
117

this procedure is available at

uploads/2021/09/typesseter-video-
demonstrations.mp4  
(visited: 7 July 2025).

III DESIGNING  AUTOMA TICALL Y
The axis modifier  operator adjusts the value on a typeface’s axis. 
By default, it modifies two axes: stretch and weight. However, it can also 
handle other axes when they are defined in the configuration file. The axis 
to be modified is randomly chosen among the available options. The stretch 
axis ranges between a maximum value (default is ultra-expanded or 200%) 
and a minimum value (default is extra-condensed or 50%). When this axis 
is modified, its value decreases in a font-stretch keyword value (i.e. around 
16.6%). The weight axis can range between 950 (Extra Black) and 100 (Thin). 
Whenever this axis is modified, its value decreases by 10. 
The axes’ values are reset to their defaults once they reach a minimum, 
and the size has been changed at least four times since the last axis mod-
ification. When a customised axis is selected for modification, it starts from 
a randomly chosen initial value and is decreased by a predefined increment. 
Algorithm 7.1 provides a summary of this method.
Algorithm 7.1. Pseudocode for the proposed greedy algorithm used in typesetting.
1:  Import settings (such as width, height, maxAttempts, and minRowHeight) 
from the file.
2: Define the typeface and its features as specified by the styling method.
3: Define content as input text split into lines.
4: Define grid with one column and rows equal to the number of content lines.
5: Define fontsize to the default value from settings.
6: Define grid row heights as fontsize plus leading (specified in settings).
7: Render content into text boxes using the grid layout, typeface, and fontsize.
8: Define currentHeight as the sum of row heights in the grid.
9: Define maxWidth as the content's maximum width.
10: attemptCount = 0.
11: sizeModifierCount = 0.
12:  WHILE currentHeight > height OR maxWidth > width OR 
attemptCount > maxAttempts DO:
13:  IF random(0, 1) > 0.5 AND the typeface has variable axes THEN:
14:   Define axis as a random axis from typeface to modify.
15:   Decrement the axis value by 10.
16:   sizeModifierCount = 0.
17:  ELSE:
18:   Define decrement based on attemptCount and typeface settings.
19:   fontsize -= decrement.
20:   Update the row height in the grid.
21:   Increment sizeModifierCount.
22:  IF sizeModifierCount >= 4 OR axis value is at minimum THEN:
23:   Set the axis value to its default value.
24:   Render content into text boxes using the grid layout, typeface, 
and fontsize.
25:  Redefine currentHeight and maxWidth.
26:  Increment attemptCount.

7.2 TOOL
We have developed an online tool that allows people to create designs 
using this proposed greedy typesetting approach. This tool streamlines 
the design process by allowing users to input their own textual and imagery 
content. Accessible through a standard web browser, it offers an accessible 
and user-friendly way for generating computational designs on nearly any 
digital device.
Our motivation for creating this tool was to allow people without 
access to design software or design education to easily create their own 
designs, particularly for personal use. To do that, we defined a set of visual 
variables that characterise the output designs. Next, we developed a tool 
that allows users to adjust these visual and typography characteristics to 
their preferences. Users can export the final outputs for immediate use or 
further refine them using other design software. The tool uses only the 
proposed typesetting method and does not include emotional analysis for 
defining visual features. The visual features are not automated and are 
entirely set by users.
We conducted workshop sessions to define the visual variables and 
constraints of this tool. We selected participants who were highly familiar 
with digital media and regularly used computer devices, whether portable 
or stationary, for communication, entertainment, and visual creation. In 
this sense, we organised a series of seven workshop sessions with 27 Por-
tuguese upper-secondary students, around 15 years old, from the 10th year 
of the visual arts course at ESJF in Coimbra, Portugal. Each session lasted 
90 minutes. 
We consider that, as digital natives with no formal education in GD, 
these participants are likely to go beyond traditional interactions with 
design software tools and offer innovative methods for creating visuals. 
We were also motivated to develop a tool that would empower individuals 
to create designs that amplify their voices and facilitate the dissemination 
of their ideas. As a result, we focused on gathering requirements and gen-
erating poster designs for social and cultural activism, providing an oppor-
tunity to collectively envision the future needs and constraints of social 
and cultural activism. 
These workshop sessions were named Pedir a Palavra and were part 
of the educational project of Convento São Francisco in Coimbra, within the 
context of the exhibition Primaveras Estudantis: da crise de 1962 ao 25 de Abril 
and in the commemorations of the 50 th anniversary of  the Portuguese 
Carnation Revolution. Since one of the focuses of these sessions was fos-
tering collective discussions about the role of posters in social activism, 
these sessions began with examining and reflecting on the strategic impor-
tance of posters during the student protests against the Portuguese dic-
tatorship in the 1960s in the cities of Lisbon and Coimbra. Álvaro Garrido 
(2022) provides a comprehensive overview of the exhibition and the his-
torical context of these student protests. 
The workshop sessions were structured into three stages. The initial 
stage, which included the first three sessions, focused on conducting 
brainstorming sessions to identify the tool’s requirements. The second 

196III DESIGNING  AUTOMA TICALL Y
stage, consisting of two sessions, was centred around collaboratively 
defining, evaluating, and refining the tool’s interface. In the final stage, 
consisting of the two last sessions, we evaluated the outputs by generating 
poster designs with two purposes: creating posters only with the tool or 
using the tool to create a starting point for the generation of new designs. 
Figures 7.6 to 7.8 document the workshops.
We began the initial workshop sessions by defining what a poster is, 
presenting its historical characteristics, and discussing how posters connect 
with recent technological advances and to the participants’ personal expe-
riences. This way, we discussed various poster examples with participants, 
examining both their technical aspects and sociocultural context. We began 
this discussion by presenting examples of cultural and social activism 
posters, with a particular focus on those originating from the student 
protests of Coimbra in 1969 (examples that were part of the exhibition 
that provided the context for workshops). At the end of each session in 
this conceptualisation stage, we conducted brainstorming sessions to 
define a list of characteristics a poster must include and, consequently, 
the features the tool should allow users to modify (see Figure 7.8). Subse-
quently, we encouraged the participants to select poster examples and 
perform a similar discussion on these chosen designs. We then collabora-
tively designed several “handmade posters” to evaluate whether the defined 
characteristics met the participants’ needs (see Figure 7.9). This first stage 
lasted for three sessions. After each of these sessions, we reanalysed and 
updated the tool features list, aligning it with the characteristics and pref-
erences observed in the posters created by the participants. Figure 7.10 
presents the final set of features that poster designs created by the tool 
must present.
Next, during the second stage, we developed the tool and organised 
sessions to enhance and refine its functionalities and design iteratively. 
In these sessions, we demonstrated the tool and requested participants to 
explore and use it freely. Throughout their interaction, we closely observed 
their behaviour, inquiring about any challenges or problems they encoun-
tered while creating their designs. Participants used various computing 
devices to interact with the tool, including smartphones, tablets, and 
laptops. Figures 7.11 and 7.12 provide visual records of participants using 
the tool at this stage. At the end of each session, we organised a brief group 
discussion, where we presented and reviewed the identified interface issues 
and collectively comprehended the reasons behind them. We then compiled 
a list of issues to address and evaluate in the upcoming sessions. Among 
the resolved issues from these discussions were the incorporation of images 
into the project, increasing the size of the poster visualisation in the tool, 
and fixing bugs and minor technical problems.

Figure 7.13 displays screenshots of the final interface that has been 
developed. The interface is divided into three sections, each dedicated to 
defining specific characteristics of the generated visuals.
The first section focuses on defining the text content and the general 
features of the poster designs (see Figure 7.13b). In this section, users can 
input text, determine the poster size, specify text alignment, and select the 
background visual style. To input text, users must use a specific delimiter 
to define text lines (default as semicolon). The poster size is set as a per-
centage of the width, with the ratio automatically updated whenever a new 
size is selected, considering that the width is always 1. Alignment options 
include top, centre, and bottom, while background visual styles offer three 
choices: solid colour; gradient between two colours; and a halved triangular 
shape with two distinct colours. Users can also choose colours for these 
styles. Furthermore, this section allows users to toggle the visibility of the 
grid and text container and adjust the size of the poster visualisation. 
Changes to the poster’s size, general alignment, and text content trigger a 
new run of the typesetting method. Users modify these features through 
text inputs, dropdown menus, and checkboxes.
The second section of the interface allows users to individually modify 
each text box in the generated poster after its creation (see Figure 7.13c). 
Each line in the generated output corresponds to a separate text box. Users 
can select each of these text boxes and modify them in a specific panel. In 
this section, users can adjust various visual and typographic attributes, 
such as the text case, text line alignment, font weight, horizontal motion, 
and size. These adjustments can be made within predefined ranges based 
on the employed typeface using sliders, checkboxes, and text inputs. The 
interface also enables the selection and collective modification of multiple 
text boxes. Users can use this feature by opening one text box and checking 
the respective checkbox on other text boxes. This way, the transformations 
are applied synchronously across all selected text boxes.

199
 GREEDY  T YPESETTING  A PPROACH7
The third section of the interface enables the input of images (see 
Figure 7.13d). Users can upload images and specify their position and size 
in this interface. A grid constrains the placement and size of images, and 
images are automatically cropped based on their centre according to the 
defined size. After uploading an image, users can resize, move, or remove 
it, similar to text boxes. Additionally, users have the option to toggle 
the visibility of a specific grid, which aids in accurately placing images 
on the poster.
This tool also lets users download their final outputs in raster (PNG 
file) and vector (SVG file) formats. Due to the rapid processing of the 
proposed typesetting method, the tool generates designs in real time. As 
a result, user changes are immediately reflected in the output. This applies 
whether a fundamental characteristic is modified, triggering the rerun of 
the greedy typesetting approach, or when a visual adjustment is made.
We evaluated the tool’s capabilities and functionality in the final 
two workshop sessions. This evaluation encompassed two tasks. First, we 
requested participants to create posters only using the tool. Figure 7.14 
presents some of the designs produced by the participants. Second, we 
encouraged participants to use the tool to automate the typesetting of 
posters and combine the generated typographic compositions with illus-
trations. To support this, we created a series of typographic posters based 
on messages defined by the participants and then invited them to use these 
compositions as a starting point (see Figure 7.15).
The results demonstrate that our approach and tool allow for the 
production of designs that meet the participants’ requirements, particularly 
in conveying messages related to sociocultural issues.  Furthermore, we 
observed that the outputs display significant visual diversity. This way, we 
consider that our approach could be useful when integrated into GD pro-
cesses. Also, our observations reveal that the tool interface is easy to use 
and provides a straightforward way to define the visual features of the designs.
At the conclusion of the workshop sessions, we were invited to 
produce a small exhibition documenting and showcasing the tool, its 
development processes, and the generated output designs. As part of this,

7.3 ESSYS* SHARING #UC
We have created the media art installation ESSYS*  Sharing #UC, which 
explores the online content shared about the university and the city of 
Coimbra, Portugal. The installation aims to foster reflection on the con-
temporary meaning of location by merging online data with its corre-
sponding physical space, creating an environment where digital and 
physical representations of a place coexist.
The motivation behind this installation is to create a physical space 
that allows the audience to visualise online data about a location. It serves as 
a space where a location’s digital and physical dimensions blend, offering 
insight into the evolving nature of a location in the present day. The exhi-
bition space is designed to explore how a physical space can be mirrored, 
visualised, perceived, and defined online. It is designed to encourage 
the audience to reflect on the impact of online data on defining the char -
acteristics of a location and influencing the behaviour of its inhabitants 
and visitors.
This installation is designed to be accessible both online and in 
an art gallery located in the Coimbra Historic Centre (CHC), Portugal. In 
both formats, visitors can observe a collection of poster designs generated 
automatically from collected tweets, accompanied by an ever-changing 
ambient sound. The audiovisual elements are created to reflect the emo-
tional tone of the tweets. Figures 7.18 to 7.20 depict the installation in the 
two configurations.

III DESIGNING  AUTOMA TICALL Y
The online installation features an ever-changing audiovisual envi-
ronment, with posters floating on the screen coupled with ambient audio 
(see Figure 7.18). On the other hand, the physical installation consists of 
a collection of posters spanning various dimensions and layouts, comple-
mented by four speakers that play ambient audio reflecting the emotional 
context of the tweets (see Figures 7.19 to 7.20). The audio for the physical 
installation is controlled by the online version, which is displayed on a 
television within the physical space.
The posters showcased in the installation are generated automatically 
using the previously described greedy typesetting method, which employs 
emotion recognition and stylisation techniques (see Section 7.1). Further-
more, we used the ESSYS system (Seiça et al., 2018) to generate the MIDI 
sonic compositions through a probabilistic rule-based approach, also 
based on the gathered emotional context derived from the input pro-
cessing method. The audience indirectly contributes to the audiovisuals 
on the installation, as their tweets affect the creation and characteristics 
of the outputs.
This installation was specifically designed for the MUSEU art gallery 
of CAPC in the CHC. The gallery was created by the Portuguese artist 
Francisco Tropa and built for anozero 2015, the first edition of the Coimbra 
Biennial of Contemporary Art (2015). This space has a participatory and 
easily accessible nature, functioning simultaneously as an urban sculpture 
and an always-open exhibition space.118 ESSYS* Sharing #UC was exhibited 
in this space between July and December 2021. This artwork was commis-
sioned by the Institute of Interdisciplinary Research of the UC to mark 
the university’s 730 th anniversary and was selected from a proposal sub-
mitted in a specific call.119
We developed a system to support the online installation. The system 
continuously searches for and collects related tweets via the Twitter API. 
It then preprocesses, analyses, and stores the tweets and the resulting data 
in a database. Simultaneously, the system also chooses tweets to drive the 
audiovisual generation. This way, 10 times per second, the system queries 
the database and selects 20 tweets based on their newness. Then, a RWS 
method selects one tweet based on its creation date and time, giving more 
recent tweets a higher chance of selection. Each tweet is assigned a random 
lifespan between 1 and 3 minutes. Due to the space constraints on the 
standard computer screens, the online installation displays only five posters 
simultaneously. When this maximum is reached, the selection is paused 
until one poster is removed. 
When a user accesses the website, its client browser requests infor-
mation about the tweets selected at the moment, generates and displays 
the posters, and triggers the emotional-related audio stream produced 
by ESSYS. The client also checks for updates on the selected tweets once 
per second. Whenever a tweet is added or removed from this list, it handles 
updates on the poster visualisation and audio. To streamline the connec-
tion between the system components, we developed a REST API. Figure 
7.21 shows a blueprint of the web-based system’s workflow.

The generated poster format is randomly selected based on the 
regular ISO standards formats (A, B and C). We loaded a set of OTVFs into 
the system and empirically defined their emotional relationship defined 
previously based on the works of Beth E. Koch (2012) and Sarah Hyndman 
(2016) considering type design features such as the weight, serifs, terminal 
shape, and horizontal motion (see Table 6.2, Sec. 6.2.4). Table 7.1 provides 
an overview of the typefaces in this experiment. Also, we defined the col-
our-emotion relation mappings empirically based on the colour defined 
in the emotion wheel of Robert Plutchik (1980). These emotional associ-
ations were established in their respective configuration files.120

We selected typefaces empirically, focusing on those that embody 
visual features traditionally linked to poster aesthetics and that visually 
complement the default background styles we used. As a result, we opted 
for sans-serif typefaces over serif ones, as they better matched our aesthetic 
preferences for this installation. The typefaces were also picked based on 
the possibility of varying both weight and character width (or stretch). Figure 
7.22 showcases some example posters displayed in the installation.
We employed the ESSYS  system (Seiça et al., 2018) to generate 
the ambient sound based on the prevailing emotion recognised in the 
messages displayed on the currently exhibited posters. This sonic compo-
sition is generated by a rule-based audio generation system, where the 
musical parameters are dynamically chosen according to predefined prob-
abilities, which depend on the emotion being portrayed.
The audio generation is guided by two major musical aspects: melody 
and harmony. The melody is understood as a set of notes whose type 
(scale note, chord note or chromatism) and duration (from whole to eighth 
notes) are parameterised, as well as the intervals between them that 
shape the leaps of the melodic line. Each note is sequentially chosen 
depending on the probabilities of these parameters, guided by a melodic 
scale that is, in turn, defined by the harmonic progression chosen for each 
emotional context. These progressions are predefined for each emotion. 
Finally, multiple timbres of mostly synthesised sounds were chosen for 
each emotional context. This method is based on the previously developed 
work of Mariana Seiça et al. (2018) but adapts the timbres of synthesised 
sounds to use free VST plugins, more specifically the Spitfire Audio LABS4 
virtual instruments.121
121
More information about the free-to-use 
Spitfire Audio LABS VSTs is available

(visited: 7 July 2025).

 GREEDY  T YPESETTING  A PPROACH7
Since this installation was displayed in a public space, it allowed the 
presentation of a set of subjects and matters regarding the city of Coimbra 
that, although often discussed online, rarely have been transposed to the 
city’s urban space. This way, the installation was not only a showcase of 
the most common online Coimbra-related discussions but also provided 
one dedicated site to present them in the corresponding urban space. 
The topics covered included the Portuguese colonial inheritance 
and its legacy on Coimbra city and university, current housing and gentri-
fication issues in CHC, regional perceptions of national and worldwide 
political circumstances, the consequence of the COVID-19 pandemic, the 
national and worldwide influence of research institutes present on Coimbra.
The audiovisual outputs were indirectly created by the audience 
through their online participation, revealing multiple (often opposing) 
personal viewpoints on the same subjects. In this sense, we consider that 
this installation functioned as a collective visualisation of the city, reflecting 
predominant thoughts and perceptions. When viewed collectively and 
over time, we find that the installation’s outputs serve as an archive of 
how both residents and visitors perceive and experience the city in its 
various dimensions.
We also developed two alternative variations of this installation. The 
first is an online happening designed to capture people’s perceptions of 
current trending subjects. This artwork functions as a happening  perfor-
mance conducted by a system that independently collects recent tweets, 
recognises the emotions expressed by their author and then translates 
these emotions into data-driven audiovisuals. 122 This artwork aims to 
question the role of the audience within contemporary art and design 
Figure 7.22. Posters displayed 
at the installation. For additional 
documentation including more poster 
designs download https://cdv.dei.
uc.pt/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/
essys-s-uc-evaluation-doc.pdf 
(visited 7 July 2025).
122
Happening art is a performative 
type of art that emerged in the 
mid-twentieth century. It is characterised 
by unscripted and ephemeral live 
performances that integrate various 
media, audience participation, 
unconventional settings, and 
improvisation. The term was first used 
by the American artist Allan Kaprow 
during the 1950s to describe 
unconventional performative events 
that aimed to break away from traditional 
artistic media and practices at the time. 
For further information, for instance, 
consult Allan Kaprow (1993).

206
III DESIGNING  AUTOMA TICALL Y
computational systems. While the system autonomously generates an 
audiovisual environment, it remains connected to human input by basing 
its creations on the emotional analysis of the collected tweets, which we 
consider raises questions about authorship in computationally generated 
content. Despite the system’s autonomous creation of the audiovisual 
environment, it is designed to mirror current human opinions, reflecting 
both positive and negative perspectives.
The system behind this fully online artwork employs three distinct 
methods. The first method conducts a textual analysis of the tweets through 
a lexicon-based approach, identifying metadata and recognising the emo-
tions conveyed by each tweet’s author during tweet creation. The remaining 
two methods are dedicated to generating the audiovisual components, 
encompassing both visual and auditory elements.
For each collected tweet, the system uses a lexicon-based approach 
to detect emotions and identify the specific parts of the text contributing 
to them. This analysis is carried out in the following eight sequential steps: 
(i) translation of the text to English, when necessary; (ii) removal of the 
contracted word forms; (iii) replacement of emojis with their corresponding 
meanings; (iv) replacement of abbreviations and slang expressions by their 
formal equivalents; (v) conversion of words to their lemmas; (vi) replace-
ment of negations with antonyms; (vii) removal of stop words; and, finally, 
(viii) tokenisation of the text. After preprocessing, the system conducts 
a lexicon-based analysis of each word in the resulting text, using a word-emo-
tion association lexicon developed by Saif M. Mohammad and Peter D. 
Turney (2010). When an emotion is recognised in a word, the original 
words and the emotion recognised are saved. The system then calculates 
the intensity of the relationship between the recognised emotions and the 
text by summing the number of recognised emotions and identifying the 
most prominent one, i.e. the emotion with the highest value. In addition 
to this, the method saves some metadata related to the tweet, such as 
emojis, mentions, and hashtags.
After that, these collected data serve as the foundation for generating 
the audiovisual environment of the installation. Similar to the main version 
of the installation, the audio is generated using the ESSYS system (Seiça 
et al.,  2018) based on the most prominent emotion recognised at that 
moment. The visuals consist of a coloured background displaying the most 
rated and representative words or one of the saved metadata fields (such 
as emojis, mentions, or hashtags). These elements are centrally positioned 
on the canvas and presented in a typeface that corresponds to the recog-
nised emotion. The mapping of emotions to colours and typography is 
established using the previously introduced mappings, which are incor -
porated into the system via configuration files. Figure 7.23 provides exam-
ples of visuals obtained during the happening of this online artwork.
In May 2022, we presented a second version of the installation as 
part of the commemoration of the 250 th anniversary of the Faculty of 
Science and Technology of UC. 123 This version maintained the default 
configuration used in the CAPC installation but introduced a new hardware 
arrangement that involved only three LCD screens (see Figure 7.24).

7.4 EV ALUA TION
We conducted two experiments using the proposed typesetting method to 
evaluate its potential for automating GD tasks and assess the generated 
posters’ visual features and emotional impact.
First, we assessed the generative capability and performance of the 
greedy typesetting method. Then, we conducted interview sessions with 
12 individuals to study how the approach outputs are experienced in terms 
of visual diversity and expressiveness. During this evaluation phase, we also 

208
III DESIGNING  AUTOMA TICALL Y
investigated how the outputs are perceived within the context of the ESSYS* 
Sharing #UC installation, particularly when combined with ambient audio 
created by ESSYS. Furthermore, we asked participants about the potential 
application of this method in other scenarios.
7.4. 1 PERFORMANCE EVALUA TION
We conducted evaluation experiments generating posters using the pro-
posed greedy typesetting method to assess its performance in generating 
poster designs. For this purpose, we selected 16 texts of varying lengths 
and emotional content. The length of these texts ranged between 22 and 
219 characters. Table 7.2  presents the selected texts along with their asso-
ciated data. We employed the default input processing method to divide 
the text into lines and determine each text’s emotional context. To enhance 
the visual diversity in terms of background styles, colours, and typefaces, 
we set the minimum recognition score threshold to a lower value of 0.2. 
This resulted in recognising a broader range of emotions within the ana-
lysed texts. The rightmost column in Table 7.2 presents the normalised 
scores assigned to the recognised emotions within each text.

Emotion recognition is inherently subjective and can vary based on 
individual interpretation. To promote visual variety in the outputs, we 
reduced the threshold for recognising a score as a valid emotion from 0.5. 
However, from our perspective, the predominant emotion (identified as 
the emotion with the highest weight and listed first) generally aligns with 
the content of the text. We applied the same stylising and typesetting 
method to each text using the default setup. For each text, we generated 
300 posters. Figure 7.25 displays a selection of these resulting outputs.
The results demonstrated that the proposed method consistently 
produced finished and legible poster designs across all evaluation runs. 
Moreover, it was found that the method can generate poster designs with 
relatively few operations (mean [x̄ ]: 61.25, median [x̃]: 31.50) and, conse-
quently, required relatively short periods (x̄ : 0.88 seconds, x̃: 0.27 seconds) 
to execute in a standard web browser.
Our observations revealed that the number of operations is related 
to the number of line divisions rather than the number of characters 
or words. Figure 7.26 displays the relationship between the number of 
typesetting attempts required to generate a poster and the number of line

7.4.2 INTERVIEW EVALUA TION SESSIONS
We conducted interview-based evaluation sessions to understand how 
viewers perceive the generated poster designs in terms of visual diversity, 
coherence, and predefined emotional mapping. We were also interested 
in determining whether the perception of these outputs was enhanced or 
diminished when paired with ambient audio generated by ESSYS  within 
the context of the ESSYS* Sharing #UC installation. In addition, we aimed 
to assess the potential utility of the proposed approach in various com-
mercial design scenarios and social interactions, along with their implica-
tions, particularly from the perspective of graphic designers.

During these sessions, we presented several posters, sometimes

invitations. Half of them (6) were professional graphic designers (G1), with 
work experience ranging from two to eight years. In this sense, we incor -
porated various design professional perspectives and insights to study the 
potential of this approach in commercial scenarios. The other half (G2) 
came from different professional backgrounds. Table 7.3 provides further 
details about the participants.

The interviews took place in person, where participants responded 
verbally, and we recorded their responses. They are divided into four stages. 
In the first stage (s1), participants viewed a collection of posters displayed 
on a screen. After the viewing, they were asked, “On a scale of 1 to 5, how 
would you rate the visual coherence of the following posters?” where 1 
means “not cohesive” and 5 means “very cohesive.” Participants were also 
asked to provide a verbal explanation for their rating. The first collection 
(s1.1) featured posters with the same typeface but different background 
styles. The following four collections (s1.2 – s1.5) included posters with 
the same typeface and background styles. The final collection (s1.6) pre-
sented posters with distinct typefaces and background styles.
During the second stage ( s2), we presented seven posters one by 
one on screen. We asked participants the open-ended question, “What 
emotion(s) do you recognise in the content of the following poster, based 
on its content and design?” (s2.1 – s2.7). We also encouraged participants 
to comment on their choices.

212
III DESIGNING  AUTOMA TICALL Y
In the next stage (s3), we presented five posters as a video file, dis-
playing each poster individually on a screen. Each poster was paired with 
an audio sample that conveyed the same emotional context. We asked 
participants to perform the same task as in s2 by responding to the open-
ended question, “What emotion(s) do you recognize in the content of the 
following poster based on its content, design, and sound?” (s3.1 – s3.5). 
We also encouraged participants to justify and elaborate on their answers. 
Two of these posters were also displayed in s2. Finally, we asked the par -
ticipants about the significance of audio on their perception of the posters’ 
message by inquiring, “In your opinion, does audio increase the effective-
ness of how the message is transmitted?” and asked them to justify their 
answer (s3.6).
In the final stage (s4), we asked participants to respond to the open-
ended question, “How do you envision the potential advantages and dis-
advantages of these computational methods affecting our everyday access 
to information and social interactions?”. For those who are graphic designers, 
we also expanded the question, requesting they also “consider commercial 
and professional contexts.” The data collected from these evaluation ses-
sions can be accessed at https://pf.dei.uc.pt/7/eval (visited: 7 July 2025).
In evaluating the visual diversity and coherence of posters (s1), 
the evaluation sessions demonstrated that this approach generated diver-
sified poster designs. However, participants noted that the method is 
particularly efficient at producing visually cohesive outputs. We found that 
the perception of visual diversity is more closely associated with background 
style than typographic style. Table 7.4 presents the quantitative results of 
this evaluation stage.

All interviewed participants indicated that the relationship between 
colours used across the collection of posters plays a crucial role in estab-
lishing visual diversity or coherence. They noted that a chromatic connec-
tion could be identified even when the posters had different backgrounds 
and typography styles. Nevertheless, around 67% (4) of graphic designers 
(g1) and 50% (3) of other participants (g2) said that posters with distinct 
backgrounds and typography were diverse enough to be used in different 
contexts or designed by various designers. 
Among the background styles created, the one that produced the 
most coherent output was the halved diagonally, primarily due to its easily 
recognisable triangular composition. Every participant found the collection 
of posters with this background style visually cohesive, with most of both

groups (g1:4, g2:4) even rating them as highly cohesive. In contrast, most

As previously noted, defining emotional charge is a subjective task 
influenced by the observer’s social and cultural context. The results from 
the s2 interview stage highlighted this, often revealing contradictory 
responses for the same poster. Even when two individuals identified the 
same emotion, they frequently provided different justifications. During 
the interviews, participants based their answers on their examination of 
the posters’ features, including visual style, typographic style, colour palette, 
and message. Table 7.5 summarises the findings from this evaluation stage.
