7.5 FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS 
In this chapter, we introduced a greedy typesetting method and experi-
mented with it to automatically create typographic poster designs. This 
method adjusts the typographic features of text boxes iteratively. The text 
in these boxes is composed using OTVFs with multiple axes. The process 
continues until all text box content fits within the designated container. 
The method uses various operators to manipulate the text size and the 
variable fonts’ axis values. We explored this method with varying levels of 
autonomy and expertise.
In this sense, we also developed a default automatic approach to 
apply this method when generating posters. This approach incorporates 
a neural NLP technique for emotional recognition and uses the resulting 
data to define the visual features of the designs. It also divides the text 
into lines.
In addition to the automatic approach, we developed a tool to give 
users easy and fast access to this method. This tool was developed in 
a collaboration workshop with upper-secondary students aged around 
15 years old. We selected this group based on the expectation that, due to 
their familiarity with digital media and lack of formal training in GD soft-
ware, they would likely explore new ways of interacting with design tools 
and offer innovative methods for creating visuals. We also intend to create 
a tool that enables individuals to design easily, helping them to share their 
ideas and thoughts. This way, in the workshop sessions, we focused on 
developing the tool primarily to create posters for sociocultural activism.
The workshops consisted of seven sessions divided into three stages. 
The first stage involved brainstorming to identify the tool’s requirements 
(3 sessions). The second stage focused on collaboratively defining, evalu-
ating, and refining the tool’s interface (2 sessions). The final stage involved 
evaluating the tool’s outputs by creating posters only with it or using it as 
a starting point for new designs by combining the generated outputs with 
custom illustrations (2 sessions).
The developed tool automatically enables users to create legible 
designs from input text and images. After the typesetting process is com-
plete, users can define the poster’s features by modifying the visual attrib-
utes of each text box and image individually, as well as the overall features 
of the poster. It also enables users to download their final designs in both 
raster and editable file formats. In this generative process, the tool uses 
only the proposed typesetting method and does not include emotional 
analysis for defining visual features. The visual features are not automated 
and are entirely set by users. 

216
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
Our observations and the results from the final workshop sessions 
revealed that the tool and its interface enable users to use the proposed 
typesetting method to produce designs quickly and easily. The designs 
present social and cultural messages, demonstrating that the tool supports 
users in expressing their opinions and personal views. These sessions also 
showed that combining system-generated typography with illustrations 
highlights the tool’s and method’s potential for applications beyond fully 
automated design creation. The resulting designs were showcased in a 
small exhibition, where participants also presented visual diaries describing 
the process behind the tool’s development.
We experimented with this method by applying its standard auton-
omous approach to create an audiovisual public art installation titled 
ESSYS* Sharing #UC . This artwork presents generative posters created 
using the proposed typesetting approach and emotion-visual defined maps, 
with emotion-driven ambient audio generated by the ESSYS system. In this 
context, we employed an approach requiring more expertise , where the 
system automatically defines the visual features of the resulting designs. 
Beyond the typical skills needed for typesetting text, we used the text’s 
recognised emotional tone to define all the installation’s visual and sonic 
elements. The installation’s audiovisuals were automatically generated 
based on tweets about the city and the university of Coimbra, reflecting 
the emotional context related to those places. Beyond technical experi-
mentation, our motivation was also to create a space where digital and 
physical aspects of a location intertwine, encouraging reflections on the 
contemporary definition of a place.
The installation was accessible both in a physical art gallery (the 
continuous-open MUSEU art gallery of CAPC in CHC) and online. The 
physical installation featured a series of typographic generative posters 
displayed on walls, accompanied by an ever-evolving soundscape that 
sonified the emotional dynamics of the posters. The online installation 
offered a constantly changing environment where visitors could experience 
the live generation of poster designs and ambient sound based on the 
real-time emotional charge of gathered tweets. The online installation was 
also presented on the physical display, shown on a television.
We conducted a series of evaluation experiments to investigate and 
analyse the performance of this approach and the perception of its outputs. 
This included a performance evaluation to assess the capability of the 
greedy typesetter method and its automated approach in generating various 
poster designs for different purposes. Simultaneously, we held interview 
sessions with people, including GD professionals, to understand how the 
installation outputs were perceived, focusing on aspects such as diversity, 
expressiveness, and potential applications in other scenarios.
The performance evaluation results showed that the proposed method 
consistently produced legible poster designs. Each poster is created in 
relatively few operations and in a short period in a standard web browser. 
We also observed this during the tool’s development. However, we noted 
that this type of algorithm tends to favour compositions with narrower 
fonts, likely due to their space-saving properties.

217
 III DESIGNING  AUTOMA TICALL Y
The interviews showed that this approach can produce both visually 
cohesive and diverse posters. Participants observed that background style 
and colour choices impact visual diversity and coherence more than typo-
graphic style. Despite recognising the overall coherence of the outputs, 
most participants considered posters with distinct visual features diverse 
enough to be used in different contexts or designed by different designers.
We also assessed whether the automatic styling map based on emo-
tions is understandable to users of the created designs. Although emotional 
perception is a subjective task influenced by the viewer’s social and cultural 
background, our interviews indicated that certain emotions identified by 
the neural classifier, especially joy, anger, and sadness, are frequently per-
ceived by participants in the posters, regardless of whether they are accom-
panied by the audio component.
Most participants recognised that the approach could enhance social 
media and digital content, with its automatic, emotion-driven features 
potentially improving message comprehension. However, they cautioned 
that widespread use could have the opposite effect. All interviewed graphic 
designers recognised the approach as having the potential to support their 
design practice. They noted that it could be used to create design frame-
works that others can easily use (as we explored in the online tool). Most 
also highlighted its potential to inspire new visual and conceptual ideas.
The findings reveal that expert strategies can be applied with varying 
levels of generality, ranging from the creation of a system to operate spe-
cific tasks (typesetting text as used in the tool) to the complete automation 
of designs (as seen in the artwork). With the proposed tool, we introduced 
a design-support tool that integrates an expert strategy to facilitate the 
generation of designs. We believe this highlights the potential for incor -
porating expertise into design tools to develop further efficient cooperative 
strategies. Our experimentation also demonstrates how a system’s exper-
tise can be increased and achieved through various techniques. This exper-
iment explored several methods, from neural classification techniques 
(such as emotion recognition) to a rules system using an emotion-to-style 
map. This way, the findings suggest that designers should choose the most 
appropriate method to give expertise to the system based on the problem.
In conclusion, despite the limitations of the proposed greedy approach, 
the findings suggest that it facilitates fast design generation and can be 
adapted to create other tools or even fully automated processes. Further-
more, this experiment indicates that integrating a degree of expertise into 
the computational systems could enable it to automate various aspects of 
the design process.

218
III DESIGNING  AUTOMA TICALL Y

219 AUTOMATED D ESIGN P RACTICES8
CD methods, particularly those involving AI and CC, have recently driven 
the introduction of novel GD practices and production processes, including 
in the typography and layout domains (Armstrong & Stojmirovic, 2011; 
Reas et al., 2010; Richardson, 2016). These procedures, particularly those 
requiring higher expertise, demonstrate considerable potential for encour-
aging automation. They can replicate various actions and procedures 
that graphic designers perform during work hours. These methods can 
address various applications with differing generality and expressive power, 
from executing specific tasks to fully generating designs. We also observed 
that they can assist designers with discovery and exploration tasks, poten-
tially resulting in the creation of unexpected designs. Furthermore, our 
analysis of related work demonstrates that this can be achieved at various 
levels of autonomy, with computational systems offering potential both as 
fully automated expert strategies and as cooperative strategies. Chapter 
2 provides an overview of the foundational knowledge and current appli-
cations of CD in typography and layout design.
In this part of the thesis, we presented our research on using CD 
approaches to automate the generation of poster designs. We focused on 
investigating the potential uses of CD for automation, ranging from specific 
tasks to broader discovery and exploration activities. In this sense, we devel-
oped two expert strategies for generating designs from scratch. The first 
approach involves evolutionary experiments aimed at creating typographic 
posters. The second approach employs a greedy approach to text typeset-
ting. We explored these strategies to create designs with varying autonomy 
and purposes. In both approaches, we incorporated methods that involve 
users in the generation process, allowing them to guide the creation of 
designs according to their preferences. However, these approaches are not 
fully cooperative, as they retain the capability (or expertise) to generate 
designs entirely automatically without requiring direct user intervention.
The first approach focused on developing poster generation systems 
using EC (see Chapter 6). This approach involved the sequential develop-
ment of three experiments using a GA to generate posters based on user 
content. This approach draws inspiration from traditional letterpress 
techniques of the nineteenth century. During that time, typographers 
worked closely with clients to compose designs until every available space 
was filled with typography, highlighting the most important elements 
through visual and layout emphasis (Meggs & Purvis, 2016). 
We developed experiments that allow the autonomous generation 
of designs. However, we introduced techniques that allow users to partic-
ipate in the evolution by influencing the features and evaluation of design 
AUTOMA TED  
DESIGN PRACTICES
8

220
III DESIGNING  AUTOMA TICALL Y
by expressing their preferences while it unfolds automatically. We devel-
oped these methods with the goal of making the guidance of evolu-
tionary processes less time-consuming, less tiring, and more controlled, 
addressing the common problems found in IEC and automatic evalua-
tion approaches.
The three experiments present a similar workflow. Users start by 
inputting content, and after, the system generates a random set of poster 
designs. These designs are then evolved based on the users’ preferences. 
We establish an initial set of preferences for each experiment based on 
empirical observations. Users can further refine these preferences using 
configuration files or in an interface.
The initial evolutionary experiment employs a GA to create black -
-and-white typographic posters from user-provided text (see Section 6.1). 
In this experiment, users can orient the evolution process by interactively 
specifying their typographic preferences, particularly concerning horizontal 
motion and weight. For the fitness assignment, we use a multi-criteria 
hardwired fitness strategy that considers three criteria: (i) layout, which 
assesses the effective use of the poster’s space; (ii) legibility, which assesses 
the legibility of text on the poster; and (iii) typography, which measures 
if the chosen typefaces align with the user’s typographic preferences. The 
experimental results demonstrate that the system can produce legible 
designs that align with user-expressed preferences, particularly when these 
preferences do not interfere with the legibility of the designs.
In the second evolutionary experiment (see Section 6.2), we used 
a GA to create colour typographic posters from user-provided text. This 
experiment expanded the first by introducing more expressive power capa-
bilities, evaluation methods, and content analysis strategies. We employed 
a lexicon-based approach to recognise the text’s emotions, sentiments, 
and colour associations and automatically divide the text into lines. This 
information was used to define the desired features of the outputs, including 
which parts of the text should be highlighted. We decided that the layout 
should emphasise the most emotionally significant text parts. This system 
expanded the design possibilities compared to the previous experiment 
and added more expertise to the evolution process. Through a dedicated 
interface and configuration files, users can specify their visual preferences 
and set the range of possible visual variations for the outputs.
The system evaluates the generated designs based on three criteria: 
(i) legibility , which assesses the text’s legibility on the poster; (ii) aes-
thetics, which assesses the aesthetic features of the poster; and (iii) seman-
tics, which evaluates if the poster visuals align with the semantic analysis of 
the text. Each criterion considers a specific set of design measures. We devel-
oped three separate strategies for assigning fitness. These strategies include 
a multi-criteria hardwired fitness function, a multi-objective optimisation 
approach, and a hybrid strategy that combines the other two. The system 
allows for combining these evaluation strategies within the same evolu -
tionary run.
Using the developed evaluation strategies, we tested this system 
by evolving typographic posters for various text contents, lengths, and 
purposes. The results showed that the multi-criteria hardwired fitness 
and hybrid strategies produce finished posters with similar performance. 

221
 AUTOMATED D ESIGN P RACTICES8
The hybrid strategy offered slightly better visual diversity and legibility  
scores, while the multi-criteria hardwired strategy performed better in 
semantic evaluation and convergence speed. On the other hand, the multi-
-objective optimisation approach led to unstable populations and did 
not consistently produce legible designs. Empirical observation showed 
that the issue arose from treating legibility as equally important as aes-
thetics and semantics. We consider that a poster with low legibility  
fails to communicate its message, even if it performs well in aesthetics  
and semantics.
Additionally, we adapted this system to create an autonomous poster 
generator tool that uses content retrieved from Twitter and employs the hybrid 
evaluation strategy. The results of this experiment further demonstrated 
the system’s capability to create visually diverse and legible designs, indi-
cating its suitability for automated design generation within a design project.
In the third evolutionary experiment, we refined our approach using 
a GA by evaluating individuals with a stochastic ranking method (see 
Section 6.3). This method enables constrained evolution by combining a 
hardwired fitness assignment strategy (aesthetics and semantics criteria) 
with a penalty function strategy (legibility  criterion). This system intro-
duced several improvements, including enhanced input analysis, new 
individual representation, and refined evaluation criteria. We integrated 
a neural NLP approach with a lexicon-based method to assess the content’s 
local and overall emotional tone. Domain-driven design was used to define 
poster representation, and the genotype was structured in JSON format, 
allowing for greater human comprehension and expressive power. Also, 
We added new evaluation measures for all criteria and updated the user 
interface, workflow, and configuration file formats. In addition to text 
input, users can provide their own emotion-to-visual mappings and images 
for the system.
We conducted experiments to evaluate the creation of typographic 
poster designs for content of different lengths and purposes and to assess 
how various evaluation criteria affect the designs. The results demonstrated 
the efficiency of our method and evaluation criteria in creating legible 
posters. However, when multiple measures are evolved simultaneously in 
this constrained environment, some measures may stabilise or progress 
more slowly. Further research is needed to understand how individual 
aesthetics and semantics measures evolve individually and interact with 
legibility constraints.
Next, we focused on developing a greedy typesetting technique 
(see Chapter 7). This method functions as a local search, iteratively adjusting 
text features until the text fits within the specified container. The text is 
represented in text boxes and composed using OTVFs with multiple axes. 
The method uses various operators to adjust text size and features by 
modifying the variable font axis values.
We experimented with this method alongside a default automatic 
approach to create typographic poster designs with varying levels of 
autonomy and expertise. Similar to the evolutionary approach, it incorporates 
neural NLP for emotional recognition, uses the resulting data to define the 
visual features of the designs, and automatically divides the text into lines.

222
III DESIGNING  AUTOMA TICALL Y
We developed a tool to give users easy and fast access to this method. 
This tool was designed during a collaborative workshop with upper -
-secondary students around 15 years old. We chose these participants 
because we considered their familiarity with digital media, and limited GD 
training would likely lead them to explore new ways of interacting with 
design tools and creating designs. We aimed to create a tool that empowers 
individuals to express their opinions. This way, during the workshop, we 
specifically focused on developing the tool for creating posters for socio-
cultural activism. The workshops comprised seven sessions, including 
brainstorming, interface design and refinement, and evaluating the outputs.
This tool explores the method cooperatively by automating only 
text typesetting while users define the remaining visual features. After 
typesetting, users can customise the poster’s elements and features before 
downloading the final design. Observations from the workshop showed 
that the tool interfaces allow users easy production designs. In the final 
workshop sessions, participants used the tool to create posters either 
by only using the tool or by combining generated typography with custom 
illustrations. The resulting designs showcase the tool’s ability to effectively 
create designs with both text and images. Moreover, integrating system-gen-
erated typography with illustrations indicates the potential of this tool 
(and the method) for applications beyond full design automation. 
We used the proposed typesetting method and standard automatic 
workflow to create the public audiovisual art installation called ESSYS* 
Sharing #UC. This installation features posters created with our typesetting 
method and ambient audio produced by the ESSYS System. Both elements 
are created based on the emotional context gathered from tweets about 
the city and the university of Coimbra, Portugal. In addition to technical 
exploration, we aimed to create a space that blends the digital and physical 
aspects of a location, encouraging reflection on the contemporary concept 
of place. In this experiment, we explored the same method approach with 
more autonomy and expertise.
We conducted evaluation experiments to assess the method and 
the autonomous approach’s performance in generating posters for various 
contents and purposes, as well as the perception of its outputs by people. 
The results showed that the proposed method efficiently produces legible 
posters for various text contents and features.
The perception of the outputs was evaluated through interviews 
with various individuals, including GD professionals. These interviews 
focused on gathering feedback regarding diversity, coherence, and poten-
tial applications in other contexts. Participants noted the overall coherence 
of the outputs while considering that some posters present diverse features 
to be used in different contexts or designed by different designers. We also 
evaluated the comprehensibility of the emotion-based automatic styling 
map for users. Our interviews showed that most participants recognised 
certain emotions, such as joy, anger, and sadness, in the features of the 
posters, regardless of whether the audio component was present. However, 
since the perception of emotions in audiovisual content is subjective and 
shaped by individual social and cultural backgrounds, the approach allows 
users to customise the styling maps to suit the specific needs of a project 
or the target audience.

223
 AUTOMATED D ESIGN P RACTICES8
Finally, most participants acknowledged that this type of approach 
could potentially improve visualisation in digital media content and enhance 
message comprehension. However, they also suggested that extensive use 
might lead to opposite effects. All graphic designers interviewed recognised 
the potential of the approach to support their design practice, noting that 
it could help create design frameworks accessible to others (as also demon-
strated with the online tool). Many also highlighted its potential to encourage 
exploring new visual and conceptual ideas.
The findings suggest that expert strategies can significantly support 
and automate GD practices. In the experiments, we used domain-specific 
knowledge to automate design tasks such as input analysis, text division, 
and typesetting, as well as to oversee the entire design process. We also 
tested different methods for integrating domain-specific knowledge into 
the system, including ML models, rules, and measures.
We also observed that designers should select the appropriate method 
based on the required level of expertise, the design problem, and the current 
state of technology. Rule-based knowledge can be challenging to model 
but has proven effective in automating the design process, especially when 
the features of the final design are well-defined. Similarly, domain-specific 
measures can assist in the preliminary evaluation of designs, particularly 
concerning aesthetic characteristics. ML models have shown promise in 
enhancing a system’s autonomy and expertise, particularly in recognition 
and evaluation tasks, as demonstrated in the emotion recognition methods 
of these approaches. However, the lack of annotated data in the GD field 
makes applying these models to more specific design tasks challenging.
The experiments also show that expert strategies can assist design 
processes by conducting specific design tasks. Our experiments reveal that 
these methods can support design practices by facilitating data extraction 
and operating routine tasks. Several developed methods demonstrate 
this potential. For instance, the input analysis methods proved useful for 
extracting initial data and conducting preliminary assessments of designs. 
Similarly, the developed typesetting method enabled faster text composi-
tion in real-time. These findings suggest that expert strategies could 
minimise graphic designers’ workloads, which we consider would give 
them more scope to focus on the creative aspects of their work.
Simultaneously, these approaches can also automate the entire 
design generation. Our findings indicate the potential of expert strategies 
to automate design generation for two primary purposes: creating new 
designs that follow specific guidelines or facilitating discovery and explo-
ration. Depending on the purpose and computational representation, 
they can be explored with different levels of expressive power. The findings 
indicate that more expressive power benefits discovery tasks but is not 
necessary for designs that have well-defined visual features.
Our experiments with EC showed that it can be advantageous in 
design processes. Evolutionary approaches have proven effective in facil-
itating GD discovery and exploration, primarily due to their stochastic 
optimisation capabilities. By defining the range of expected features (the 
search space) and setting appropriate evaluation criteria, designers can 

224
III DESIGNING  AUTOMA TICALL Y
use EC approaches to search for new designs automatically. This way, we 
identify that these approaches can streamline design processes, allowing 
designers to simultaneously explore multiple design variations while 
encouraging serendipity in the design process. However, defining the 
search space, the expressive power, and the appropriate evolutionary criteria 
can be challenging, especially in subjective evaluation contexts.
Our results further indicate that EC is more effective for complete 
design generation than simple design tasks. Although EC has proven 
capable of handling simple tasks, its lengthy processing times and high 
computational demands generally make it inefficient for such tasks. Nev-
ertheless, complementary computational methods can be combined with 
these approaches to automate narrower tasks, such as line division or 
colour generation.
This evolutionary approach draws inspiration from nineteenth-
-century letterpress techniques. We found that this approach involves the 
transmediation of algorithm design practice from analogue to computa-
tional media, converting the procedures and processes’ representations 
to promote automation, which can significantly enhance the efficiency 
and capabilities of the original hand process.
Despite observing that the greedy typesetting method has limited 
search capabilities and lacks expressive power, our experiments reveal that 
it can facilitate faster design generation both in a cooperative setting 
(as part of a design support tool) and autonomously when combined with 
other methods.
Recently, deep generative techniques have demonstrated success in 
synthesising visuals. However, the lack of annotated data in the field of GD, 
coupled with inaccuracies and noise in the generated text and typographic 
details, still makes employing these techniques in the context of typographic 
design generation challenging (see Figures 8.1 and 8.2). In comparison to our 
results, the typographic limitations are visually apparent. However, ongoing 
developments are promising for future applications. We anticipate that 
upcoming advancements in the field will soon address most of these limitations.
Also, the experiments conducted in this part of the thesis reveal that 
incorporating expertise into computational systems can further enhance 
cooperative strategies, which we see as contributing to more efficient 
processes and results. An example of this is the design-support tool devel-
oped using the greedy typesetting method. With this tool, users only need 
to modify the visual features of posters, while some actions, such as text 
typesetting, are automated.

Additionally, we proposed a method that allows users to express 
and progressively refine their visual preferences to guide an evolutionary 
process. User preferences are incorporated into the fitness assessment 
of potential candidate solutions. Our initial observations indicate that this 
approach effectively integrates user preferences into the evolutionary 
system, making the process more controllable than fully automatic evo-
lution while avoiding the time-consuming aspects of traditional IEC 
approaches. However, further testing with users is necessary to refine 
the interface and the measures.
Although these experiments show promising advancements in auto-
mating design generation, we recognise the need for further research 
and testing, especially regarding user interaction. Future research should 
include further testing with diverse experimental settings and evaluations 
involving participants and design experts. This testing should encompass 
assessing the system’s capabilities to allow users to apply their desired 
visual mappings and incorporate images.
In summary, the experiments reveal that expert strategies can 
enhance and automate GD practices by providing daily support and auto-
mation across various tasks, including visual discovery. Our findings also 
suggest that integrating expertise into cooperative strategies improves 
and accelerates collaborative design processes and creative support tools.

COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
In this part of the thesis, we detail our investigation of the use of Computa-
tional Design (CD) approaches to creating designs, which extends our explo-
ration beyond the creation of poster design. This investigation covers the 
development of computational approaches for generating print design, such 
as books and music album covers (Chapter 9), as well as  digital design, 
including a brutalist website generator and two internet artworks, namely 
Portraits of No One and Sonar (Chapter 10). Finally, in Chapter 11, we present 
our conclusions on the application of CD in contexts beyond poster design 
scenarios, drawing on insights and findings from these experiments.

229
 IV EXPANDING  COMPUT A TIONAL  PRACTICES
This chapter presents a preliminary study on the developed CD approaches 
for generating print designs beyond posters. In this study, we aim to explore 
how computational approaches can be used to generate other types of print 
designs beyond posters. Specifically, we developed two distinct approaches 
for creating books and music album covers.
For generating book designs, we have created an approach that 
procedurally creates books from user-provided input, including text and 
images. This system automatically designs book layouts by executing 
a series of operations grounded in established typographic knowledge 
while matching the users’ preferences and restrictions expressed before 
the generation process. This system was developed to explore the feasibility 
and potential of using CD to automate the generation of book designs.
Moreover, this system operates within the traditional computerised 
design software, Adobe InDesign, a widely used tool for creating editorial 
and book designs. The generated designs are created as editable InDesign 
files. This experiment also seeks to investigate how computational approaches 
can be integrated into conventional Graphic Design (GD) tools, eliminating 
the need for designers to learn and work with new tools. By doing so, 
designers can include computational tools in their regular processes and 
refine them within their familiar working environment.
For album cover design generation, we developed an online tool that 
creates designs based on the audio characteristics of tracks from a user-se-
lected album. The system automates cover generation using a template  
strategy, with visual features defined by a data-driven method. In this sense, 
we have implemented various drawing modes that process the acquired 
data, resulting in diverse visual representations of the album. The primary 
aim of this work is to explore how template strategies and data-driven 
approaches can enhance user design customisation.
Although the created album covers are primarily designed for print, 
our work also explores how computational media can transmediate tradi-
tional print designs to create new possibilities. Thus, it also allows the cre-
ation of digital album covers with animation features.
The following sections summarise these preliminary works and 
provide an overview of the findings.
9 .1 BOOK DESIGNS
We developed a computational tool for automatically generating book 
layouts from given input content, including text and images, that operates 
inside the Adobe InDesign environment. This system takes advantage of the 
9 COMPUT A TIONAL GENERA TION 
OF PRINT DESIGNS

230IV EXPANDING  COMPUT A TIONAL  PRACTICES
Figure 9.1. Examples of books generated 
with the presented system.
typeset functionalities available in InDesign , which can be controlled 
through scripting, allowing users to easily create and refine designs in a 
familiar working environment.
This system generates book layouts that comply with previously 
defined typographic rules and knowledge while aligning with the user’s 
preferences specified before the generation process. The system relies 
on a framework of typographic rules, styles, and principles taken from 
well-known works in the field. Encoding these rules into the system enables 
the sequential generation of typographic designs, where the system sys-
tematically applies the rules one by one to determine the typographic 
features of the book. The reference works include works by Robert Brin-
ghurst (1997), Josef Müller-Brockmann (1981), Andrew Haslam (2006), 
Jost Hochuli and Robin Kinross (2004), Jost Hochuli (2008), Ellen Lupton 
(2014), and Jan Tschichold (1991). The rules are stored in a configuration 
file (JSON file) containing the possible values (or ranges of values) for 
each typographic attribute, along with probability rates where applicable. 
Users can easily edit this file anytime due to its domain-specific design 
and accessible format. The default configuration file can be found at https://
pf.dei.uc.pt/D/rules.json (visited: 7 July 2025). Figure 9.1 showcases some 
books generated by the system.
Before generating a book, users can define a set of constraints and 
visual characteristics for the output, including format, size, grid, and type-
face, in a specific interface. Alternatively, they can choose automatic settings 
based on predefined rule values. The system’s engine then typesets the 
input content automatically, following the user-defined settings and the 
predefined typographic rules and principles.
The system’s automatic typesetting process follows a series of steps 
to create the final book design. First, it analyses the input content to extract 
data such as text length, image count, and the text-to-image ratio. This helps 
classify the book type ( e.g. long reading, short reading, text and images, 
or image-only) and guide typographic decisions. Next, the system defines 
the document size and grid based on the book type, sets margins, columns, 

231
 COMPUT A TIONAL  GENERA TION  OF PRINT  DESIGNS11
and baselines, and creates parent pages with running headers and page 
numbers. Then, it selects typefaces based on the user’s preferences, maps 
them to available ones, or chooses based on the book type. After that, 
paragraph, character, and image styles are set according to user preferences 
and rules. Finally, once the styles are applied, the content is placed and 
typeset, including the generation of image captions, a table of contents, 
and a colophon.
Optional experimental features can be applied before typesetting. 
These features include the definition of coloured page backgrounds, colour 
gradient margins, or random paragraph indentations. Users can customise 
or expand these features and easily add new ones. At the end of this gen-
erative process, the system creates a typographic cover for the book fea-
turing its title and author on a solid-coloured background. Experimental 
features can also be introduced at this stage. By default, this system presents 
one that maximises the title’s font size to the largest possible.
The system presents the generated book composition to users as 
an editable Adobe InDesign document. Users can then choose to accept 
the generated book as the final design, use it as a starting point for further 
changes, or continue generating designs until a more suitable one is found. 
It also lets users save a configuration file that stores the settings used 
to generate the book. Later, this settings file can be imported into the system, 
allowing the typesetting of different books with the same settings. This helps 
users generate different books while maintaining consistent visual features. 
The files, installation instructions, source code, and other supplementary 
materials are available at https://cdv.dei.uc.pt/2019/scriptedpages (visited: 
7 July 2025).

232
IV EXPANDING  COMPUT A TIONAL  PRACTICES
We conducted experiments using this system to evaluate its ability 
to autonomously generate diverse book layouts as well as visually coherent 
books. This involved two tasks. First, to evaluate visual diversity, we selected 
a public domain book and generated 15 designs using the system. Second, 
to evaluate visual coherence, we exported the settings of one design from 
the initial set and used them to generate five new books with different 
content. Figures 9.2 and 9.3 present the results of each task, respectively. 
At the end of each task, participants reviewed each set of designs and 
assessed the layout diversity or coherence through a five-point scale survey. 
Appendix D further describes the system’s generative process and the 
evaluation experiments conducted.
 Briefly, generated books exhibit varied visual features influenced 
by typographic principles and rules, with probabilistic mechanisms 
enhancing diversity in some attributes. Also, designs created using imported 
settings show clear visual similarity to their source. The evaluation survey 
shows that the system can generate both diverse and cohesive book designs. 
For the first set, most participants found the designs visually diverse. 
In contrast, for the second set, most participants observed a high level 
of coherence among the designs.
9.2 MUSIC ALBUM COVER DESIGNS
We developed a computational tool to design music album covers. Users 
can search for an album using text and generate a custom cover. The covers 
are generated using a template strategy that translates the audio features 
of the album’s tracks into visuals. These album data and characteristics

are accessed through the Spotify API.124 We have developed various drawing 
modes that explore different shapes and methods of translating sound 
data into visuals. Moreover, this tool provides a range of methods for users 
to redefine or completely modify the visual features of the outputs to align 
with their visual preferences once the generation process is complete. 
The system also offers the ability to produce animated versions of the 
covers, where visual elements are animated based on data.
The generative process starts with users either searching for a spe-
cific album by entering a text string (album or artist name) or selecting 
from popular albums displayed on the homepage. The searched album 
must be available on Spotify and accessible through its API. When users 
enter a term, the results are sorted by popularity. Afterwards, the system 
retrieves information from the selected album and generates an initial 
cover design based on its audio features. Users can then customise the 
design through an interface, adjusting colours, shapes, and typography 
and adding animations. Figure 9.4 shows screenshots of the tool.
Based on user input, this system retrieves information about the 
album, artist, and track features, including the number of tracks, release 
date, and the music genres associated with the artist. Then, for each track, 
it gathers details such as estimated tempo (in Beats Per minute [BPM]), 
loudness (in decibels), mode (major or minor), and key (tonality). The album 
cover is generated using one of five drawing modes: (i) ellipse, (ii) rec-
tangle, (iii) circle, (iv) dash, and (v) shape. Each mode translates the 
retrieved data into visual elements based on predefined settings. For instance, 
shape size corresponds to loudness, visuals’ colours represent key or genre, 
and animation speed is connected to the album’s BPM. Common album 
details, such as name, artist, and release year, are consistently placed in 
the layout across different modes. Some modes incorporate stochastic  
methods to introduce variation, with the initial mode selected randomly. 
After the cover is generated, users can refine the output through a dedicated 
interface, where they can adjust visual features, text elements, and anima-
tions. Figure 9.5 displays some outputs generated by this system.

IV EXPANDING  COMPUT A TIONAL  PRACTICES
We conducted preliminary evaluation experiments with invited 
designers to assess the system’s potential to support creative tasks and 
automation in GD practice. The participants in the evaluation sessions, 
aged 22 to 30, included designers with diverse backgrounds in GD. The eval-
uation involved two stages: in the first stage, participants generated album 
covers using the tool, and in the second, they evaluated the visual quality of 
the outputs and the tool’s capabilities through a question survey. During this 
evaluation stage, they created 46 cover designs. Appendix E further describes 
the system’s generative approach and the evaluation experiment conducted.
Preliminary findings reveal that most participants considered that 
the proposed approach generates outputs with limited visual diversity, 
primarily due to the visual constraints imposed by the template strategy. 
Some participants considered the coherence high enough for all the outputs 
to be considered part of the same collection. However, they also acknowl-
edged some visual diversity, particularly in terms of colour and shapes,

and recommended that typographic options be expanded to enhance 
the diversity of the system’s outputs. Participants also expressed that this 
tool (or similar ones) could be valuable for their creative processes, par -
ticularly for brainstorming, visual discovery, and exploration. Participants 
suggested various applications beyond cover designs, including creating 
playlist images, advertisements, and merchandise materials for bands.
9.3 FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS
We have presented two preliminary works on generating book and album 
covers, expanding our investigation into the use of CD approaches to create 
print designs beyond posters. In both experiments, we developed compu-
tational methods to support contemporary GD practices, aligning with 
the objectives this thesis outlined earlier. The generation of books follows 
an expert strategy based on recognised typographic knowledge. This 
approach aims to study the feasibility and potential of using CD to auto-
mate book design generation, similar to the research presented in Part III 
of this thesis. The generation of album covers, on the other hand, uses 
a template strategy, relying on data to determine the visual characteristics 
of the outputs and explore how this approach can enhance design custo-
misation, aligning with the exploration presented in Part II of this thesis.
The book generation approach creates designs using user-provided 
text and images, operating within the Adobe InDesign software, using its 
scripting capabilities. This system does not require users to predefine any 
visual feature, allowing them to generate books entirely from scratch. Users 
can then modify the results within the familiar InDesign environment and 
print them as needed.
If they desire, users can impose specific constraints or preferences 
on the system through a dedicated interface. Throughout the generation 
process, the system will take into consideration these restrictions. More-
over, the system allows the introduction of new rules and functions, and the 
design rules can be exported to create other designs.
The experiments demonstrated the system’s ability to consistently 
generate book designs that adhere to traditional typographic rules. We eval-
uated the system with participants to determine its ability to generate 
visually diverse books from varied content and visually coherent books 
from diverse content. The results showed that the system can produce 
visually diverse books when operating without restrictions and maintain 
visual coherence when strict constraints are applied.
Despite its local search nature and certain limitations in autonomy 
compared to other expert strategies, we observed that the proposed 
system has proven to be a functional design tool. The preliminary findings 
indicate that it can assist designers in automating book typesetting and 
facilitate the exploration and discovery of new visual possibilities. 
The generative book process, mainly guided by predefined typo-
graphic principles, incorporates probabilistic mechanisms that occasion-
ally introduce variation, enhancing visual diversity and increasing the tool’s 
exploratory value. Users can limit the system’s autonomy by specifying 

236
IV EXPANDING  COMPUT A TIONAL  PRACTICES
desired features, making it useful across different stages of the design 
process, from earlier and exploratory stages (when designers can take 
advantage of random generation to look for new types of layouts) to the 
final stages (when designers need to fine-tune specific graphic attributes).
Furthermore, the system allows users to export data into settings 
files, which encode the book’s design and, later, can be loaded into the 
system to create other visually similar books. Users have the flexibility 
to input their desired book properties directly into the system interface 
or modify the typographic principles and rules the system uses. Therefore, 
we found the system to be a valuable tool for creating books that follow 
specific typographic and visual attributes, such as those required for a 
collection or series.
This system also promotes a more seamless and smoother incorpo-
ration of computational methods in the design processes, allowing designers 
to work within their familiar environment and eliminating the need to learn 
new tools. This way, designers can effortlessly edit or refine the output 
designs directly. However, it is worth noting that not all traditional Com-
puter-aided Design (CAD) software currently supports scripting and devel-
opment of computational tools. We also highlighted that this integration 
enables the development of approaches with a higher level of expressive power.
The album cover generative system employs a template strategy 
to generate designs. In this approach, the visual features of the design are 
determined by data from the user-selected album and its tracks. We used 
the Spotify API to gather these data. We also developed an online tool that 
allows users to customise the designs according to their tastes and pref -
erences after the generation.
We conducted evaluation experiments with designers, inviting them 
to generate album covers using the tool and subsequently collecting their 
feedback. Preliminary findings indicate that the tool is user-friendly and 
facilitates the creation of visually coherent album covers. The outputs 
demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed template strategies in gener-
ating designs with consistent visual characteristics, supporting automation 
in scenarios, particularly in scenarios where designs should share similar 
visual traits. Also, participants suggested various applications beyond the 
creation of cover designs, including creating playlist images, advertisements, 
and merchandise materials for bands.
This experiment demonstrates an example of one transmediation 
of album covers from print to digital media, incorporating new features 
like animation, interactivity, and reactivity, similar to our work with moving 
posters.
These two experiments presented in this chapter demonstrate how 
CD processes can automate the generation of different GD artefacts. 
Despite exploring two distinct methods, the findings indicate that both 
approaches present significant potential for a wide range of print design 
scenarios where the generation of custom-made designs is needed. We 
consider that they are particularly relevant for print-on-demand applica-
tions and for creating designs for existing collections or series.

237
 COMPUT A TIONAL  GENERA TION  OF PRINT  DESIGNS11
The book design experiment demonstrates the potential of expert 
approaches for automation. These approaches can potentially optimise 
routine tasks and assist in the exploratory and discovery phases of the 
design process. Although more limited visually, the template-based 
approach used on album cover designs shows potential for creating cus-
tomised designs that can adapt to various contexts, which we consider 
could promote more personalised communication with the audience. These 
findings align with conclusions drawn in other sections of this thesis.
Both approaches offer mechanisms that enable users to customise 
and add new features according to their preferences using configuration 
files. In the case of the first experiment, users can even introduce new 
computational methods (referred to as “experiment features”). We consider 
that this flexibility allows users to modify the existing approaches, adapting 
the system to meet specific needs. Also, by enabling the introduction 
of novel visual elements, we consider that these customisations can poten-
tially enhance the distinguishability of the output designs.
In conclusion, these works highlight two distinct applications of CD 
methods in the domain of print designs, each offering varying levels of 
autonomy and expertise. 

238
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES

239 IV EXPANDING  COMPUT A TIONAL  PRACTICES
We have developed preliminary work by conceiving computational 
approaches to create digital designs, particularly websites. These methods 
aim to research how the studied computational techniques can be extended 
to website design. We have developed three works in this context: a web 
page generator and two internet artworks.
The web page generator uses computational methods to create 
designs inspired by brutalist web aesthetics, 125 automatically retrieving 
content based on user input. Users can refine the generated outputs through 
a dedicated interface to align with their tastes and preferences. This 
system was developed as a preliminary study to explore how computational 
approaches can support web design automation and the development 
of customised interactive visuals. We conducted preliminary evaluation 
experiments to assess the system’s ability to generate websites. We used 
this system to create a design installation that autonomously generates 
content from random inputs, intending to encourage reflection on the 
advantages and limitations of automating design practices.
We also present two internet artworks: Portraits of No One and Sonar. 
Portraits of No One is an online participative artwork that generates artifi-
cial human portraits by recombining facial components from its audience. 
Additionally, it creates ambient crowd noise based on the interactions of 
the participants. This audiovisual work challenges viewers to question the 
authenticity of the content it presents. On the other hand, Sonar is an 
online audiovisual artwork that offers an interactive exploration of the 
Portuguese Carnation Revolution of 25 April 1974, which ended the Por -
tuguese Estado Novo dictatorship. It features a collection of testimonies 
from individuals who experienced this historic event, sharing their expe-
riences before, during, and after the revolution. The testimonies are linked 
to the authors’ locations at the time of writing, with the Sonar system 
autonomously selecting and sequentially presenting the corresponding 
testimonies based on these locations. The audience interacts with the 
installation by choosing one of the tracked testimonies, which is then 
presented as a multimodal audiovisual experience, including an auditory 
narration, typographic compositions, and illustrations.
These preliminary works demonstrate the practical use of compu-
tational design methods to promote automation and customisation in 
digital design creation. The following sections briefly present these works 
and provide an overview of the preliminary findings.

We developed a computational system that generates brutalist web pages 
using content sourced from Wikipedia and based on user input text. 
The system combines an expert strategy with textual analysis and tem-
plate-based methods. It also allows users to customise the outputs after 
generation. The system’s primary goal is a preliminary study using CD 
methods to automate web design generation. It aims to create outputs 
that challenge traditional interaction design principles and facilitate visual 
and interactive design discovery tasks.
The generation process starts when a user enters a search term. 
The system retrieves the content and displays it to the user, who can modify 
it before starting the generation. Figure 10.1 displays screenshots of the 
interface at different stages.

web pages automatically from random inputs. The audience could watch

every few minutes after creating a page to simulate user interactions like

Its main goal was to encourage reflection on the advantages and 
disadvantages of CD techniques and their impact on future information

10.2 PORTRAITS OF NO ONE
We designed and developed the online artwork Portraits of No One, which 
explores the computational generation of imagery at the borderline between 
the real and the artificial. The project focuses on creating photorealistic 
portraits of artificial human faces and simulating crowd noise. This online 
artwork is based on a physical installation of the same name presented at 
the Portuguese National Museum of Contemporary Art — Museu do Chiado 
(NMAC) in Lisbon, Portugal, and the Círculo de Artes Plásticas de Coimbra 
(CAPC), Portugal. Appendix G of this thesis outlines the development 
process and technical details behind the physical installation. This online 
artwork allows remote participation for those unable to visit the physical 
installation and supports installation setup at venues where creating 
a custom capturing device is impractical.
The installation generates and displays photorealistic portraits 
of human faces in real-time by recombining facial parts from audience 
members who interacted with the artwork (see Figures 10.5 to 10.7). More-
over, it generates crowd noise using sound samples captured during these 
interactions. The installation space comprises an array of artificial faces 
and ambient audio of crowd noise. As people interact with the installation, 
they will immediately see their facial components and hear the sound 
of their interaction, influencing the dynamic installation environment. 
Interaction is facilitated through custom-made capturing equipment. Across 
both exhibitions, the installation recorded over 10,000 visitor interactions.
The portraits’ photorealism challenges viewers to question the 
veracity of what they see, blurring the lines between real and artificial. 
Furthermore, the installation promotes a symbiotic relationship with its 
audience, being fed and needing people’s interaction to evolve. The Portraits 
of No One project explores portraiture within the realm of contemporary 
digital and new media art, focusing on artificial synthesis techniques. 
Its primary objective is to provoke critical thinking on how recent tech-
nological advancements reshape our perception of imagery.

IV EXPANDING  COMPUT A TIONAL  PRACTICES
The online artwork presents an ever-changing audiovisual experience, 
featuring artificial face portraits combined with ambient crowd noise, both 
generated by recombining user-provided inputs. Each portrait remains 
on the screen for a randomly chosen duration of one to three minutes. 
When a portrait disappears, it is replaced after a random pause of one 
to seven seconds. Similar to the physical installation, when users access 
the website, the portraits are loaded sequentially. The system randomly 
selects a position on the grid and pauses for one to seven seconds before 
placing a new portrait. This process continues until the grid is filled. Fol-
lowing web browser policies regarding audio autoplay, the ambient sound 
is muted by default. Users can activate the sound by clicking a speaker 
icon in the website header. Once enabled, the system plays a set of five 
sounds simultaneously. These sounds begin sequentially, with random 
intervals of silence between each, ranging from 1 to 2 seconds. Figure 10.8 
displays some screenshots of the artwork. 
 
Users can participate in the installation by clicking the “Participate” 
button located in the top-right corner of the web page header. The inter -
action begins with a description which outlines how their contributions 
(the facial components and recorded interaction sounds) will be incorpo-
rated into the artwork (see Figure 10.9a). If the user agrees to participate, 
they enter the input recording mode; otherwise, they return to the instal-
lation’s home page. Users must also grant permission for the web page 
to access the camera and microphone of their computer.
We have implemented a system that automatically detects, captures, 
and extracts facial components from users while recording the sound 
of their interactions. In the installation’s recording mode, users see a live 
video stream from their web camera, and their faces are automatically 
detected and highlighted (see Figure 10.9b). If multiple faces are recognised, 
the system prioritises the largest one. When ready, users click the “Capture 
Photo” button at the bottom of the screen. Next, a three-second countdown 
starts, and at the end of this countdown, the photo is taken (see Figure 
10.9c). Sound is recorded during the countdown. After capturing, the inputs 
are processed and saved to the file (see Figure 10.9d). Finally, a confirma-
tion screen displays the captured photo to the participant (see Figure 
10.9e). On this screen, users can access the artwork wall by clicking the 
“See Portraits of No One” button at the bottom of the page. 
Figure 10.8. Screenshots of the Portraits of 
No One online artwork. A demonstration 
video of the artwork running is available 
at https://pf.dei.uc.pt/10/2/demo.mp4 
(visited: 7 July 2025).

245
 COMPUT A TIONAL  GENERA TION  OF DIGIT AL  DESIGNS12
Alternatively, if a processing error occurs, a message appears to inform 
the user of the issue and offers a hint for a possible solution. In these cases, 
users are invited to participate again by clicking the “Retry” button or giving 
up participation. In this process, we used the OpenCV.js library  126 to rec-
ognise the face on the video stream and the Face-api.js library 127 to retrieve 
the facial landmarks of each processed face. 
We developed a server-side system to manage the distribution of faces 
and sounds, operating as a REST API service. When the client side of the 
artwork requires a new portrait or sound, it sends a request to the server, 
which provides the resource to be displayed. The server-side system works 
independently of browser clients. Regarding the generation of artificial 
faces, it produces 60 new faces per minute and stores them in a queue, 
where each face can remain for up to three minutes. If not requested within 
this time, the face is discarded and replaced by another one. Once a face 
is requested, it is sent to the client and immediately replaced in the queue.
New faces are generated using the X-Faces system (Correia et al., 
2016, 2019), which recombines input faces provided by participants. The 
system selects five faces from the dataset using a tournament method that 
prioritises the most recent photos. In this process, one face is chosen as 
the target (the base face), while the other four act as sources, contributing 
features such as eyebrows, eyes, nose, and mouth. The system ensures 
the source faces have similar head poses to the target for a seamless blend. 
For a more comprehensive overview of the face generation process used, 
see Appendix G.
The selection of sounds is similar to the process of selecting artifi-
cial faces. The server maintains a queue of 30 sound samples, distributing 
them based on client requests. Sounds are chosen from the dataset using 
a four-position tournament method, prioritising newer recordings. When 
a sound is sent to the client, it is replaced by a new one. Any sound that 
remains in the queue for more than three minutes without being selected 
is discarded and replaced.

The proposed system architecture ensures each client artwork pre-
sents distinct audiovisuals. However, it still prioritises selecting and pre-
senting more recently captured inputs. We consider that this approach adds 
more dynamism and customisation to the online artwork while maintaining 
the core idea of the physical installation.
Nevertheless, we have observed that this artwork presents a different 
visual environment than the original installation. This is mainly due to the 
uncontrolled conditions during the capture process, which led to variations 
in lighting and background. While we consider that this affects the visual 
uniformity of the portraits, it also adds visual diversity to the installation.
The online artwork has supported the presentation of the project in 
the online exhibition Human and AI Generated Multimedia and supported the 
installation of Portraits of No One in the collective exhibition Omnisciência: 
Estratégias de Fratura e Fuga (2021, see Figure 10.7) at Forum Maia, Portugal.
10.3 SONAR
Sonar is an online interactive audiovisual artwork that tracks testimonies 
about the Portuguese Carnation Revolution, which occurred on 25 April 
1974, marking the end of Portugal’s Estado Novo dictatorship. This artwork 
presents a figurative representation of sonar to detect testimonies, featuring 
an aerial view of a location tracked by 360-degree radar equipment searching 
in a clockwise motion. The location is randomly chosen from those with 
available testimonies. The artwork is available in both Portuguese and 
English. Sonar can be accessed online at https://sonar.dei.uc.pt (visited: 
7 July 2025). This project includes custom illustrations, animations, and 
sound effects. Full technical details and acknowledgements are on the 
website.
This work was developed using standard web technologies, including 
P5.js for canvas creation and rendering and Mappa.js with the Mapbox API for 
map rendering and styling.128 It was initially designed for a physical exhi-
bition but was adapted to an online format due to COVID-19 restrictions.
The artwork’s visuals were designed to evoke a dark, shadowy atmos-
phere resembling an underwater environment (see Figure 10.10). The land 
is navy blue, and map features (e.g. seas, rivers, or streets) are rendered 
in a dark blue tone. Additionally, we incorporated a fog effect above the 
map and integrated a custom sonar resonance loop sound as ambient audio. 
Ambient audio and sound effects are muted at the start to adhere to current 
web browser audio auto-play regulations. Users can enable sound by clicking 
the pop-up message in the bottom-right corner of the browser.
When a testimony is detected, a beep sounds, and a circular marker 
blinks at the location where the author was when the testimony was written. 
The colour and blinking speed of the marker vary based on the timestamp 
of the testimony. Testimonies from before the revolution are displayed in 
blue (#375D81), blinking between 25 % and 40 % opacity. Testimonies from 
during the revolution are presented in a light lavender (#FFE6FA), blinking 
between 15 % and 30 % opacity. Testimonies from after the revolution are

shown in light blue (#97B4CF), blinking between 15 % and 30 % opacity. 
We empirically chose these colours based on the desired environment 
for the artwork. The marker stays visible for a few seconds until the sonar 
antenna finds it again. Users can select and view a testimony by clicking 
on it. The sonar moves to a new random location if no action is taken. 
After viewing a testimony, the sonar “flies” to another random location, 
and the map adjusts to the new destination.
The collected testimonies include poems, diary entries, and inter -
views covering events before, during, and after the revolution. This col-
lection features 21 authors, including writers, politicians, and musicians. 
The collected testimonies are written in 11 different locations: Algiers 
(Algeria), Beira (Mozambique), Coimbra (Portugal), Geneva (Switzerland), 
Heidelberg (Germany), Lisbon (Portugal), Moscow (USSR), Paris (France), 
Santa Barbara, CA (USA), Sintra (Portugal), and Vancouver, BC (Canada). 
This research was previously conducted by Daniela Côrtes Maduro (see 
Appendix H). This artwork uses a database that links locations to testimo-
nies and assets, allowing for easy addition of new ones.
Each testimony page is designed using a template-based strategy. 
It features an audio reading of the testimony, a dynamic typographic com-
position, and an animated line illustration inspired by the content, occa-
sionally accompanied by sound effects. Table 10.1 summarises the 
characteristics of the illustrations and sound effects. In the bottom-left 
corner, the author’s initials and their location coordinates at the time 
of the testimony are displayed.

The animations and illustrations are created specifically for this 
artwork based on the text of the testimonies. The illustration starts with 
a small point (simulating a drawing pencil) on the left side of the screen, 
gradually sketching. Once the declamation ends, the illustration is erased 
progressively, line by line. A single testimony may have multiple animations 
associated with it. Examples of these testimony representations are shown 
in Figures 10.11 to 10.13.
The typographic composition was created using the Maquina de Ouver 
system (Couceiro e Castro et al., 2019), which maps speech features to 
typographic elements. Voice intensity is represented by font size, word 
duration by letter spacing, and pauses by the space between words. The 
typeface used is Zeitung Mono .129 At the end of each testimony, the com -
position gradually fades out, letter by letter.
The audio declamations and text of the testimonies are available 
in both Portuguese and English. The recording, editing, mastering, and 
mixing of the testimonies are performed by Miguel Alves, Vitor Torpedo, 
and João Luis, and the voice-overs of testimonies are from Maria Manuel 
Almeida and João Paulo Janicas (from the theatre company Cooperativa 
Bonifrates),130 as well as Tracy Vandal and João Luis. 
The Sonar artwork was designed to provide a discovery-based, inter-
active, and customised way of exploring diverse historical perspectives on 
the Portuguese Carnation Revolution. Additionally, we designed this 
artwork to serve an archival purpose, ensuring easy access to the collection 
of testimonies and demonstrating how new digital media and electronic 
literature can be used to voice social concerns. Sonar was featured in the 
collective online exhibition (un)continuity — a virtual exhibition (Maduro 
et al., 2020)131 and included in the fourth volume of the Electronic Literature 
Collection (Maduro et al., 2021).
