COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES

251
 IV EXPANDING  COMPUT A TIONAL  PRACTICES
11 COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN  
BEYOND POSTERS
This part of the thesis introduced a set of preliminary experiments that 
expand our investigation of using CD in GD and Typography scenarios 
beyond the creation of poster design. Our investigation explores the appli-
cation of computational methods across both print and digital media.
In the context of print media, we developed two computational 
approaches to generate books and music album covers. We explored an 
expert strategy to produce book layouts from user-provided text and images. 
This approach operates within Adobe InDesign, a widely used computerised 
software for editorial design, and it is informed by typographic knowledge 
or expertise retrieved from recognised literature on the field. This system 
allows users to set constraints or express preferences for the design fea-
tures and introduce new rules. Our preliminary evaluations of the system’s 
outputs showed that it can produce visually diverse and coherent designs, 
whether or not user restrictions are applied. We also observed that inte-
grating these approaches in traditional design tools helps ease incorporating 
computational methods into conventional design practices, allowing 
designers to work within a familiar environment. Our preliminary findings 
indicate that expert strategies have great potential, both in automating 
routine tasks and assisting in the exploratory and discovery phases of the 
design process.
For computationally creating album cover designs, we employed 
a template-based approach that uses data to define the visual character -
istics of the design. The album covers are created based on a user-selected 
album, analysing its metadata and sonic data. stochastic methods are 
used to introduce visual variation. We also developed an online tool that 
allows users to customise the resulting designs according to their tastes 
and desires after the generation. Preliminary evaluation experiments show 
that the system generates visually coherent album covers with consistent 
visual characteristics. We observed it valuable for supporting design in 
scenarios where shared visual traits are desirable, such as creating collec-
tions for the same artist or label. Also, we found that this approach demon-
strates the potential to automate the creation of customised print designs 
to align with specific data or audience preferences. Furthermore, our 
findings demonstrate the capacity of CD methods to facilitate transmedi-
ation from print to digital media. In this case, we present a musical album 
cover that can incorporate new features like animation, interactivity, and 
reactivity in their digital versions.
Considering our findings, our analysis indicates that CD processes 
can also automate and support the creation of print GD artefacts, aligned 
with the methods for poster design explored in other parts of this thesis. 

252
IV EXPANDING  COMPUT A TIONAL  PRACTICES
The proposed approaches show significant potential for scenarios requiring 
custom-made designs, such as print-on-demand applications, or for cases 
where designs are expected to share similar features, like those in existing 
collections and series.
In digital media, we conducted experiments on developing three 
works featuring a web page generator and two internet artworks. The web 
page generator introduces an automated design process, generating web 
pages that align with the principles of brutalist web design. Web pages are 
generated using an expert approach, sourcing content online based on 
user-provided search terms. The creation process uses a set of rules, style 
functions, and features based on content analysis. It also integrates tem-
plate and stochastic methods. We designed an interface to allow users 
to refine designs after generation.
We preliminary tested the system with both designers and non -
-designers to evaluate its outputs and potential. The evaluation results 
demonstrate that this approach can create visually diverse and distinctive 
web pages. Although testing participants viewed the outputs as exploratory 
and not directly usable on the web, they also recognised the system’s 
potential for automating the exploration and discovery of new visual and 
interactive design possibilities. This experiment also reveals that sto-
chastic methods allow for the introduction of visual variation in designs. 
We also developed a design installation in which the system autonomously 
generates web pages from random terms, demonstrating its potential for 
contextual and autonomous web page generation.
The two internet artworks, Portraits of No One and Sonar, use com-
putational methods to create customised web pages. Portraits of No One 
explores the creation of artificial portraits and crowd noise by recombining 
data from the audience, including facial portraits and sound samples. This 
artwork extends a namesake physical installation to allow remote partic-
ipation by a broader audience. This online artwork is also designed to 
facilitate the physical installation of artwork in sites where custom -capturing 
devices cannot be implemented.
Sonar provides an interactive exploration of the Portuguese Carna-
tion Revolution’s history based on written testimonies from people who 
lived through the events. This artwork uses a figurative version of sonar 
to track the testimonies across various global locations. Each testimony 
is presented as an audiovisual representation, which includes a spoken 
declamation of testimony,  a line art illustration, and a typographic depic-
tion of the same declamation. 
Both artworks use template strategies to create visuals (such as 
faces or representations of testimonies) and the layout of the websites. 
Our experiments with these artworks suggest that computational approaches, 
particularly template strategies, can effectively create customised designs 
and interactive experiences for the audience, as observed in other parts 
of this thesis.
The work presented in this part of this thesis demonstrates how CD 
methods can be applied to create both print and digital media, extending 
beyond poster designs. These approaches offer varying degrees of autonomy, 

253 COMPUT A TIONAL  GRAPHIC DESIGN  BEYOND  P OSTERS13
expertise and expressive power and can address different contexts and objec-
tives. Our experiments also indicate that CD can automate the production 
of GD, particularly in creating series and collections.
The book and brutalist web page generator systems employ expert 
strategies where the generation is based on domain-specific knowledge about 
the field. The book system relies on typographic principles derived from 
specialised literature in the field, while the brutalist generator employs 
default rules, styling functions, and data-driven methods. Both systems also 
use probabilistic and stochastic methods to introduce visual variation.
Our experimentation with these two systems highlighted the auto-
mation potential of high-autonomy and expertise approaches, particularly 
expert strategies. The findings indicates that, depending on the approach’s 
goals, this potential applies to both routine design tasks and the discovery 
stages of the design process. On the other hand, although visually more 
limited, the template-based approaches used in album cover design and 
internet artworks reveal the ability to create customised designs, which 
we consider creating more personalised communication with the audience. 
We have noted that modifying and refining the outputs of compu-
tational systems can be challenging. To address this issue, in these exper-
iments, we developed user interfaces and configuration files that facilitate 
easy customisation and adjustment of these outputs. Preliminary results 
indicate that this approach enhances flexibility, allowing output designs 
to be corrected and modified without the need to rerun the entire process.
Similarly, the book design system generates new designs within the 
environment of a computerised design tool, allowing designers to modify 
the design entirely after generation. Our preliminary observations indicate 
that this approach provides high flexibility to designers and facilitates 
more accessible and widespread use of CD approaches in GD practices. 
Moreover, we observed that using the scripting capabilities of typical 
computerised design tools enables the creation of systems with greater 
expressive power, as they can utilise all the functions and features available 
on these software applications.
In summary, our preliminary experiments on the generation of designs 
beyond posters reveal that CD approaches can be used in various contexts, 
including print and digital media. Our preliminary experimentation shows 
that CD processes can enhance and reshape GD practices by promoting 
automation and customisation, aligning with findings in other parts of this 
thesis. The expert approaches employed in the website and book gener -
ators showed the potential for automating routine tasks and aiding design 
exploration. The template strategies explored in the album generator and 
internet artworks demonstrated potential for design customisation.

254
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES

255
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
Part V
EPILOGUE

256
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES

257
 V EPILOGUE
CONCLUSIONS
The evolution of Graphic Design (GD) and Typography is closely inter -
twined with technological advancements. Even before the rise of modern 
computing, algorithmic and systematic approaches were being explored 
within the domain. For instance, traditional typography and letterpress 
methods utilised modular techniques, and designers in the early twentieth 
century experimented with grid systems for organising layouts and creating 
visual variations.
The introduction of Graphical User Interfaces (GUIs) and the devel-
opment of early electronic typesetting and word-processing software 
facilitated using computers in the GD context. In the later years of the 
twentieth century, the development of Desktop Publishing (DTP) tools 
expanded access to GD tools, encouraging experimentation and new aes-
thetics. Today, designers primarily work with computerised tools. Several 
designers are also increasingly exploring Computational Design (CD) 
approaches to generate their own tools and systems. CD approaches in GD 
have shown the potential to reshape design practices. Designers can shift 
from creating individual designs to developing systems that systematically 
generate multiple designs. We observe this in contemporary design trends, 
such as dynamic branding and responsive designs. These approaches are 
designed with diverse degrees of autonomy, expertise, and expressive power. 
The primary objective of this thesis was to investigate the application 
of CD methods in the GD context, mainly focusing on typography and layout 
design challenges. The research hypothesis posits that the use of CD 
approaches can lead to innovative communication methods and design 
techniques while automating certain design tasks. To test this hypothesis, 
we conducted a series of computational experiments to create GD artefacts. 
The primary motivation of these experiments was to evaluate how com-
putational methods affect design practices and outcomes. We selected 
poster design for this study due to its historical importance in GD and its 
significance in self-expression and reflection for designers. Moreover, 
the single-page layout and simple information hierarchy of posters allow the 
application of our findings to other types of artefacts. The development 
process explored various computational and Artificial Intelligence (AI) 
methods, ranging from rule-based systems to more sophisticated approaches, 
like Evolutionary Computation (EC) and Machine Learning (ML) models.
Our investigation followed a research through design process involving 
the iterative experimentation, reflection, and documentation of design 
works that address real-world problems and client specifications. It is struc-
tured into three main stages. The first stage explored how computational 
processes facilitate the development of new practices of communicating 
with audiences, encouraging responsiveness and customisation (Part II). 
14

258
V EPILOGUE
The second stage addressed the challenges and opportunities of automa-
tion in design processes (Part III). In the last stage, we investigated whether 
the findings of other stages could be applied to design artefacts beyond 
posters across both print and digital media (Part IV).
Our findings demonstrate that CD, especially template strategies, 
can support the creation of designs that promote engagement and com-
municate messages more effectively to audiences, providing a positive 
answer to research question A (“Can CD support the creation of designs 
that promote audience engagement and effectively communicate their 
messages?”). 
We concentrated on tailoring designs to the audience using CD 
methods, which led us to investigate responsive and data-driven design 
techniques. Our investigation involved creating artefacts for different 
media, including real-time modification of moving posters and customised 
print designs. Additionally, we conducted preliminary studies on creating 
other types of artefacts, such as album covers that react to sound features 
and user preferences and internet artworks customised with user data.
Our experiments with moving posters revealed that computational 
approaches allow for the creation of context-aware designs that adapt to 
various audience behaviours and environmental conditions in their display 
environments (Chapter 3). Computer Vision (CV) and sensor data proved 
effective for modifying responsive designs. These methods enable real-time 
interaction, provide immediate feedback on audience movement, and allow 
for design customisation, which we consider enhances audience engage -
ment. Consequently, our findings suggest that these approaches may lead 
to more effective message transmission for the audience in moving poster 
designs. Our observations from the two internet artworks created reveal 
similar conclusions and findings (Chapter 10).
Additionally, CD facilitates the creation of customised designs that 
incorporate data provided by the audience. This capability enables the 
generation of new visuals tailored to audience-specific information. The 
results also show that this approach further enhances engagement, as 
demonstrated by the Phomotaton installation (Chapter 4). Evaluations of 
the album cover design experiments indicate similar results (Chapter 9). 
This customisation, combined with audience engagement, can also drive 
the development of new businesses and services. This is exemplified by 
the creation of a print-on-demand service developed by the Torre Literaria 
exhibition staff to sell the Photomaton outputs.
template  strategies, which offer limited autonomy  and expertise , 
have been shown to be effective in creating responsive and custom designs. 
With this approach, designers predefine actions based on data, including 
animations or procedures. Moreover, stochastic and expertise-based 
methods have helped introduce further visual variation into templates or 
generate assets for these visuals. We observed that these approaches can 
provide different levels of expressive power, with designers determining the 
suitable level based on their objectives. Nevertheless, our results also 
indicate that only a few feature variations are sufficient to introduce 
noticeable dynamism into designs. 

259
 CONCLUSIONS14
Our experiments illustrate how reactive and interactive approaches 
can be employed in this context (Chapter 3). However, we consider that 
each approach offers a different design visualisation experience for the 
audience. While reactive posters modify visual elements without altering 
the core message, interactive posters allow for the gradual communication 
of the message through interaction, which may lead to more personal 
engagement.
As digital media and techniques for gathering environmental data 
continue to advance, we anticipate that GD practices will increasingly 
integrate computational strategies, leading to more responsive designs.
The work conducted in this thesis demonstrates that automation 
through CD approaches can improve design practices, including those 
related to typography and layout. Addressing the research question B 
(“What are the automation possibilities of integrating CD techniques into 
GD practices, especially for typography and layout challenges?”), the find-
ings show that these approaches can automate a wide range of tasks, from 
specific routine tasks to discovery and exploration processes. Our exper -
imentation reveals that CD approaches provide support both as expert  
and cooperative strategies, offering varying levels of autonomy.
Our experiments focused on developing expert strategies for gen-
erating posters using evolutionary approaches (Chapter 6) and a greedy 
typesetting method (Chapter 7). We explored additional computational 
methods to automate various specific routine design tasks, including cre-
ating a design-supporting tool that employs a cooperative strategy. With 
this goal in mind, we conducted studies on generating books, album music 
covers (Chapter 9), and web pages (Chapter 10).
The findings suggest that computational approaches incorporating 
domain-specific knowledge (or expertise) can automate design tasks when 
integrated into designers' processes. expert strategies, characterised 
by their high level of autonomy and expertise, have proven effective in 
this context.
Our experimentation shows that CD can support design practices 
by facilitating data extraction and handling specific routine design tasks. 
This may reduce graphic designers' workload, allowing them to focus on 
the creative aspects of their work. Several methods we developed illustrate 
this by handling tasks such as input analysis, colour palette generation, 
line division, and typesetting. Combining multiple of these specific methods 
can fully automate the entire design process, as demonstrated by the 
posters created for the ESSYS* Sharing #UC installation (Chapter 7). Our 
experiments also revealed that these techniques can facilitate the crea-
tion of series and collections of designs. Beyond poster creation, initial 
results also indicate similar conclusions in the generation of books 
(Chapter 9) and web pages (Chapter 10). 
While EC can be less appropriate for handling specific routine design 
tasks due to its lengthy processing times and high computational demands, 
it has proven valuable for discovery and exploration tasks (Chapter 6). By 
defining the range of expected features and setting appropriate evaluation 
criteria, designers can use evolutionary approaches to generate new designs 
simultaneously, promoting serendipity and leading to unexpected discov-
eries in the design process. 

260
V EPILOGUE
We observed that, even without advanced expertise, preliminary 
experiments with books and web pages revealed that stochastic strate-
gies offer comparable discovery potential (Chapters 9 and 10). Neverthe-
less, the findings indicate that incorporating expertise in the approaches 
leads to more effective practices.
CD methods with advanced expertise  have also shown potential 
for integration into GD practices in a cooperative manner. For example, 
the greedy typesetting method allows users to focus on defining the visual 
features of posters while automating text typesetting (Chapter 7). Similarly, 
the developed evolutionary approaches enable users to express and refine 
their preferences to guide the design process (Chapter 6). We consider 
that incorporating these approaches can lead to faster and more efficient 
design processes as well as a more controlled use of CD.
Depending on the purpose and computational representation used, 
CD approaches for supporting design practices can vary in their level 
of expressive power. The observations reveal that higher expressive power 
benefits all-purpose systems and discovery tasks but is unnecessary for gen-
erating designs with well-defined visual features. 
Various methods, including ML models, rules, and measures, have 
proven effective in integrating domain-specific knowledge into the system. 
The choice of the most suitable method should depend on the required 
level of expertise, the specific design problem, and the current state of 
technology.
The use of CD faces several challenges and obstacles that affect its 
widespread adoption among graphic designers. Concerning research ques-
tion C (“What limitations may emerge from the employment of CD in GD 
and Typography practices?"), we found that primary barriers include the 
overwhelm and fatigue associated with the design generation process, 
challenges in defining characteristics and evaluation methods of CD 
approaches, and difficulties in editing the outputs. Also, graphic designers' 
lack of coding literacy can be a significant obstacle to integrating CD into 
design processes.
Our experimentation indicates that responsive and data-driven 
approaches, often based on template strategies, can enhance design 
visualisation and improve the effectiveness of message transmission. 
However, our findings also suggest that extensive use of these methods 
may result in opposite effects, creating repetitive outputs and audience 
fatigue (Chapter 3). We also observed that higher autonomy methods can 
be used to introduce visual variation into the designs.
Appropriate evaluation of outputs is crucial when using CD approaches 
in GD practices. While this rarely affects routine design tasks with well-
-defined goals, we observed that inadequate assessment of outputs can 
limit the ability of techniques, such as EC, to introduce variation and 
discover new designs (Chapter 6). Our work with expert and stochastic 
strategies for discovery, including the evolution of posters and preliminary 
work with websites and books, highlights this. The evaluation in GD pre-
sents particular challenges due to its personal and subjective nature. 
Historically, CD approaches have used interactive evaluation techniques 
where users assess the outputs. However, these approaches can be time-

261
 CONCLUSIONS14
-consuming and may lead to user fatigue. Alternatively, some works have 
explored automatic evaluation models and measures to replicate experts' 
assessments. While these methods can ease the process, they also face 
challenges in control and limit the diversity of results. Our findings indicate 
that enabling users to express their preferences and constrain design 
generation can address these issues, especially when allowing user-friendly 
modifications of these preferences.
Defining the characteristics of a CD approach can be challenging. 
Designers must base these characteristics on the design problem and 
the current state of technology. High-autonomy processes are shown to be 
challenging to control, while low-autonomy processes have proven to be 
time-consuming. Methods allowing users to express their preferences have 
been shown to be effective but can be complex to develop. While increased 
expertise offered several improvements to design practices, incorporating 
and modelling domain-specific knowledge remains difficult. Limited expres-
sive power reduces CD's discovery potential, but it has proven unnecessary 
for carrying out simple routine tasks.
CD approaches may produce outputs that are not easily adaptable 
or editable by designers, often resulting in raster formats. To partially 
address this issue, designers should, when possible, opt for approaches 
that produce outputs in vector formats, as these are easier to edit with 
computerised design tools. Several of our experiments explored this, sup-
porting the use of outputs in exhibitions (Chapters 6 and 7) and applying 
the generated typographic portraits in various formats (Chapter 4). More-
over, some computerised software supports scripting, enabling designers 
to incorporate CD approaches into their standard toolkits. This integration 
offers greater flexibility and control over the final outputs, as demonstrated 
by our preliminary experiments with book design generation (Chapter 9).
Finally, many graphic designers lack the coding literacy needed to 
develop CD approaches, which hinders the seamless integration of CD 
into their design processes. While several creative coding frameworks, 
including visual programming tools, have been developed to support coding 
in creative and design contexts, they still require a certain level of coding 
literacy and a systematic approach from designers. In this regard, some 
design schools are including computer programming courses in their 
curricula to help designers acquire the necessary technological skills. 
Moreover, recent advancements in generative AI techniques may help 
overcome this limitation.
This thesis is organised into five main parts. We began by establishing the 
foundation of our research in Part I. First, in Chapter 2, we outlined the 
core concepts (Section 2.1) and provided a historical overview of algorithmic 
and computational approaches for visual generation and manipulation 
(Section 2.2). We also examined the use of CD in GD and Typography 
(Section 2.3) and analysed CD primary strategies in layout and typographic 
design (Section 2.4). In addition, in Section 4.1, we reviewed related work 
on typographic portraits essential to the research work presented in that 
chapter. This study identified key approaches, opportunities and challenges 
to guide the experimental research presented in the later parts of the thesis.

262
V EPILOGUE
In Part II of the thesis, we explored how computational approaches 
can be used to develop responsive designs by using environmental data. 
We developed experiments with creating responsive moving posters (Chapter 
3). We experimented with data-driven and context-aware methods to create 
reactive and interactive moving posters. These approaches incorporated 
CV, physical computing, and access to georeferenced sources. Also, we 
introduced a responsive poster generator that adapts designs based on 
georeferenced and environmental data. The system was tested in the urban 
space, and its outputs were preliminarily evaluated by people. Appendices 
A, B, and C further describe these works in creating reactive and interactive 
moving posters, as well as the environmentally responsive poster gener -
ator, respectively. In Chapter 4, we presented Photomaton, an interactive 
installation that generates custom designs. These designs combine a 
typographic portrait of the user and a text, both defined based on user 
input. This installation was part of a permanent exhibition on Lusophone 
literature, and we evaluated it based on museum requirements. Overall, 
these experiments demonstrate that CD approaches, especially template 
strategies, can effectively support the creation of adaptable designs, which 
findings have indicated are more efficient and engaging, addressing research 
question A. In this context, our experimentation reveals that this type 
of strategy can foster the emergence of new business opportunities and 
services, as exemplified by the print-on-demand service created from the 
Photomaton installation. While template strategies enable faster and more 
controlled design production, the findings indicate that their extensive 
use can be time-consuming, illustrating the concerns discussed in research 
question C. Our observations show that stochastic and expert methods 
can be useful for introducing variation.
In Part III of this thesis, we explored the automation potential CD 
approaches in GD practice, experimenting with strategies that differed in 
autonomy and expertise. Chapter 6 focused on EC methods, presenting 
three evolutionary approaches for generating posters and including user-
-guided evaluation. In each experiment, we used various measures and 
automatic fitness evaluations to assess the outputs based on legibility , 
aesthetics, and relevance of semantics. In these approaches, users could 
express their preferences to guide the evolution of the designs. We tested 
this approach to autonomously generate typographic poster designs while 
allowing user guidance. Chapter 7 introduced a greedy typesetting method. 
We used this method to develop a design-support tool for creating posters 
and an automated workflow, which was applied in the development of the 
ESSYS* Sharing #UC media art installation. In the work presented in both 
chapters, additional CD approaches were used to automate specific routine 
design tasks, such as input analysis, line division, and colour palette gen-
eration. Overall, our experimentation demonstrates that CD approaches 
can significantly support design practices by promoting the automation 
of tasks with varying generalities and complexity, providing insights into 
research question B. We also observed that developing methods to model 
evaluation in the GD context remains a challenge, and even with user guid-
ance, outputs often require further modification by designers, addressing 
research question C.

263
 CONCLUSIONS14
Lastly, in Part IV, we examined the application of our findings to 
other GD and typography artefacts beyond poster design. Chapter 9 addressed 
print design through two experiments, focusing on book design and music 
album covers. Appendices D and E provide more details on the work related 
to generating books and album covers, respectively. Chapter 10 addressed 
digital media with three experiments, including a system for generating 
brutalist web pages and two internet artworks, Portrait of No One and Sonar. 
Appendix F gives more details about the brutalist web page generator. 
Portrait of No One generates artificial portraits and audio using audience 
data, while Sonar presents perspectives on the Portuguese Carnation 
Revolution through written testimonies from that period. Appendices G 
and H present support work related to these internet artworks, respectively. 
These works explored different levels of autonomy, expertise, and expressive 
power. The results highlighted the applicability of our findings in poster 
designs, showing how CD techniques can be used to create various artefacts 
and enhance automation in several GD practices. Our experimentation 
demonstrates that data-driven approaches and template strategies can 
improve customisation in design artefacts, resulting in more engaging and 
personalised artefacts, approaching research question A. These works also 
demonstrate that CD approaches can automate a range of design tasks, 
from specialised to discovery tasks, as addressed in research question B. 
They have proven to efficiently support the creation of a series of artefacts, 
text typesetting, and generating multiple outputs from the same content. 
Meeting the objectives of research question C, our experiments reveal 
similar limitations and barriers. We observed that integrating CD into 
traditional design tools partially helps designers edit outputs more easily. 
Moreover, our experimentation reveals that developing tools for refining 
outputs offers some support in addressing this same challenge. Allowing 
users to specify desired output features through configuration files and 
interfaces has also proven valuable in guiding the design process.
The work presented in this thesis highlights the transmediation 
potential of computational media for traditional GD artefacts and practices. 
For instance, moving posters exemplify this transformation by adapting 
print poster designs into dynamic digital media with interactive and respon-
sive elements (Chapter 3). Furthermore, we found that expert strategies 
can facilitate this transition from analogue to computational media. This 
process adapts traditional procedures and representations to promote 
automation, which can improve the efficiency and capabilities of the orig-
inal craft. This is exemplified by the developed evolutionary experiments, 
which drew inspiration from nineteenth-century letterpress techniques 
(Chapter 6).
Several of our works demonstrate that computational media can 
support both artistic practices and social activism. We conducted exper -
iments to explore artistic concepts and also tested some of our systems 
with social activism content. These experiments include generating posters 
with social quotes, the design of the artwork ESSYS*: Sharing #UC, which 
reflects on contemporary notions of place, and the Pedir a Palavra, featuring 
posters addressing current issues affecting young people (Chapters 6 and 7). 

264
V EPILOGUE
Similarly, Metamorphosis addresses human impacts on climate change 
(Chapter 3). Also, the internet artwork Portraits of No One explores the 
effects of artificial synthesis techniques, while Sonar provides an interac-
tive presentation of the history of the Portuguese Carnation Revolution 
(Chapter 10).
Finally, we highlight that, within this thesis, we conducted several 
experiments that address client briefs, including works such as Desenhar Car-
tazes com / para o Caminho (Chapter 3), Photomaton (Chapter 4),  and ESSYS*: 
Sharing #UC (Chapter 7). Also, these projects received some coverage in 
regional and national Portuguese newspapers and news agencies. We con-
sider these experiments to be successful examples of how CD techniques 
can be effectively integrated into contemporary GD practices. 
Regarding disseminating our research, most of our contributions have 
been presented at international conferences and published in interna-
tional journals. Below, we provide a list of resulting publications organised 
according to the experimental parts of the thesis.

sive designs resulted in five publications.

V EPILOGUE
The evolutionary experiments conducted were supported by a schol-
arship from SPECIES, the Society for the Promotion of Evolutionary 
Computation in Europe and its Surroundings. Posters created using evo-
lutionary methods (Chapter 6) were exhibited at the Centro Arte Compu-
tulense in Madrid, Spain (S. M. Rebelo et al., 2018), the art gallery of the 
Faculty of Fine Arts at the University of Porto, Portugal (S. M. Rebelo et 
al.,2019), and were also selected for Mostra Jovens Criadores (2019). Fur -
thermore, we organised workshops named Pedir a Palavra, where we col-
laborated with secondary students from Escola Secundária José Falcão in 
Coimbra, Portugal, to develop the design-supporting tool (Chapter 7). The 
results were showcased in an exhibition at Convento São Francisco (CSF) 
in Coimbra, Portugal (2023). These workshops were part of a mediation 
project linked to the exhibition Primaveras Estudantis: da crise de 1962 ao 
25 de Abril, supported by Câmara Municipal de Coimbra and CSF.
In this same context, we also created the art installation ESSYS*: 
Sharing #UC at MUSEU art gallery of Círculo de Artes Plásticas de Coimbra 
(CAPC), Portugal, from August to December 2021 (Chapter 7). A prelim-
inary study for this installation was presented in the performance sessions 
of the 9th Conference on Computation, Communication, Aesthetics & X (Seiça 
et al., 2021), and a minimal version of this installation was featured in 
a session commemorating 250 years of Faculty of Science and Technology 
of UC (2022). This artwork was partially funded by the Institute of Inter-
disciplinary Research of the UC.
In Part IV, we extended our investigation to other design artefacts, resulting 
in subsequent publications.

The outputs generated by the brutalist website generator were fea-
tured in various collective exhibitions: Future Visions (J. N. Rebelo et al., 
2021b) online, Contingency (J. N. Rebelo et al. 2021) in Aveiro, Portugal, and 

267
 CONCLUSIONS14
{Between} (J. N. Rebelo et al., 2021) in Coimbra, Portugal. The internet 
version of the Portraits of No One was featured in Human and AI Generated 
Multimedia at the ACM Multimedia 2020 conference in Seattle, USA, and sup-
ported the installation of Portraits of No One in the collective exhibition 
Omnisciência: Estratégias de Fratura e Fuga (Martins et al., 2021b) at Forum 
Maia, Portugal. The artwork Sonar appeared in the online exhibition (un)
continuity (Maduro et al., 2020) at the ELO 2020 conference in Orlando, USA, 
and was later included in the Electronic Literature Collection (Maduro et al., 
2021, vol. 4). 
Portraits of No One was based on a physical installation displayed at 
the National Museum of Contemporary Art—Museu do Chiado (NMAC) 
in Lisbon, Portugal, as part of the SONAE Media Art Award  exhibition 
(Martins et al., 2019), at CAPC in Coimbra, Portugal (Martins et al., 2021a), 
and was selected for the Golden Bee 14 (un)real Global Biennale of Graphic 
Design 2020 in the interactive video installations category.
In addition to the contributions from each part of this thesis, a selection 
of the poster designs created in the context of this thesis, named Poster 
Factory, was nominated and shortlisted in the interactive video installation 
category of the Golden Bee 14 (un)real Global Biennale of Graphic Design, and 
presented at HSK Gallery in Moscow, Russia. It was also featured in the 
Y, Desenhar Portugal exhibition as part of the Porto Design Biennale 2019 in 
Matosinhos, Portugal, from November 2019 to February 2020, and in the 
Do Acaso a Condição artwork the Montra-Relâmpago exhibition by Há Baixa 
Association in Coimbra, Portugal.
Our findings provide a starting point for continued research and practice 
in Computational GD. For future work, we plan to extend our investigation 
into other GD artefacts and domains such as visual identity design, type 
design, and information visualisation. We also aim to investigate new 
automation techniques, focusing on expert and cooperative strategies, 
particularly by integrating generative AI methods. Furthermore, we plan 
to conduct additional experiments and tests on compositions that integrate 
typography and imagery and continue investigating approaches that enable 
users to guide the design creation process by expressing their preferences. 
We also seek to develop more seamless methods for integrating CD tools 
into GD processes, which might involve incorporating these tools into 
existing computerised design tools. This study will involve testing with 
design experts, as well as observational and phenomenological testing 
with users.

REACTIVE

A02
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
This appendix presents an experiment investigating Computational Design 
(CD) approaches in Graphic Design (GD), specifically in Poster Design. The 
goal is to explore these methods for creating new communication strategies 
to engage audiences, as described in Chapter 3. The work in this appendix 
features a responsive moving poster that reacts to environmental data.

A03 APPENDIX  A REACTIVE  MOVING  P OSTERS
REACTIVE MOVING POSTERS
Poster design is among the most well-established, enduring, and resilient 
design practices, having played a key role in visual communication throughout 
history (Blauvelt, 2011b; Sontag, 1999). Even in ancient times, primitive 
types of posters were already observable, and over the centuries, they 
adapted, changing their characteristics and production methods as tech-
nology advanced (Blauvelt, 2011b; Guffey, 2015). This way, they have adapted 
to novel social and technological contexts while maintaining their funda-
mental purposes of conveying messages (Hollis, 2001; Meggs & Purvis, 2016).
Over time, CD and Computational Creativity (CC) methods have 
been used in GD. Chapter 2 provides an overview of how computational 
techniques are explored in the context of GD and Typography. We observed 
that these computational methods have led to the emergence of responsive 
designs, where visual features and elements dynamically adapt to data 
during visualisation and production. For example, responsive designs might 
change based on real-time data feeds or environmental factors such as 
location or time. We found that these responsive designs have the poten-
tial to create designs that encourage greater audience engagement, sug-
gesting they can effectively communicate their messages. An example is 
the use of reactive and interactive graphics in moving poster designs. 
Moving poster designs are a recent type of design that, although 
resembling traditional posters, incorporate animation and video to enhance 
the message delivery, aiming to engage their audience better. These posters 
serve various purposes, including advertising, entertainment, and educa-
tion. Although they deviate from traditional posters in their use of motion 
and digital elements, moving posters are designed to adhere to the con -
ventions, standards, and formats of classic print poster designs (Benyon, 
2016; Schaub, 2022). The rise of these approaches is amplified by the 
increased proliferation of digital media in physical spaces and the wide-
spread use of mobile computing in contemporary times (Conrad, 2021). 
Unlike their traditional print counterparts, moving posters are typically 
crafted for mass digital display rather than for mass print production.
There is no typical way of animating a moving poster, ranging from 
simple animations to more complex filmic posters, often employing loop-based 
animations and video. The Moving Poster Archive (Schaub, 2022) offers a 
wide collection of examples. Moreover, we have recently noticed an increase 
in discussions about moving posters at various GD events and conferences, 
including the Le Signe Design Biennale (Chaumont, France),1 the  Golden Bee 
Graphic Design Biennale (Moscow, Russia),2 the DEMO Festival (Amsterdam, 
Netherlands),3 or the Weltformat Poster Festival (Lucerne, Switzerland).4
As moving posters gained popularity, several designers started incor-
porating reactive and interactive behaviours, experimenting with compu-
tational technologies like physical computing, Computer Vision (CV),

A04
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
or Augmented Reality. Within this context, template strategies have shown 
significant potential. These strategies allow designers to predefine varia-
tions in visual features based on collected data, giving them greater control 
over the characteristics of the design at each stage.
The work present in this appendix focuses on developing and stud-
ying reactive moving poster designs. These are context-aware artefacts in 
which features and elements respond to data, primarily related to the 
location where the poster is displayed. These data add dynamism to the 
design without altering its core information and content. We experiment 
with template  strategies to examine their potential in developing reactive 
moving poster designs. The developed responsive poster employs con-
text-aware techniques and environmental data to adjust its visual fea-
tures automatically in response to viewers’ behaviour and the surrounding 
environment. This way, each visualisation of a reactive poster is different, 
influenced by the time and characteristics of the space in which it is observed. 
We intend to investigate different data-gathering techniques to 
understand their potential use in this context. The proposed approaches 
collect environmental data by observing the behaviour of the poster’s 
audience and the state of the surrounding environment. We experimented 
with real-time environmental data collected through CV, sensors, and 
georeferenced data to understand the differences and impact of each on 
poster designs.
Our main motivation was to create reactive moving posters that are 
directly linked to the environment and, consequently, to their audience. 
This way, we aimed to avoid random approaches for defining features, 
which might produce autonomous moving posters but would not introduce 
new forms of interaction with the environment.
In the following sections, we present two approaches for devel-
oping reactive moving posters, each employing a different strategy for col-
lecting data from the surrounding environment. In the first section, we 
present an approach where the visual appearance of poster elements is 
modified using CV techniques and data collected based on the location 
where the poster is being viewed. The following section introduces a tem-
plate strategy for designing moving posters that react to data collected 
through physical computing methods. The experimentation with this approach 
included a hands-on workshop with upper-secondary students. The final 
section summarises the main findings and conclusions.
A .1  EXPERIMENTING WITH COMPUTER VISION  
AND GEOREFERENCED DA T A
This first approach involved developing and designing a reactive moving 
poster. This work is an initial study intended to investigate the impact of 
environmental data on creating reactive moving poster designs. For this 
matter, we employ a template strategy for designing moving posters using 
two types of data gathering: one that facilitates real-time interaction with 
the audience (CV) and another that incorporates environmental georef -

A05 APPENDIX  A REACTIVE  MOVING  P OSTERS
erenced data, which changes more gradually and is not dependent on the 
audience. We opted for these types of data due to their easy retrieval with 
existing frameworks, along with the widespread availability of cameras 
and internet access on devices.
This poster consists of reactive elements that can sequentially vary 
their appearance. These elements begin as two-dimensional shapes, revealing 
a three-dimensional aspect only in response to the data (see Figure A.1).
The poster comprises three types of visual elements: boxes, spheres, 
and letterforms. The viewers’ position determines the shape of these 
visuals, while their colour is based on the air temperature of the location 
where the poster is viewed. For this, the visual features of these visuals 
react to data from the environment gathered using a video capture camera 
and CV methods, as well as using georeferenced weather data.
The poster was designed for presentation in both the physical world, 
such as a physical installation at the entrance of a building, and the online 
world, such as a reactive web banner. We used Processing Java for poster 
development, integrating the OpenCV 5 framework for CV and the Temboo 
software toolkit for collecting weather data.6 Figure A.2 presents the created 
poster in its initial state.
The poster’s visual elements respond to the audience’s behaviour 
when they are in front of it. In this case, we detect the audience’s movement 
using a face detection algorithm, the off-the-shelve OpenCV Haar-cascade 
face detector. When a person is detected in front of the poster, a random 
element is selected, and the position of the person’s face is used to control 
the appearance of this element, thereby defining the animation of the 
selected visual element. To achieve this, we normalised the position of the 
person’s face, both x and y coordinates, from the camera capture to a

A06
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
two-dimensional coordinate ranging between -2π  and 2π. The resulting 
value is then used to control the animation of the selected visual element. 
In other words, when the viewer’s face is motionless in front of the poster, 
the poster does not change; however, the more the viewer’s face moves, 
both horizontally and vertically, the more pronounced the change in the 
visual element on the poster (see Figure A.3). When multiple people are 
in front of the poster, it calculates the midpoint between their positions 
and uses this position. The element is swapped after a person interacts 
with it for more than one minute, with the current transformations pre-
served on the last selected visual.
Each type of visual element reacts differently to the audience’s 
motion. The sphere elements move in one of the axes. In other words, the 
centre of spheres moves horizontally, i.e. in the direction of the x-axis, 
or vertically, i.e. in the direction of the y-axis (see Figure A.4). The maximum 
movement on the axis is defined randomly when the shape is created 
in a predefined range of values from 5 to 20. When people are detected on 
the capture, their position is mapped. When people are in the centre of the 
capture, there is no movement on the shape; however, when they are at 
the edges of the capture area, the movement on the sphere is the predefined 
maximum value. The sphere movement is directional and can be positive 
or negative along the defined axis.
Similarly, the box elements rotate on a single axis. The rotation axis 
of each box is defined randomly when the shape is initialised. To empha-
sise the rotation of the box elements, we used directional lights to create 
shadows on the sides of the boxes (see Figure A.6).
Letterform elements have three different types of animation. The first 
one, called rotation, involves the letterform rotating around its centre on 
both the vertical and horizontal axes (see Figure A.7). 
In the second type of animation, called rotation with traces, letter -
forms rotate around their upper right corner in both axes, leaving traces 
during the rotation. This effect has two modes: fixed and non-fixed. In the 
fixed mode, traces are pre-existing on the poster, and the rotation of 
the letter only modifies the spacing between these traces. The number 
of traces depends on the initial rotation angle of the letter. Therefore, the 
higher the initial angle, the greater the probability of creating more traces. 
In the non-fixed mode, new traces are only generated during the rotation 
of the element. The mode, direction of rotation, and the initial number of 
traces (in the fixed mode) are randomly defined on the initialisation of 
the letterform element. Figure A.8 illustrates the behaviour of the two modes.

Figure A.10. The poster at different air

The third and final type of animation, named  translate with traces, 
involves changing the position of a letterform, leaving behind an accordion-
-like trace. The letterform is initially created with traces, and when people 
are detected, both the primary letterform and its traces are translated. 
This effect is similar to the sphere’s movement, and the maximum trans-
lation value is randomly defined within a range of 10 to 5 (see Figure A.9).
We used weather data, specifically air temperature forecasts, asso -
ciated with the location where the poster is being displayed to determine 
its colour palette. The poster’s location is identified based on the public 
Internet Protocol (IP) address of the device running the system. Subse-
quently, this location is used to obtain the current air temperature via the 
Open Weather API.7 Temperature information is updated every 15 minutes, 
and the current temperature is normalised relative to the average minimum 
and maximum temperature values for the poster’s location.8 
We constrain the colours of elements to a predetermined spectrum 
consisting of four distinct hues, each with various tints. The swatches in 
Figure A.10 present the key tones across this colour spectrum. We empir-
ically determined the element’s hue. The tint is then mapped based on the 
temperature value: more saturated colours represent warmer temperatures, 
while less saturated colours indicate cooler temperatures (see Figures A.5 
and A.10). This colour spectrum is defined in a configuration file and can 
be modified as necessary.
We observed that even a small number of inputs, such as the number 
and position of viewers and the current air temperature, is sufficient 
to introduce reactivity into a moving poster. Our experimentation also 
reveals that CV is effective in creating reactive elements, allowing real-time 
interaction and responding instantly to audience movement. This use 
of CV holds significant promise for creating more engaging and customised 
visualisation experiences for the audience. Also, the easier implementation 
of contemporary CV frameworks simplifies the development process, 
making it more accessible and practical for use in various applications. 
Moreover, integrating online contextual data, such as weather information, 
showed that the moving poster can adapt to less dynamic environmental 
data. Since these data change more slowly, we used them to adjust a less 
noticeable feature, such as the colour palette. Our observations reveal that 
this approach appears to enhance the poster’s dynamism, especially when 
viewed sporadically over time.

A09 APPENDIX  A REACTIVE  MOVING  P OSTERS
A.2 EXPERIMENTING WITH PHYSICAL COMPUTING
In the second approach, we created moving posters that respond to sensor 
data from the physical world. We aimed to further investigate the impact 
of real-time environmental interaction data on creating reactive moving 
posters. We were also interested in studying how data gathered by sensors 
affects design, particularly when compared with other real-time environ-
mental data techniques. Although sensors provide more precise environ-
mental readings, this approach requires the development of a  custom 
hardware interface.
We developed a template poster and a code framework to simplify 
rendering dynamic elements, mapping sensor data to visuals, and handling 
communication between an Arduino microcontroller (which captures the 
sensor data) and the poster via serial communication.
The poster combines typography and shapes. The typographic ele-
ments include a headline, a running header (with information such as the 
authors’ names and the creation date), and a bar of logotypes. All typo-
graphic elements use the same type family and have fixed positions on the 
layout. On the other hand, the geometric shapes can vary in position and 
are placed based on a grid using the provided code framework. This frame-
work allows for the creation of geometric shapes such as rectangles, tri-
angles, and ellipses.
The framework allows for dynamic adjustments to the size (width 
and height) and colour of each geometric shape, as well as changes to 
the typographic weight of the text elements. It includes methods to collect 
data from simple voltage dividers electronics, such as potentiometers 
or Light Dependent Resistors (LDR) photoresistors. These sensor data 
are then used to adjust the features of the visuals on the poster. Specifically, 
the data are mapped onto a scale between a maximum and minimum value 
for each visual characteristic. For instance, if the sensor reading reaches 
its maximum value, the text will be typeset in the boldest weight, or the 
geometric shape will be rendered at its largest size. Otherwise, if the sensor 
reading is at its minimum value, the text will be typeset in the lightest 
weight, or the shape will be rendered at its smallest size.
We also provide support for reading data from pushbuttons. This 
functionality allows for the triggering of events within the computational 
system of the poster. For instance, a button can trigger a change in the current 
colour scheme or freeze the modifications made to the poster. This frame-
work was developed using Processing and Arduino. Figure A.11 presents 
variations of the same poster created using the proposed code framework.

A10
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
We tested the proposed template and framework for creating reac-
tive moving posters using a physical computing approach in a hands-on 
workshop with 17 Portuguese upper-secondary students aged 15 to 18. 
The participants had no education in multimedia, design, coding, or related 
domains. In this workshop, the participants created a reactive poster design 
that responds to sensor data from the physical world. The framework 
allows the inclusion of two types of reactive visual elements: ellipses and 
rectangles. In the workshop, we provided three sensors, a potentiometer, 
an LDR photoresistor, and a pushbutton, assembled on a circuit and con-
nected to an Arduino Uno microcontroller (see Figure A.13). The workshop 
lasted two hours, with students divided into six teams of two or three 
members. Each team was tasked with producing two outputs during the 
workshop: a reactive moving poster and a static version of the poster to 
be printed at the end of the workshop (see Figure A.12).
This workshop was conducted in the context of the  Summer School 
of the UC  in 2019, in the thematic track of Design and Multimedia, with 
the support of the Department of Informatics of the UC. Figures A.13 to 
A.17 present some photographic documentation of the workshop.
Our workshop observations and the outputs created indicated that 
physical sensor data can create real-time reactive visuals. This suggests 
that such data can also enhance audience engagement. We mainly observed 
this with sensors that capture unintentional audience motion, such as LDR 
photoresistors. 
Moreover, sensors that require voluntary user actions and interac-
tions, such as potentiometers and pushbuttons, allow for creating tangible 
interfaces for real-time customisation and fine-tuning of designs’ visual 
features. This indicates that these types of sensors have the potential

to adjust the poster without needing to redesign the entire system. For 
instance, they can adapt the design to new locations with lighting condi-
tions. We find that this aspect offers designers a more user-friendly and 
flexible design process.
Although this approach requires more setup than our initial one, it 
shows that custom physical interfaces can offer the same or even more 
tailored audience experiences compared to traditional setups that use only 
CV. From the workshop results, we infer that the developed template  
strategy and code framework were able to streamline the design process 
for creating sensor-reactive designs and customisation. This is evident 
as even participants without specialised expertise were able to create their 
own designs.
Despite being created from the same template, due to their reactive 
nature, the resulting outputs showcase diverse visual characteristics, 
including various colour schemes, geometric shapes, and arrangements. 
This analysis shows that template strategies can be useful for introducing 
visual customisation in a controlled way.

A13 APPENDIX  A REACTIVE  MOVING  P OSTERS
A.3 FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS 
We conducted two works using template strategies to create moving 
posters that react to environmental data from the surroundings in which 
they are displayed. We explored various methods of gathering data from 
the environment, including CV, sensor data and online gathering of geo-
referenced data. We intended to investigate different data-gathering tech-
niques to understand their potential use in this context. 
In the first work, we used CV and georeferenced data to modify 
a poster’s visual features. In the second project, we focused on sensor data 
and introduced an approach with slightly greater expressive power, enabling 
the dynamic creation of visual geometric shapes in multiple locations. 
We also tested this second approach in a hands-on workshop with upper-sec-
ondary students without prior education in the field. Both approaches 
successfully created reactive moving posters. 
The widespread availability of capture cameras in devices and the 
straightforward application of contemporary CV frameworks simplify 
the development of reactive posters, making this technique accessible and 
practical for various applications. Although using sensor data requires 
more setup, custom physical interfaces can provide the same or even more 
tailored audience experiences.
In the initial work, we also explored using georeferenced weather 
data (such as air temperature forecasts) to modify the poster’s colour 
scheme. Even though in both approaches, we focused on using methods 
that quickly respond to feedback from viewers, data that changes gradually 
and has limited or no direct impact on the audience, such as weather 
information, was used to adjust less noticeable design elements. This 
approach seems to enhance the poster’s dynamism, especially when viewed 
sporadically over time, thereby mitigating the repetitive nature of the 
designs. However, further testing is needed to understand how different 
data types, which are not directly retrieved from the environment, impact 
our design decisions.
In both approaches, we observed that only a few inputs are needed 
to introduce reactivity in a poster. We observed that CV and sensor data 
are effective techniques for creating reactive elements, enabling real-time 
interaction and instant response to audience movement. Therefore, these 
methods hold significant promise for delivering more engaging and cus-
tomised design visualisation experiences for the audience than traditional 
print or moving posters.
Based on the outputs of the second approach workshops, we  con-
clude that the developed template strategy offers sufficient flexibility 
for customisation, allowing people without specialised expertise to create 
their own designs. The workshops also revealed that tangible interfaces 
enable real-time customisation, allowing adjustments to visual features 
without the need to redesign the entire system. We consider that this 
approach provides designers with a user-friendly and flexible way to adapt 
their designs to environmental conditions.
Despite using template strategies, the variations in the output 
designs of both approaches highlight the potential for controlled visual 
changes. The reactivity introduces variations in designs without funda-
mentally modifying the poster’s message. Therefore, we do not consider 
that it significantly affects how people perceive the poster’s message.

B02
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
This appendix presents an experiment exploring Computational Design 
(CD) approaches for developing responsive Graphic Design (GD) artefacts 
similar to those discussed in Appendix A. However, in this work, we explored 
an interactive approach where computational methods and environmental 
data are used to modify core content and introduce new information on 
posters. The primary aim of this approach is to explore the communication 
potential of these methods in engaging audiences, as discussed in Chapter 
3. This appendix presents a  collection of interactive posters on climate 
issues, titled Metamorphosis, along with their development process and 
preliminary evaluation.

B03 APPENDIX  B INTERACTIVE  MOVING  P OSTERS
Interactive moving posters are a type of responsive design where features 
and elements respond to data, either altering the core content or adding 
additional information. These data are mainly gathered from the environ-
ment, primarily related to the location where the poster is displayed. In 
contrast to reactive moving posters, where data does not alter the core 
content, these moving posters use interactive animation techniques to 
modify the core content and introduce new information interactively based 
on the data values. Interactive moving posters can include visuals that 
respond reactively and interactively.
In this appendix, we present a collection of seven interactive moving 
posters named Metamorphosis, which address the current climatic changes 
on Earth. These posters aim to inform viewers about the causes and con-
sequences of current environmental problems, focusing on human impact 
on them. Each poster includes several visual elements that react to audi-
ence behaviour and the state of the surrounding environment. In this 
experiment, we are motivated to study whether the interactive dynamism 
of visual elements on a poster enhances the communicative value of the 
design. The posters were created using a template strategy. Like reactive 
moving posters, the visuals’ animation stages were predefined based on 
possible data variations. However, unlike reactive posters, these animations 
modify the posters’ content.
Like reactive moving posters, interactive posters are influenced by 
data collected from the environment in various ways. Some data are gath-
ered by observing the environment, such as tracking viewer behaviour and 
monitoring conditions using Computer Vision (CV) and sensors. Other 
data are obtained online through georeferenced information. Additionally, 
we experimented with stochastic methods, including simulation and 
generative techniques, to introduce visual variations into the templates.
These posters were designed for both physical (see Figure B.1) and 
online (see Figure B.2) interaction. The only setup required is access to 
a video camera and microphone. The posters were developed using web tech-
nologies (HTML, CSS, and JavaScript). We used the P5.js library to manip-
ulate and render the posters, the ML5.js library to facilitate access to Machine 
Learning (ML) models, 1 and the Matter.js library as a physics engine.2 
We conducted testing sessions to assess whether the designed inter-
active moving posters would be more engaging and communicate more 
efficiently compared to print and only animated moving posters. The test 
results reveal that, in most cases, the interactive versions of the posters 
convey the message in a more engaging and efficient manner. The findings 
suggest that these posters personalise the messages by linking them to 
the audience’s actions.

B04
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
The work presented in this appendix is partially supported by the  
M.Sc. dissertations of Ricardo Gonçalves (2021) from the Design and 
Multimedia programme of the Faculty of Sciences and Technology of 
University of Coimbra. In the following sections, we describe the design 
and development of this collection, outline the evaluation experiments 
conducted, and discuss the findings and conclusions.
B. 1 DESIGN AND DEVELOPMENT
We designed seven interactive moving posters, each addressing a different 
environmental subject. The explored subjects are (i) air pollution, (ii) bio-
diversity loss, (iii) deforestation, (iv) global warming, (v) noise pollution, 
(vi) rubbish production, and (vii) water pollution.
Each poster has been designed as a self-contained communication 
artefact, reflecting a different subject. However, all the posters share 
common visual features to maintain visual cohesion and,  therefore, be 
recognised as a collection. These features include the use of GT Flexa  
typeface,3 the typeset of a centre-aligned awareness message, and a running 
footer with information about the poster collection (see Figure B.11). The 
characteristics of posters  (e.g. format, size, elements placement position, 
etc.) were defined parametrically. Next, we comprehensively describe 
the development processes behind each poster.
B. 1. 1 AIR POLLUTION
Air pollution is the contamination and alteration of the atmosphere’s 
natural characteristics by chemical, physical, and biological agents (Vallero, 
2014). To raise public awareness about this issue, we designed a moving 
poster displaying real-time data concerning the Air Quality Index (AQI) and 
the number of pollutants near the place where the poster is being observed.
This poster is composed of three main variable visual elements: 
(i) a message informing about the current air index; (ii) an illustration 
presenting the quantity of each pollutant nearby; and (iii) a system of smog 
particles. Figure B.3 presents three different states of this poster. To access 
these data, we used the online weather forecast service Open Weather  4 
and its air pollution API to retrieve the current AQI and the pollutants 
in a given location.

B05 APPENDIX  B INTERACTIVE  MOVING  P OSTERS
Figure B.3. Variations of the air pollution 
theme poster, ranging from a location with 
good AQI (left) to one with hazardous

The interactive version can be accessed at 
https://pf.dei.uc.pt/B/demo/AirPollution 
(websites visited 7 July 2025).
We placed a message on the poster informing about the current air 
quality. It adjusts itself based on the current AQI value from good (1) to 
hazardous / very poor (5). Furthermore, we created a visualisation to illus-
trate each pollutant in the atmosphere. Each pollutant is represented by 
a circle that varies its area according to data retrieved from the API. The 
size of the circle is proportional to the pollution values. It increases with 
unhealthy aQi levels and decreases with good AQI levels. The presented 
pollutants are Carbon Monoxide (CO), Nitrogen Monoxide (NO), Nitrogen 
Dioxide (NO2), Ozone (O3), Sulphur Dioxide (SO2), and Fine Particles 
Matter (PM2.5). The area of each circle is determined by a logarithmic 
function that maps the pollutant values according to a minimum and 
maximum value for each. These minimum and maximum values are defined 
according to the prejudice of each substance to the air quality.
The colour fill of the variable part of both the message and circles 
changes based on the AQI value; for each AQI value from 1 to 5, green, 
yellow, orange, red, and purple were used.
We also implemented a system of smog particles on the poster. It 
was specially designed to represent the human-related causes of air pol-
lution figuratively. This way, when a person is detected in front of the poster 
(using a face recognition method), the system creates particles in a random 
position near the bottom edge of the poster. These particles move on the 
canvas, making the readability of the poster’s contents troublesome. When-
ever no one is recognised, the particles begin to disappear. The brightness 
of the smog particles is also defined based on the AQI value. If it is good (1), 
the particles are lighter; if AQI is hazardous / very poor (5), they are darker.
B. 1.2 BIODIVERSITY LOSS
Biodiversity loss is the decrease in the number and variety of species 
on Earth. Most of the current diversity loss is caused by human actions 
(Cardinale et al., 2012). We have created a poster to alert us to the negative 
impact of present-day human activities on natural ecosystems. This poster 
illustrates an ecosystem. Figure B.4 displays some of the variations of 
this poster.


B06
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
Figure B.4. Variations of the biodiversity 
loss theme poster. From left to 
right, (i) the poster in its initial stage,

(websites visited 7 July 2025).
The ecosystem is a particle system where each particle is associated 
with a species and is rendered by a pictorial depiction of a living being. 
The pictorial representation of each particle is randomly selected from 
a collection of images related to each species. The species of each particle 
is defined by a stochastic selection method, guided by the estimated per-
centage of current known species, according to the taxonomic group 
defined by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).5  
By default, these particles are moving to an attractor in the centre of 
the poster. At a predefined time (empirically defined at 10 seconds), a par-
ticle is removed from the poster, symbolising the extinction of a species. 
The probability of extinction is based on the estimated threatened species, 
which are also sourced according to IUCN data. The species and parti-
cles are selected to be extinct using a Stochastic Universal Sampling 
(SUS) method.6
A pictorial representation of a human appears whenever a person 
is recognised near the poster. The position of this representation on the 
poster’s canvas is based on the position in the physical world. The viewer’s 
position is identified using a face detection method and mapped on the 
poster based on a mapping of the size of the poster in the camera range. 
This representation follows the person when interacting with a poster. 
Since this poster intends to communicate the impact of human activity 
on diversity loss, when a human appears, the particles’ lifespan is reduced 
to half. Also, when a person interacts with a poster, the message concerning 
the number of endangered species is presented in the centre of it. This infor-
mation is also based on data from IUCN.
B. 1.3 DEFOREST A TION
Deforestation leads to various economic, social, and climatic consequences 
in the affected regions, such as loss of water and soil resources, flooding, 
biodiversity loss, and climatic change. The causes of deforestation can vary, 
but they are often linked to human activities such as converting forests to 
agricultural land, grazing areas, or urban developments (Chakravarty 
et al., 2012)

B07 APPENDIX  B INTERACTIVE  MOVING  P OSTERS
Considering this environmental issue, we designed an interactive 
moving poster highlighting the importance of forests on our planet and the 
impact of their destruction. The poster is composed of three illustrations 
of trees. When a human is detected near the poster, the tree illustrations are 
“cut” and become stumps, one by one. When no more trees are displayed, 
the stumps begin to emit smoke, alluding to the impact that the transfor-
mation of forest on non-forest has on the increase of CO2 levels in the 
atmosphere. Viewers are detected using a face detection algorithm. We imple-
mented a particle system to create the smoke effect on the tree stumps 
and empirically defined the visual features of the smoke. Figure B.5 presents 
three different states of the poster.
When no human is detected in front of the poster, the stumps stop 
producing smoke, and progressively, the tree grows again. When a person 
is detected in front of the poster, a message appears in the centre of the 
canvas, which displays the forecast of the number of trees destroyed 
this year. This forecast number is computed based on the Global Forest Watch 
platform data.7
B. 1.4 GLOBAL WARMING
Global warming is the long-term increase in Earth’s surface temperature 
observed since the pre-industrial era, primarily due to human activities. 
It raises sea levels, increases CO2 in the atmosphere, and causes polar 
glaciers to shrink and melt. Climate change promotes the loss of diversity 
and species extinctions (Dawson & Spannagle, 2008).
We designed an interactive moving poster, keeping in mind one of 
the most visible consequences of global warming: the shrinking and melting 
of polar glaciers and the consequent rise of the sea level. The poster com-
prises one lettering displaying the designation “Global Warming” and a rec-
tangle that changes its height according to the air temperature where the 
poster is located. Figure B.6 presents this poster in different locations and 
weather conditions.
The rectangle’s height varies based on the air temperature in the 
location where the poster is being visualised. The temperature value is 
mapped into a specific range where the maximum and minimum represent 
the most extreme temperatures registered on Earth. 8 The rectangle’s fill

(coldest temperature) to red (hottest temperature).
The overlapping of the lettering and the rectangle produces a dis-
tortion in the lettering, resembling a melting effect. This effect is achieved 
by manipulating the SVG filter feDisplacement-Map  and varies according 
to the collected air temperature. The higher the temperature, the greater 
the distortion. Similar to the other posters in the collection, a message 
regarding the issue is displayed when a viewer’s face is detected in front 
of the poster. In this case, it displays “Reduce your carbon footprint.”
Depending on how it is displayed (physically or digitally), the poster 
employs a different method for collecting the air temperature. When 
installed in the physical world, it gathers the air temperature from the phys-
ical surroundings using an Arduino Uno and an LM35 temperature sensor. 
Otherwise, the online version uses the browser’s native Geolocation API 
to get the viewer’s location. Then, the Open Weather API is used to retrieve 
the air temperature forecast for that place and time.9
B. 1.5 NOISE POLLUTION
Noise pollution is linked to various physical and mental health problems 
in humans and animals (Anees et al., 2017). We designed a poster to warn 
about the impact of noise pollution and loud sounds on people. This poster 
is composed of a dynamic typographic composition that behaves as a noise 
indicator. As noise levels increase, the poster’s readability decreases. Figure 
B.7 displays the poster under different sound conditions.
The composition involves repeatedly typesetting the word “noise”, 
with the repetitions increasingly overlapping from the centre to the post-
er’s edges. The word “noise” is repeated 24 times, 12 in each direction. 
The number of repetitions depends on the amplitude of the surrounding 
sound, measured using a microphone. Higher sound amplitudes result in 
more repetitions. In this sense, this animation functions similarly to a 
symmetric volume indicator.
Furthermore, a dotted halftone pattern texture makes the lettering’s 
readability harder when the noise increases. The size of the dots and the 
blur of the texture adjust according to the ambient sound amplitude within 
a specified range. As noise levels rise, the text becomes more distorted

B. 1.6 RUBBISH PRODUCTION
Human-generated rubbish poses significant problems for both water and 
land (Hoornweg et al., 2013). Rubbish is generated faster than other pol-
lutants, making its management a significant challenge. We developed an 
interactive moving poster to simulate the impact of human litter, alerting 
that much of it ends up in landfills or open dumps. This poster metaphor-
ically represents an open landfill. Figure B.8 presents different variations 
of this poster.
The poster features litter elements that are dropped onto it at regular 
intervals (empirically set to 10 seconds). According to data from the 
Municipal Solid Waste reports of the United States Environmental Pro-
tection Agency,10 the type of rubbish is selected based on a certain prob-
ability using a SUS selection method. The  visual representation of each 
rubbish item is randomly chosen from a predefined set of images for each 
type. We employed a physics engine to simulate the dropping and inter -
action of rubbish items. After a set time, each item begins to “decompose,” 
i.e. it is removed from the poster. This time is based on the forecast decom-
position rates of each type of rubbish. As in other posters, we employ 
a non-linear logarithmic function to adjust the removal time of items 
with low and high decomposing times.
When a viewer is detected in front of the poster (using face detec-
tion), a specific number of rubbish items, empirically set to 40, is “dropped 
off.” Simultaneously, a message appears showing the average daily waste 
production (0.74 kg), and a video of the viewer’s face is displayed within 
the glyph “o” of the word “you.”
B. 1.7 WA TER POLLUTION
Water is vital for all life forms. Although water covers nearly three-quarters 
of the Earth’s surface, only a tiny fraction (around one per cent) is safe to 
drink. Consequently, one of the major environmental issues today is the
