COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
increasing contamination of freshwater systems, mainly due to human 
activities (Goel, 2006). Single-use plastics and their improper disposal in 
water are significant contemporary environmental problems. To raise 
awareness of this issue, we designed an interactive moving poster high-
lighting the vast amounts of rubbish in our oceans and providing informa-
tion about its decomposition time.
This poster simulates a part of the ocean. One rubbish item is added 
to the poster every time interval (empirically defined at 10 seconds). The 
types of items included are based on the top 10 rubbish items found in the 
ocean.11 Each item has a specific probability of being chosen, reflecting 
the frequency of its recovery. A figurative representation of each item is 
randomly selected from a predefined set of images. Once added to the 
poster, each item’s lifespan is determined by its decomposition time. Due 
to the wide variance between the minimum (paper items, around five 
weeks) and maximum (glass, around one million years) decomposition 
times, we used a non-linear logarithmic function to make these times 
perceptible to viewers. Items float on the poster and reappear on the 
opposite side when they exit one side. A physics engine simulates floating 
and collisions realistically.
The poster’s background colour changes according to the number 
of rubbish items present. Whenever the number of items increases, the water 
becomes darker. The water colour ranges from light blue with no trash 
to dark blue when there are over forty items. Figure B.9 displays some 
variations of this effect.
When a person is detected near the posters, additional items are 
automatically dropped off on the poster. The system uses face detection 
to recognise individuals; each detected person adds ten items. Simultane-
ously, a message appears estimating the amount of rubbish dumped into 
the ocean annually. Viewers can also adjust the trajectory of the litter items 
with their hand position, effectively “cleaning” the poster. Nevertheless, 
the items reappear on the other side, emphasising that solving water pol-
lution requires not only cleaning but also reducing waste production and 
increasing recycling. The PoseNet model is used to estimate hand positions.12

B11 APPENDIX  B INTERACTIVE  MOVING  P OSTERS
B.2 EV ALUA TION 
We assessed the posters designed through testing sessions with people.
The primary aim of the evaluation was to assess how effectively the posters 
conveyed their intended message as well as the impact of the interactive 
features. These evaluation sessions were conducted during the COVID-19 
pandemic. At that time, we could not ensure a safe, physically controlled 
environment for observational testing sessions where participants could 
freely interact with posters. Therefore, the evaluation was conducted online 
through the remote completion of a survey by people.
The seven posters were evaluated individually and their commu-
nicative and visual features were assessed separately. Furthermore, the 
posters were evaluated collectively as a collection, considering their 
common communicative and visual features. Since the evaluation involved 
subjective information, we collected both qualitative data (through open-
-ended questions) and quantitative data (through multi-choice Likert  
scale questions).
Each test was divided into two stages. The first stage ( s1) focused 
on evaluating each poster individually. During this stage, we examined 
the quality of the posters’ visuals and assessed whether the interactive 
features enhanced message transmission compared to print and animated 
versions. The second stage (s2) focused on the overall evaluation of using 
animated and interactive techniques in poster design. For this evaluation, 
we created a print version and a moving-only version for each interactive 
moving poster developed, enabling a comprehensive comparison.13
We conducted 11 evaluations. The participants, aged between 22 and 
30, visualised and interacted with posters in their online versions (see 
Figure B.10). They were recruited via social media posts and personal 
invitations. Even though more participants could have improved the results, 
the sample size was sufficient for drawing conclusions given the study’s 
constraints and qualitative focus. The data collected in the evaluation 
sessions are available at https://pf.dei.uc.pt/B/eval-results.xlsx (visited: 
7 July 2025).
The first evaluation stage (s1) determined whether interactive moving 
posters improve message transmission compared to printed and mov-
ing-only posters. Thus, we asked participants to view the same poster on 
a screen in three different formats: print, moving, and interactive moving.

They viewed the posters in the same format in order to familiarise them-
selves with their features and context and then see if new features improved 
them. Afterwards, participants were asked to perform the following four 
tasks: (s1.1) for each poster, rate “How attention-grabbing does this poster 
look?” on a scale from 1 to 3, where 1 is low attention-grabbing, and 3 is 
highly attention-grabbing, and then explain their rating; (s1.2) to answer 
the question “What environmental issue is this poster addressing?”; (s1.3) 
to order the three different posters version based on the effectiveness of 
the message they convey by selecting the posters that “Which version of 
this poster communicates the message more effectively?” and “Which 
version of this poster communicates the message less effectively?”, followed 
by a open-ended explanation for your choices; and, finally, (s1.4) openly 
respond to the question, “Is there anything you would change to enhance 
the effectiveness of the poster message?”. Participants answered these 
questions by selecting multiple-choice options and providing written 
responses. Table B.1 presents the quantitative results of tasks s1.1 and s1.3. 
The posters were shown to users in this order: rubbish production, global 
warming, deforestation, water pollution, air pollution, noise pollution, and 
biodiversity loss.

B13 APPENDIX  B INTERACTIVE  MOVING  P OSTERS
On average, participants found all versions of the posters to be 
attention-grabbing (s1.1). Each version received a positive rating, with aver-
ages above 1.5, and there were no significant differences in their attention-
-grabbing effectiveness. When questioned, participants noted that inter -
activity often added contextual information. However, they also mentioned 
that each poster format was equally effective at grabbing attention, with 
each being more effective in different contexts. In task s1.2, participants 
clearly understood the subject, or the issues, addressed by the posters.
Participants preferred the interactive versions in almost all posters 
when asked which version best conveyed the message (s1.3). On the other 
hand, many participants found the printed version less effective. Exceptions 
included the global warming, deforestation, and water pollution posters. 
Participants found the moving version more effective for the global warming 
poster and the interactive version less effective. For the water pollution 
poster, participants preferred the moving version and found the print 
version less effective. Opinions were divided for the deforestation poster, 
with participants finding both moving and print versions the most and 
least effective. When asked about their choice, participants generally 
highlighted that interactivity makes posters more engaging and personal, 
which enhanced the effectiveness of conveying and sensitising the message. 
However, some noted that interactive versions could sometimes be unnec-
essary and difficult to understand. This feedback was most common for 
the global warming, deforestation, and water pollution posters. We consider 
this because these posters feature complex interactions that are hard 
for users to grasp.
Finally, most of the change suggestions from people (s1.4) were 
related to performance issues in the interactive versions. The posters that 
most participants gave suggestions about were the ones concerning global 
warming (7) and deforestation (9). In the global warming poster, people 
suggested making the word “warming” more readable, increasing the blurry 
effect, and changing the rectangle behaviour to be more like the ocean. 
Conversely, two people suggested making the interaction more straight -
forward for the deforestation poster. 
In the second evaluation stage (s2), we assessed whether animation 
and interactivity improved message comprehension on posters. This way, 
we asked people three questions: (s2.1) to answer if animation helped 
in the comprehension of the message and explain more comprehensively 
their answer; (s2.2) to answer if interactivity helped in the comprehension 
of the message, especially compared with animation,  and explain more 
detailed their answer; and, finally, (s2.3) to select the version which they 
thinks will stand most in people’s memory.
Most participants (8) considered that animation helped with message 
comprehension (s2.1). On the other hand, two people thought it mostly 
helped, but it depended on the context of the subject and visualisation.  
The other person considered that animation did not help with message 
comprehension. Detailed responses often highlighted that animation helps 
to tell a story, allowing viewers to realise and pay attention to the problem. 
Regarding the use of interactivity (s2.2), most participants (9) believed it 
helped in the comprehension of the message. At the same time, two people 

B14
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
considered that it mostly helped but depended on the subject. However, 
we recognise that further testing is needed to study how animation helps 
and improves comprehension, especially for more complex messages.
Also, most participants noted that the use of interaction methods 
allowed them to establish a connection between themselves (viewers) 
and the design, making the message more engaging and personal. Almost 
all people (10 of 11) chose the interactive version as the one they thought 
would stand most in people’s memory (s2.3), with only one person selecting 
the animated version instead.
B.3 FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS
In this experiment, we created a collection of interactive moving posters 
employing a template strategy. The posters were composed of responsive 
visuals, where animations responded interactively to environmental data. 
The animations were designed to introduce new communication signifi-
cance in the posters’ message, with different animation stages reflecting 
the possible data variations. The topics covered by the posters were related 
to climate problems, all focusing on human impacts on the natural envi-
ronment. These subjects included air pollution, biodiversity loss, deforest-
ation, global warming, noise pollution, rubbish production, and water pol-
lution.
We conducted evaluation experiments to assess how effectively 
these designs conveyed their intended messages and the impact of the inter-
active features compared to their print and animated versions. Participants 
found the posters attention-grabbing and considered their subjects easy 
to understand. In the context of these posters, most participants consid-
ered that animation and interactivity helped to transmit messages effectively. 
The interactive version was generally viewed as more effective. 
The findings suggest that this type of poster gives viewers a more 
memorable experience. However, further testing is needed to explore this 
effect on the audience in greater detail. Nevertheless, some interactive 
versions were seen as less effective, particularly those on global warming, 
deforestation, and water pollution. Participants noted that the static 
and animated versions conveyed the subject matter more effectively in 
these cases. These interactive versions sometimes seem complex, unnec-
essary and challenging to understand. 
Our results also indicate that designers should be careful about adding 
animation and interactivity when designing this type of poster. Our exper-
imentation reveals that designers should include such features only when 
expected to enhance the poster’s communication value. Moreover, when 
such features are added, designers must ensure that interactions are simple, 
provide clear feedback, and are accessible for the audience to understand.
In conclusion, our findings indicate that interactive moving posters 
can be effective in conveying messages. Our experimentation also indicates 
that the added interactivity must be straightforward enough for the audi-
ence to understand. Otherwise, it may have the opposite effect.

C02
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
This appendix presents our research on creating an environmentally respon-
sive poster generator informed by data collected from their physical sur-
roundings. The work focuses on the study of the system’s responsive 
capability to adapt its visual elements based on environmental feedback. 
Also, we aim to examine their impact on communication and engagement 
of design with the audience, as described in Chapter 3. This appendix 
details the system’s development, experimentation and findings.

C03 APPENDIX  C ENVIRONMENT ALL Y  RESPONSIVE  P OSTER  GENERA TOR
ENVIRONMENT ALL Y RESPONSIVE  
POSTER GENERA TOR
C
This appendix presents our research on creating designs that incorporate 
environmental data collected from the physical surroundings near the site 
where they are displayed. Our primary goal is to study whether including 
computational data-driven methods enables the production of more note-
worthy designs. In this context, we introduce an environmentally respon-
sive poster generation system that creates designs informed by environ-
mental data. Additionally, this generator adjusts its creation processes 
based on the environmental feedback received from previous designs. 
Therefore, our primary motivation for developing this work is to create 
a computational system that produces designs that blend seamlessly with 
the conditions and dynamics of the surrounding environment.
This environmentally responsive poster generator operates as follows. 
Each poster comprises variable and static visual elements. Static visuals 
remain constant (both in content and appearance) across different gen-
erations and are not influenced by environmental data. Variable visuals, 
however, are placed on the composition with a specific lifespan that decreases 
over time. The system rewards variable visuals by extending their lifespan 
based on environmental feedback data, such as people’s behaviour near 
the installation. Furthermore, the system replicates outputs, or part of them, 
that have previously proven successful in similar environmental conditions. 
Figure C.2 presents some outputs generated by this system.
We installed this system in an urban environment to observe its 
behaviour (see Figure C.1). The installation was placed in the Coimbra 
Historic Centre (CHC) between March and April 2019. This neighbourhood 
enabled us to situate the installation in streets with varying environmental 
conditions and people fluxes. The selected shops encompassed diverse 
types of businesses. The installation remained in place for four weeks, 
occupying the store windows of four different shops, with each shop hosting 
the installation for one week. In the first week, it was at Estúdio Diorama,  
a traditional photography laboratory and shop. The second shop, Jorge 
Mendes, Irmão & Ca, Lda., is a traditional clothing store. In the third week, 
the installation was placed in Chronos’ Paper, an independent bookbinding 
and restoration workshop. Lastly, it was housed at the ellayne clothing 
shop during the fourth week. The map in Figure C.3 shows the installation 
locations over these four weeks, while Figure C.4 provides photographic 
documentation of the installation in each location. 
We evaluated the outputs from the installation by gathering feedback 
from people. We aimed to assess two main creative aspects of the system:  
(i) whether the system can translate the gathered environmental data 
into outputs, and (ii) whether the system’s adaptive capabilities are per -
ceptible in the generated designs.

COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
C .1 APPROACH
The proposed poster generator operates sequentially, continuously creating 
designs using environmental data from the surrounding area. It autono-
mously generates outputs by combining template and stochastic methods. 
These designs consist of two types of visuals: variable and static.
Static visuals are predefined elements that maintain their position, 
appearance, and typographic features across different system runs. Although 
their content can dynamically change over time, we do not consider them 
variable visual elements because they are not influenced by environmental 
data and are used to communicate details about the output (see Figure C.5). 
This content includes fixed information (e.g. installation supporters or 
technical information) and dynamic information (e.g. location address, date, 
or time, textual content about the system and installation).
Variable visuals, on the other hand, are shapes created and  placed 
autonomously by the system on the poster. The system determines their 
position, style, and colour based on environmental data and feedback 
(see Figure C.5). The system gathers environmental data by directly 
observing the environment, mainly through Computer Vision (CV) and 
physical computing, and by accessing online data collections. A set of 
predefined settings, including a set of source shapes and a base colour 
palette, constrains the generation of these visuals. We defined and designed 
these constraint elements, which are loaded dynamically at the initialisa-
tion of the system from a specific file folder. This method of loading con-
straints allows for easy modification and updating of these settings without 
altering the core system. Also, this enables other generation systems to 
contribute with assets to this system.
The system creates posters continuously. Initially, it displays com-
position with only static elements. Over time, variable visuals are added 
to the poster at a specific interval, each with a lifespan that decreases as it 
remains visible (see Figure C.6). Visual elements stay on the poster until 
their lifespan expires.
Variable visuals can receive rewards by extending their lifespan 
(or the time placed on the poster) based on people’s behaviour in the 
environment near the poster. Thus, the system monitors the surrounding 
environment to answer three questions: (i) “How many people are near 
the poster?”; (ii) “How close the people are to the poster?”; and (iii) 
“How many are attentive to the poster?”.
Data on the people surrounding the poster (distance and attention) 
are collected through video capture and CV methods. For each detected 
person, the system calculates their distance from the camera and checks 
if they are looking directly at the poster. We use a body detection method 
to recognise people on the capture and a face detector method to detect

C07 APPENDIX  C ENVIRONMENT ALL Y  RESPONSIVE  P OSTER  GENERA TOR
the faces in those bodies. If a face is detected, the system checks for eyes 
on that region to assess attentiveness. We assumed that an attentive person 
was directly looking at the poster. This way, we presumed that whenever 
two eyes are recognised, the person to whom those eyes belong is more 
attentive than when only one eye is recognised. If no face or eyes are 
detected, the system considers that the detected body is from a passer -by. 
We used the off-the-shelve OpenCV Haar-cascade classifiers for body, 
face, and eye detection. The proximity of detected people is estimated 
based on the size of their bounding boxes. A larger bounding box indicates 
a closer distance. Based on these data, variable visual elements are rewarded. 
It considers that a person closer and more attentive to a poster must assign 
a higher reward to its visuals. We defined the maximum and minimum 
values of reward through empirical exploration. A minimum reward is 
assigned when only a passer-by is detected; a maximum reward is given 
when a person is detected looking directly at the poster up close (a minimum 
predefined value). 
The fitness value (f) of a poster is calculated as the arithmetic mean 
of the lifespan of its variable visuals. Accordingly, this fitness value is 
directly influenced by the current environmental conditions and is defined 
as:
)C.1  (
 
where Np is the total number of variable visuals in the poster p, and Lifespan 
(i) represents the lifespan of the variable visual i.
Furthermore, this system can save and manage history entries for pre-
vious outputs, enabling it to create outputs based on its previous design expe-
riences. The system saves each generated poster and creates a history entry 
in the file. Each entry contains (i) a description of the output, (ii) the state 
of the environment, and (iii) both raster and vector versions of the output 
(PNG and PDF files). This ability allows the system to redraw specific 
outputs or simulate data from a particular environment. New variable 
visuals can be placed on the poster based on two methods: (i) generation at 
random, i.e. when a new shape is randomly generated; or (ii) generation based 
on experience, i.e. when a previously generated shape that had obtained 
positive environmental feedback is selected to be placed again on the poster. 
To choose the method for creating a new variable visual, the system 
analyses the average fitness of previous outputs generated under similar 
environmental conditions and assigns a probability for each method. 
The system is more likely to use the random generation method if it does 
not achieve successful outcomes in similar conditions. Otherwise, if past 
designs were successful in similar environmental conditions, it  is more 
probable to use the generation based on experience  method. Algorithm C.1 
summarises the main steps of this system.
Thus, when the system has not created successful designs, it con-
tinues experimenting with different visuals, seeking new ways of capturing 
the attention of passers-by. Nevertheless, when the system has previously 
been successful in a similar environment, it is more likely to use visuals 

C08
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
that have proven effective under comparable conditions. This way, this 
system adapts to the dynamic of the place where it is settled. The following 
sections describe each placement method in detail. 
Algorithm C.1. Environmentally Responsive Poster Generator
1: Load constraints and interval value from file.
2: Define startTime as the current time.
3: Define variableVisuals as empty list.
4: WHILE True DO:
5:  Display poster.
6:  Gather environmentalData
7:  elapsedTime = millis() - startTime
8:  IF elapsedTime >= interval THEN:
9:   IF environmentalData is similar to previous conditions THEN:
10:    newVisual = GenerationBasedOnExperience()
11:   ELSE:
12:     newVisual = randomGeneration()  
13:  ADD newVisual TO variableVisuals  
14:  Define startTime as the current time.  
15:  Update lifespans of variableVisuals.
16:  Remove visuals from variableVisuals that have expired lifespans.
17:  Calculate the fitness of the current poster.
18:   Save the current poster state to history.
C.1 .1 RANDOM GENERA TION
The random generation of a new shape involves defining both visual fea-
tures (i.e. shape, colour, scale, and rotation) and placement features (i.e. posi-
tion and lifespan). These features are determined based on random factors 
and environmental data.
The system initially determines the visual features. First, it selects 
a shape from those preloaded into the system. It then determines the colour 
of the visual. Colours are assigned using the Hue-Saturation-Brightness 
(HSB) model, where hue and saturation are influenced by environmental 
data collected directly and indirectly, while brightness remains constant 
across all visuals. The hue is randomly chosen from a subset of the provided 
colour palette, which is selected based on the current air temperature 
of the location where the poster is visualised. Warmer temperatures lead 
to the use of warmer hues and vice versa. This subset is determined using 
weather forecast information for the current location and time.14 Satura-
tion is based on the luminosity of the environment, more precisely, the 
amount of direct incident light that falls on the poster, measured using an 
LDR photoresistor sensor placed on top of it. The sensor data are mapped 
to a saturation value ranging from 0.3 to the highest possible saturation 
value (1).
14
We used the Open Weather API to obtain 
the air temperature forecast, which 
offers hourly temperature predictions 
for any location worldwide.

C09 APPENDIX  C ENVIRONMENT ALL Y  RESPONSIVE  P OSTER  GENERA TOR
Subsequently, the system decides on geometric transformations 
to apply. It determines whether to apply rotation, scaling, or both and 
defines the value of these transformations. The range of possible values 
is predefined empirically, allowing visuals to be rotated fully or scaled from 
one-third to three times their original size.
Finally, the visual is placed on the poster. The coordinates for its place-
ment are randomly defined, and the visual is assigned an initial lifespan con-
sistent across all visual types. This process is summarised in Algorithm C.2.
Algorithm C.2. Pseudocode for the random generation function.
FUNCTION randomGeneration()
1: Select a random shape from preloaded shapes.
2: Select colourPaletteSubset based on temperature.
3: Choose random hue from colourPaletteSubset.
4: Set saturation based on current enviromental luminosity [0.3 – 1]
5: Set brightness to 1.
6: IF random decision THEN:
7:  Set random rotation [0 – 2π].
8: IF random decision THEN:
9:  Set random scale [0.33 – 3].
10: Set random position (x, y) on the poster.
11: Set initial lifespan.
12: ADD newShape to the poster.
13: RETURN newVisual.
C. 1.2 GENERA TION BASED ON EXPERIENCE
When generating a new shape based on its previous design experience, 
the system selects and places visuals that are copies of ones that have 
previously achieved high attention levels under similar environmental 
conditions and, therefore, achieved longer lifespans.
The system starts by choosing an output to copy a visual element. 
To pick the output, it selects designs created under similar environmental 
conditions, such as (i) the number of passers-by, (ii) the number of atten-
tive people, (iii) time, (iv) air temperature, and (v) environmental light. 
Next, the system ranks these designs based on how well they match the 
current environmental state. This ranking is based on an appropriateness 
value computed from the sum of the poster’s fitness value (when initially 
created) with a reward that reflects the similarity between past and current 
environmental conditions. The reward is the maximum when the data 
gathered in the two environments (past and current) are in the same range. 
The variation and reward value ranges must be empirically defined based 
on the environment. 
The ranking list is then truncated to a predefined size, and each 
element is assigned a probability of selection based on its appropriateness 
value. Next, one output is randomly selected using a SUS method.

C10
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
Lastly, a visual is chosen from the selected poster and placed on the 
current poster with the same visual features and position as in the original 
design. Also, the system forces the selection of a visual not already present 
in the composition to avoid placing the exact visual multiple times. This 
process is outlined in Algorithm C.3.
Algorithm C.3. Pseudocode for the generation based on experience function.
FUNCTION GenerationBasedOnExperience()
1: Search previousOutputs under similar environmental conditions.
2: FOR each output IN previousOutputs DO
3:  Calculate appropriateness values for each output.
4: Sort previousOutputs by appropriateness value.
5: Truncate previousOutputs to a predefined size.
6: FOR each output IN previousOutputs DO
7:  Calculate selection probabilities for each output.
8: Random choose a selectedVisual based on the calculated probabilities.
9: WHILE selectedVisual IS IN currentPoster DO
10:  Random choose a new selectedVisual. 
11: ADD selectedVisual to the poster.
12: RETURN selectedVisual.
C.2 INST ALLA TION
We conducted an experiment to deploy our system, turning it into a phys-
ical installation named Desenhar Cartazes com / para o Caminho and placing 
it in a real urban environment. The system was set up using a single-board 
computer connected to a monitor (for displaying the current output), 
a web camera (for capturing the environment), and an LDR photo- resistor 
sensor (for measuring environmental light levels). Figure C.7 displays 
the blueprint of the installation’s hardware.
From March to April 2019, we installed the system on the streets of 
the CHC neighbourhood. It was placed in the windows of four shops, 
spending one week at each location. When relocating the installation, 
we rebooted the system and cleaned any data about the previous site. 
This way, we ensured that outputs generated in each site were only influ-
enced by the data collected in that place. Figures C.1 to C.4 document the 
system’s installation.
We selected this neighbourhood for its variety of street types and 
dynamics despite its small area (less than one square kilometre). This 
variety allowed us to test the system in different environments with minimal 
Figure C.7. Blueprint of the 
installation’s hardware.

C11 APPENDIX  C ENVIRONMENT ALL Y  RESPONSIVE  P OSTER  GENERA TOR
logistical effort. Also, this neighbourhood is historically known for shopping 
and business activities, where posters and advertisements frequently attract 
passers-by’s attention.15
Each location had distinct environmental characteristics and urban 
dynamics. The first location was a traditional photography laboratory 
in Rua dos Esteireiros, a narrow and uncrowded street near the neighbour-
hood’s busiest squares. The second place was a historic clothing shop 
in Praça do Comércio (also known as Praça Velha), a historic square known 
for its historic shops. The third location was a bookbinding workshop on 
Rua Adelino Veiga, a narrow and busy street connecting the historic train 
station and city hall. Unlike the first place, this is a busy street with mul-
tiple shopping places. Finally, the last location was another clothing shop 
in Largo do Poço, a busy square near the city hall and one of the most 
well-known concert halls in the city.
The experimental setup was determined empirically. Figure C.8 
shows the designed vector shapes, and Figure C.9 displays the 11-colour 
palette used in the experiment. The installation did not record personal 
data about the people recognised in the nearby environment. Over the 
four weeks, the system identified 12,722 passers-by (an average of 490 
people by day and 3,430.5 by week). The busiest location was Largo do Poço, 
with 3,970 people per week, followed by Rua Adelino Veiga (3,512 people 
per week), Praça do Comércio (3,306 people per week) and Rua dos Estereiros 
(2,934 people per week). The installation operated in an unsupervised 
manner, so we could not guarantee that all recognised individuals were 
actual people or that the system identified every passer-by. The placement 
of this installation was part of the event 21st Cultural Week of the University 
of Coimbra (UC) under the theme “Caminhos.”
This experiment demonstrated that the system could generate poster 
designs from scratch. Figures C.10 to C.13 show some of the generated 
outputs. The outputs reveal how the environmental conditions around 
the installation changed over time. For instance, Figure C.12 demonstrates 
outputs generated during warmer air temperatures, while Figure C.11  
displays outputs created at different times of the day, distinguishing between 
night and day designs. Furthermore, Figure C.10 illustrates how the number 
of passers-by influenced the generated outputs. Figures C.6 and C.13 display 
the sequential generation of outputs by the system.16
During the installation of the system, we identified some unexpected 
issues. First, we faced problems with the shops’ electrical conditions. 
Most of them are established in old buildings with inadequate electric 
installations. This issue led to irregular voltages, affecting our single-board 
computer’s performance and processing power. We also detected image 
captures where the system incorrectly identified faces or people (false 
positives). This issue rarely occurred when we tested the system in a con-
trolled environment (such as an indoor space). Nevertheless, during the 
routine maintenance, we found false positives in walls or parked cars. This 
way, visual compositions might be erroneously rewarded based on false 
positives in the urban environment. As it did not save the captured images 
(to ensure people’s privacy in public space), we cannot qualify how much 
the false positives influenced the outputs.

C.3 EV ALUA TION
We conducted evaluation sessions to assess the capability of the system’s 
outputs to communicate the environmental features of a place and whether 
the system’s experience and adaptive features were visible in the outputs.
Each testing session was divided into three stages, each aiming 
to evaluate a different aspect of the generated outputs. The first stage (s1) 
focused on assessing how well the environmental conditions of the place 
where the system is running are perceived in the outputs created. The 
second stage (s2) focused on understanding if the system’s adaptive capa-
bilities were perceived in its outputs. Finally, the third stage (s3) focused 
on collecting overall evaluation and thoughts about the system, installation, 
and output.
The testing sessions began with an introduction to the system and 
the context of its installation in the urban space. This introduction did not 
reveal the visual mapping of environmental data. Afterwards, we asked 
each participant to respond to a multiple-choice form divided into three 
sections. Each section corresponds to an evaluation stage. 
Figure C.13. Outputs created by the 
system, every three minutes, between 
10:48 and 10:56 on 12 March at Estúdio 
Diorama (Rua dos Esteireiros).

C14
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
We conducted testing sessions with 35 people aged between 20 
and 34, with an average age of 25.8 (see Figure C.14). The testing sessions 
were conducted in person, where participants completed an online survey 
by selecting from multiple-choice options and writing in responses under 
our supervision. Participants were recruited through social media announce-
ments and personal invitations. The tested materials and  data collected 
during these evaluation sessions are available at https://pf.dei.uc.pt/C/eval 
(visited: 7 July 2025).
In this first evaluation stage (s1), we focused on understanding 
if the generated outputs communicate the environmental conditions 
surrounding the installation. In this stage, each participant chose an output 
from a set of three posters that, in their opinion, best expressed the char-
acteristics mentioned in the question. Each question included one output 
specifically designed to express the requested characteristic better. We chose 
this poster by looking at the installation’s outputs and data, selecting the 
one that better represents the characteristic in evaluation, i.e. the output 
with the highest value in saved data. The rest of the collection consisted 
of designs with different visual characteristics. Participants could also 
respond that all present designs represented the feature equally. We ensured 
that the examples used were composed of visual elements placed using 
the random generation method.
We asked participants seven questions in this stage: (s1.1) “What is 
the generated composition when more people were in front of the instal-
lation?”; (s1.2) “What is the composition sequence generated when there 
is a more regular and constant flow of passers-by?”; (s1.3) “What is the 
compositions sequence generated when there are a higher number of 
passers-by?”; (s1.4) “What is the generated composition when the air 
temperature is warmer?”; (s1.5) “What is the generated composition when 
the sensor caught more direct light in the environment?”; (s1.6) “What is 
the composition generated during the night?”; and ( s1.7) “What is the 
composition generated during the day?”. In most questions, participants 
selected one option from a set of static outputs, except for questions s1.2 
and s1.3, where the answer comprised selecting a sequence of poster designs.
During the testing session, we displayed the outputs only with their 
variable visuals and without any information related to the place and time 
of their generation. We did not display the time and location information 
to avoid influencing the participants’ answers. Table C.1 unveils the results 
of the first testing stage.

The only environmental feature that most people did not directly 
recognise in the output was the amount of light the installation caught from 
the environment (s1.5). In this question, 65.71% of the testing participants 
(23) chose incorrectly. As mentioned earlier, the system modifies the colour 
saturation of visual elements based on the direct luminosity caught 
in the environment. Since the background of the posters is white, when the 
system caught low light, the visual elements became lighter and blended with 
the background. We noted that this confused the participants, especially 
when they observed the designs without the context of the installation.
The participants could only slightly identify the sequence of designs 
generated based on the number and regularity of passers-by. Only 51.40% 
(18) correctly selected the poster sequence when the flow of people was 
greater, i.e. when there were more passers-by near the installation (s1.2). 
Similarly, only 54.30% (19) correctly selected the sequence of posters when 
the flow of people was more constant, i.e. when passers-by were captured 
in more regular intervals (s1.3).

C16
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
In the second testing stage (S2), we focused on perceiving whether 
the generation based on experience method was noticeable in the posters. 
We measured the similarity between the generated outputs. During this 
testing stage, we calculated the similarity error, computing the likeness 
between posters according to the system’s perspective based on the saved 
data. Afterwards, we invited participants to repeat the same task, i.e. to 
observe the outputs and visually assess the similarity of the environments 
by rating “On a scale of 1 to 5, how related are these posters?”. In the end, 
we compared the results between the two classifications.
The similarity error allows us to compute how the generation based 
on experience method has been applied to the outputs. In other words, it 
correlates the visual similarity between two posters with the similarity of 
the environmental conditions at the time of generation. We assume that 
the system gains expertise in designing for the place where it is located 
when its outputs become more visually similar under similar environmental 
conditions. On the other hand, when two posters generated in the same 
environmental conditions are visually distinct, we assume that the system 
is not effectively generating for the surrounding environment.
The similarity error between the two posters is calculated based 
on environmental and visual factors. The environmental similarity between 
the two outputs is the difference between their surrounding environments 
concerning the (i) amount of people interacting with the installation, 
i.e. the number of passers-by nearby, their distance and the number of 
people looking directly at the installation, (ii) the air temperature, and 
(iii) the direct light caught from the environment. The visual similarity 
between two outputs is calculated based on the difference between the 
visual elements (and their features) on the outputs. We compute the dif -
ference between the outputs in terms of (i) the number of visual elements 
placed, (ii) the current fitness value, (iii) the average of the colours of visual 
elements, and (iv) the number of visual elements with the same shape. 
Each part of the equation has the same weight in the computation.
We selected five outputs generated at different time intervals and 
with distinct environments and surroundings. Afterwards, we computed 
the arithmetic mean of the error of similarity in the sequence, and we 
asked participants to perform the same task, using a scale from 1 to 5, where 
1 indicates that the set of posters is visually indistinct and 5 implies that 
the outputs are nearly identical. The outputs were grouped based on their 
characteristics. The first collection (s2.1) consisted of outputs generated 
on the same day and placed only in the afternoon (13h – 19h). The second 
collection (s2.2) consisted of posters created on the same day in the same 
place, between daylight hours (9h – 19h). Finally, the third (s2.3), fourth 
(s2.4), and fifth (s2.5) collections aggregated posters generated at the same 
time (13h, 9h, and 23h, respectively) and placed over consecutive days. 
The posters were displayed to participants in chronological order.
Similar to the s 1 stage, we presented participants with outputs 
containing only variable visuals. This way, they did not observe the infor-
mation related to time and place. Table C.2 reveals the average computed 
similarity error between the sequences and the evaluation results with people.

C17 APPENDIX  C ENVIRONMENT ALL Y  RESPONSIVE  P OSTER  GENERA TOR
The collection of outputs selected for testing presented a high sim-
ilarity error. The less similar sets were the first (s2.1) and second (s2.2), 
which were generated at different times on the same day and responded 
to varying environmental conditions. However, since they were generated 
in the same exact location and processed similar environmental data, the 
outputs were not entirely different. On the other hand, as expected, the 
third (s2.3), fourth (s2.4), and fifth (s2.5), which were produced over 
consecutive days, revealed greater similarity. This is expected because, in 
those cases, the system collects more data over time, often promoting the 
employment of generation based on experience method.

Although visual similarity is a subjective and personal concept, some 
patterns emerged from the survey responses. In the first collection (s2.1) 
and the second collection (s2.2), the majority of participants rated a sim-
ilarity error close to the computed value, with 48.60% of participants (17), 
selected the value closest to the computed value. We also noted that, in 
all the questions, most participants’ answers clustered around the com-
puted similarity error and the two values immediately adjacent to it. These 
findings suggest that the system’s adaptive capabilities were noticeable 
over time; however, the similarity between posters is only slightly percep-
tible to people, mainly when the similarity value is higher.
Finally, in the last and third stages of evaluation (s3), we focused 
on measuring the visual quality of the generated outputs and collecting 
some feedback on the system. This way, we asked people to rate, on a scale 
from bad (1) to exceptionally good (5), “How they visually liked the gen-
erated poster compositions” (s3.1). We also invited them to provide written  
feedback, thoughts, and comments about the system and installation (s3.2).
Despite the fact that the visual quality of poster design is a subjective 
matter, all participants rated the generated poster designs as at least sat -
isfactory, with a minimum rating of 3. Particularly, 51.43% (18) rated the 
visual quality as good (4), and 31.43% (11) rated it as exceptionally good 
(5). Table C.3 presents the results of this evaluation.

Only five participants (14.28%) provided comments about the system 
and outputs (s2.2). The majority of feedback focused on incorporating 
more environmental data into the designs. We highlight the following four 
comments: (i) the system should also use environmental data to influence 
the rendering and composition of static elements; (ii) it should employ 
a method to organise visual elements orderly in the composition, e.g. using 
a grid or avoiding overlaps; (iii) the visual elements could react to the 
direction of the most frequent passer-by traffic; and (iv) the visual shapes 
used could be more complex. 
In summary, the testing sessions reveal that the presented system 
can create visually appealing outputs; however, more environmental data 
and a more reactive approach could enhance the audience’s visualisation 
experience in the urban space.
C.4  FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS
In this experiment, we introduced an environmentally responsive poster 
generator system that creates new designs based on environmental data. 
This system uses a template strategy to generate the outputs and sto-
chastic methods to enhance the visual diversity. The posters consist of 
both static and variable visuals. Static visuals are predefined elements that 
maintain their position and appearance. In contrast, the system autono-
mously creates variable visuals using environmental context data collected 
through CV and physical computing (light intensity data).
This system operates continuously and sequentially, dynamically 
adjusting the output compositions by adding or removing variable visuals 
at specific intervals. The lifespan of each visual diminishes when it is on the 
composition; however, the attention of nearby people increases it. This way, 
this system tracks the number of people, their proximity to the installation, 
and their attention using CV techniques. This reactive approach allows 
the system to generate new designs in response to the evolving environ-
mental context where it is inserted. Moreover, the system can save and 
manage historical data, allowing it to adapt its generative process gradually. 
Over time, it gains expertise and starts replicating outputs (or parts of 
them) that have previously been successful under similar conditions.

C19 APPENDIX  C ENVIRONMENT ALL Y  RESPONSIVE  P OSTER  GENERA TOR
We installed the poster generator in four shop windows on different 
streets in CHC over four weeks (one week per store). This experiment 
demonstrated that the system could create designs from scratch with visual 
variation and diversity, suggesting that it effectively reflects different 
environmental conditions in urban spaces. Following this, we conducted 
evaluation sessions with participants to assess the system’s ability to 
communicate environmental features and whether its adaptive capabilities 
were visible in the output designs. These sessions showed that most par -
ticipants recognised the environmental conditions reflected in the outputs, 
indicating that the system successfully creates poster designs that integrate 
with the dynamics of the surrounding environment. However, the system’s 
adaptive capabilities were only slightly noticeable over time, mainly when 
the similarity value was higher. Also, participants found the generated 
outputs visually appealing. 
Furthermore, our observations during the installation revealed that 
the generated designs are more noticeable in urban spaces due to their 
reactive nature than traditional print designs. This allows us to conclude 
that the system’s capability to adapt designs in real-time to the current 
environmental context enhances visibility and engagement. Nevertheless, 
some participants suggested that incorporating more environmental data 
and reactive elements could provide the viewers with a more distinctive 
visual experience.

OF BOOKS

D02
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
This appendix outlines our initial experiments on computationally gener-
ating book designs from user-provided inputs, such as text and images. 
The system generates book layouts by following established typographic 
principles and rules as well as incorporating users’ specified preferences 
and constraints defined before the generation process. The primary purpose 
of this experiment is to explore the feasibility and potential of computa-
tional methods to be employed to create other print design media beyond 
posters, as discussed in Chapter 9 of this thesis. The development of this 
system also aims to explore the potential of computational methods for 
automating Graphic Design (GD) tasks, similar to the work discussed in 
Part III of this thesis. This appendix details the system’s development, 
initial experiments, and results.

D03 APPENDIX  D COMPUT A TIONAL  GENERA TION  OF BOOKS
We explored a computational approach for procedurally generating book 
layouts from user-provided input, including both text and images. The system 
automatically designs layouts by executing a series of operations that are 
grounded in established typographic knowledge while matching the users’ 
preferences and restrictions expressed before the generation process. 
The development of this system primarily aims to examine how compu-
tational generative techniques can be employed to generate other print 
GD artefacts beyond posters.
The developed system operates inside the Adobe InDesign environ-
ment, automatically generating books from given input content, including 
text and images. This system takes advantage of the typeset functionalities 
available in InDesign, which can be controlled through scripting. The purpose 
of integrating this software with the system was to allow users to easily 
create and refine design variations in a familiar working environment.
This system enables the generation of layouts that comply with 
previously defined typographic rules and knowledge while aligning with 
the user’s preferences set before the generation process. Prior to creating 
compositions, users define a set of constraints and visual characteristics 
for the output, including format, size, grid, and typeface. The system then 
automatically typesets the content according to the predefined typography 
rules and principles. Finally, the system presents the generated composi-
tion to the user as an editable Adobe InDesign document.
To install the system in the InDesign environment, users simply need 
to copy the folder that contains the system files into the “scripts” folder 
within the application directory. To make accessing the system easier, we 
also provided a script that creates a dedicated tab for the system in the 
InDesign navigation menu. The installation files, source code, and other 
supplementary files, including demonstration videos and examples of books 
generated, are available at https://cdv.dei.uc.pt/2019/scriptedpages (visited: 
7 July 2025).
We conducted preliminary experiments using the system to demon-
strate its ability to autonomously generate diverse compositions from the 
same input content while producing visually coherent compositions for 
different input content. Figure D.1 illustrates several books created using 
this system. 
This appendix is supported by the M.Sc. dissertation by Diogo Fer-
reira (2021) from the Design and Multimedia programme at the Faculty 
of Sciences and Technology of the University of Coimbra. The following 
sections describe the developed approach and summarise our findings.

D.1 INTERFACE
Figure D.2 displays various snapshots of the user interface, which is designed 
to enable interactive control of the system’s inner workings. The user 
interface consists of five tabs, each allowing users to set specific properties 
of the composition. Users can either manually configure these properties or 
opt for automatic selection based on a set of predefined rule-based values.
The first interface tab, labelled “Document” (see Figure D.2a), con-
cerns the document’s structural characteristics. It allows users to set the 
page size, margins, number of columns and gutter width. Additionally, 
there is an option to import settings from a stored file.
In the second tab, named “Input” (see Figure D.2b), users provide 
the content for the book. To that end, the interface offers two options. 
The first option is to load a Microsoft Word file containing only text, only 
images, or both. The second option is to load a Microsoft Word  file con-
taining just the text alongside a folder containing the corresponding images. 
In this case, users must indicate where each image should be placed within 
the text by using the tag @imageFileName@, which will be  replaced by 
the image with the matching name from the loaded folder. Users can also 
choose whether to generate a table of contents and a colophon for the 
book. The final option in this tab allows users to select the input text’s 
language to ensure proper word hyphenation.
The third tab, titled “Styles” (see Figure D.2c), focuses on defining 
and mapping paragraph styles. Users can choose from three options. The 
first option is to retain the styles imported from the input Word document. 
The second option is to map each style from the input document to another 
paragraph style, which can be selected manually or randomly from a list 
comprising all fonts installed on the computer. The remaining paragraph 
attributes are preserved. The last option is to let the system generate the 
styles, suggesting font combinations based on the rules entered in the 
system (these rules are explained in the following subsection).

D05 APPENDIX  D COMPUT A TIONAL  GENERA TION  OF BOOKS
In the fourth tab, labelled “Experimental” (see Figure D.2d), users can 
toggle experimental features to be applied to the generated book. The 
current version of the system offers four experimental features: (i) applying 
a colour background on half of each book page; (ii) applying a colour 
gradient to both the inner and outer margins of the pages; (iii) randomly 
indenting text paragraphs; and (iv) making the cover title as large as pos-
sible. These features aim to enhance the distinctiveness of the resulting 
designs. Moreover, users can select the “Surprise me” checkbox to let 
the system randomly decide whether to apply any of these experimental 
features. Furthermore, new features can be implemented and added to the 
system at any time.
After configuring the settings across the four tabs, users can initiate 
the creation of book designs by clicking the “Create” button located at the 
bottom right corner of the interface. This action triggers the system’s 
engine to automatically generate a new InDesign document and typeset a 
new book according to the content and settings specified by the user.
Upon completion of the typesetting process, the output is provided 
to the designer as an editable InDesign document. From there, users have 
three options: (i) adopt the generated book as a final design; (ii) use the 
generated book as a starting point for making further changes or refine-
ments; or (iii) continue using the system to generate additional designs 
until a more suitable design is found.

There is another interface tab, entitled “Properties” (see Figure D.2e), 
which not only provides an overview of the settings used in the generation 
of a book but also enables users to save those settings to a file. Later, this 
settings file can be imported into the system using the first interface tab, 
as mentioned earlier. This functionality can be helpful, for example, to 
facilitate the typeset of different books using the same settings. This last 
tab only becomes accessible after a book is generated. Additionally, a button 
becomes visible after generation, enabling users to generate a new book 
while maintaining the same input document and predefined settings. 
D.2 ENGINE
The system is built upon a set of typographic rules, styles, and principles 
derived from well-recognised literature in the field. Encoding these rules 
into the system enables the sequential generation of typographic designs, 
where the system systematically applies the rules one by one to determine 
the typographic features for all composition attributes. The reference 
works include those by Robert Bringhurst (1997), Josef Müller-Brockmann 
(1981), Andrew Haslam (2006), Jost Hochuli and Robin Kinross (2004), 
Jost Hochuli (2008), Ellen Lupton (2014), and Jan Tschichold (1991). 
The rules are stored in a configuration file (JSON file), which con-
tains possible configurations (i.e. values or a range of values) and, when 
applicable, the probability rate for each typographic attribute. Due to its 
easy comprehension and accessible format, users can easily edit this file 
anytime. The default configuration file is available at https://pf.dei.uc.pt/D/
rules.json (visited: 7 July 2025).
The typesetting process employed by the system consists of seven 
different sequential steps: (i) input processing; (ii) document size and grid 
definition; (iii) typeface definition; (iv) typographic styles definition; 
(v) document typesetting; (vi) experimental features application; and  
(vii) cover design. Next, we further describe each step.
INPUT PROCESSING
The first step involves loading and processing the input content. Once 
the content is loaded, the system conducts an analysis to extract data, 
such as the text length, the number of images, and the proportion of text 
to images. This analysis is important since it allows the system to classify 
the type of book that it is typesetting, whether it is a long reading book 
(i.e. 50,000 words or more), a short reading book (i.e. less than 50,000 
words), a book combining text and images, or a book containing only 
images. This categorisation informs the subsequent typographic decisions 
made during the following steps of the typesetting process.
DOCUMENT SIZE AND GRID DEFINITION
The next step is to create a new document with the page format and size 
tailored to the specific type of book. The configuration file contains a set 
of predefined book sizes and associated probability rates for selection 
based on the book type. Then, the book size is selected at random based 
on those probability rates. 

D07 APPENDIX  D COMPUT A TIONAL  GENERA TION  OF BOOKS
In this step, the system also defines the document grid, which includes 
defining the size of the margins, the number of columns, and the document 
baseline. Margins are randomly defined within a predetermined range. The 
number of columns in the grid is calculated by dividing the width of the 
available text block by a random integer value selected from a predefined 
range while also considering a minimum text block width. Thus, for smaller 
page sizes, it only creates single-column grids. 
The system also generates template pages for the document by cre-
ating text boxes and placing the running header (with the section name) 
and page numbering. The section name for each page is the last title found 
in the input document file. The position and sizing of these elements are 
defined empirically based on observation and analysis of example layouts. 
Currently, the system supports five different ways of composing headers 
and page numbering.
TYPEFACE DEFINITION
Next, the system defines the typefaces based on the users’ preferences. 
Users can choose to (i) keep the typefaces used on the input document, 
(ii) map those typefaces to new ones installed on the computer, or (iii)  
let the system select the typefaces.
When users opt to map the fonts from the input document to new 
ones, they must specify the style for each font using typefaces installed 
on their computers. Fonts not selected for mapping will maintain the same 
style as in the input document. Users also have the option to let the system 
randomly map one or more fonts at random. In this last case, the typefaces 
are chosen from predefined pairs or combinations as outlined in the con-
figuration file. When selecting the fonts, the system considers the type of 
book (e.g. long reading or short reading) and includes pairs of fonts where 
one is used for titles and the other for the text body, along with specific 
typographic features for each font.
TYPOGRAPHIC STYLES DEFINITION
The process continues with the definition of the paragraph, character, 
and image styles. Each paragraph style includes properties such as font, 
weight, size, leading, first-line indentation, paragraph indentation, space 
before and after the paragraph, alignment, vertical alignment, hyphenation, 
language, and colour. 
The font, weight, text leading, language, initial text size, and colour 
are set according to the preferences expressed beforehand by the user. 
The final text size is determined based on the selected document grid. 
During this process, the system checks whether the initial typeface size 
falls within the limits specified by the loaded rules. It then creates a text 
box and ensures that its average number of characters per line is within 
a predefined range. If the average number of characters is lower or higher 
than the limits, the system decreases or increases the text size, respectively. 
This adjustment process continues until an appropriate text size is reached. 
If necessary, the document grid may be modified, including adjustments 
to the margins and the number of columns. Finally, attributes such as the 
first line indentation, paragraph indentation, space before and after the 
paragraph, text alignment, vertical alignment and hyphenation are defined 
stochastically based on the type of book.

D08
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
The character styles are then defined based on the input document 
and the paragraph styles, which will facilitate the use of italics, bold text, 
and small caps, among other features. Similarly, the image styles are decided 
based on the input document and the paragraph style, which include 
aspects like positioning, size, text wrap, and effects.
DOCUMENT TYPESETTING
Once the base document is created and all the styles are defined, the system 
proceeds with the book’s typesetting. It begins by placing the body text, 
and subsequently, the previously defined typographic styles are applied 
to the entire document’s content.
Titles are organised into three levels of hierarchy, based on their 
text size in the input document: (i) chapter titles, i.e. titles in the largest 
size and preceded by a page break; (ii) section titles, i.e. titles larger than 
the main text font and preceded by a page or column break; and (iii) sub-
section titles, i.e. titles in the same size as the body text. 
Chapter titles are placed on a separate page. Section titles are typeset 
on the following page of the document. In multi-column documents, section 
titles are placed on the first column alone; otherwise, they are placed at 
the top of the page. Subsection titles are composed inline on the text of 
the same size as the body text.
After applying the typographic styles, the system automatically places 
the images and their corresponding captions. Initially, images are placed 
inline, matching the width of the column where they are placed. If the 
book has a multi-column grid and the image is placed on the leftmost 
column of the document, the system randomly decides whether to change 
its size to fulfil more than one column. In such cases, the text layout adjusts 
to accommodate the image’s placement. Captions are created automatically 
based on the name of the input images. For each document, the system 
determines a caption style, considering the available inner space on margins 
as well as the existence of headers and page numbers. By default, captions 
can be positioned below the images, aligned to the left, or placed alongside 
the images, centred, and vertically rotated 90º.
Finally, the system generates the table of contents and colophon. 
As mentioned earlier, the user can choose whether to create a table of 
contents and a colophon. When these options are selected, a table of 
contents is added to the beginning of the book using the titles from the 
input document, formatted with the same paragraph style as those titles. 
On the other hand, the colophon containing information about the gen-
erated book is typeset at the end of the book in the same style as the body 
text. It includes a description of the project and parametric details about 
the specific design of that book, such as size, margins, and the number of 
columns, among other relevant information.
EXPERIMENTAL FEATURES
Experimental features are optional and are only used when selected by 
the user through the interface. As mentioned before, new features can be 
developed and added to the system.

D09 APPENDIX  D COMPUT A TIONAL  GENERA TION  OF BOOKS
By default, the system presents three experimental features regarding 
the book’s interior. The first one adds a coloured background on half of each 
page, in a specific layer beneath the text. The second feature applies a gra-
dient along the inner or  outer margins of the pages. The margins where 
the gradient is applied are chosen randomly, allowing the system to create 
gradients on either or both margins. For both experimental features, the 
background colour is also chosen randomly from a predefined set of colours 
as soon as the first feature is used. The default set includes the following 
seven CMYK colours: cyan (100,  0, 0, 0); light orange (0, 40, 100, 0); 
orange (0, 60, 100, 0); red (0, 100, 100, 0); pink (0, 39, 3, 0); yellow (0, 0, 
100, 0); and beige (2, 14, 38, 0). The final feature adds random indentation 
to randomly selected text paragraphs.
COVER DESIGN
The final step in the process is designing the book cover. We have developed 
a method that generates simple typographic compositions, placing the 
book title at the top margin and the author’s name at the bottom margin, 
both in uppercase letters and using the same typeface as the text. The back 
cover features information about the computer system responsible for 
generating the book. The cover background colour is randomly chosen 
from a set of predefined colours. The book title and author(s) must be 
defined in the input document using a specific paragraph style. If this 
information is not provided, the system automatically sets the title to 
the first sentence of the paragraph composed using the largest text size in 
the document.
Moreover, new experimental features can be developed and applied 
to the covers. For example, the presented version of the system includes 
experimental features that typeset the cover title in the largest font 
size possible.
D.2. 1 EVALUA TION
We conducted experiments to evaluate whether the proposed system 
can automatically generate book layouts with different purposes and styles. 
Our focus was on studying the ability of the system to accomplish two 
design tasks: (i) creating books with distinguishable layout designs, i.e. 
generating a set of books that present several visual characteristics; and 
(ii) creating visually coherent books, i.e generating a collection of books 
that follow and share the same visual style between them. To assess these 
aspects, we conducted a survey to evaluate the visual diversity and coher-
ence of designs created with the proposed system.
For the evaluation of visual diversity, we conducted the following 
actions. Initially, we selected a public domain book as the source content 
for the evaluation. Then, we input this content into the system and gen-
erated fifteen books without manually setting any visual or typography 
attribute. In other words, the system randomly defined these attributes 
within predefined ranges based on its default principles. Lastly, we pre-
sented the 15 generated book designs to a group of 42 participants and 
asked them to assess the layout diversity and coherence within the set.

D10
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
The selected content was the book Contos, written by the Portuguese 
author Eça de Queiróz and published in 1992.1 This book comprises thirteen 
short stories, each one structured as a chapter, composed of approximately 
73,330 words.
To evaluate visual coherence, we followed the following steps. Ini-
tially, we selected a book design from the set of 15 generated earlier to 
evaluate visual diversity. We then exported the settings used by the system 
to generate the selected book. Table D.1  overviews the visual and typo -
graphic features of the chosen book design. Subsequently, we input these 
settings into the system and created book designs for five different contents. 
Lastly, we presented the generated designs to the same group of partici-
pants and asked them to evaluate the layout diversity (or coherence) within 
this set.

The two sets of books were evaluated by the same group of partic-
ipants in a survey. First, participants were shown a set of 15 randomly 
generated designs, followed by a new set of five designs created using the 
settings from one design selected from the first set. After observing each 
set of designs, each participant was invited to “Classify the layouts’ diver-
sity and coherence on a scale ranging from 1 (very coherent) to 5 (very 
diverse)?”. This testing group consisted of 42 individuals, with ages ranging 
from 19 to 49 years old, who evaluated the design remotely through an 
online survey. Participants were recruited via social media posts and per-
sonal invitations.

D11 APPENDIX  D COMPUT A TIONAL  GENERA TION  OF BOOKS
Figure D.3 displays several pages composed automatically by the 
system for the first part of the evaluation experiment, where the visual 
features were randomly defined. Upon examining the resulting designs, 
we noticed that most of the designs (12 out of 15) are portrait-oriented. 
This is due to the automatic classification of the input content by the system 
as a long reading book, resulting in a higher probability of selecting a por-
trait format. Nevertheless, the format of the generated books shows slight 
variations between them.
Regarding the text boxes, grids, and typefaces used, we observed 
the influence of the typographic principles and rules encoded in the system. 
Most designs present the body text typeset in justified alignment (13 out 
of 15) over a one-column grid (12 out of 15), which are characteristics 
considered suitable for long reading books. However, we noticed diversity 
in other aspects. The dimensions of the margin and the size of the grid 
gutter (when present) vary between books. The font, text size, leading, 
and placement of running headers and page numbers also vary. Addition-
ally, various experimental features, used individually or in combination, 
were observed in six of the generated designs.
When examining books created using system settings imported from 
a previously generated book, it becomes evident that the resulting designs 
share several visual characteristics. These characteristics include the book 
format and size, page margins, grid, and typefaces used. Furthermore, these 
designs exhibit a noticeable similarity to the source design. Figure D.4  
shows pages from the book that sourced the settings file (see Figure D.4a), 
which was selected from the set used in the first part of the experiment 
(see Figure D.3), along with pages of some books used in the second part 
of the experiment (see Figure D.4b).

The evaluation survey conducted indicates that the system is capable 
of generating both diverse and cohesive book designs. The chart in Figure 
D.5 shows the distribution of answers obtained in the survey. When we 
asked the survey participants to assess the diversity and coherence of the 
first set of books, which were generated at random by the system, the 
majority of participants (35 out of 42) considered them as diverse (19) or 
very diverse (16). Only a few participants considered this set of books to 
be very cohesive (2) or cohesive (5).
In contrast, when participants evaluated the second set of books, 
which were generated from a specific settings file, the majority of partic-
ipants (38 out of 42) considered that the generated designs were visually 
coherent. Most of them (30) considered that this second set of designs 
presented a high level of coherence among them.
Results also indicate that variables and properties defined by the 
system can create visually diverse layouts. Although the system engine 
determines book features based on predefined typographic rules and prin-
ciples, it also employs probabilistic mechanisms to define some attributes.  
We observed that this probabilistic approach occasionally results in the 
definition of attributes in an unexpected manner, promoting visual varia-
tion in the resulting layouts. This is visible, for instance, in the first part 
of the experiment, where books are created with different formats  even 
though the system tends to avoid using landscape format in long reading. 
The experimental features incorporated into the system can be 
observed in some of the generated books. We consider that they contribute 
to the diversity and variation of the outputs. However, we noted that some 
generated designs show certain graphic limitations because they comply 
with the same default typographic rules and principles. Although users 
can manipulate these rules, this will primarily change the typeset of the 
book, but it will not include new visual features.

D13 APPENDIX  D COMPUT A TIONAL  GENERA TION  OF BOOKS
D.3 FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS
We have presented a Computational Design (CD) approach for generating 
book designs. This approach follows an expert strategy drawing on typo-
graphic knowledge from recognised literature in the field. Its main aim 
is to explore how CD can support contemporary GD practices beyond 
poster design, aligning with the objectives outlined earlier in this thesis.
This book generation approach creates designs using user-provided 
text and images, operating within the Adobe InDesign software, making 
use of its scripting capabilities. This system does not require users to pre-
define any visual feature, allowing them to generate books entirely from 
scratch. Users can then modify the results within the familiar InDesign  
environment and print them as needed.
If they desire, users can impose specific constraints or preferences 
on the system through a dedicated interface. Throughout the generation 
process, the system will take into consideration these restrictions. More-
over, the system allows the introduction of new rules and functions, and the 
design rules can be exported for applications to create other designs.
The preliminary experiments revealed the system’s capability to con-
sistently generate book designs that comply with traditional typographic 
design rules. We assessed the system’s ability to generate visually diverse 
books from different content and visually coherent books with diverse 
contents. The outputs were assessed with 42 participants, and the results 
demonstrated the dual ability of the system to create visually diverse books 
when the system operates without restrictions and visually coherent books 
when subject to strict constraints.
Despite the proposed process having a local search nature and certain 
limitations in autonomy compared to other expert strategies, the system 
has proven to be a functional design tool. The findings show that it can 
assist designers in automating book typesetting and facilitate the explo-
ration and discovery of new visual possibilities.
The generative book process, primarily guided by predefined typo-
graphic expertise, occasionally introduces variation through probabilistic 
mechanisms. This probabilistic approach can lead to unexpected attribute 
definitions, which we consider to enhance visual diversity in the layouts 
and increase the exploratory value of the tool. Users can also limit the

D14
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
autonomy and expertise of the system by specifying the desired features for 
the outputs. Our analysis recognised that the system could be suitable for 
use in different stages of the design process, from the earlier and explor-
atory stages (when designers can take advantage of random generation to 
look for new types of layouts) to the final stages (when designers need to 
fine-tune specific graphic attributes).
Furthermore, the system allows users to export data into settings 
files, which encode the book’s design and, later, can be loaded into the system 
to create other visually similar books. Users have the flexibility to input 
their desired book properties directly into the system interface or modify 
the typographic principles and rules the system uses. 
This way, we noted that the proposed system is also a useful tool 
for automating the design of books and editorial designs that need to follow 
a set of restricted typographic and visual attributes (e.g. when it is neces-
sary to design new books that will be part of a collection or a series). 
This system was designed to integrate with traditional computerised 
editorial design tools, which we believe promotes a more seamless incor-
poration of computational methods into the design process. Our obser -
vations indicate that allowing designers to work within their familiar 
environment eliminates the need to learn new tools, enabling them to 
effortlessly edit or refine the generated designs directly. However, not all 
traditional Computer-aided Design (CAD) software currently supports 
scripting and the development of computational tools. We also highlighted 
that this integration enables the development of approaches with a higher 
level of expressive power.
We incorporated a mechanism called “experiment features,” allowing 
users to customise and add new functionalities through configuration files. 
We consider that this flexibility allows users to modify the existing approaches, 
adapting the system to meet specific needs. Also, by enabling the intro-
duction of novel visual elements, we consider that these customisations 
can potentially enhance the distinguishability of the output designs.
Overall, this experiment demonstrates the potential of CD processes, 
especially expert strategies, to automate the creation of print GD artefacts, 
particularly book layouts. These approaches have the potential to optimise 
routine tasks and assist in the exploratory and discovery phases of the 
design process. These findings align with conclusions drawn in other sec-
tions of this thesis. Moreover, the findings suggest that this approach 
presents significant potential for a wide range of print design scenarios 
where the generation of custom-made designs is needed. We consider that 
they are particularly relevant for print-on-demand applications and for 
creating designs for existing collections or series.
