E02
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
This appendix presents an experiment on the computational generation 
of music album cover designs. In this context, we developed an online tool 
that creates covers based on the audio characteristics of an album’s tracks. 
This approach automates the generation of designs through a template  
strategy, where visual features are defined by a data-driven method. This 
work examines the application of computational methods to other print 
designs, expanding beyond posters, as detailed in Chapter 9. Also, this 
experiment investigates how template strategies and data-driven methods 
can enhance customisation, aligning with the works presented in Part II  
of this thesis.

E03 APPENDIX  E COMPUT A TIONAL  DESIGN  OF  MUSIC ALBUM  COVERS
We developed a Computational Design (CD) approach to automatically 
generate music album cover designs. Users can experiment with this 
approach through an online tool that allows them to create covers by 
searching for an album. The features and visuals of output designs are 
defined based on the audio characteristics of the album’s tracks.
We generate album covers through a template strategy, incorpo-
rating visual features derived from data related to the album. We used the 
Spotify API to access a dataset of the music album and retrieve the audio 
characteristics and details concerning the album and its tracks.1 We have 
developed several drawing modes that employ different shapes and methods 
of translating sound data into visuals.
Moreover, the system provides a range of methods for users to refine 
or completely modify the visual features of the outputs to align with their 
visual preferences once the generation process is complete. Beyond gen-
erating static outputs, the proposed approach can create animated versions 
of album covers by animating the visual elements based on data. In this 
sense, this experiment investigates how computational media can trans-
form traditional print designs into digital scenarios, similar to our work 
with moving posters (see Chapter 3).
We conducted a series of preliminary experiments using this approach 
to evaluate its generative capability by inviting graphic designers to 
produce covers and then evaluate the quality of the outputs and their overall 
design experience. The computational creation of album covers aspect 
is beyond the scope of the state-of-the-art covered in Chapter 2  of this 
thesis. The work on this appendix is supported by the M.Sc. dissertation 
by  Marília R. Martins (2022) from the Design and Multimedia program at 
the Faculty of Sciences and Technology of the University of Coimbra. 
Subsequent sections provide an overview of the computational creation 
of album covers and detail the approach and the preliminary experi-
ments conducted.
E .1 COMPUT A TIONAL CREA TION OF ALBUM COVERS
Initially intended for record protection, music album cover designs began 
to be depicted as a design medium in the 1940s. Graphic designer  Alex 
Steinweiss played a key role in this evolution while employed by Columbia 
Records. He explored new types of designs to capture the music’s essence 
and symbolism and attract new customers (Heller, 1992; Medel, 2014; 
Meggs & Purvis, 2016). Several album covers with contemporary cultural 
significance and recognition were created in the following decades. Exam-
ples include Andy Warhol’s iconic banana cover for The Velvet Underground 
and Nico’s debut album (1967), Iain Macmillan’s Abbey Road cover for The

OF MUSIC ALBUM COVERS

E04
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
Beatles (1969), and Jamie Reid’s provocative portrayal of the British mon-
archy on the Sex Pistols’ God Save the Queen album (1977).
Over time, several authors have explored the algorithmic generation 
of visuals using sound-to-visual representation. Examples of these explo-
rations include An Optical Poem (1938)2 by Oskar Fischinger (Moritz, 2004), 
Fontana Mix (1958) by John Cage, and Pithoprakta (1957) by Iannis Xenakis 
(Harley, 2004). Recently, computational approaches have begun to be used 
in the same context. Examples include works such as ESSYS system (Seiça, 
2018), Computerized Forms (Givens, 2017), P5Live (Davis, 2019), XYScope 
(Davis & Hieda, 2019), Reading Machines (Dingsun, 2020), and Undulations 
in C (Ezekiel, 2020).
While the use of computational approaches for generating music 
album covers, as far we know, remains relatively scarce and limited, we 
identify several works that explore this subject, generating visuals that 
represent audio or an entire album. Angela Lorenz (2016) produced covers 
by remixing sound fragments from albums, employing screen interference 
and image details as patterns (Shaughnessy & Lorenz, 2003). Beethoven 
Generative Music Artworks by Mindaugas Dudenas, Modesta Kalkyte, and 
/ kazkas (2020) transformed the data from song analysis with Fast Fourier 
Transform into circular frequency spectra and used rectangles to represent 
songs on the album. Tiziana Alocci (2019) designed covers for several 
artists based on the album content, including spectrum-based and network 
representations of tracks. While these works allow the computational 
generation of album cover designs, they are custom generative tools whose 
outputs lack visual versatility and seldom incorporate visual mapping of 
audio attributes such as loudness and Beats Per Minute (BPM).
More recently, several works also explored the use of generative 
deep learning, mostly Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN), for creating 
album cover imagery. Alexander Hepburn et al. (2017) experimented with 
generating album covers based on genre tags using an Auxiliary Classifier 
GAN approach trained with a dataset of 50,000 images separated into five 
genres, which were retrieved using the Spotify API. Vera van de Seyp (2020) 
explored a Style-based GAN as a tool to generate album cover designs, 
training the model on a dataset of 150,000 album covers. Valeria Efimova et al. 
(2022) proposed a GAN-based approach called CoverGAN that can generate 
vector graphics cover designs based on a set of audio features from album 
tracks, including the emotions associated with them. James Marien et  al. 
(2022) used a deep-learning framework to generate cover artworks informed 
by audio features, employing an evolutionary approach to optimise the 
generated cover. Nevertheless, these generative approaches are difficult 
to control and require high computational power and extensive training data.
E.2 APPROACH
The system utilises a template strategy for album cover designs. This system 
was developed using web technologies and the Spotify API to retrieve 
information and audio features from the album’s tracks.
We designed a tool to assist the generation process (see Figure E.1). 
The generative process begins with users searching for a specific album 
by entering a text string that includes the album or artist name. Users

input the search term on the top of the page and click the “search” button 
(see Figures E.1a and E.1b). This album must be available on Spotify and 
accessible through its API. 
When accessing the tool, the homepage presents a selection of the 
current most popular albums. Users can choose one of these albums 
to generate a cover. If users enter a search term, the results are shown 
sorted by popularity.
Afterwards, the system retrieves information from the selected 
album and creates an initial cover design based on the audio features 
of the album. At the end of the generation process, users can modify 
the output through a dedicated interface, adjusting visual features such 
as colours, shapes, and typography, as well as introducing animations. 
(see Figures E.1c to E.1e). A high-level scheme of the architecture of the 
system is depicted in Figure E.2. The developed system is available at http://
soundshape.dei.uc.pt  (visited: 7 July 2025 ). The following subsections 
outline the engine and the refinement interface.
E.2. 1 ENGINE
The system’s generative approach consists of two distinct stages. The first 
stage involves retrieving information based on the user’s inputs. The second 
stage uses a sequential process to generate the album covers.
The system gathers information about the album, artist, and track 
features from the Spotify API. It begins by performing a search based on 
the user’s input to find albums and artists that match the query. For each 
result, it retrieves details such as the album name, artist’s name, popularity, 
and the original cover image. This information is displayed on the results 
screen, helping users to select the desired album.

E06
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
Next, based on the user’s selected album, the system retrieves infor-
mation about the album, the artist, and the audio features of the tracks. 
Initially, it collects data such as the number of tracks on the album, the 
release date, and the music genres associated with the artist. Then, for 
each track on the album, the system gathers information such as its esti-
mated overall tempo in BPM, the overall loudness (or volume) in decibels, 
the mode of the song (major or minor), and the key or tonality of the song.
This system creates visual compositions using five different drawing 
modes: (i) ellipse; (ii) rectangle; (iii) circle; (iv) dash; and (v) shape. In all 
these modes, a set of shapes is used to represent the tracks on the album. 
In each mode, the retrieved information is mapped to create visuals according 
to predefined settings. In some modes, stochastic-based methods are 
used to introduce visual variation. The initial mode for the output is 
selected randomly.
In all drawing modes, the size of the shapes corresponds to the 
loudness of the track it represents. The colour is based on the key, or genre, 
of the same track. When animated, the movement speed of the shape 
relates to the BPM of each song. The system uses a sine wave animation 
for shape size, with the increment defined by the BPM of each track. 
In the circle mode, the ring’s appearance represents the track’s mode 
(major or minor), with the inner circle indicating the major mode and the 
outermost ring representing the minor mode. In the dash mode, the number 
of dashes is random. In shape mode, the shape is randomly selected from 
triangles, half-circles, circles, squares, or diamonds.
Table E.1 presents the visual mapping employed in this system, which 
we have defined empirically. These values are stored in a dedicated con-
figuration file, allowing users to customise these features as desired.
By default, the colour of a visual element on the cover represents 
the track’s key. This mapping is based on Leonid Sabaneyev ’s analysis of 
the relationship between tones and colours of Alexander Scriabin (Galeyev 
& Vanechkina, 2001). Additionally, we have established an alternative 
colour mapping based on the music genre of the track, informed by a survey 
conducted by Jukka Holm et al. (2009). Figure E.3 illustrates these rela-
tionships. To simplify the number of genres, we have grouped similar ones 
into fifteen broader genres, including Pop, Dance, EDM, Hip-Hop, Rap, 
R&B, Latin, Rock, Metal, Classical, Jazz, Blues, New Age, World, and Folk.

Since we use a template-based approach, certain information is 
consistently positioned in all generated outputs. This information includes 
the album name, the artist, and the release year. These elements are posi-
tioned at the top-right, top-left, and bottom-right corners of the cover, 
respectively. The album name is typeset in the Magtis Extra Bold typeface,3 
while the artist and release year are in the Inter Bold typeface.4 If the album 
or artist names are too long, the system automatically breaks them across 
multiple lines. Also, the background of the cover is always defined as white, 
and the text elements are black.

E.2.2 REFINEMENT INTERFACE
Once the user chooses an album, the system generates and displays an 
album cover. Users can then refine the visual characteristics of the output 
cover. Although the system initially defines these features based on pre-
defined visual decisions related to the album’s track features, users have 
the option to adjust them according to their preferences.
The refining interface offers three editing modes, each accessible 
through its respective tab on the left side of the interface. Users can switch 
between these modes to manipulate several characteristics of the visual 
elements on the album cover. These characteristics include shape mode, 
colour, position, blend mode, size, rotation, and motion speed. Certain 
attributes like blend mode, background colour, and rotation are only 
modified during this stage. Additionally, users have the option to save the 
generated album covers to a file. Figure E.4 displays multiple results created 
after the fine-tuning of this interface.
In the shape and colour editing mode, users can adjust various visual 
attributes. They can change the shape mode, set the blend mode for over-
lapping shapes, customise the background colour, and select the colours of 
visual elements on the cover based on the key or genre. Additionally, they 
can also manually assign a colour to shapes according to their preferences.
In the text editing mode, users can resize the text elements on 
the album cover, including the album name, artist name, and release year. 
They also can choose a different colour for the typography.

Finally, in the animation editing mode, users can adjust features 
related to shapes and their animation. This includes the size of the shapes 
(both width and height separately) and the animation velocity (with minimum 
velocity indicating that the animation is stopped). During animation, the 
size of the shape reflects its maximum value. Additionally, in ellipse and 
rectangle modes, users can alter the rotation of the shapes.

E.3 EV ALUA TION
We conducted an evaluation session to assess the creative and automation 
potential of the approach in the Graphic Design (GD) practice. We invited 
14 designers in the fields related to visual communication to interact with 
the system and evaluate the tool’s automation capabilities and the visual 
quality of the outputs. These testing sessions were divided into two stages. 
First, participants experimented with the tool to generate album covers. 
Then, they evaluated both the outputs, the tool itself, and the applicability 
of the approach to their professional practice.

E09 APPENDIX  E COMPUT A TIONAL  DESIGN  OF  MUSIC ALBUM  COVERS
In the testing sessions, we asked participants to follow three steps: 
(i) access the website (on a computer or tablet); (ii) search for any artist 
or music album and generate an album cover; and (iii) explore the tool’s 
capabilities by creating at least three covers for the same album, and then 
downloading them.
After completing the tasks, participants were asked to complete a 
survey of 22 questions, divided into two stages. The first stage focused on 
the visual quality of the generated outputs (S1), while the second stage 
assessed the tool’s capabilities and usability (S2). These questions were 
structured to gather quantitative and qualitative feedback. Typically, each 
question consists of two parts: first, participants rate various aspects on 
a five-point scale, and then they answer open-ended questions to provide 
justifications for their evaluations.
In the initial stage (S1), participants were asked to answer five ques-
tions related to the designs of the generated outputs. First, we asked them 
to “rate the visual quality of the generated outputs using a scale from 1 (low 
quality) to 5 (high quality)”, and then to describe their visual characteris-
tics freely. Next, we requested they to “Classify whether the generated 
covers display visual cohesion among them, using a scale from 1 (few 
cohesive) to 5 (very cohesive)?” and next to explain their reasoning freely 
(S1.2). Subsequently, participants rated, on the same scale, where 1 (low 
potential) and 5 (high potential), if they “Consider that this tool had the 
potential to create diverse outputs?” and then justified their responses 
(S1.3). On the same scale, they were then asked whether they “Consider 
the designs to be distinctive?” (S1.4). Finally, participants were invited to 
“share suggestions regarding the visual aspects of the generated covers” (S1.5).
The second stage (S2) focused on evaluating the developed tool, 
which comprised six questions evaluated on a scale from 1 (low value) to 
5 (high value). The first question was, “Are the available options for refining 
the cover designs sufficient?” (S2.1). Next, participants were asked to 
answer, “After using the tool, how has your perception of this approach 
as a support tool in the creative process of designing album covers changed?” 
along with providing justifications for their views (S2.2). Following this, 
we inquired, “How perceptible it was that the approach used information 
from the album to inform visual elements on the cover?” asking participants 
to freely identify at least three features where this was noticeable (S2.3). 
On the same scale, we asked, “How easy is the tool to use?” (S2.4). Lastly, 
in open-ended questions, we requested  participants to reply to “What 
potential future applications of this tool do you see in commercial con -
texts?” (S2.5) and invited participants to provide “suggestions for improving 
the tool” (S2.6).
The designers who participated in the evaluation sessions were 
between 22 and 30 years old. Participants were selected through per -
sonal invitations and participate in the survey on-site under our supervi-
sion. Among the participants, 9 (64.3%) identified as graphic designers, 4 
(28.6%) as multimedia designers, and 1 (7.1%) as a digital designer. Regarding 
their prior knowledge of the system’s subject matter, 10 participants (71.4 %) 
had no previous experience in sound design, while 4  (28.6 %) indicated 
they did not often have an interest in computational design or creative 
coding. Table E.2 summarises the profile of the participants.

During this experimentation stage, participants created 46 cover 
designs, averaging 3.33 covers per participant. Three participants created 
more covers than the three minimum required for the evaluation. Figures 
E.5 and E.6 display examples of covers generated during this stage. The 
collected data and all the generated covers from these evaluation sessions 
can be accessed at https://pf.dei.uc.pt/E/eval (visited: 7 July 2025).
Among the 46 covers created, we observed that participants used the 
key colour mode to fill the visual elements in 25 covers (54.3 %), experimenting 
with various blend modes. The most frequently used drawing mode was the 
circle(13 covers, 28.2 %), followed by the Rectangle (10 covers, 21.7 %), the 
Dash (9 covers, 19.6 %), the Shape (8 covers, 17.5 %), and the Ellipse 
(6 covers, 13.0 %). Table E.3 summarises the quantitative results of the survey.

E11 APPENDIX  E COMPUT A TIONAL  DESIGN  OF  MUSIC ALBUM  COVERS
The results of the first stage (S1) reveal that participants consider 
that the proposed approach is able to generate quality outputs, with most 
users rating the visual quality of the outputs (S1.1) as high (mean [x̅ ]: 4.07, 
median [x̃]: 4.00). When we asked participants to define the visual char -
acteristics, words, such as “appealing” (3), “inspiring” (3), “interesting” (2) 
and “minimalist” (2) were used. 
Regarding the visual coherence of the covers (S1.2), all participants 
agreed that the approach produces visually coherent designs, with every 
participant rating the coherence as at least high (x̅ : 4.07, x̃: 4.00). Many par-
ticipants justified this by highlighting the visual limitations imposed by 
the available options for styling the covers, which ensure that all results 
share similar visual characteristics, mainly due to the typographic fea -
tures (6). Two participants also noted that the results could be identified 
as covers that are part of the same collection.
Although participants acknowledged the system’s ability to create 
coherent designs, they also noted that it could produce somewhat visually 
diverse designs (S1.3, x̅ : 3.57, x̃: 4.00). Some users emphasised that the 
outputs have visual diversity in terms of colour and shapes, but not in terms 
of typographic features (5). The tests also revealed that the outputs present 
certain limitations in terms of distinctiveness (S1.4), even though they are 
still considered distinct by the average of users (x̅ : 3.21, x̃: 3.00). Regarding 
suggestions (S1.5), most participants (11) recommended increasing the 
typographic options in the tool would enhance the diversity of the sys-
tem’s outputs.

COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
The second survey stage (S2) revealed that participants are generally 
satisfied with the tool and perceive some information about the album in 
the outputs. They also expressed a willingness to include this tool in their 
design processes. The tests revealed that participants are relatively satis-
fied with the current typographic refinement options (S2.1). However, they 
acknowledge that there is room for improvement (x̅ : 3.42, x̃: 4.00). Addi-
tionally, participants considered that this approach could be valuable 
in their designer processes for exploratory purposes (S2.2, x̅ : 3.79, x̃: 4.00) 
with most participants rating its exploratory value as high, with 28.6% (4) 
assigning a value of 4, and 35.7% (5) assigning a value of 5. In the optional 
justifications, three users noted that the approach is a valuable tool for brain-
storming and discovery tasks in their projects.
The album information was perceived in the outputs (S2.3) by the 
average of the users (x̅ : 3.21, x̃: 3.00). However, most users only identified 
direct information, such as the album name, artist name, year, and colour 
assignments based on keys and music genre. Regarding the usability of the 
tool (S2.4), the results indicated that participants found the interface 
straightforward to use (x̅ : 4.64, x̃: 5.00). For future applications of this tool 
in commercial contexts (S2.5), participants suggested a range of uses, 
including generating multiple covers for each song on an album, creating 
cover images for playlists, and producing advertisements and merchandise 
materials for a band. In the final question (S2.6), users’ suggestions revolved 
around increasing editing options, especially the typographic ones.
We also noted that there were no significant patterns between the 
responses of participants with previous knowledge of sound design and 
those with an interest in computational design and creative coding.
E.4  FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS
We have presented a CD approach for generating music album covers, 
expanding our investigation beyond posters. The primary goal of this 
experiment is to examine the potential of computational methods to support 
contemporary GD practices, aligning with the objectives outlined earlier 
in this thesis.
The covers are created using a template strategy, with the visual 
features of the design determined by data from the user-selected album 
and its tracks. We used the Spotify API to gather these data. The developed 
online tool also allows users to interactively customise the designs according 
to their preferences after the generation.
We conducted preliminary evaluation experiments by inviting 14 
designers to use the tool to generate album covers. Following this, we asked 
them questions about the visual quality and usability of the tool. The testing 
sessions revealed that the tool is user-friendly and facilitates the quicker 
and easier creation of album covers.
Our preliminary findings indicate that the proposed system effec-
tively facilitates the generation of coherent album cover designs. The 
testing outputs unveil that the proposed template strategies are efficient 
in generating album covers that share consistent visual characteristics. 

E13 APPENDIX  E COMPUT A TIONAL  DESIGN  OF  MUSIC ALBUM  COVERS
Our experimentation also reveals that this approach supports automation 
in the process of creating album covers, particularly in scenarios where 
designs should share similar visual traits, such as when creating album 
cover collections for the same author or label.
The drawing modes developed for creating cover illustrations allow 
some visual diversity in the designs. However, we noted that the outputs 
share similar typographic features, such as typefaces and their positions 
on the layout, which limits overall visual variation. Testing participants 
highlight that introducing broader typographic variation methods could 
enhance the overall visual variation of the designs. For example, enabling 
changes to the typeface or its position within the design could contribute 
to a more varied visual outcome.
The developed approach demonstrates the potential of using tem-
plate strategies to create print designs. We observed that this approach 
encourages the creation of new design types that can be customised for 
different personal and data contexts. We consider that this encourages 
crafting tailored designs that align with the audience’s preferences. Par -
ticipants also suggested expanding the proposed approach to create not 
only album cover designs but also other artefacts, such as collections of 
album covers, advertisements, playlist cover images, and custom merchan-
dising materials.
Moreover, we assert that this experiment demonstrates the trans -
mediation of album covers from print to digital media, enabling the inclu-
sion of new features such as animation, interactivity, and reactivity.
Despite its preliminary nature, this experiment demonstrates the 
potential of CD processes to automate the creation of custom designs 
for print. We consider that this approach presents significant potential for 
a wide range of print design scenarios where the generation of custom-made 
designs is needed. Moreover, the use of one template-based approach 
reveals potential for creating customised designs that can adapt to various 
contexts, which we suggest could promote more personalised communi-
cation with the audience. These findings align with conclusions drawn 
in other parts of this thesis.

F02
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
This appendix presents an experiment exploring the computational crea-
tion of brutalist websites. The system generates these designs using auto-
mated processes that combine several computational approaches. Like 
other studies in this thesis, this experiment investigates how Computational 
Design (CD) methods can be applied to Graphic Design (GD) artefacts 
beyond posters, focusing specifically on Web Design. This work is part of 
a series of initial experiments examining the impact of computational 
techniques on digital design, as discussed in Chapter 10. Moreover, it 
explores how computational methods can automate the creation of web 
designs, building on the approaches outlined earlier in Part III of this thesis.

F03 APPENDIX  F BRUT ALIST  WEBSITE  GENERA TOR
BRUT ALIST WEBSITE GENERA TOR
We developed a computational system that generates web pages and pop-
ulates them with content sourced from a user-provided input string on 
Wikipedia. This system defines web page features using an expert strategy 
that combines textual analysis to extract information from the content 
with template-based and stochastic methods. Users can customise the 
generated web pages, allowing them to adjust the designs according to 
their tastes and preferences. The primary aim of this work is to conduct 
an initial study on how computational approaches can be applied to digital 
design, particularly to automate the generation of web and interactive 
designs, similar to the approaches discussed earlier in Part III of this thesis.
The generated web pages are designed to embody the aesthetics of 
brutalist web design.1 Web brutalism is an alternative movement that encour-
ages designers to challenge interaction design principles and reflect on their 
current practices, exploring new visual styles and user usability approaches 
(Ganci & Ribeiro, 2017). By adopting this brutalist style, the system is also 
intended to support discovery tasks in visual and interactive design.
We conducted a preliminary user evaluation to assess the usability 
and visual features of the system’s outputs. Also, we created an installation 
where the audience can observe the autonomous performance of the 
system, generating content sequentially based on a set of random inputs. 
The primary purpose of this installation is to create a space of reflection 
about the potential advantages and disadvantages of CD techniques to auto-
mate design practices. The work presented in this appendix is partially 
based on the M.Sc. dissertations of José N. Rebelo (2020) from the 
Design and Multimedia programme of the Faculty of Sciences and Tech-
nology of University of Coimbra. The following sections detail the gener-
ative approach, the development of the refinement interface and the exper-
iments conducted.
F.1 APPROACH
This system automatically creates web pages from content retrieved online 
from Wikipedia. The content is selected based on a user input term, which 
is searched and queried via the MediaWiki API.2 Users can optionally modify 
the retrieved content before the generation process begins. The generation 
of web pages involves two key sequential stages: (i) content analysis; 
and (ii) styling.
The generation process initiates when the user inputs a search 
term into an interaction form (see Figure F.1a). After clicking the “search” 
button, the system performs content analysis by querying the API to

COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
retrieve and display the resulting data (see Figure F.1b). Users can edit the 
gathered data, and once they are satisfied, they submit it for further anal-
ysis. This analysis includes recognising emotional and semantic data within 
the content (see Figure F.1c). Next, it employs content styling methods to 
define the visual styles and render the web page. This process uses an 
expert strategy combined with stochastic and template methods. Once 
the page has been generated, users may fine-tune the output by adjusting its 
visual features through a dedicated interface, allowing them to customise 
the design according to their preferences (see Figure F.1 d). Figure F.2 
presents some output pages created with this system. 
F.1 .1 CONTENT ANAL YSIS
The content analysis stage involves retrieving site content and performing 
an analysis of the content. The process starts by retrieving online content 
based on a user-input text search in the Wikimedia API. Subsequently, the 
search result is presented to the user in a specific editable interface, allowing 
them to make any desired edits. Once users are satisfied, they can proceed 
to submit the content for automatic web page generation.
The content analysis process begins by counting the frequency 
of words and the HTML tags in the content. Following that, it preprocesses 
the text for analysis, which involves several steps: removing HTML ele-
ments such as hyperlinks, section markers, tags, and inline styles; expanding 
contractions; converting all words to lowercase; and removing non -alpha-
betical and special characters. Following this, it identifies and corrects any 
spelling mistakes and, finally, removes stop words.
Afterwards, a lexicon-based approach is used to recognise the colours 
most related to the content. This involves searching the content tokens 
against a word-colour lexicon developed by Saif Mohammad (2012a). This

F05 APPENDIX  F BRUT ALIST  WEBSITE  GENERA TOR
lexicon associates content with 11 colours: black; blue; brown; green; grey; 
orange; purple; pink; red; white; and yellow. The results of the analysis are 
then used in the content styling stage to define the visual features of the 
website. In the end, the presented analysis provides five key data points: 
(i) the frequency of words in the content; (ii) the usage frequencies 
of HTML tags within the content; and (iii) the identification of colours 
associated with the content and the intensity of these associations. In the 
implementation of this analysis, we  used HTML technologies, Node.js,  
and the NLP.js toolkit.
F . 1.2 CONTENT STYLING
In the content styling stage, the web page is generated using the data col-
lected in the semantic analysis. The styling process is composed of three 
stages. First, the main typographic and visual features of the content are 
defined based on the analysis. Next, a set of styling functions is determined 
to be applied to the content. Finally, a web page structure is selected, and 
the page is generated.
Initially, the content is placed on the web page using OpenType 
Variable Fonts (OTVF), adjusting its features based on the data from the 
analysis. We have chosen a set of four available typefaces: Bandeins,3 Hela,4 
Movement,5 and Recursive. 6 One typeface is randomly selected from this 
collection. The weight of each word is determined by its frequency,  with 
more frequent words being typeset in a bolder style. The boldest word is 
the most frequently occurring word in the text, while lighter weights are 
used for less frequent words. The remaining typeface characteristics are 
defined at random within the specified ranges for each axis.
The background colour is randomly selected from the five most 
associated with the content. The remaining colours are used for typography 
in different sections of the page. Next, the system defines the size of the 
page by setting the width of the main container according to the number 
of words in the text, with a narrower container for fewer words. The 
margins of the container are randomly assigned. We established the colour 
values for all 11 colours in advance.
Then, the system selects a set of styling functions to apply to the 
content sequentially. We have developed eight of these functions with the 
intent of enhancing the interactive experience and increasing the diversity 
of results. These functions can be combined, with a minimum of one and 
a maximum of five being used in each instance. The selection of styling

The first function, named hideCommonWords, places a pink rectangle 
over the most common words in the content, hiding them (see Figure F.3a). 
The second function, modifyTextPosition, randomly selects a different 
text direction (left to right or right to left) and writing mode (horizontal

oriented upright, allowing it to be typeset vertically (see Figure F.3b).

across the page. To prevent excessive overlap, the placement of the text 
is restricted to quarters of the page width. The function randomly decides 
how many times the text will be repeated, with a range from 1 to 3 repeti-
tions (see Figure F.3c).

F07 APPENDIX  F BRUT ALIST  WEBSITE  GENERA TOR
The fourth function, interactiveSplit, overlays four copies of the 
content and generates a random rectangular mask for each. Users can 
interactively adjust the mask  size based on their mouse position, with 
increments and directions determined randomly (see Figure F.3d). 
The perspectiveCards function divides the content using the secondary 
headline tags (h2) and arranges the sections horizontally to create the 
illusion of a three-dimensional web page space. This function alters the 
perspective and angle of the containers based on their horizontal position 
on the page. Containers farther from the top of the page are presented as 
if they are positioned further back. This function also allows users to 
interactively scroll within this simulated three -dimensional space, adjusting 
the position and aspect of the containers and simulating a camera move-
ment (see Figure F.3e).
The sixth function, randomStyle, divides the text into sections based 
on h2 tags and randomly modifies some of these sections’ visual and layout 
features. Modifications include changing border size and style, selecting 
different colours for the background and typography, and randomly adjusting 
margins and paddings (see Figure F.3f). 
Following the same section division, the overlapSections function 
places the sections in containers at random locations on the page. Users 
can uncover hidden sections by clicking on the page and dragging the most 
visible section to different positions (see Figure F.3g). 
Finally, the eighth function, distortCommonWords, targets the most 
frequently occurring word in the content and applies a liquid distortion 
effect to them. The extent of distortion varies according to the mouse’s 
vertical position (see Figure F.3h).
These content styling options are exclusively applied when the result 
is a Wikipedia article. However, if the API returns a disambiguation page,7 
it is directly formatted using the perspectiveCards function without needing 
prior text analysis (see Figure F.3e).
In the final stage of styling, we applied placement rules based on 
the primary styles and predetermined styling functions. We have empiri-
cally developed 16 default sets of rules that define the initial basic placement 
features, including the headlines’ default appearance, the position of the 
first section, and the default margins and paddings of elements. This process 
uses standard web technologies and the JavaScript library blotter.js for 
shader implementation.
F .2 REFINEMENT INTERFACE
After generating the brutalist website, the output is displayed with a special 
header component at the top of the page. This component allows users to 
refine certain design features by opening the “refine” tab through the 
“controls” button. Figure F.4 displays the refinement tab. The header also 
provides access to additional project information and a gallery of previously 
created websites (see Figure F.5).

This interface allows users to adjust various aspects of the website. 
Specifically, users can adjust the colour and typography. For colour adjust-
ments, users can change the main typography colour and the background 
colour. For typography, users can customise the main font size and adjust 
the default values of the typeface axes used on the web page.
F .2. 1 EVALUA TION
We conducted a preliminary evaluation of the system’s outputs to assess 
its ability to generate distinctive and diverse outputs in terms of visual 
and interactivity. Furthermore, in this evaluation, we aimed to gain insights 
into the applicability of these outputs in web design. To this end, we carried 
out a survey with 33 participants in which we presented various outputs 
and collected quantitative data regarding the participants’ perceptions 
of them.
The testing sessions were organised into four stages. Participants 
observed a set of system outputs in the first three stages and then com-
pleted a survey. The goal was to study the diversity and distinctiveness of 
results from the same and different content. In the first (S1) and second 
stages (S2), participants viewed five outputs created using the same input 
terms, “joker” and “mercury,” respectively. The main aim was to observe 
if the results differed when the same content was used and to determine 
if the results changed with different terms. In the third stage (S3), we

assessed the system’s ability to create diversity with different content. 
Participants reviewed five outputs, each generated from a different input: 
“joker”, “mercury”, “Seneca the Younger,” “fire,” and “pizza.” The five 
terms used were defined randomly.
The survey contained three questions, with responses rated on 
a five-point scale, where 1 means “not agree” and 5 means “totally agree.” 
The first question (Q1) asked, “Do you find the result distinctive from what 
you currently see in contemporary web design?”. The second question 
(Q2) asked, “Are the generated outputs suitable for use in other contexts 
and content?”. The third question (Q3) asked, “Are the outputs visually 
diverse?”. Then, in the last stage (S4), we invited participants to provide 
their “comments and suggestions for future improvements.”
The participant group consisted of individuals aged between 18 and 40 
years, with the majority of participants (17, 51.5 %) in the 25 to 30 age range. 
Participants were selected through personal invitations and social media 
posts, and they responded to the survey online. We aimed to create a diverse 
testing group, including professional designers who could use the system 
to automate aspects of their daily work and individuals from other fields 
who might use the system to create web pages. Thus, most participants (17, 
51.5 %) were designers, while the remaining participants came from various 
fields of study, including Architecture, Medicine, Sociology, and others. The 
chart in Figure F.6 provides a summary of the profile of the participants in 
this evaluation. The data collected during the testing sessions is available 
at https://pf.dei.uc.pt/F/eval (visited:7 July 2025). Tables F.1 to F.3 summa-
rise the results of the first three stages.

Regarding the distinctiveness of the results compared to the current 
web design scenario (Q1), the average responses indicate that participants 
find the outputs distinctive (with a minimum average and median score 
of 4.00 across all stages). In each evaluation stage, over 70% of participants  
(S1: 28, S2: 25, S3: 24) rated the outputs as at least distinctive (4), with 
more than 42.4% (S1: 15, S2: 14, S3: 14) rating them as very distinctive (5).
Although the outputs generated for the same term (S1 and S2 stages) 
were perceived as slightly more distinctive, the difference between stages 
is minimal. In all evaluation stages, participants did not find the outputs 
distinctive in only three cases. We did not observe significant differences 
between the two profiles of participants. However, we noted that designers 
(d) tended to rate the results as very distinctive (5) more frequently than 
non-designers (n).

Regarding the potential use of the generated outputs with other content 
and in different contexts (Q2), participants were asked to classify the nature 
of the results as either exploratory (not suitable to use in other contexts) 
or suitable (possible to be employed in other contexts). The results indi-
cate that most participants consider the system outputs to be exploratory 
and cannot be directly used in other contexts and scenarios. The average 
classification is around 2 (exploratory) for all tested sets. 
In the first stage (S1), approximately 72.7 % of participants found 
the results to be very exploratory (11, 33.3 %) or exploratory (13, 39.4 %). 
Similarly, in the second stage (S2), 66.4 % of participants considered the 
results to be very exploratory (36.4 %, 12) or exploratory (27.3 %, 9). The 
outputs in the third stage (S3) received the highest approval for imple-
mentation. The most common selected option was that the outputs were 
neither exploratory nor suitable (11, 33.3%). Nevertheless, about half of 
the participants rated the results as very exploratory (8, 24.2 %) or explor-
atory (9, 27.3 %). We noted that non-designers tend to perceive the outputs 
as more suitable results compared to designers.
In all stages, when asked about the visual diversity of the outputs 
(Q3), the majority of the participants (over 75.8 % in all evaluation stages) 
considered the outputs to be visually diverse, whether for generating the 
same content (S1 and S2) or different contents (S3). In the first and third 
stages, the most frequently selected option was the one indicating that

In the final stage (S4), only three participants provided comments. 
Two of them noted that the approach has the potential to be used as an 
exploratory tool. The third comment suggests enhancing the system by 
integrating other types of media elements.
F .3 INST ALLA TION 
We created an artwork that uses the developed system to automatically 
generate brutalist websites from random inputs. Presented as an installa-
tion, this artwork invites the audience to observe the autonomous web 
page generation in real time. The main goal of this installation is to create 
a reflective space where viewers can contemplate the potential advantages 
and disadvantages of CD techniques for automating design development 
and their impact on our future consumption of information. By showcasing 
this work, we aim to stimulate a broader conversation about the role of 
computational GD systems in automatically customising visual and inter-
active design elements.
The installation displays the system running automatically, presented 
either as a projection or on a computer screen. Throughout the installation 
time, the system continuously generates websites, pausing for a few minutes 
(between two and four) between each generation. During these intervals, 
the system automatically scrolls through the website and performs several 
clicks to simulate user interaction. The words used for generating the 
content are randomly selected from a predefined list.8 
This installation was featured in three exhibitions: Future Vision 
(J. N. Rebelo et al., 2021b), Contingency (J. N. Rebelo et al., 2021a, see Figure 
F.7) in Aveiro, Portugal, and {Between} (J. N. Rebelo et al., 2021, see Figure 
F.8) in Coimbra, Portugal.

F.4 FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS
We presented a web page generator that explores an expert strategy 
to create brutalist web pages, extending our investigation to digital GD. 
The proposed system extracts content from Wikipedia based on a text 
string provided by the user. Nevertheless, users can modify the retrieved 
content before it is generated. The web page generation process involves 
two main stages: content analysis and styling.
The content analysis stage involves recognising semantic data within 
the content, such as word frequency and tag use. Also, a lexicon-based 
approach identifies colours associated with the content. The content styling 
stage incorporates the analysis results to define the output’s visual, typo-
graphic, and interactive features. This modification was carried out using 
styling functions. The final web page is generated using predefined sets 
of rules, style functions, and features based on the analysis. Users can 
further refine the generated output through a dedicated parametric inter-
face, which allows for adjustments to colour and typography.
We conducted preliminary evaluation experiments to assess the 
system’s outputs and potential, involving both designers and non-designers. 
The evaluation focuses on whether the system produces distinctive, final-
ised, and visually diverse outputs. Participants observed and interacted 
with outputs during the evaluation and then completed a survey.
The preliminary results indicate that the system produced visually 
distinctive and diverse outputs. However, most participants view the 
outputs as exploratory and not directly suitable for use, mainly due to their 
exploratory aesthetic and interactions. Our experimentation also indicates 
that stochastic methods allow for the introduction of visual variation. 
Thus, findings reveal the potential of this system to facilitate and automate 
the exploration of new visual and interactive possibilities in the realm of 
Web Design.
Furthermore, we experimented with this system to create an auto-
matic setup, which was presented as a design installation that sequentially 
generated outputs based on random inputs. This experimentation displays 
the system’s automation capabilities, which we consider creates a space 
for reflecting on the benefits and limitations of using CD techniques 
to automate design practices and shaping our future interactions.
Figure F.8. The system at the {Between} 
exhibition, running on the second 
computer from the right. 2021.

F13 APPENDIX  F BRUT ALIST  WEBSITE  GENERA TOR
Our findings suggest that computational methods can be effectively 
employed to create web designs. The expert  strategy indicated that the 
CD could be explored to automate GD processes, including visual and 
interactive design discovery tasks. However, our preliminary evaluation 
of this system’s outputs shows that they are only sometimes applicable 
and require further refinement. To address this, we have integrated an inter-
face that allows for design modifications, although it still offers limited 
control over visual features. 
Nevertheless, we consider that this integration allows for the inclu-
sion of customised elements in web designs, enhancing their overall quality 
and adaptability.

D02
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
This appendix presents our work on the computational generation of face 
images, particularly the design and conceptualisation of the interactive 
installation Portraits of No One. Although this work falls outside the direct 
scope of this thesis, it directly influences the generative approach explored 
in the namesake online artwork. This online artwork explores the inter -
section of computational generation processes in digital media, as detailed in 
Section 10.2. By including this information in the appendix, we provide 
readers a comprehensive description of the generative processes behind 
the generation of artificial face designs as well as the design and develop-
ment of physical installation at the Portuguese National Museum of Con-
temporary Art (NMAC) — Museu do Chiado in Lisbon, Portugal, (2019), 
in the context of the SONAE Media Art Award 2019, and the Círculo de 
Artes Plásticas de Coimbra (CAPC), Portugal (2021). The content of this 
appendix is based on the article The X-Faces Behind the Portraits of No One 
by João Correia et al. (2021).

D03 APPENDIX  G PORTRAITS  OF  NO ONE
G PORTRAITS OF NO ONE
This appendix presents the design and development of Portraits of No One, 
an interactive installation exploring the generation of photorealistic arti-
ficial images. This work explores the recent advances in Artificial Intelli-
gence (AI) and Computer Vision (CV) to present a method for seamlessly 
creating photorealistic facial imagery through recombining or blending 
different facial components.
This installation is built upon the previously developed generative 
design system, X-Faces (Correia et al., 2016, 2019). This system is capable 
of generating new face imagery examples recombining other existing faces. 
This process employs CV and Computer Graphics (CG) techniques to facil-
itate the automatic recombination, or exchange, of the facial parts, including 
eyebrows, eyes, noses, and mouths, from pre-existing face images. This gen-
erative system has demonstrated its effectiveness when integrated with 
an automated fitness function evolutionary approach for producing realise 
composite faces which challenge the face classifiers (Correia et al., 2016) 
and performs data augmentation on face detection datasets, contributing 
to improving classifiers’ performance (Correia et al., 2019).
We explored the capabilities of the developed approach within the 
context of new media art by developing the present interactive Media Art 
installation, Portraits of No One (Martins et al., 2019, 2020). This installation 
generates and displays portraits of human faces by recombining the facial 
parts that are retrieved from the faces of its audience (see Figure G.1). 
Additionally, the installation generates and plays crowd noise as ambient 
audio based on captured sound inputs from the audience.1 Whenever users 
interact with the installation, they will immediately see parts of their inputs 
becoming part of the ever-changing portraits that are projected on the 
walls and ambient sound. In a way, one could say that the installation feeds 
on the faces of people who interact with it. 
The photorealism of the portraits makes the audience question them-
selves about the boundary between reality and what they are seeing, which 
is located somewhere on the borderline between the real and artificial. This 
installation was designed for the Sonae Media Art Award 2019,2 selected as a 
finalist artwork, and exhibited at the MNAC in Lisbon, Portugal, from 28 
November 2020 to 2 February 2021. More recently, a new version of this 
installation was featured as a solo exhibition at Edifício Sede gallery of CAPC, 
in Coimbra, Portugal, from 24 April to 19 June 2021.3 For further documen-
tation, information, and news clipping about the Portraits of No One consult 
https://cdv.dei.uc.pt/projects/portraits-of-no-one (visited: 7 July 2025).

D04
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
The next section provides an overview of related work, covering 
both the computational generation of human face images and the use of 
generated faces in visual art. The third section presents our approach to 
generating face images. The fourth section outlines the application of the 
presented approach to create interactive media art installations. The last 
section presents our conclusions and outlines directions for future work.
G .1 RELA TED WORK
This work focuses on computationally generating human faces for various 
purposes. These include studying related work on computational creation 
of face images and using artificially generated human faces in creative 
visual artworks, particularly in New Media and Digital Art.
G. 1. 1 COMPUT A TIONAL GENERA TION OF FACE IMAGES
The computational generation of new face image instances has been using 
various generic image processing techniques, including simple transfor -
mations, like rotation, scale, flip horizontally or vertically, as well as more 
complex operations, such as adding noise, filters, or distortions (Krizhevsky 
et al., 2017). Nevertheless, most of these works do not exploit knowledge of 
the underlying problem domain to generate new instances (Masi et al., 2016).
However, our review has identified a set of approaches that take 
advantage of domain-specific knowledge. For instance, Dalong Jiang et al. 
(2005) proposed a three-dimensional reconstruction methodology to 
create face images in different poses, illuminations, and expressions. Hoda 
Mohammadzade and Dimitrios Hatzinakos (2013) explored subspace 
projection techniques to generate new facial expressions. Seyyede Z. Seyyed-
salehi and Seyyed A. Seyyedsalehi (2014) used a Deep Neural Network (DNN) 
Figure G.1. The environment 
of the installation Portraits of No One 
at MNAC (2019) during the installation 
start-up. Photography by José Paulo Ruas /
DGPC 2019.

D05 APPENDIX  G PORTRAITS  OF  NO ONE
approach to extract expression, pose, and identity information from a 
collection of face images captured under unconstrained conditions, allowing 
the generation of new faces based on an input image. Similarly, Yuval 
Nirkin et al. (2018) used a DNN for face swapping under unconstrained 
conditions to create new face images and improve the base model on 
face recognition.
More recently, Jiang-Jing Lv et al. (2017) introduced face augmen-
tation algorithms that involve landmark perturbation and synthesis methods 
to generate face images with variations in glasses, haircuts, poses, and 
illuminations. Their study also demonstrated that models trained with 
these generated face images achieve a similar performance compared to 
deep models trained with larger datasets. Furthermore, the introduction of 
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) enables the generation of high-res-
olution images based on several datasets, including faces (Karras et al., 
2019, 2020). One of the most notable deployments of this model is the 
This Person Does Not Exist project (Wang, 2019), which showcases photo-
realistic faces generated using the StyleGAN approach. These GANs produce 
impressive results, but their use and training remain computationally 
expensive and challenging to control.
In parallel, certain works employ Evolutionary Computation (EC) to 
generate new face images by employing the outputs of face classifiers to 
assign fitness to the generated images. Jie Chen et al. (2007) used a Genetic 
Algorithm (GA) to generate faces, with individual encodings represented 
as vectors of integers denoting pixel intensity values, while variation 
operators consisted of image filters. On the other hand, Penousal Machado 
et al. (2012) used Genetic Programming (GP) to evolve images that do not 
contain faces, aiming to enhance the performance of face classifiers.
G. 1.2 ARTIFICIAL FACES IN VISUAL ART
Visual arts widely explored portraiture, and the human face was a subject 
of study. In the context of new media arts, this subject is mainly explored 
through the exploration of video capturing and face detection techniques. 
Early media artwork addressing this subject includes, for instance, the 
installations Video Narcissus by Jeffrey Shaw (1987, see Figure G.2) or Sol-
itary by Simon Biggs (1992). With the recent advancements in CV methods, 
these kinds of tools have gained popularity in the realm of the arts.
Several artists have explored CV to create interactive artistic expe-
riences that involve using audience inputs to create artworks. The inter -
active installation Reface by Golan Levin and Zachary Lieberman (2007, 
see Figure G.3) generates group portraits of its audience by grouping video 
excerpts of the mouths, eyes and eyebrows of different people who interact 
with the installation. People can interact with the artwork using eye blinks. 
Similarly, Sarah Howorka (2015) developed a digital mirror that displays 
the average face of all individuals who have stood in front of the installation. 
Sameh Al Tawil (2019) presented the installation IDEMixer, which gener-
ates live portraits by blending pairs of faces captured by two different 
Figure G.2. Video Narcissus. Jeffrey Shaw. 
1987. © Jeffrey Shaw. 

D06
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
cameras. H. Cecilia Suhr (2019) presented the interactive multimedia 
performance I, You, We in which the audience is invited to take photos. 
These photographs are then combined with each other and other visuals 
in a live video that plays in the background. Simultaneously, the performer 
improvises with a violin or a cello to change the video’s colours.
Other artworks explore facial input and computational technologies 
to create innovative ways for the audience to interact with the artwork and 
each other. The installation Sharing Faces by Kyle McDonald (2013) acts as 
a mirror connecting Anyang, South Korea, and Yamaguchi, Japan. It tracks 
users’ facial expressions in one location and mirrors them in real-time with 
those of individuals who interacted with the installation in the other loca-
tion. Karen Lancel et al. (2019) developed the installation Saving Face, an 
artwork realised in multiple geographies between 2012 and 2016. This 
installation blends portraits of users and displays them on public screens, 
with the intensity of blending determined by the number of “take care” 
gestures made by users on their faces. Rafael Lozano-Hemmer (2015) 
designed the interactive installation Level of Confidence, which employs 
a face recognition system trained to find similarities between a given face 
and the faces of forty-three students who disappeared during a cartel-related 
kidnapping in Iguala, Mexico, in 2014. When users stand in front of the instal-
lation, it captures their faces and reveals the most similar students and 
the accuracy of the match. Antonio Daniele (2016) created This is Not Private, 
in which facial features of the audience slowly merge with the face of a 
person being interviewed on a video at the exhibition.
Alternatively, some artworks focus on developing and exhibiting 
portraits of artificial people. The series Portraits of Imaginary People of Mika 
Tyka (2017) presents a series of portraits generated with a GAN trained 
with thousands of photos of human faces. João Martinho Moura and Paulo 
Ferreira-Lopes (2017) explored the creation of imagined faces, which 
resemble ghost faces, based on false-positive detections of visual random-
ness. Mario Klingemann (2018) developed the Neural Glitch technique 
involving the random manipulation of GANs’ trained weights to generate 
new images, including artificial portraits (see Figure G.4).
Contemporary methods for the generation of artificial faces pre-
dominantly rely on DNNs and GANs. While these approaches can produce 
photorealistic results, they are computationally intensive and time-
-consuming when it comes to training models that provide control over 
the generated faces. Consequently, they have not been appropriate for gen-
erating face images in the context of participatory media art, which demands 
the real-time creation of photorealistic faces using an ever-changing 
dataset of face examples. The presented X-Faces system (Correia et al., 2016, 
2019) addresses the generation of faces by automatically recombining 
facial parts from previous existing faces, which results in a faster, scalable, 
and less expensive approach. Therefore, this system offers a suitable 
approach for computationally creating facial portraits in participatory 
Media Art installations.

D07 APPENDIX  G PORTRAITS  OF  NO ONE
G.2 X‑FACES: GENERA TING FACES
The X-Faces system was aimed to meet the following requirements: (i) auto-
matically generate a large number of photorealistic faces, and (ii) maintain 
control over the generative process of the composite faces to expand the 
set of face composites rapidly. As far as we know, existing approaches are 
not able to deliver on these requirements. Therefore, João Correia et al.  
(2016, 2019) developed a computational system that creates photorealistic 
face images by assembling parts from existing examples. The system gen-
erates new faces by performing the following steps: (i) decomposition 
of facial parts from multiple images; (ii)  assembly of composite images 
from the separated facial parts; and (iii) exploration of different face 
composite images. The processes incorporate various techniques, including 
CV, CG, and Machine Learning (ML). 
G.2. 1 FACE DECOMPOSITION
To generate new faces from a dataset of face images, we employed a face 
detector and landmark classifier to extract essential data. These data 
included facial landmark points and head pose information for each face 
found in the dataset. The process for each image in the input dataset 
is detailed in João Correia et al. (2019) and comprises the following steps. 
First, it uses a pretrained face detector to identify potential face regions 
within the image. This detector observes the image, locates faces, and pro-
vides information about their positions and sizes. Second, we employed 
a pretrained facial landmark predictor inside each detected face region. 
This predictor positions a sequence of 68 points along the contours of 
various facial structures, including the jaw, eyebrows, nose, eyes, and mouth. 
Finally, after obtaining the landmark points, we used them to estimate 
the head pose, which defines the orientation of the face in space. In the 
end, we save to file the following data (i) facial landmark points, (ii) pose 
information, and (iii) the image path. The result of the stage is a set of files, 
with one file for each face found in the input dataset. As a result, the dataset 
only needs to be preprocessed once, regardless of the number of new 
instances to be generated.
G.2.2 ASSEMBL Y OF COMPOSITE IMAGES
With the facial landmarks and poses calculated for all faces within the input 
dataset, new instances can be generated. The process of creating a new 
face instance involves selecting a face from the dataset and then replacing 
its elementary parts (eyebrows, eyes, nose, and mouth) with parts from 
other faces. Consequently, each new face consists of a recombination, 
or a blend, of different faces. However, the automatic recombination 
of facial parts, particularly in an unconstrained environment, requires 
special care with their alignment to attain natural and seamless facial 
blends. The process of generating a new face instance is schematised 
in Figure G.5.

D08
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
The data extracted during the preprocessing of the input dataset 
begins the generation process by randomly choosing one face among all the 
preprocessed faces. This face becomes our target face, i.e. the face whose 
parts will be replaced with others from other faces. Next, we randomly 
select one additional face for each part we want to replace. These faces 
will be our source faces, i.e. the faces that will provide the parts to be 
blended into the target. The selection of the source faces is performed 
by considering the pose of the selected target face. That is, the source faces 
must possess a head pose like that of the target face.
Before blending parts of the source faces onto the target face, it first 
aligns each source with the target, more specifically, the facial landmarks 
of each source with the landmarks of the target. Since we know the position

D09 APPENDIX  G PORTRAITS  OF  NO ONE
of the 68 landmark points in the faces (Figure G.5a), we can use this infor-
mation to warp each source to match the target. To achieve this, the system 
uses OpenCV 4 to compute the Delaunay triangulation of each face, using 
specific points of its landmarks, as well as a few additional points, such 
as two points on both sides of the nose and six points above the eyebrow, 
which are calculated relative to the landmarks (see Figure G.5b). The Delaunay 
triangulation divides each face image into triangles (see Figure G.5c). These 
resulting triangles correspond to facial regions in both the source and target 
faces, and we can identify which triangle in a source face corresponds 
to a triangle in the target face (see Figure G.5f). The next step involves 
warping each source face triangle to match the corresponding triangle 
in the target face. We use OpenCV  to calculate the affine transform for 
each source face triangle, which maps its vertices to the vertices of the cor-
responding triangle in the target face. This affine transform is then used 
to transform the pixels within the source face inside the triangle (before 
transforming) to the target face. The result is source faces that have been 
transformed to achieve a complete alignment with the target face (see 
Figure G.5e).
Once each source face is aligned with the target face, the subsequent 
step is to blend them in a natural fashion. To achieve this, it employs 
the seamless cloning algorithm provided by OpenCV , based on work by 
Patrick Perez et al. (2003). This algorithm enables us to seamlessly copy 
a region from each warped source face and place it onto the target image, 
creating a new photorealistic face. To delineate the regions of the warped 
source faces that should be blended into the target face, it creates masks 
that delimit the different facial parts: left eyebrow, right eyebrow, left eye, 
right eye, nose, and mouth (see Figure G.5f). It computes the specific 
vertices of the Delaunay triangles to calculate the mask of each facial part. 
Each mask includes a margin, which causes the mask to contain a larger 
area than the one defined by the vertices used to create it. The purpose 
of this margin is to expand the area of each shape to cover some skin 
around each facial part, which is helpful for the smooth assemblage of 
parts to generate new faces. The outcome of this process is a composite 
face image that combines different facial parts from various source images.
G.3  PORTRAITS OF NO ONE:  
INTERACTIVEL Y GENERA TING FACES 
We explored the creative capabilities of the X-Faces system in the interac-
tive Media Art installation Portraits of No One. This installation employs 
the generative process outlined in the previous section to create and exhibit 
photorealistic artificial portraits based on the captured facial features 
of the audience. As a result, the installation can invoke the capabilities 
of AI to generate content that makes people question the veracity of what 
they are observing.

D10
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
This installation was initially conceptualised and designed for the 
Sonae Media Art Award 2019, where it was selected as a finalist artwork. 
As a result, it was exhibited at the MNAC in Lisbon, Portugal. During 
this exhibition, from late November 2019 to early February 2020, the cap-
turing box was used about 5,000 times. The installation’s environment 
is depicted in Figure G.6.
The room of the installation at MNAC was tailor-made for the purpose, 
measuring six meters in length and four meters in width. The installation 
space was divided into an input area and an output area. The input area, 
located near the entrance to the room, contains the capturing box attached 
to one side of a pillar. The capturing box allows the audience to capture 
their faces and, this way, feed the installation. The output area was located 
at the back of the room, following the input area, and it encompassed an 
immersive video projection of 12 meters wide on three walls. This projec-
tion contains an array of portraits that are continuously generated by the 
installation. Each portrait is displayed in a size that is like a real face. This 
area also included a speaker attached to the ceiling of the room that repro-
duces an intertwined combination of sounds recorded during the users’ 
interactions with the capturing box. This audio promotes the creation of 
a more lifelike and reflective environment for the installation, resembling 
crowd noise, where only a few words create a sensation that the portraits 
are engaging in conversation with one another. This sonic environment 
fosters the viewers to engage with the identities embodied by the artificial 
portraits they see on the walls of the installation.
A typical user interaction with the installation unfolds as follows: 
(i) people enter the installation space; (ii) people approach the capturing 
box and observe their face on the screen in a mirror-like fashion; (iii) if 
the system recognises their face, the button turns white and blinks rapidly; 
otherwise, the button remains red and blinks slowly; (iv) when the button 
is white and the reflected image pleases the participants, they press 
the button to capture the face; (v) a countdown of three seconds begins 
and then the face is captured; (vi) the capturing box pauses for a couple 
of seconds to avoid frequent captures and the button turns off until a new 
face can be captured; and, finally, (vii) users steps into the output area 
to see new portraits being generated using their facial features.

D11 APPENDIX  G PORTRAITS  OF  NO ONE
More recently, the Portraits of No One installation was featured 
at CAPC between April 2021 and June 2021 in the Edíficio Sede gallery. 5 
In this presentation, the installation occupies all three rooms of the two-floor 
gallery. The ground floor space was conceptualised as the input area, while 
the first floor was the output area. Given the circumstances of the COVID-19 
pandemic, a human assistant captured photographs. The ground floor area 
comprises two rooms. The first room houses a capturing box (see Figure 
G.7a). Participants need to ask the assistant to operate the capturing box 
to take a photograph. The sound capture is automated trigged by the sound 
detection. In the other ground floor room, the audience can view two real 
photographs of participants of the installation, selected randomly based 
on novelty (see Figure G.7b). On the first floor, people can visualise the 
resulting artificial environmental audio and portraits on two adjacent walls 
(see Figure G.7c).
In this version of the installation, the typical interaction proceeds 
as follows: (i) visitors enter the gallery and request an assistant to take 
their picture; (ii) the assistant takes a picture, and the sound is automat -
ically captured; (iii) participants move to another room to view their 
picture along with pictures of other participants; (iv) people then goes 
to the output area, on the first floor, to observe new portraits being gen -
erated using their facial features.
The development of this installation required both hardware and soft-
ware components. The computer serves as the core component of this 
installation, connecting all hardware and software parts of the installation 
as well as managing the inputs (i.e. the people’s faces and their interaction 
sound) and outputs ( i.e. the array of portraits and the ambient sound). 
We also use a microcontroller to allow the computer to communicate with 
hardware contained in the capturing devices and to trigger some software 
events using this hardware. The following subsections comprehensively 
describe the installation’s hardware and software.
G.3. 1 HARDWARE
The installation’s hardware is responsible for gathering data from the audi-
ence, displaying audiovisual outputs generated by the installation’s system, 
and providing feedback to the participants. Figure G.8 presents the main 
hardware components and their data flow.
Figure G.7. Different rooms of the 
installation Portraits of No One at CAPC. 
From left to right: (a) capturing room; 
(b) input visualisation room; 
and (c) output room.

D12
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
People interact with the system in the input area, which is equipped 
with the necessary hardware to collect the data from the people for the instal-
lation to operate. These data include the images of users’ faces and the 
sounds produced by users during their interaction. In the first version 
of the installation, the input area presents a capturing box that integrates 
several pieces of hardware, including a video camera to capture the faces, 
an LED ring that encircles the camera to provide even illumination with 
few shadows visible in the captured faces, an LCD display to offers par -
ticipants a live preview of their faces before capturing, a microphone 
to record some seconds of audio during each interaction, and a pushbutton 
with an RGB LED that allows participants to trigger the face capturing 
while providing colour-coded feedback. The video camera and the LED 
ring were situated on the top of the display, while the microphone was posi-
tioned beside the video camera, oriented forward to pick up sounds pro-
duced in front of the capturing box. The push button is located at the bottom 
of the screen.
In the second version of the installation, we reconfigured the cap-
turing box to occupy the entire room space while keeping the same hard-
ware components. The microphone is now positioned on the floor of 
the room to continuously capture ambient sounds, only recording when 
the detected sound amplitude exceeds a predefined threshold. Two cus-
tom-made external light boxes have replaced the LED ring that was part 
of the capturing box. We have also integrated a Raspberry PI micro-com-
puter to manage the photos taken by a web camera and incorporated an 
external button for capturing images. This revised capturing box also offers 
the flexibility to adjust its height as needed. Also, it presents a screen to 
inform the assistant if the gathered picture is valid.
The installation employs video projectors and one loudspeaker 
to create an ever-changing audio-visual environment consisting of images 
of generated portraits and ambient sounds generated from data collected 
from the audience. In the first version of the installation, three video 
projectors were attached to the ceiling of the room, each facing a different 
wall, to create a single continuous projection. This resulted in a surrounding 
video projection spanning 12 meters wide on three walls, with a total image 
size of 5760 by 1080 pixels. Alternatively, we create a different audiovisual 
environment in the second version when we present the portraits on two

G.3.2 SOFTWARE
The installation software is developed in Java and relies on open-source 
libraries Processing, OpenCV and Dlib.6 We also use Max for sound recording, 
processing, and playback. In the first version, communication between 
the computer and other hardware is facilitated by an Arduino Uno micro-
controller, while in the CAPC version, a Raspberry PI 4 microcomputer is 
used for this purpose
This functionality is achieved through the utilisation of off-the-shelf 
solutions from the OpenCV and Dlib libraries. These libraries enable the anal-
ysis of each frame of the video camera feed, facilitating the detection 
of people’s faces and their facial landmarks when positioned in front of 
the capturing box. In the context of this work, we require neutral frontal 
poses for the portraits. This is not only advantageous to the accurate 
extraction of the facial features but also to ensure visual coherence between 
different portraits. To achieve this, we implemented a set of detection 
filters that determine whether a detected face should be considered valid. 
The system necessitates explicitly neutral frontal poses for the portraits. 
This requirement enhances the accuracy of facial feature extraction and 
ensures visual consistency across different portraits. To enforce this con-
dition, a series of detection filters have been implemented to  determine 
the validity of a detected face.
When more than one valid detection occurs, the system focuses on 
one face based on two preference criteria: (i) faces horizontally centred in 
the captured image and (ii) faces with large bounds. The area used to gen-
erate a new portrait is the boundary box of the detected face with a certain 
margin. The aspect ratio of the crop rectangle is always 3 : 4 (vertical). 
The size and position of the rectangle are determined in relation to the 
detected facial landmarks. This way, we ensure the faces shown in the por-
