D14
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
traits are always roughly aligned with each other. In the capturing box 
in the MNAC, when a valid detection occurs, a rectangle around the face 
is drawn on the live preview shown on the screen. In addition to drawing 
a rectangle around the valid face detection, the system also invites the user 
to capture the face by pressing the push button. In the second version, 
a message is presented to the assistant, indicating that a face is detected.
Upon pressing the capture button, the system initiates a three-second 
countdown. When the countdown ends, the system captures the face 
and saves the related data needed to generate new portraits. The count -
down timer was presented to both the participants (displayed near the video 
camera) and to the assistant (presented on the information screen). Addi-
tionally, in the first iteration of the installation, the system turns off the LED 
of the push button for a brief period until a new face can be captured. This 
feature is part of a delay mechanism we implemented to prevent excessive 
photos from being taken in quick succession.
The installation continuously generates and displays new artificial 
faces in the output area. To accomplish this, we use the X-Faces generative 
system to create artificial faces from the facial features extracted from users’ 
faces (see Section G.2). Thus, captured face images are passed to the X-Faces 
system, which automatically extracts their facial components and recom-
bines them to synthesise new ones. This process involves the generated 
faces to satisfy several requirements, namely matching facial pose and 
ensuring proper scaling and alignment of facial parts. Each portrait pro-
jected on the walls has a random lifespan ranging from 10 to 20 seconds. 
When this lifespan expires, the X-Faces system generates another artificial 
portrait, replacing the old one. This process is repeated whenever the lifespan 
of a portrait is over. The collection of face images used by the X-Faces  
system for generating portraits is continuously updated with new faces 
captured by the users. This allows the installation to quickly adapt to new 
face images captured by the users, so whenever a new face is captured, 
its facial parts will contaminate the artificial portraits shown on the walls. 
The seamless transition between portraits makes users aware of the subtle 
changes on the walls of the installation that are populated with numerous 
portraits. Additionally, the installation employs a mechanism that places 
a few real faces, selected at random, among the artificial ones to make 
the audience question the authenticity of the portraits they observe. Figures 
G.10 to G.12 display the environment of the installation, with users observing 
the walls populated with numerous portraits, real and artificial.
The installation also captures sound samples during the audience 
interaction. In the MNAC installation, this sound recording occurs a few 
seconds before the face capture process, while in the CAPC installation, 
it is triggered automatically when sound is detected. These sound record-
ings contribute to the creation of an ambient soundscape played through 
the loudspeaker. The sound is generated by intertwining a total of 12 
samples randomly selected from the set of all recorded samples of audience 
interaction. Since most interactions happen in silence, we decided to play 
a background sound sample with a volume lower than the main samples. 
This background sound consists of a sample, in the loop, of crowd noise 
that was recorded previously. The frequency and pitch of the recorded 
sound samples are digitally attenuated and made homogeneous through

mostly perceive imperceptible sounds resulting from the blending of cap-

sentences. This creates an environment where the users have the percep-
tion that the people whose faces are projected on the walls are talking 
to each other.
G.4  CONCLUSION
We introduced our research on the computational generation of photore-
alistic face images by combining facial parts from existing faces. We described 
the X-Faces system as one that automatically recombines facial parts from 
different faces and, this way, creates new face composites. This work, 
developed by João Correia et al. (2016, 2019), has demonstrated significant 
potential across diverse domains. It has proven valuable for expanding 
face detection datasets by generating new instances and identifying vul-
nerabilities in face detectors. Furthermore, it has found applications 
in Media Art by generating artificial portraits based on the faces of the 
audience (Martins et al., 2019, 2020).
In this appendix, we presented the X-Faces system, which has explored 
the creation of the interactive Media Art installation Portraits of No One  
to create an ever-changing audio-visual environment composed of photo-
realistic human portraits constructed with the facial parts captured from 
its audience and an ambient sound generated by intertwining sound samples 
of users’ interactions. Whenever the audience members give their faces 
to the installation, they will immediately see their facial parts contaminating 
the portraits that are displayed on the walls. As the installation takes 
advantage of participants’ facial traits to feed itself and grow, the partici-
pants’ facial parts become part of the artwork. This aspect of the installa-
tion creates an engaging experience for the audience by allowing them to 
directly participate in the generation of new artificial identities in the form 
of portraits.
The artificial portraits created by the installation encourage critical 
thinking about how recent technological advances are changing our rela-
tionship with others and the world. The photorealism of the generated 
portraits places blurs the line between reality and artifice, prompting users 
to question the veracity of the faces they encounter. Therefore, this opens 
a window of opportunity to discuss the veracity of the images that we see in 
other contexts and environments and whether we should consider them 
as unquestionable proofs of the truth.
Within the installation, one can observe diverse relationships and 
interactions between users, as well as between the users and the artificial 
identities generated by the installation. Most of the audience see the por-
traits on the walls as other people, starting to judge and talk about their 
visual appearance. However, when they recognise themselves, or a familiar 
face part, in a portrait of no one, their behaviour undergoes a shift. At this 
moment, the audience engenders empathy with this artificial person and the 
others who, like them, are blended to generate their portraits. 

D17 APPENDIX  G PORTRAITS  OF  NO ONE
The presented installation was initially conceived for the Sonae Media 
Art Award in 2019 and exhibited at the MNAC in Lisbon, Portugal, in the 
same year. Subsequently, it was also showcased at the CAPC in 2021. In 
Section 10.2, we explore an extension of this concept beyond the confines 
of a physical exhibition space, introducing an online artwork that can be 
adapted to create a lighter version of the installation, as exemplified at the 
presentation of the installation at Forum Maia, Portugal, in late 2021.
The future work on this installation encompasses the following areas 
of exploration: (i) exploring the animation of generated portraits and their 
reactiveness to external data, such as the presence of people in the room; 
(ii) experimenting with the blending of audio recorded from the audience 
with computationally generated sounds; (iii) setting up Portraits of No 
One in other locations.

E02
COMPUT A TIONAL GRAPHIC DESIGN AND TYPOGRAPHY PRACTICES
This appendix presents the selected testimonies presented on Sonar artwork 
(see Section 10.3). Collecting these testimonies involved searching for 
and georeferencing them, a task by Daniela Côrtes Maduro before the pro-
duction of the artwork. The list includes text passages from 21 Portuguese 
individuals written before, during, and after the Carnation Revolution of 25 
April 1974. The authors come from various fields, including writers, poli-
ticians, and musicians. The testimonies cover texts from authors in Portugal 
and abroad, most in exile. They span 11 locations across nine countries in 
Europe, America, and Africa. All the locations have one associated testi -
mony, except Lisbon, which is associated with the 11 testimonies.
